removed: describes inert matter; does not say to consider the cause apart from it
God controls matter, but no word of reason; 92.1 is plainer
calm from discussing causes, not from the world being governed; proposed for the claim on calm, not added
asks who built the universe, but “beginnings” is plural; 65.12 says “one”
unruffled because all follows divine law; fits the claim on calm; proposed, not added
God and man of the same nature; same point as 92.1, already used
reason a portion of divine spirit; same point as 92.1
the universe is one and is God; same point as 95.52
care of him who governs all things; about why things last
seeming harms preserve the world, not “follow from good”; Article 3 uses it
fate, God or chance: Article 3 already uses it for the same doubt
our spirit imitates the soul of the universe; about seeking honour
reason judges good and evil in us; not about the world
honour paid to great men, not to what governs the world
reason copies nature; about what a good is
nature tempers the world by opposites; about change
all things perish in their time; about decay, not order
justice without reward; unrelated

articles.title: What I was made for

claims.t: Everything that exists, the gods included, is made for something and bears fruit in its own time.
claims.shared: Both passages name the gods: 8.17 has the Sun and “the other gods”, 9.8 has “god”. What they say of them differs: 8.17 says each thing has come to be for something, 9.8 says a human being, god and the universe bear fruit, each in its own seasons.
claims.changed: “Made for something” and “bears fruit” are kept as two phrases, each from its own passage. “Made for” is the claim’s plain English for 8.17’s “has come to be for”; the Greek names no maker. “Everything that exists” is 8.17’s “each thing”. 9.8 names only a human being, god and the universe; when the claim says that everything bears fruit, it widens 9.8. Drops the horse, the vine and the Sun as examples.

support.quote: Each thing has come to be for something: a horse, a vine.
gives: Everything that exists
is made for something
support.follows: Each thing has come to be for something, as a horse or a vine has.

support.quote: Even the Sun will say, “I have come to be for some work,” and so will the other gods.
gives: the gods included
is made for something
support.follows: Even the Sun would say it has come to be for some work, and the other gods would say the same.

support.quote: A human being bears fruit, and so does god, and so does the universe
gives: the gods included
bears fruit
support.follows: A human being, god and the universe each bear fruit.

support.quote: each bears it in its own seasons
gives: in its own time
support.follows: Each of them bears its fruit in its own seasons.

claims.t: I was not made to please myself, but to keep exercising reason and fellowship. Reason turns toward other people, and its fruit is shared as well as its own.
claims.shared: Two passages say that reason is not a private thing, in different words: 6.13 honours rational soul “as civic” and keeps the soul “rational and social”; 9.8 says reason has fruit “both shared and its own”. “Social” and “shared” translate Greek words of one family. “Turns toward other people” is the claim’s phrase for both; neither passage uses it. The rest is one passage each: 8.17 asks whether I am for pleasure, 6.13 names the keeping of the soul, 9.8 the fruit.
claims.changed: 8.17 asks what I am for, offers pleasure as an answer and says “See whether the idea holds up.” It expects a no and does not say it; the claim says it. The “but” that answers the question is the editor’s, and is marked.

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I am for and challenges only pleasure as an answer. The answer is the editor’s, taken from 6.13 and 9.8, which do not say what I have come to be for.

support.quote: So what are you for? For pleasure?
gives: not made to please myself
support.note: The question is put to the reader. Its verb is understood from the Sun’s words just before it: what have you come to be for?
support.follows: I should ask what I am for, and whether it can be pleasure.

support.quote: See whether the idea holds up.
gives: not made to please myself
support.follows: I should test whether that idea holds up; Marcus expects that it will not, and leaves the verdict to me.

support.quote: before everything else preserves their own soul rational and social in its condition and its movement
gives: to keep exercising reason and fellowship
support.follows: Such a person, before everything else, keeps their own soul rational and social, in its state and in what it does.

support.quote: whoever honours rational soul as such, and as civic
gives: Reason turns toward other people
support.follows: This person honours rational soul as such, and as civic: as something that belongs to a community.

support.quote: from it come other things of much the same kind as reason itself
gives: its fruit
support.follows: What comes from reason is of much the same kind as reason itself.

support.quote: reason has fruit, both shared and its own
gives: Reason turns toward other people
its fruit is shared as well as its own
support.follows: Reason has fruit that is shared and fruit that is its own.

claims.t: What looks rotten or old to me looks different to someone who knows nature well. Nature throws nothing away: she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, and it has something pleasing of its own.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the rotten and the old, and both appeal to a person who knows nature, who sees them differently: in 8.48 “a person who studies nature” laughs at the complaint, in 3.2 only “the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works” is struck by the beauty. What that person sees differs: 8.48 says nature reuses such things, 3.2 says they are pleasing as they are.
claims.changed: Does not make “by-products” the common term. They are the subject of 3.2 from its first sentence (“what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature”), but 8.48 has shavings and trimmings only as a comparison. The claim rests on the two things both passages say outright. The claim calls nature “she”; the translation says “it”.

support.quote: changes into itself everything inside that seems to be decaying and growing old and to be useless, and that it makes other, fresh things again out of these very things
gives: What looks rotten or old
she takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it
support.follows: What seems spoiled, old or useless, nature changes into herself and makes into new things.

support.quote: you will be laughed at by a person who studies nature
gives: looks different to someone who knows nature well
support.follows: A person who studies nature would laugh at me for asking why such things came to be.

support.quote: they, at least, have somewhere to throw these, whereas the nature of the whole has nothing outside it
gives: Nature throws nothing away
support.follows: Nature has nowhere outside itself to discard anything.

support.quote: in olives ripened on the tree, the very nearness to rotting adds a certain beauty of its own to the fruit
gives: What looks rotten or old
it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: In olives ripened on the tree, being close to rotting adds a beauty of its own to the fruit.

support.quote: will be able to see a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man
gives: What looks rotten or old
it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: That person will be able to see a kind of prime and ripeness in an old woman and an old man.

support.quote: which will not convince everyone, will strike only the one who has become truly at home with nature and its works
gives: looks different to someone who knows nature well
support.follows: Such things will not convince everyone; they will strike only someone who has become truly at home with nature and its works.

support.quote: even what comes about on top of the things that come about by nature has something graceful and attractive about it
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: Even what comes about as an extra, on top of what nature produces, has something graceful and attractive about it.

support.quote: there is almost nothing, even among the things that happen as consequences, that will not seem to that person to be put together in a way that somehow gives pleasure
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
support.follows: Even among nature’s side effects, that person will find pleasure in almost every one.

single.label: A practice
single.t: If the cucumber is bitter, I set it aside; if brambles are in the way, I go round them. That is enough.
single.quote: A bitter cucumber? Leave it. Brambles in the path? Turn aside. That is enough.
single.why: Only 8.48 gives the practice. Its second half is the next item.
single.follows: I should set the bitter thing aside, go round the obstacle, and leave it at that.

single.label: A prohibition
single.t: I do not go on to ask why a bitter thing came to be in the universe at all.
single.quote: Do not go on to say, “And why did these things come to be in the universe at all?”
single.why: Only 8.48 forbids the question. Its reason is under “If I doubt it”: nature throws nothing away. Marcus does not say how this fits with 8.17, where each thing has come to be for something.
single.follows: I should not go on to ask why such things came to be in the universe at all.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I follow what is done impulse by impulse, and I see at once what aim each one is directed at.
single.quote: what is done impulse by impulse; and in the latter case see at once what aim it is directed at
single.why: Only 7.4 asks about the aim of what is done, impulse by impulse. It speaks of what is said and done, not of what each thing has come to be for, so it backs no claim.
single.follows: I should follow what is done impulse by impulse and see at once what aim it is directed at.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 6.13 is 6.14, 8.17 is 8.19, 8.48 is 8.50, 9.8 is 9.10 and 11.5 is 11.6; 3.2 and 7.4 are the same.
Uses 6.13 and 9.8 to answer the question that 8.17 asks and leaves open. The step is marked as the editor’s: “namely” in the statement, “but” in claim 2.

Fuses 8.17 with 9.8 only on what both say: the gods are included. “Made for something” is 8.17’s and “bears fruit” is 9.8’s, and the claim keeps them apart. “Everything that exists” is 8.17’s “each thing”; 9.8 names a human being, god and the universe.
Fuses 6.13 with 9.8 on reason turning toward other people. The phrase is the editor’s for 6.13’s “civic” and “social” and for 9.8’s fruit “both shared and its own”.
Fuses 8.48 with 3.2, the most central passage of the section, on the rotten and the old and on the person who knows nature. That nature reuses them is 8.48 alone; that they are pleasing is 3.2 alone.
Keeps 7.4 as a said-once practice. It was a witness to claim 1 without backing any of its words.

8.17 says each thing has come to be for something; 8.48 forbids asking why a bitter thing came to be at all. The translation has “come to be” in both because the Greek has one verb in both. Neither passage mentions the other, and the article keeps both without reconciling them.

Withdraws “by nature” from the statement and from claim 2, and “of its own kind” from claim 1. They rested on words Casaubon added: “naturally sociable” in 6.13, where the Greek has “civic”; “of a diffusive nature” and “every one in their kind” in 9.8, where the Greek has nothing.
Keeps “made for” in the title, the statement and the claims as plain English for 8.17’s “has come to be for”. The Greek names no maker.

Keeps “I was not made to please myself”, although 8.17 only asks “For pleasure?” and says “See whether the idea holds up.” Casaubon turned that into a verdict; the Greek leaves the verdict to the reader.
articles.limit: This is the smallest and loosest section: seven passages, six used. Claims 1 and 3 rest on two passages and claim 2 on three, and in each claim only part of the sentence is said by two passages: the gods in claim 1, reason’s turn toward others in claim 2 (the phrase is the editor’s), the rotten and the old and the person who knows nature in claim 3. The rest of each claim is one passage’s. That what I was made for is reason is the editor’s step; no passage of this section says it.

aside.11.5: What tragedy and comedy were brought on for. Purpose applied to drama, with nothing for a rule of life.

statement.t: Like everything that exists, the gods included, I am made for something, namely to use my reason, which turns toward others.

parts.words: Like everything that exists, the gods included
to use my reason, which turns toward others

inferences.why: 8.17 asks what I am for and challenges only pleasure as an answer. That the answer is reason is the editor’s, from 6.13 and 9.8.

statement.kind: A rule, its application to me, and its hardest case
statement.form: A rule, its application to me, and the case that seems to break it. “If I doubt it” answers the objection that some things are plainly useless or flawed. “I am made for something” rests on 8.17 alone (“Each thing has come to be for something”, then “So what are you for?”), so it carries no source line here; claim 1 shows it. That it is not for my own pleasure is also 8.17 alone and stays in claim 2.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes failing at one’s purpose.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, each claim gains a second author on one of its parts, and the article gains three things Marcus leaves out here: the answer to what I was made for, what failing at it looks like, and the joy that is left when pleasure is ruled out.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains its missing step. Marcus asks what I was made for and does not answer in this section; Seneca says outright that it is reason brought to perfection.

items.quote: In each thing that quality should be best for which the thing is brought into being and by which it is judged.
gives: is made for something
items.follows: In each thing, the quality that should be best is the one the thing was brought into being for.
items.context: Seneca is proving that the honourable is the only good. “That quality” is each thing’s own excellence: a vine’s yield, a stag’s speed, a dog’s scent.

items.quote: this wisdom I have declared already to be, both the good of others, and also his own
gives: its fruit is shared as well as its own
items.follows: Wisdom is the good of other people and also the wise man’s own.
items.context: Seneca is showing that hardship cannot stop the wise man from acting. “This wisdom” is what he still practises then; “his own” means the wise man’s.

items.quote: none of the objects which vanish from our gaze and are re-absorbed into the world of things, from which they have come forth and are soon to come forth again, is annihilated
gives: she takes it back into herself
items.follows: Nothing that vanishes is destroyed: it is taken back into the world it came from and will come out of it again.
items.context: Seneca is arguing against the fear of death. The “objects” are whatever dies or disappears, which he says will return; he is not speaking of waste or flaws.

items.quote: Let us cherish and love old age; for it is full of pleasure if one knows how to use it. Fruits are most welcome when almost over
gives: it has something pleasing of its own
items.follows: Old age is full of pleasure for one who knows how to use it, as fruit is most welcome when it is almost over.
items.context: Seneca has just scolded his decaying house, his gnarled trees and an old slave, and seen his own age in them. “It” is old age; the fruit is his comparison.

items.label: why
items.t: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason. Reason brought to perfection is the good that nature designed me for at birth, and when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good.
items.why: Marcus asks in 8.17 what I am for, and whether it is pleasure, but this section never gives the answer. Seneca gives it in so many words.

support.quote: What then is peculiar to man? Reason.
gives: What is peculiar to me as a human being is reason
support.follows: What belongs to a human being alone is reason.
support.context: The same proof that the honourable is the only good. “Peculiar to man” means what a human being has and animals and plants do not.

support.quote: It is soul, and reason brought to perfection in the soul.
gives: Reason brought to perfection
support.follows: What is a person’s own is the soul, and reason brought to perfection in it.
support.context: Seneca is saying what to praise in a person: not his slaves, house or income, which are outside him. “It” is the property peculiar to a human being.

support.quote: man’s highest good is attained, if he has fulfilled the good for which nature designed him at birth
gives: the good that nature designed me for at birth
when I fulfil it I have reached my highest good
support.follows: A person reaches the highest good by fulfilling the good that nature designed him for at birth.
support.context: The close of the same argument. “The good for which nature designed him” is the reason just named, brought to perfection in the soul.

items.label: action
items.t: I am not to go without gladness. Real joy is a stern matter, and I rejoice only in what comes from my own store.
items.why: Marcus asks whether I am for pleasure and expects a no (8.17). He does not say in this section what joy is left; 9.8 says only that reason has fruit of its own. Seneca says what joy remains and where it comes from.

support.quote: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness
gives: I am not to go without gladness
support.follows: Seneca does not want his friend ever to be without gladness.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius to learn how to feel joy and denies he is taking pleasures from him. “Gladness” is the kind born inside a person, not a gift of chance.

support.quote: Real joy, believe me, is a stern matter.
gives: Real joy is a stern matter
support.follows: Real joy is serious, not light.
support.context: “Real joy” is that of a person who can despise death, face poverty and curb his pleasures. Seneca sets it against laughter and a cheerful face.

support.quote: rejoice only in that which comes from your own store
gives: I rejoice only in what comes from my own store
support.follows: I should rejoice only in what comes from within myself.
support.context: Said after telling Lucilius to trample what glitters outwardly. “Your own store” is, in his next words, your very self, the best part of you.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself. If I creep into a hole and grow torpid, I have died before I am dead; and if I go into hiding out of fear, I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust.
items.why: Marcus has no passage in this section on what failing looks like. Seneca describes it twice: the man who is of use to no one, and the man who hides out of fear.

support.quote: He really lives who is made use of by many; he really lives who makes use of himself.
gives: I really live when many make use of me and I make use of myself
support.follows: To be really alive is to be of use to many and to make use of oneself.
support.context: The letter attacks living for the belly. “He” is set against those who obey their appetites, some of whom Seneca has just counted among the dead.

support.quote: Those men, however, who creep into a hole and grow torpid are no better off in their homes than if they were in their tombs.
gives: If I creep into a hole and grow torpid
support.follows: People who hide away and go numb are no better off at home than in a tomb.
support.context: “Those men” are the opposite of the man of use to many: people who withdraw into sloth, in a letter about living for the belly.

support.quote: he has died before he is dead
gives: I have died before I am dead
support.follows: Such a man has died before his death.
support.context: “He” is the same torpid man. Seneca says his name may be carved on the lintel of his house as on a tomb.

support.quote: who through fear has taken to concealment
gives: if I go into hiding out of fear
support.follows: The man in question has gone into hiding out of fear.
support.context: Seneca is at the villa of Vatia, who was famous only for his leisure, and separates leisure from hiding. “Who” is the man fled from affairs and from men.

support.quote: this person is not living for himself; he is living for his belly, his sleep, and his lust
gives: I am living not for myself but for my belly, my sleep and my lust
support.follows: A man who hides like that does not live for himself; he lives for his belly, his sleep and his lust.
support.context: “This person” is the man who has hidden from affairs and people out of fear and failed desires. It is not anyone at rest, nor anyone enjoying himself.

amend.t: , for reason brought to perfection is the good that nature designed me for at birth

searches: made for / designed / brought into being
for pleasure; pleasure with cattle or animals
common good / good of others / live for
acquainted with nature / secrets of nature

rejected.why: was in use twice; its “appointed times” are those of birth and destruction, not of bearing fruit, and 36.10 says the reuse more fully
the vine’s own virtue is fertility; 41.8 beside it says the same of man and was used
reason is best in man; 76.10 says it shorter
pleasure is the good of cattle; about the highest good, says nothing of what I was made for
pleasure is low and shared with animals; a list of maxims, not about purpose
born for more than serving the body; about fear and the soul’s freedom, not pleasure
man born to fulfil his life; about leaving the body behind
live for your neighbour; said of friendship, no mention of reason
naturally born to love all men; said about praise, and of nature, not reason
philosophy promises sociability; about not making oneself odd
nature made us related; about nature, not reason, and belongs to Article 1
the wise man’s good is common; 85.37 names wisdom outright and was used
what seems to perish merely changes; 36.10 says where it goes and was used
pleasures of the last years of life; 12.4 says it more plainly
four natures, each perfect in its kind; about what the Good is, not about being made for something
every animal looks out for itself first; a different doctrine
nature’s secrets disclosed after death; not the person who knows nature now
complaining is the only evil; near the bitter cucumber but about misfortune
verses on what each country bears; about produce, not purpose

articles.title: What the whole sends in its season

claims.role: What comes is good, and on time
claims.t: What the whole brings me is good for me, and it comes at the right time: nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me.
claims.shared: Both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to (10.21: “good for each”; 4.19: “fruit to me”). Both add the time: 10.21 that it is good when nature brings it, 4.19 that what is timely for the universe is never too early or too late for me.
claims.changed: 10.21 says “each”; the claim says “me”, as 4.19 does. 4.19 speaks to the universe and to nature as “you”; the claim speaks about them and calls both “the whole”, 10.21’s word.

support.quote: What the nature of the whole brings to each is good for each
gives: What the whole brings me is good for me
support.follows: Whatever the nature of the whole brings to anyone is good for that one.

support.quote: it is good at the time when nature brings it
gives: it comes at the right time
support.follows: It is good at the time nature brings it.

support.quote: Nature, everything your seasons bear is fruit to me.
gives: What the whole brings me is good for me
support.follows: I count whatever nature’s seasons bear as fruit.

support.quote: Nothing that is timely for you is too early or too late for me.
gives: it comes at the right time
nothing that is timely for the whole is too early or too late for me
support.follows: What comes at the universe’s right time does not come at a wrong time for me.

claims.t: I take the universe’s side: what it loves to bring about, I love along with it, and whatever fits well with it fits well with me.
claims.shared: Both passages are spoken to the universe, and in both the speaker puts himself on its side: in 10.22 he loves along with it; in 4.19 what fits it fits him.
claims.changed: Both passages say “you” to the universe; the claim speaks about it. “I take the universe’s side” is the editor’s summary of what the two say in their own words.

support.quote: the universe loves to bring about whatever is to come
gives: what it loves to bring about
support.follows: The universe loves to bring about whatever is going to happen.

support.quote: So I say to the universe: “I love along with you.”
gives: I take the universe’s side
I love along with it
support.follows: Marcus tells the universe that he loves along with it.

support.quote: Universe, everything that fits well with you fits well with me.
gives: I take the universe’s side
whatever fits well with it fits well with me
support.follows: Whatever fits the universe well fits Marcus well.

single.label: Different parts, one work
single.t: The sun does not do the rain’s part, and no god does another’s. The parts of the world differ, and they work together toward the same thing.
single.quote: Surely the sun does not think it should do the rain’s part? Or Asclepius the part of the fruit-bearing goddess? And what of each of the stars? Are they not different, yet working together toward the same thing?
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the parts of the world and their separate tasks. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Each power keeps to its own part; the parts differ and work together toward the same thing.

single.label: One source
single.t: Everything is from nature, in nature, and goes into nature.
single.quote: All things from you, all things in you, all things into you.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names a source, a place and a destination; it does not say that things work toward an end.
single.follows: All things are from nature, in nature and go into nature.

single.label: A practice
single.t: As one man says “Dear city of Cecrops” of Athens, I say “Dear city of Zeus”.
single.quote: One man says, “Dear city of Cecrops.” But you, will you not say, “Dear city of Zeus”?
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. They are kept as the article’s practice.
single.follows: If one man can call Athens dear, I am asked to say “Dear city of Zeus”.

single.label: A practice · how to pray
single.t: If I pray, I pray simply and like a free person, as the Athenians prayed for rain on their land.
single.quote: A prayer of the Athenians: “Rain, rain, dear Zeus, down on the ploughland of the Athenians and the plains.” Either one should not pray, or one should pray like this: simply and like a free person.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It says how to pray, not for whom.
single.follows: If one prays at all, one should pray as in this prayer: simply and like a free person.

single.label: Meeting an obstacle
single.t: When something stands in my way, I do not force my way and I do not fall. I stand and give light to whatever receives it; what gives the light no passage deprives itself of it.
single.quote: It should not lean on the obstacles it meets with force or like a torrent, nor fall down, but stand and light up whatever receives it. For whatever does not give the beam passage will deprive itself of the beam.
single.why: Only this passage says how to meet what resists me. It shows what failing looks like, forcing or falling, and the way back.
single.follows: Meeting an obstacle, thought should neither force its way nor fall, but stand and light up what receives it.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.21 is 10.20, 10.22 is 10.21, 4.19 is 4.23, 6.38 is 6.43 and 8.54 is 8.57; 5.7 is the same.
Reads “the nature of the whole” (10.21), the universe and nature addressed in 4.19, and the universe of 10.22 as one whole.

Keeps only two fused claims. In claim 1 both passages say that what nature brings is good for the one it is brought to, and both speak of its time. In claim 2 the words the two share, “I take the universe’s side”, are the editor’s summary of two sentences spoken to the universe. The parts of the world working together (6.38) and all things from, in and into nature (4.19) are each said by one passage and stand alone.
Withdraws the earlier claim that I pray “for everyone, not for myself alone”. It rested on a clause Casaubon added to 5.7; the Greek ends at “simply and like a free person”.
Reads “Dear city of Zeus” (4.19) as said of the world. The Greek does not say what the city of Zeus is.
Leaves out the poet’s line and the last sentence of 10.22, a remark on a Greek turn of phrase.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept whatever happens. What this article adds is the time: what comes is good when it comes, never too early or too late. It adds little else. Six passages give two fused claims, and 4.19 feeds both, so the article leans on one passage. It states a trust and does not argue for it.

statement.t: What the whole brings me is good for me and comes at the right time, so I take its side.

parts.words: What the whole brings me is good for me
comes at the right time
I take its side

inferences.why: No passage joins these two. In 10.22 Marcus’s own “So” runs from the universe’s love to his; the step from “good for me” to taking its side is the editor’s.

statement.kind: A ground and the stance that answers it
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: what the whole brings is good for me and comes at the right time. Claim 2 is the stance Marcus takes toward the universe. The “so” that joins them in the statement is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers that what the whole brings might not be good for me; the article states the trust and does not argue for it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, taking the universe’s side gains two witnesses, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: the hard things, paid willingly as a tax; words for a setback; a test for prayer; how to stand under pain; an answer when a death seems too early; and what holds if I doubt it. He backs nothing in the first claim, and he limits the second: he does not crave hardship itself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the hard things: I take the whole’s side, and what is hard in what it brings I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive. He does not say that I should want it.

items.quote: I have trained myself not merely to obey God, but to agree with His decisions
gives: I take the universe’s side
items.follows: Seneca has trained himself to agree with what God decides, and not only to obey it.
items.context: Seneca answers a complaining Lucilius. “His decisions” are God’s: the illness and losses Seneca has just listed as his own, which he says come by order and not by accident.

items.quote: Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God
gives: I take the universe’s side
items.follows: A person should be pleased with whatever has pleased God.
items.context: On the inner defence against Fortune: not chafing at what happens to one. “Whatever has pleased God” is whatever happens, including what seems to bring harm.

items.label: action
items.t: The hard things are a tax on being alive, and I pay it willingly. Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax, and I do not hope or try to escape it.
items.why: In this section Marcus calls what comes fruit and says it is timely; none of his passages names the hard part of it. Seneca names it, and calls it a tax, not a fruit. He says how to receive it: willingly. He does not say that I should want it.

support.quote: I shall pay up all my taxes willingly.
gives: I pay it willingly
support.follows: Seneca will pay every tax he owes, and pay it willingly.
support.context: From Letter 96, where Seneca tells Lucilius to agree with what God decides. The “taxes” are not money: the next sentence says they are everything in life that makes us groan or recoil.

support.quote: Now all the things which cause us to groan or recoil, are part of the tax of life—things, my dear Lucilius, which you should never hope and never seek to escape.
gives: The hard things are a tax on being alive
Whatever makes me groan or shrink back is part of that tax
I do not hope or try to escape it
support.follows: What makes us groan or recoil is part of the price of living, and we should neither hope nor try to escape it.
support.context: Said to Lucilius, who had feared for his life in an illness. The things that make us groan are the illness, losses, toil and fear listed just before.

items.label: practice
items.t: Whenever something turns out against what I expected, I say to myself: “Heaven decreed better.”
items.why: Marcus gives words to say of the world: “Dear city of Zeus”. Seneca gives words to say at each setback. They say that what was decided is better than what I expected; they do not say, as 10.21 does, that it is good for me.

support.quote: say to yourself, whenever things turn out contrary to your expectation: “Heaven decreed better!”
gives: Whenever something turns out against what I expected
Heaven decreed better
support.follows: When things go against what I expected, I should tell myself that the gods decided better.
support.context: On holding what Fortune gives without leaning on it. He first offers “Heaven decreed it otherwise” for every mishap, then this, as braver and nearer the truth.

items.label: practice
items.t: I speak with God as if other people were listening. The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires.
items.why: 5.7 says to pray simply and like a free person, and gives no test. Seneca gives one, and ties it to freedom as well: whoever asks only for what he could ask for openly is free of his desires.

support.quote: Know that thou art freed from all desires when thou hast reached such a point that thou prayest to God for nothing except what thou canst pray for openly.
gives: The day I ask for nothing that I could not ask for openly, I am free of my desires
support.follows: A person is free of his desires once he prays only for what he could pray for openly.
support.context: Seneca has just told Lucilius to drop his old prayers and ask for a sound mind. The saying is Athenodorus’s; to pray “openly” is to ask only for what others may hear.

support.quote: Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening
gives: I speak with God as if other people were listening
support.follows: I should live as if God saw me and speak with God as if people heard me.
support.context: Seneca’s own advice, drawn from that saying: people whisper to the gods the base wishes they hide from men. To “speak with God” is to pray.

items.label: breaks
items.t: In pain or illness, if I give way to my suffering, it beats me. It is like a wall falling toward me: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back.
items.why: 8.54 is about an obstacle in my way: I do not force it and I do not fall. Seneca speaks of something else, pain and illness that press on me, and says to stand up to them. He resists suffering that has to be borne; he does not attack an obstacle, so the two do not conflict.

support.quote: if he once gives way, he will be vanquished; but if he strives against his sufferings, he will conquer.
gives: if I give way to my suffering, it beats me
support.follows: Whoever gives way to his sufferings is beaten; whoever strives against them wins.
support.context: A letter on bearing illness and pain, to Lucilius, who is ill; Seneca recalls his own sickness. “He” is anyone in the midst of troubles, striving against his sufferings.

support.quote: but if you hold your ground and make up your mind to push against it, it will be forced back.
gives: if I hold my ground and push against it, it is forced back
support.follows: What leans on me is forced back if I hold my ground and push against it.
support.context: Same passage. “It” is a falling ruin that leans on you: Seneca’s image for pain, which presses harder on the one who backs away from it.

items.label: breaks
items.role: When a death seems too early
items.t: When a death seems to come too early, I ask which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me. How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference, and a short life can be a perfect one.
items.why: The time is this article’s own point: nothing is too early or too late for me. Seneca meets it in one case only, a death that seems to come too soon, and his answer is not Marcus’s. He does not say the time was right; he says the length of a life does not decide whether it is complete.

support.quote: do you consider it fairer that you should obey Nature, or that Nature should obey you? And what difference does it make how soon you depart from a place which you must depart from sooner or later?
gives: which is fairer: that I obey nature, or that nature obey me
How soon I leave a place I must leave anyway makes no difference
support.follows: Seneca asks which is fairer, that I obey nature or that nature obey me, and what difference it makes how soon I leave a place I must leave.
support.context: Lucilius mourned the philosopher Metronax as dead too soon; Seneca calls such complaints railing at Fate. The “place which you must depart from” is life.

support.quote: Just as one of small stature can be a perfect man, so a life of small compass can be a perfect life.
gives: a short life can be a perfect one
support.follows: A short life can be a perfect life, as a small man can be a perfect man.
support.context: Letter 93, on the philosopher Metronax, mourned as dead too soon: a life is to be measured by what was done in it, not by how long it lasted. “A life of small compass” is a short life.

items.label: doubt
items.role: Even if it is a disaster
items.t: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong, it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if what comes is not good for me. Seneca’s answer is that even a disaster cannot make virtue smaller. He uses the sun for it, as 8.54 uses a sunbeam for the mind.

support.quote: obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it is no smaller, but merely shines with less brilliancy.
gives: my virtue shines less brightly, but it is no smaller
support.follows: Obstacles take nothing away from virtue; it only shines less brightly.
support.context: Seneca argues that a good man is happy even under misfortune. “Obstacles” are what stands in virtue’s way as an object stands before the sun, which is no smaller for it.

support.quote: Disasters, therefore, and losses, and wrongs, have only the same power over virtue that a cloud has over the sun.
gives: Even if what comes is a disaster, a loss or a wrong
it has no more power over my virtue than a cloud has over the sun
support.follows: Disasters, losses and wrongs have no more power over virtue than a cloud has over the sun.
support.context: The conclusion of that comparison: a cloud hides the sun and takes nothing from it. “Virtue” is the good man’s, which Seneca holds to be his whole good.

items.t: Seneca stops short of Marcus’s word “love”. He agrees with what God decides and receives it without complaint (Ep. 96.2), but he says he is not so mad as to crave a hardship: what he wants is the virtue that bears it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He would rather be spared beforehand and agrees once it comes; and of his own death he says he should desire whatever circumstances demand (Ep. 61.3).

support.quote: Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly.
support.follows: Seneca does not want illness; if he must be ill, what he wants is to do nothing unrestrained or weak in it.
support.context: Lucilius asked whether every good is desirable, since bravery under torture is a good. Seneca separates the hardship, which he does not want, from his conduct in it.

support.quote: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
support.follows: What is desirable is not hardship but the virtue that lets us bear hardship patiently.
support.context: Seneca’s own summing-up of his answer to that question. The “hardships” are the torture, war and illness he has just named.

support.quote: Let us therefore so set our minds in order that we may desire whatever is demanded of us by circumstances
support.follows: I should bring my mind to want whatever circumstances require of me.
support.context: Seneca, now old, writes that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. What circumstances demand is, above all, his death.

amend.t: ; what is hard in it I pay willingly, as a tax on being alive
; but I do not crave hardship itself, and what I want, if it must come, is the virtue to bear it

searches: timely, too early, too late, untimely, appointed time

rejected.why: About everything perishing: the “appointed times” are those of birth, growth and destruction, and the “same goal” is dissolution. Says nothing of a time that is right for me. Both old pieces removed.

Sets a puzzle (how can goods be equal if they are of three kinds?) that the letter answers by calling them equal. Its rule on prayer was aimed at a claim now withdrawn. Ep. 67.4 asks the question directly.
Nature rules by changing seasons, storm after calm. Says the soul must adjust to this law, not that what comes is good for me or on time.
Do not rail at Nature; endure what cannot be reformed. Already in Article 3, and about enduring, not about taking the universe’s side.
“Welcome our orders with energy”, following a universe into which future sufferings are woven. Says what 96.2 and 74.20 say; a third witness for the same words was not needed.
Cleanthes’s prayer. “The willing soul Fate leads” argues that refusing is useless; Article 3 uses it for that. Here it would only repeat obedience.
The great soul has given himself over to Fate. Same point as 96.2, in a letter already used in Article 3.
Its first half (apparent harms work for the preservation of the world) is about the good of the world, not good for me; used in Article 3. Only “pleased with whatever has pleased God” is used here.
Fortune gives only the raw material of goods and ills. A possible limit on “good for me”, but it is about Fortune, and three sections on he says Heaven decreed better. Not a clear disagreement.
“Beholden to the seasons”, though they were not apportioned for my benefit. About gratitude for goods shared with all, in a letter on rulers and peace.
The good man endures whatever happens because it comes by divine law. An argument that only the honourable is good; about enduring.
The wise man wills what necessity is about to force on him. About leaving life; 61.3 says the same more generally and is quoted.
Endure “willingly and with alacrity”: the oath of one who has enlisted as a good man. About enduring trials, not about what they are.
If God is pleased to add another day, welcome it. Welcomes a gain, in a letter on living each day as the last.
The wise man taught us to welcome the gifts of chance as divine commands. One item in a list about what philosophy discovered; no context of its own.
The perfect man as citizen and soldier of the universe, taking what happens as his orders. A portrait of acceptance as duty; nearer to Article 3.
A prayer that Fortune not keep Lucilius in luxury. Against softness, said for a friend; not a wish for hardship.
Even an untimely death leaves a full life. Same point as Ep. 93, which is quoted and is fuller.
On the untimely dead: every life is short beside eternity. A different consolation; does not speak of the right time.
Wheat has its good only when ripe. About when a thing’s own good exists, not about what comes to me.
Olive trees “bearing fruit in due season”. Literal farming.
We are parts and members of God. Whole and part, but it backs neither claim, and the said-once items on the parts of the world take no backing.
We are the parts of one great body. About what people owe one another; Article 1’s subject.
Pray for a sound mind and good health of soul. Says what to pray for; 5.7 is about how. The next section, 10.5, is used.
Foolish to pray for a sound mind when you can get it from yourself. About where understanding comes from.
Stop thinking prayers can bend divine decrees. A line of Virgil used against the fear of death; 5.7 does not say prayer is useless.
In praying for a life of honour I pray also for the hardships it may include. Shows he can pray for hardship indirectly; left out to keep the item to his direct answer in 67.4.
Do not regard obstacles to an honourable act as evils. “Obstacle” here is a hindrance to a deed, in an argument that honourable acts are voluntary.
Obey God cheerfully, Fortune defiantly. Already in Article 3.

articles.title: My judgment is up to me

claims.t: Everything is a matter of judgment: how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it. What troubles me rests on my judgments. It is not outside me but inside.
claims.shared: 12.16 and 2.13 open with the same words, that all things, or everything, are “judgment”. 9.30 and 9.11 both put what presses on me in “judgment”: 9.30 says the things that trouble me “rest wholly on your judgment”, 9.11 that what hemmed him in was “in my judgments”.
claims.changed: 9.30 says “many” of the things that trouble me rest on judgment; 9.11 says “all that hemmed me in”. The claim says “what troubles me” and leaves the number open. 9.11 speaks of what hemmed him in; the claim uses 9.30’s word “trouble” for both. 12.16 and 2.13 give only the bare saying, “all things are judgment” and “everything is judgment”; the claim says “a matter of” judgment, and the words after the colon, that how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it, are the editor’s reading of the saying, backed by no quote of their own.

support.quote: That all things are judgment
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment
support.follows: All things are a matter of judgment.

support.quote: That everything is judgment.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment
support.follows: Everything is a matter of judgment.

support.quote: those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments
support.follows: Many of the things that trouble me are needless and rest wholly on my own judgment.

support.quote: for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments
It is not outside me but inside
support.follows: What hemmed Marcus in was not outside him. It was inside, in his judgments.

claims.t: My judgment is up to me. I am able to form the judgment I ought, and free to form none, and I need not be troubled: things themselves do not produce my verdicts, and what is outside my mind is nothing to my mind.
claims.shared: All three passages say that judging lies with me: 12.16 that the judgment “is up to you”, 7.2 “I am able to form the judgment I ought”, 6.47 “One is free to form no judgment”. 7.2 and 6.47 both go on to being disturbed or troubled, and both then turn to “things”: things do not produce our verdicts, and things outside the mind are nothing to it.
claims.changed: 7.2 says “disturbed” and 6.47 “troubled”; the claim says “troubled” for both. The colon stands for the “for” of 6.47, which gives the reason itself. In 7.2 the sentence about things outside the mind only follows the question, without a “for”. Both passages speak of “this”, the matter in front of Marcus; the claim speaks generally.

support.quote: this judgment is up to you
gives: My judgment is up to me
support.follows: The judgment I form is up to me.

support.quote: I am able to form the judgment I ought about this.
gives: My judgment is up to me
I am able to form the judgment I ought
support.follows: Marcus is able to form the judgment he ought to form about the matter in front of him.

support.quote: If I am able, why am I disturbed?
gives: I need not be troubled
support.follows: Since he is able to judge as he ought, Marcus has no reason to be disturbed.

support.quote: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul
gives: My judgment is up to me
free to form none
I need not be troubled
support.follows: A person is free to form no judgment about a matter, and free not to be troubled by it.

support.quote: things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts
gives: things themselves do not produce my verdicts
support.follows: Things are not of a kind to make our verdicts for us.

support.quote: The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind.
gives: what is outside my mind is nothing to my mind
support.follows: What is outside Marcus’s mind has no bearing at all on his mind.

claims.t: When I wish, I can take away my judgment about what seems to distress me, and then I stand in the safest place: there is calm, like a bay without a wave. What hems me in I can throw out, and at once have plenty of open room.
claims.shared: 8.38 and 12.16 both say “take away” the judgment and both say what follows. The shared words are the translation’s: the Greek verbs differ (ἀφέλῃς in 8.38, ἆρον in 12.16) and are close in sense. 9.11 (“threw out”) and 9.30 (“strip away”) both speak of removing what presses on me. All four passages describe the outcome as a place: “the safest place” (8.38), “a bay without a wave” (12.16), “open room” (9.30), being out of “all that hemmed me in” (9.11).
claims.changed: 12.16 says “when you wish” and 8.38 says “if”; the claim keeps “when I wish” and drops the “if”. Only 8.38 and 12.16 name the judgment as the thing removed: in 9.11 what is thrown out is all that hemmed him in, and in 9.30 what is stripped away is needless things among those that trouble me. 9.30 is cut in mid-sentence: the Greek goes on to say by what means the room is made, by taking the whole universe in thought, with endless time and the quick change of each thing. The claim leaves that means out, so its “open room” is not to be read as coming from the removal of a judgment alone. The headland of 12.16 is left out.

support.quote: So take the judgment away when you wish
gives: When I wish
take away my judgment
support.follows: I can take the judgment away whenever I wish.

support.quote: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place.
gives: take away my judgment
about what seems to distress me, and then I stand in the safest place
support.follows: Once I take away my judgment about what seems to distress me, I stand in the safest place.

support.quote: just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave
gives: there is calm, like a bay without a wave
support.follows: With the judgment gone there is calm, as for a sailor who has rounded the headland into a bay without a wave.

support.quote: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in
gives: What hems me in
I can throw out
support.follows: Marcus got out of everything that hemmed him in that day, or rather he threw it out.

support.quote: You can strip away many needless things
gives: I can throw out
support.follows: I can strip away many needless things.

support.quote: you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself
gives: at once have plenty of open room
support.follows: I can strip away many needless things that trouble me, and I will at once make plenty of open room for myself.

claims.t: My reason does not trouble or distress itself; it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself. What happens to my body or to anything else of mine I leave to the part it happens to: the body can say so if it suffers, and whatever else of mine is in a bad way can judge that for itself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the judging part acting on “itself”: the ruling part “does not make trouble for itself” (7.13), and reason is not to be the one “to distress itself” (8.38). Both then turn to another part with “let”: let the body say so if it suffers (7.13), let whatever is in a bad way form its own judgment (8.38).
claims.changed: 7.13 says “the ruling part” and 8.38 says “reason”; the claim says “my reason” for both. 7.13 states it as a fact about the ruling part and 8.38 as an instruction; the claim states it as my rule. 8.38 does not name the body; 7.13 does. “Judge that for itself” follows the printed reading of 8.38, “let that form its own judgment about itself”; the translators’ other reading, “let it suppose so about itself”, says much the same: the part that is in a bad way, not reason, is to judge its own state.

support.quote: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself
support.follows: The part of me that rules does not make trouble for itself.

support.quote: let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself
support.follows: Reason, at least, should not be the one that distresses itself.

support.quote: it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself
gives: it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself
support.follows: The ruling part is undisturbed and unhindered unless it disturbs and hinders itself.

support.quote: Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything.
gives: I leave to the part it happens to
the body can say so if it suffers
support.follows: It is for the body to take care that it suffers nothing, and to say so if it does suffer.

support.quote: if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself
gives: I leave to the part it happens to
whatever else of mine is in a bad way can judge that for itself
support.follows: If some other part of me is in a bad way, that part may form its own judgment about itself.

claims.t: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed. When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to; I see things as they are.
claims.shared: Both passages take the case of a person who turns on me, one who “is speaking ill of you” (8.47) and one who “abuses you” (4.9). 8.47 answers that case with what has and has not been reported, and uses “see” for its second example, the sick child: “I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see”. 4.9 answers its case with “see them as they are in truth”. The shared word “see” is the translation’s: the Greek has βλέπω in 8.47 and ἴδε in 4.9, different verbs close in sense. Both refuse a judgment that goes beyond the thing.
claims.changed: In 8.47 the judgment refused is the one I would add from within; in 4.9 it is the one the abuser holds or wants me to hold. The sick child of 8.47 is a second example and is kept only in the quote. 4.9’s “in truth” is left out of the claim. The claim calls the reporters “my first impressions”, the words 8.47 itself uses later for “the impressions that lead the way”.

support.quote: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report.
gives: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report
support.follows: I should tell myself only what the first impressions report.

support.quote: It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported.
gives: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed
support.follows: The report is that someone speaks ill of me. That I have been harmed is not part of the report.

support.quote: I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see.
gives: I see things as they are
support.follows: Marcus sees that the child is sick. He does not see that the child is in danger.

support.quote: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are
gives: When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to
support.follows: I should not take things to be what the person who abuses me decides they are or wants me to decide they are.

support.quote: see them as they are in truth
gives: I see things as they are
support.follows: I should see things as they truly are.

single.label: No need either
single.t: So far as depends on itself, my ruling part needs nothing, unless it makes a need for itself.
single.quote: The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself
single.why: Only this passage speaks of need. The other passages speak of trouble and distress, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Left to itself, the ruling part needs nothing; any need it has, it makes for itself.

single.label: Or say this
single.t: Rather than adding nothing to what my first impressions report, I do say something further to myself, as someone who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.quote: Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.why: Only this passage corrects the rule to say nothing further. It does not spell out what is to be said.
single.follows: Marcus corrects himself: I may say something further, but as one who recognises each thing that happens in the universe.

single.label: Principles going out
single.t: My principles can be killed only if the impressions that answer to them are put out, and it is up to me to keep fanning those impressions back into flame.
single.quote: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame?
single.why: Only this passage says how principles are lost and how they are kept alive. It is kept as what failing looks like and the way back.
single.follows: Principles die only when the impressions that answer to them go out, and keeping those alight is up to me.

single.label: So far as true
single.t: The saying that everything is judgment can be answered, and the answers are plain. Its usefulness is plain too, if I take what is nourishing in it, so far as it is true.
single.quote: For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
single.why: Only this passage admits that the saying has plain answers and limits it to what is true in it.
single.follows: The replies to Monimus’s saying are plain, and so is its use, if one takes from it what nourishes and only so far as it is true.

single.label: “I am not reason”
single.t: The self that stands in safety is my reason. If I object that I am not reason, I grant it.
single.quote: “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted.
single.why: Only this passage raises the objection that I am more than my reason, and it grants it. The item stops where its quote stops. What still holds comes in the passage’s next sentence, which is quoted in the claim on reason and the body: reason is not to be the one that distresses itself.
single.follows: The “yourself” that stands safe is reason. To the objection that he is not reason, Marcus answers: granted.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of 1634. In modern editions 8.38 is 8.40, 6.47 is 6.52, 7.13 is 7.16, 9.30 is the opening of 9.32, 8.47 is 8.49, 12.16 is 12.22, 4.9 is 4.11, 2.13 is 2.15 and 9.11 is 9.13; 7.2 is the first part of 7.2.

Reads “reason” (8.38) and “the ruling part” (7.13) as the same thing and calls both “my reason” in claim 4. Reads the unnamed “anything else of yours” of 8.38 beside the “little body” of 7.13; the Greek of 8.38 does not name the body.

The statement says “what troubles me” without “all” or “many”. 9.30 says many of the things that trouble me rest on judgment, 9.11 says all that hemmed him in was in his judgments, and 2.13 holds “everything is judgment” only so far as it is true.

Uses “trouble” in the statement and in claims 1 and 2 for three of the translation’s words: “trouble” (9.30, 6.47), “disturbed” (7.2) and “hemmed in” (9.11). “Distress” is kept as it is in claims 3 and 4. The quotes keep the difference.

Fuses 8.47 and 4.9 into claim 5 although they share few words: both take a person who speaks against me, and both answer with “see” in the translation. The words “I see things as they are” rest on 4.9; 8.47 backs them only by its example of the sick child.

Quotes 9.30 although the passage is cut in mid-sentence. The Greek goes on to say that the open room is made by taking the whole universe in thought; claim 3 quotes only the room, and says where it lists what the fusion changed that the room is not to be read as coming from removing a judgment alone. Also leaves out “it does not frighten itself into desire” (7.13), where the translators’ note says the Greek text has been doubted, and the “little soul” of the same passage.
articles.limit: 12.16 feeds three of the five claims and two of the three parts of the statement, so the article leans on one short passage. The passages do not agree on what to do with a judgment: 6.47 says I may form none, 7.2 that I can form the one I ought, 8.47 first says to add nothing and then to add something. Claim 2 keeps 6.47 and 7.2 side by side, and claim 5 and the said-once item on 8.47’s correction keep the two halves of 8.47; the article settles neither. Article 2 already says that I take care in my judgments and that reason is not to be overpowered by the senses. What this article adds is that the trouble itself rests on the judgment, and that the judgment can be taken away.

statement.t: What troubles me rests on my judgment; that judgment is up to me, and when I take it away there is calm.

parts.words: What troubles me rests on my judgment
that judgment is up to me
when I take it away there is calm

statement.kind: A chain: where the trouble is, whose it is, what removing it gives
statement.form: Claim 1 places the trouble in my judgments, claim 2 says the judgment is mine to form or to withhold, and claim 3 says what taking it away gives. The statement joins these three in the order 12.16 itself gives them. Claims 4 and 5 apply it to two cases: my own body, and another person’s words.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first and the fifth claims gain a second author. Practice gains questions to put to myself and words for facing a feared event, and “when it breaks” gains where false opinions come from and how they are driven out. He limits the first claim (even pain with no opinion added is still slight) and the fourth (the mind is struck by feelings reason cannot rout), and he challenges the fifth: where all is in doubt, he would have me believe what I prefer.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for facing a feared event: if it does happen, perhaps it happens for my best. He limits the first claim, though: even pain with no opinion added is still slight.

items.quote: Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment
items.follows: Everything depends on opinion, and ambition, luxury and greed go back to it as well.
items.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness and pain, written to Lucilius, who is ill. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our pain; Seneca extends it to ambition, luxury and greed.

items.quote: It is according to opinion that we suffer.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments
items.follows: How much we suffer goes by our opinion.
items.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca tells the sick Lucilius not to make his pain heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what the sufferer thinks of his own pain.

items.quote: to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom
gives: I see things as they are
items.follows: I should strip from things whatever disturbs and confuses, and see what each one is at bottom.
items.context: Letter 24: Seneca tells Lucilius to listen calmly when his enemy threatens him over his case. “Things” are what he fears; stripped, they hold nothing fearful but the fear.

items.quote: Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.
gives: I see things as they are
items.follows: We should set rumour aside and value each thing by what it is, not by what it is called.
items.context: Letter 95, on principles: what opinion we ought to hold about poverty, riches, renown, disgrace and exile. “Each thing” is one of these; “rumour” is what people say of it.

items.label: practice
items.t: When people around me try to talk me into believing that I am unhappy, I consider what I myself feel and not what I hear. I ask myself whether I am tormented without sufficient reason, and whether I am turning what is not an evil into an evil.
items.why: 4.9 deals with the person who abuses me and wants me to judge as he does. Seneca deals with people who mean well and pity me, and he gives the questions to put to myself; Marcus gives none here.

support.quote: when men surround you and try to talk you into believing that you are unhappy, to consider not what you hear but what you yourself feel
gives: When people around me try to talk me into believing that I am unhappy, I consider what I myself feel and not what I hear
support.follows: When others try to persuade me that I am unhappy, I should go by what I feel and not by what I hear.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. The “men” are people who condole with Lucilius over a trouble he expects; Seneca asks him to consult his own feeling instead of them.

support.quote: Put the question voluntarily to yourself: “Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?”
gives: I ask myself whether I am tormented without sufficient reason
whether I am turning what is not an evil into an evil
support.follows: I should ask myself whether I am tormented without reason and am making an evil out of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: the last of the questions Seneca gives Lucilius to ask himself when the people around him tell him that he is unhappy.

items.label: practice
items.t: When I fear the worst, I say: what if it does happen? Let us see who wins. Perhaps it happens for my best interests.
items.why: 8.47 gives words for a report: say nothing further, or speak as one who recognises what happens in the universe. It gives none for facing an event I fear may come. Seneca does, and his words are again a judgment: he does not grant that the event would be an evil, he judges that it may be for his best.

support.quote: You yourself must say: “Well, what if it does happen? Let us see who wins! Perhaps it happens for my best interests; it may be that such a death will shed credit upon my life.”
gives: I say: what if it does happen? Let us see who wins
Perhaps it happens for my best interests
support.follows: Lucilius is to say: suppose it does happen; let us see who wins; perhaps it is for my best.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. After the mild remedy, “perhaps the worst will not happen”, Seneca gives the sterner one. “It” is the worst that Lucilius fears.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I fail when I agree too quickly with what people say and do not test the things that frighten me. My faults were not born in me: they came from outside and were heaped on me, and with frequent admonitions, from someone who keeps reminding me, I can reject the opinions that din about my ears.
items.why: 7.2 says my principles die when their impressions go out, and that keeping them alight is up to me. Seneca says where the false opinions come from, other people, and that the remedy is to be reminded often, by someone else if need be. Marcus speaks here only of what I do myself.

support.quote: we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear
gives: I agree too quickly with what people say and do not test the things that frighten me
support.follows: We accept what people say too quickly and do not test the things that frighten us.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca says we are troubled by apprehension and rumour more than by fact; “those things” are the reports that frighten us.

support.quote: For you are mistaken if you suppose that our faults are inborn in us; they have come from without, have been heaped upon us.
gives: My faults were not born in me: they came from outside and were heaped on me
support.follows: Our faults are not inborn; they came from outside and were heaped on us.
support.context: Letter 94 defends the giving of advice. Seneca has just said that parents, slaves and neighbours pass their folly on to us; “from without” means from these people.

support.quote: by receiving frequent admonitions, we can reject the opinions which din about our ears
gives: with frequent admonitions, from someone who keeps reminding me, I can reject the opinions that din about my ears
support.follows: If we are admonished often, we can reject the opinions that are dinned into our ears.
support.context: Letter 94, on the value of advice: we need a guardian to pluck us by the ear and dispel rumours. The “opinions” are those of the crowd around us.

items.t: Seneca leaves a residue. Of bodily pain he says that it is slight when opinion has added nothing to it, not that it is then gone (Ep. 78.13). The same section argues that the weight of pain depends on opinion, and it goes on to advise calling the pain nothing, a trifling matter at most; so this is one argument, and what remains is a slight pain that opinion did not make. This limits the claim that what troubles me rests on my judgments.

support.quote: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it
support.follows: Pain to which opinion has added nothing is slight.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness, to the sick Lucilius: do not make troubles heavier by complaining. The “pain” is bodily pain; “opinion” is what one tells oneself about it.

items.t: Seneca does not let reason off so cleanly. Even the mind of a man over whom fortune has lost her control will be smitten with a thrill, and he will change colour (Ep. 57.3): there are emotions that no courage can avoid, and such a feeling is not fear but a natural feeling that reason cannot rout (Ep. 57.4). The claim says that the ruling part is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself; here the mind is struck by something it did not do to itself, and reason cannot stop it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: like Marcus, he calls trembling, pain and turning pale sensations of the body, and he puts what is truly an evil in the mind only if these trials drag the mind down (Ep. 71.29). He is not fully consistent: in Letter 57 the thrill is in the mind, in Letter 71 such things are of the body.

support.quote: Even such a man’s mind will be smitten with a thrill and he will change colour.
support.follows: Even the mind of a man fortune cannot rule is struck by a shock, and he changes colour.
support.context: Letter 57, on passing through a dark road tunnel. “Such a man” is one over whom fortune has lost her control, not Seneca himself; the “thrill” is the shock of the gloom.

support.quote: there are certain emotions, my dear Lucilius, which no courage can avoid
support.follows: Some emotions cannot be avoided by any courage.
support.context: Letter 57: in a dark road tunnel Seneca felt a thrill and a change in himself. The “emotions” are such first shocks, which he says strike even a man fortune cannot rule.

support.quote: This is not fear; it is a natural feeling which reason cannot rout.
support.follows: Such a shock is not fear but a natural feeling, and reason cannot drive it out.
support.context: Letter 57, on a journey through a dark tunnel. “This” is frowning at a grim prospect, shuddering at sudden sights and growing dizzy at a precipice, in a brave man.

support.quote: the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body. Where, then, is the abode of utter distress, of that which is truly an evil? In the other part of us, no doubt, if it is the mind that these trials drag down
support.follows: Trembling, pain and pallor belong to the body even in the wise man; what is truly an evil is in the mind, and only if these trials drag it down.
support.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: human virtue does not go beyond nature. “These trials” are the trembling, pain and pallor; “the other part” is the mind.

items.t: Seneca goes further than saying nothing more. Where everything is in doubt, he tells Lucilius to decide in his own favour and believe what he prefers, and to lean toward hope even if fear has the majority (Ep. 13.13). Marcus says to add nothing to what is reported and to see things as they are in truth; a belief chosen because I prefer it is an addition. Seneca does not hold to this himself: a few lines later he says he is ashamed either to admonish Lucilius sternly or to beguile him with such mild remedies, and he goes on to a sterner one (Ep. 13.14).

support.quote: whenever all the elements are in doubt, decide in your own favour; believe what you prefer
support.follows: When everything is uncertain, I should decide in my own favour and believe what I prefer.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: Lucilius is to weigh his hopes against his fears about a trouble that may come. “The elements” are the uncertain signs on either side.

support.quote: And if fear wins a majority of the votes, incline in the other direction anyhow, and cease to harass your soul
support.follows: Even if fear has more on its side, I should lean the other way and stop harassing my soul.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca pictures hopes and fears as voting; even if fear has more votes, Lucilius is to lean toward hope.

support.quote: But I am ashamed either to admonish you sternly or to try to beguile you with such mild remedies.
support.follows: Seneca is ashamed either to admonish Lucilius sternly or to try to beguile him with mild remedies like these.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: said shortly after Seneca advises Lucilius to believe what he prefers. The “mild remedies” are that advice; a sterner one follows.

amend.t: ; and if what I fear does happen, I can say that perhaps it happens for my best interests
; yet even pain to which opinion has added nothing is still slight
; yet my mind itself is still struck by certain natural feelings that no courage can avoid and reason cannot rout
; yet where it is in doubt whether what I fear will come, I decide in my own favour and believe what I prefer

searches: near c3.s1 (25 nearest sections by vectors)
in our (your, my, his) power or control
wretched, unhappy (with think, believe, convince, opinion)
mask, what it is, at bottom, as they are
add, added (with ills, troubles, pain, grief, fear)
judgment (with pain, suffer, evil, fear, trouble)

rejected.why: Nearest by vectors. About equipping oneself against the fickleness of chance; does not place the trouble in judgment.
A soul that keeps its own sure order, which no storm ruffles. About freedom from regret through philosophy, not about removing a judgment.
Do not judge the magistrate happier than yourself. About envy of the great.
“Give your opinion” as a judge on the doctrine of causes. Another sense of opinion.
It matters with what eyes you see. Close to claim 1, but the passage is about judging great matters with greatness of soul; Ep. 78.13 says the point directly.
Virtue is a true and never-swerving judgment. About what the good is.
“A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is.” Says what Ep. 78.13 says; a third witness for the same words was not needed.
Only common opinion makes pain, loss and death formidable. Found by the word search. The opinion is other people’s talk; Ep. 78.13 is about my own.
Does unjust gossip harm a good man? Near 8.47, but it says gossip does no harm, not that the harm was never reported.
“It is you yourself who are turning it into pain.” A rebuke to a bereaved father; the same point as Ep. 78.13.
Tears fall however we try to check them. The same limit as Ep. 57.4, said of grief only.
Add nothing to natural grief. Near 8.47’s “say nothing further”, but about displays of mourning before onlookers.
Our wise man feels his troubles and overcomes them. A contrast with another school in a letter on friendship; Ep. 71.29 says it more fully.
The irrational part may be hurt; the rational part holds to its opinions. Near claim 4, but it does not say that reason is disturbed only by itself; Ep. 71.29 is quoted.
Socrates: let anyone insult you; with virtue you suffer nothing. Rests safety on virtue, not on withholding a judgment.
Strip the mask from things. The same instruction as Ep. 24.12, which is quoted.
We exaggerate, imagine or anticipate sorrow. A list of three faults about fears before the event, not about opinion as such.
A rule for telling real from imaginary sufferings by present and future. About time, which is not this section’s subject.
The mind fashions false shapes of evil and twists a doubtful word. Describes the failing; Ep. 13.8 is shorter and is quoted.
Nature’s wants are slight, the demands of opinion boundless. About desire and wealth.
The mind must make everything agreeable to itself. About places of retirement.
Nothing is heavy if accepted with a light heart. About a late supper and not adding anger to trouble; acceptance, not judgment.
The only safe harbour is scorn of the future and a firm stand. The harbour image of 12.16, but reached by facing Fortune, not by removing a judgment.
Tranquillity comes from clinging to a good judgment. The opposite movement to taking a judgment away; no clear bearing on claim 3.
The beginnings of certain things are outside our control. An argument about whether the passions can be kept within bounds once begun.
The beginning is in our power, fortune decides the issue. About actions and results; used in Article 2.
We lack the power because we refuse to believe in it. About clinging to vices.
Drive out false opinions before giving precepts. An opponent’s argument in the debate over precepts.
Tell good from bad without patterning your opinion on the populace. About birth and freedom.
