We suffer more often in imagination than in reality. Contrasts dangers imagined beforehand with dangers that come, not opinion with fact, so it does not limit claim 1; said in a milder style Seneca chooses openly.

articles.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

claims.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear. I am fitted by nature to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable. What happens to me is the kind of thing that happens to human beings, usual and natural, and I do not resent it.
claims.shared: 5.16 and 8.45 both say it of everything that happens and both end on bearing: nothing happens that a person is not “fitted by nature to bear” (5.16), nature brought nothing “that could not be borne” (8.45). 10.3 uses 5.16’s phrase, “fitted by nature to bear”, and says with 8.45 not to “resent it”.
claims.changed: 5.16 says “anyone” and 8.45 says “you”; the claim says “me”. 5.16 and 8.45 say it of everything that happens; 10.3 says only that I am fitted to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable, and allows a second case, a thing I am not fitted to bear. The claim keeps 10.3’s condition in its second sentence and does not say that everything is within my judgment’s reach; the second case stands under “If I doubt it”. The ox, the vine and the stone of 8.45 are dropped.

support.quote: Nothing happens to anyone that they are not fitted by nature to bear.
gives: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
I am fitted by nature to bear
support.follows: Whatever happens to a person, that person is fitted by nature to bear it.

support.quote: For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.
gives: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
support.follows: Whatever the common nature brought me, it was something that could be borne.

support.quote: Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable
gives: I am fitted by nature to bear
whatever my own judgment can make bearable
support.follows: I am fitted by nature to bear everything that my own judgment can make bearable.

support.quote: Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence
gives: What happens to me is the kind of thing that happens to human beings
support.follows: Only things of the human kind can happen to a human being.

support.quote: So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it?
gives: usual and natural
I do not resent it
support.follows: If what happens to each thing is usual and natural for it, there is no reason to resent it.

support.quote: So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do.
gives: I do not resent it
support.follows: If what happens is something I am fitted by nature to bear, I should bear it and not resent it.

claims.t: What troubles or harms me is not the thing outside me but my own judgment that it is bad. Unless I make that judgment I have not been harmed, and it is in my power not to make it, or to wipe it out once it is made.
claims.shared: All five passages put the trouble in the one who judges and not in the thing: “your own verdict” (8.45), “that which judges about bad things” (4.32), “unless I judge” (7.11), “the judgment” (4.7), and things that “do not touch the soul” (5.16). 7.11 and 4.7 share the words “been harmed”. 8.45 and 7.11 both say that something about the judgment is open to me (“in your power”, “possible for me”): 7.11 not to judge, 8.45 to wipe out a verdict already made.
claims.changed: “Verdict” (8.45) and “judgment” (4.7) translate two Greek words; the claim uses “judgment” for both. 4.32 speaks of what is bad for me, 8.45 of what troubles me, 7.11 and 4.7 of harm; the claim says “troubles or harms”. 7.11 says “not yet been harmed”; the claim says “not been harmed”.

support.quote: If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and to wipe that out at once is in your power.
gives: not the thing outside me
my own judgment
it is in my power
or to wipe it out once it is made
support.follows: When something outside distresses me, what troubles me is my verdict about it, and I can wipe that verdict out at once.

support.quote: What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you.
gives: not the thing outside me
support.follows: What is bad for me is not in another person’s mind and not in any change in my surroundings.

support.quote: Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all
gives: not the thing outside me
support.follows: Things themselves do not touch the soul at all.

support.quote: In the place where you have that which judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well.
gives: my own judgment
that it is bad
support.follows: What is bad for me lies in the part of me that judges things bad; if that part does not judge, all is well.

support.quote: But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed.
gives: my own judgment
that it is bad
Unless I make that judgment I have not been harmed
support.follows: Unless I judge that what has happened is bad, I have not yet been harmed.

support.quote: Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.
gives: Unless I make that judgment I have not been harmed
support.follows: Without the judgment there is no thought “I have been harmed”, and without that thought there is no harm.

support.quote: And it is possible for me not to judge so.
gives: it is in my power not to make it
support.follows: It is possible for me not to make that judgment.

claims.role: The body’s pain, the mind’s calm
claims.t: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart, the pain is for the body and its senses to see to. Nothing from outside touches my mind: it can keep its own calm, and it does not add the judgment that this is bad.
claims.shared: 4.32 and 7.39 both take the worst that can be done to the body (“is cut, is burned”; “tearing apart the little limbs”) and both leave the mind where it was. 7.39 and 8.26 share the word “calm”. 8.26 and 5.20 name the one thing the mind must not do: “judge that it is a bad thing” (8.26), “add … the judgment that it is something good or bad” (5.20). 8.26, 8.39 and 5.20 hand the pain to the body or to sensation.
claims.changed: The claim says “my mind” where the passages say “the soul” (8.26), “the mind” (7.39), “the ruling part” (5.20) and “what is the mind’s own” (8.39). 5.20 speaks of pleasure as well as pain and says “good or bad”; the claim keeps pain and “bad”. 5.20 also grants that the feeling does reach the mind; that sentence stands as a said-once item under “In action”.

support.quote: Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet.
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart
support.follows: Even if the body is cut, burned or rotting, the part that judges about these things should keep quiet.

support.quote: even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart
support.follows: I can live unforced and glad even while wild beasts tear apart the limbs of my body.

support.quote: Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to
support.follows: If pain is a bad thing for the body, it is for the body to say so.

support.quote: Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to
support.follows: Whether pain or pleasure touches me is a matter for sensation.

support.quote: let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to
support.follows: The ruling part should draw a line around itself and keep the body’s feelings within the parts of the body.

support.quote: What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it
gives: Nothing from outside touches my mind
support.follows: Nothing whatever, not fire, iron, a tyrant or slander, touches what is the mind’s own.

support.quote: For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.
gives: Nothing from outside touches my mind
support.follows: Every verdict, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to that place.

support.quote: For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm
gives: it can keep its own calm
support.follows: Nothing in all of this prevents the mind from keeping itself calm.

support.quote: But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing.
gives: it can keep its own calm
it does not add the judgment that this is bad
support.follows: The soul can keep its own calm and can decline to judge that the thing is bad.

support.quote: but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad
gives: it does not add the judgment that this is bad
support.follows: The ruling part should not add, from itself, the judgment that the feeling is something good or bad.

claims.t: Nothing that happens prevents me from being good and just; that is in my power everywhere. What comes to hand is material for virtue: using it rightly makes me better, and to bear it nobly is good fortune.
claims.shared: 10.33 and 4.41 both use the word “prevent” and both deny it: no one prevents me from being good (10.33), what has happened does not prevent me from being just (4.41). 7.29 and 10.33 both say “in your power”, and both say “everywhere”: 7.29 of behaving justly, 10.33 of acting in accordance with one’s own nature. 7.39 and 10.33 both call what is present or comes to hand “material”.
claims.changed: 4.41 lists eight qualities and 10.33 two; the claim keeps “good” (10.33) and “just” (4.41, 7.29), and “prevents me” is the word the two passages share. 10.33 speaks of material for doing what belongs to a human being, and only 7.39 says “for virtue”. 10.33’s “better” and 4.41’s “good fortune” both say that a thing handled well turns into a gain; each of the two wordings rests on its own passage. 10.33 says “everywhere” of acting in accordance with one’s own nature and 7.29 of behaving justly; the claim says it of being good and just.

support.quote: All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward?
gives: prevents me from being good
that is in my power
support.follows: Being good and straightforward is in my power, and no one prevents me from it.

support.quote: Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free
gives: Nothing that happens prevents me
just
support.follows: What has happened does not prevent me from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible and free.

support.quote: Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present
gives: just
that is in my power
everywhere

support.quote: For one must judge everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature to be an enjoyment. And it is possible everywhere.
gives: everywhere
support.follows: Acting in accordance with my own nature is possible everywhere, and I should count it an enjoyment.

support.quote: For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue
gives: What comes to hand is material
for virtue

support.quote: that is what it is for you to do, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand, the things that belong to the way a human being is made
gives: What comes to hand is material
support.follows: My part is to do what belongs to a human being with the material that is supplied and comes to hand.

support.quote: the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them
gives: using it rightly makes me better
support.follows: A human being becomes better and more praiseworthy by using rightly what befalls them.

support.quote: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”
gives: to bear it nobly is good fortune
support.follows: The thing to say is not that this is a misfortune but that bearing it nobly is good fortune.

claims.t: At every impression of harm, at every pain or distress, I apply one of the rules I keep ready. If the city, the community I belong to by nature, is not harmed, I have not been harmed; and what does not make me worse does not harm me.
claims.shared: Three passages give a rule and say when to use it, in nearly the same words: “At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule” (5.19), “At every pain, have this ready to hand” (7.35), “at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle” (4.41). 5.19 and 10.33 state the same rule about the city and the citizen. 7.35 and 4.7 both measure a thing by whether it makes me “worse”.
claims.changed: 4.41’s own principle, that to bear a thing nobly is good fortune, stands in the claim before this one; here only its instruction to use a principle is taken. 7.35 says of pain that it does not make the mind worse; 4.7 gives the general rule that what does not make a person worse does not harm them. 10.33 goes on from the city to the law; that step is left out. “The city” is glossed as the community I belong to by nature, after 10.33’s “one who is by nature a citizen”.

support.quote: At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either.
gives: At every impression of harm
I apply one of the rules
If the city
is not harmed, I have not been harmed
support.follows: Whenever I have the impression of being harmed, I should apply the rule that if the city is not harmed, I am not harmed.

support.quote: At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse
gives: at every pain
the rules I keep ready
what does not make me worse
support.follows: At every pain I should have ready the thought that pain is not shameful and does not make the governing mind worse.

support.quote: From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle
gives: distress
I apply one of the rules
support.follows: At everything that leads towards distress I should use one principle.

support.quote: nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city
gives: If the city
the community I belong to by nature
is not harmed, I have not been harmed
support.follows: Nothing harms a citizen that does not harm the city.

support.quote: What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them either from outside or from within.
gives: what does not make me worse
does not harm me
support.follows: What does not make a person worse does not make their life worse and does not harm them.

claims.t: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it: not the rest of my life, and not my opinion. Only the present weighs on me, and taken in this way it is not unbearable, and it is not everlasting.
claims.shared: Both passages use the word “unbearable” and both deny it of a thing taken without additions. 8.34 strips the present of the future and the past (“by itself alone”, “stripped bare”); 7.35 says “do not add to it by opinion”.
claims.changed: 7.35 speaks of “most pains” and credits the saying to Epicurus; 8.34 speaks of hardships and of the task in hand. The claim says “a hardship”. 7.35’s condition “if you remember the limits” is left out.

support.quote: it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and convict your mind if it cannot hold out against this, stripped bare
gives: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it
Only the present weighs on me
support.follows: Only the present weighs on me, and it shrinks when I mark it off by itself, stripped bare.

support.quote: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion
gives: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it
not my opinion
it is not unbearable
it is not everlasting
support.follows: Most pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if I remember its limits and do not add to it by opinion.

support.quote: Do not take in, in one sweep of thought, what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you.
gives: not the rest of my life
support.follows: I should not take in at one sweep all the hardships that are likely to have come on me.

support.quote: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it.
gives: it is not unbearable
support.follows: Asked what is unbearable in the task in front of me, I would be ashamed to name anything.

single.label: Good and bad alike
single.t: Nothing is bad or good that can happen equally to a bad man and a good one.
single.quote: That is, let it decide that nothing is either bad or good which can happen equally to a bad man and a good one.
single.why: Only this passage argues from the fact that the same things happen to good people and bad. It is a separate ground, and no second passage of the section gives it.
single.follows: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.

single.label: Help without alarm
single.t: When other people lose things that are neither good nor bad, I help as far as I am able and as far as is deserved. I do not form the impression that their loss is a harm.
single.quote: Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if it is in the middle things that they are coming off worse; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.why: Only this passage turns from my own hardship to other people’s losses. It keeps the help and withholds the judgment.
single.follows: I should help as far as I can even when the loss is in indifferent things, but I should not form the impression that it is a harm.

single.label: In illness
single.t: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I do as Epicurus did when he was ill: I keep to philosophy, whatever befalls.
single.quote: So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls
single.why: Only this passage gives an example to copy. By his own account Epicurus, when ill, did not talk about his body’s sufferings and went on inquiring into nature. The sentence that begins with “For” is cut off in the passage.
single.follows: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I should do as Epicurus did and not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.

single.label: Pain unnoticed
single.t: Being drowsy, overheated or without appetite is the same as pain, though I do not notice it as such. When one of these displeases me, I say to myself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.quote: many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.why: Only this passage names the small discomforts and gives words to say when I resent them. It shows what failing looks like on an ordinary day.
single.follows: Drowsiness, heat and loss of appetite are forms of pain; being displeased at them is giving in to pain.

single.label: An unconditional impulse
single.t: If I set out on something unconditionally, without keeping in mind “if nothing prevents it”, and something comes to stand in its way, that is already a bad thing for me as a rational being. If I accept the common lot, I have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.quote: Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.why: Only this passage says when an obstacle does harm me: when I wanted the thing unconditionally. It gives the failure and the way back.
single.follows: A blocked impulse is already bad for me if it was without reservation; if I accept the common lot I have not yet been harmed or hindered.

single.label: The feeling is natural
single.t: When the body’s feelings do pass up into my mind, I do not try to go against the sensation, which is natural.
single.quote: But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a body that is one, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural
single.why: Only this passage grants that the line between body and mind is crossed. It says what I do then: I let the sensation be and withhold only the judgment.
single.follows: When bodily feelings reach the mind, one should not fight the sensation, which is natural.

single.label: Outdone by ignorance
single.t: Other people stand firm and unhurt under the same things, because they do not know what has happened or because they are showing off. It is a terrible thing if ignorance and the wish to please are stronger than wisdom.
single.quote: The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.
single.why: Only this passage compares me with people who bear the same things for worse reasons. It is a rebuke for the moment I give way.
single.follows: Others bear the same things out of ignorance or to show off; it is terrible if those are stronger than wisdom.

single.label: If I cannot bear it
single.t: If something happens that I am not fitted by nature to bear, I do not resent that either: it will perish once it has used me up. When it has consumed me, it comes to an end with me.
single.quote: And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up.
single.why: Only this passage allows that something may be more than I can bear. It is the section’s own answer to a doubt about the first claim.
single.follows: What I am not fitted to bear ends once it has used me up, so it too is not to be resented.

single.label: If I am blocked
single.t: If something stronger keeps me from doing what seems sound to me, I am not distressed, for the cause does not lie with me. If life is not worth living without it, I leave life in a kindly spirit, gracious towards what stands in the way.
single.quote: “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life in a kindly spirit, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.
single.why: Only this passage follows the objection to its end: an obstacle that cannot be removed, and a life judged not worth living without the thing. 10.33 also speaks of not going on living, but as the price of not being good, not as the answer to an obstacle.
single.follows: If something stronger blocks the act, the cause is not mine and I need not be distressed; if life is not worth living without it, I may leave life kindly.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition, given here with the modern number in pairs: 8.45 is 8.46–47, 10.33 is 10.32–33, 7.39 is 7.68, 7.29 is 7.53–54, 4.32 is 4.39, 4.41 is 4.49b, 5.19 is 5.22–25, 7.35 is 7.64, 8.34 is 8.36, 5.16 is 5.17–19, 5.20 is 5.26, 7.11 is 7.14, 8.39 is 8.41a, 9.41 is 9.41a, 5.29 is 5.35–36a, 8.41 is 8.42–43, 8.26 is 8.28 and 4.7 is 4.7–9; 10.3 is 10.3 in both.

Widens the title from “Nothing happens that a human being cannot bear” to “What happens can be borne and does not harm me”. More passages of the section speak of harm and of the judgment that makes it than of bearing.

States “Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear” without a condition, as 5.16 and 8.45 do. 10.3 allows a second case, a thing I am not fitted to bear; the article puts that case, and 8.45’s exit from life, under “If I doubt it” and not into the statement.
Treats “verdict” (8.45, 8.26), “judgment” (4.7, 7.11, 5.20, 10.3) and “opinion” (7.35) as one act of the mind. The translation keeps them apart because the Greek uses different words.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one from their own sections: Article 2 that pain is not bad for me; Article 3 that none of what happens is unusual; Article 7 that what troubles me rests on my judgment, that the body’s pain is the body’s, and that I tell myself no more than my first impressions report (claims 2, 3 and 6 here); Article 11 that I keep my principles ready and that my situation is material for my reason (claims 5 and 4); Article 13 that no one can prevent me from living well and acting justly (claim 4); and Article 21 that an impulse is made with a reservation and that my mind, gathered into itself, cannot be harmed (8.39c and claim 3). What this article adds is that I am fitted to bear what happens, that harm and not only trouble lies in my judgment, and this section’s own rules: the city and the citizen, what does not make me worse, and the hardship taken bare. Its first claim is asserted and not argued: 10.3 itself allows that something may come that I cannot bear, and Seneca, with Letter 78 and Letter 24, challenges it on the same point.

aside.8.41: Says what gladdens Marcus: a sound ruling part that turns away from nothing that happens and uses each thing according to its worth. The use of what happens is already in claim 4 from 10.33 and 7.39, and its first sentence, on not causing himself distress, is a different thought.

statement.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear; what happens harms me only if I judge it bad, and it does not stop me from being good and just.

parts.words: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
what happens harms me only if I judge it bad
it does not stop me from being good and just

statement.kind: Two grounds, what follows from them, and rules for the moment
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the grounds: what happens is within what I am fitted to bear, and the harm lies in my judgment. Claims 3 and 4 say what follows for the body and for conduct. Claims 5 and 6 are exercises for the moment a thing strikes. The statement joins the two grounds and claim 4 with no step of the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second witness: nothing is beyond my power to bear, I suffer according to opinion, pain is a sensation of the body, whatever I am given is material for virtue, and pain is slight when opinion adds nothing to it. The article gains a way of turning the mind from pain, a question that catches the sorrow I add myself, and a reason to go on living when I could leave. He challenges the first claim: a pain I cannot bear may come, though it is short. He limits the third: the mind is steady only once virtue is complete.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement is challenged in its first part. That part does not stand as it is worded: Seneca, like Marcus in 10.3, allows a pain I cannot bear, and says only that it will not last, though elsewhere he says nothing is beyond my power to bear. The rest of the statement stands.

items.quote: none of these things is an evil, none is beyond your power to bear, or is burdensome
gives: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
items.follows: None of the things Seneca has listed is an evil, and none is beyond a person’s power to bear.
items.context: After the fire that destroyed Lyons, Seneca tells Lucilius what everyone must suffer. “These things” are pain, thirst, hunger, old age, sickness, loss and death.

items.quote: It is according to opinion that we suffer.
gives: my own judgment
items.follows: How much we suffer depends on our opinion.
items.context: Letter 78 is to Lucilius, who is ill, on bearing pain. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our trouble; Seneca has just said that everything depends on it.

items.quote: for a man there is no misery unless there be something in the universe which he thinks miserable
gives: my own judgment
that it is bad
items.follows: A person is miserable only if there is something that he thinks miserable.
items.context: Letter 96: Seneca answers a Lucilius who chafes and complains, and lists his own illness and losses. The one real evil in such things, he says, is the complaining.

items.quote: the wise man will tremble, will feel pain, will turn pale, For all these are sensations of the body
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to
items.follows: Even the wise man trembles, feels pain and turns pale, because these are sensations of the body.
items.context: Letter 71 argues that the honourable is the only good. Seneca grants that virtue does not rise above nature, and places real distress in the mind, if trials drag it down.

items.quote: Therefore a high-minded and sensible man divorces soul from body, and dwells much with the better or divine part, and only as far as he must with this complaining and frail portion.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to
items.follows: A sensible person keeps the soul apart from the body and stays with the complaining body only as far as he must.
items.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: the inexperienced cannot stand bodily pain because they live too close to the body. The “complaining and frail portion” is the body.

items.quote: If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit. So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty
gives: What comes to hand is material
for virtue
items.follows: As a sculptor makes the best statue his material allows, the wise man develops virtue in wealth or in poverty.
items.context: Letter 85 defends the view that poverty and pain do not harm the wise man: he makes use of evils. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in ivory and in bronze.

items.quote: Pain is slight if opinion has added nothing to it
gives: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it
not my opinion
items.follows: Pain is slight when opinion has added nothing to it.
items.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: do not make troubles heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what a person adds to the pain by what he says of it to himself.

items.quote: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all,—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
gives: not the rest of my life
items.follows: Fear of suffering to come and memory of suffering past must both go: the past no longer concerns me and the future does not yet.
items.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca wants an end to laments over what one has suffered. “The latter” is past suffering; “the former” is suffering still to come.

items.label: practice
items.t: When I am in pain I turn my mind aside to other things: to the honourable and brave things I have done, and to the brave men who have conquered pain. If pain can be conquered by a smile, it can be conquered by reason.
items.why: Marcus gives rules to recall and one example, Epicurus, who went on with philosophy in illness. Seneca makes a method of it: turn the mind away from the pain, toward my own good deeds and toward those who have beaten it.

support.quote: This, too, will help—to turn the mind aside to thoughts of other things and thus to depart from pain.
gives: I turn my mind aside to other things
support.follows: It helps to turn the mind to other thoughts and so to leave the pain.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius who is ill: having argued that pain is bearable or short, Seneca lists further helps. “This” is turning the mind to other thoughts.

support.quote: Call to mind what honourable or brave deeds you have done; consider the good side of your own life.
gives: the honourable and brave things I have done
support.follows: In pain I should recall my own honourable and brave deeds and the good side of my life.
support.context: Letter 78, Seneca’s advice to the sick Lucilius on where to turn the mind when in pain: first to what he himself has done well.

support.quote: Then think of all the brave men who have conquered pain
gives: the brave men who have conquered pain
support.follows: I should think of all the brave men who have conquered pain.
support.context: Letter 78, to the sick Lucilius: Seneca goes on to name such men, one who read a book during surgery and one who kept smiling at his torturers.

support.quote: If pain can be conquered by a smile, will it not be conquered by reason?
gives: If pain can be conquered by a smile, it can be conquered by reason
support.follows: If a smile can conquer pain, reason can.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca has just told of a man who kept smiling under torture, and argues from him to what reason can do against pain.

items.label: breaks
items.role: Three ways I add to it
items.t: When a sorrow torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all, I am exaggerating it, imagining it or anticipating it. I ask myself: am I tormented without sufficient reason, and am I turning what is not an evil into an evil?
items.why: Marcus names one way I add to a hardship, by taking in the past and the future along with it (8.34), and says not to add to it by opinion (7.35). Seneca names three ways, and gives a question that catches them.

support.quote: Accordingly, some things torment us more than they ought; some torment us before they ought; and some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all. We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
gives: When a sorrow torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all
I am exaggerating it, imagining it or anticipating it
support.follows: Some things torment us too much, some too early, some with no cause: we exaggerate, imagine or anticipate sorrow.
support.context: Letter 13 is on groundless fears; Seneca has just said that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. “We” is people in general.

support.quote: Am I tormented without sufficient reason, am I morose, and do I convert what is not an evil into what is an evil?
gives: am I tormented without sufficient reason
am I turning what is not an evil into an evil
support.follows: I should ask whether I am tormented without reason and whether I am making an evil of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: when others try to persuade Lucilius that he is unhappy, he is to consult his own feeling and put this question to himself.

items.label: doubt
items.t: Before I leave a life I could bravely leave, I ask who would not be able to bear the loss of me. Sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
items.why: 8.45 lets me leave life in a kindly spirit when it is not worth living. Seneca, who had the same impulse in a long illness, adds what held him back: his father, who could not have borne the loss.

support.quote: For I reflected, not how bravely I had the power to die, but how little power he had to bear bravely the loss of me.
gives: I ask who would not be able to bear the loss of me
support.follows: Seneca weighed not how bravely he could die but how badly his father could bear losing him.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca recalls a long illness of his youth in which he often wanted to end his life. “He” is his old father, the thought of whom held him back.

support.quote: And so I commanded myself to live. For sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
gives: Sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live
support.follows: Seneca ordered himself to live; sometimes living is itself the brave act.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca on the illness of his youth. He wanted to end his life and did not, for his father’s sake; his studies and his friends then consoled him.

items.t: Seneca gives the steady mind to the person whose virtue is complete. He agrees that pain belongs to the body and that the rational part cannot be conquered (Ep. 71.27, 71.29), but he says that until the good is fully attained the mind wavers, and that someone still on the way will slip back at times. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus says that the mind can keep its calm; Seneca says who can count on it.

support.quote: Before this is completely attained, the mind wavers in uncertainty; only when it is fully achieved is the mind fixed and steady.
support.follows: Until the supreme good is fully attained the mind wavers; only then is it fixed and steady.
support.context: Letter 71: the wise man feels pain, with an irrational part that can be hurt and a rational part that cannot be conquered. “This” is the supreme good, in the rational part.

support.quote: one will retrograde at times and there will be a certain slackening of mental effort
support.follows: A person who is not yet perfect will slip back at times and slacken.
support.context: Letter 71, on the honourable as the only good. “One” is a person who has just begun or is still on the way to virtue, set against the man whose virtue is complete.

items.t: Seneca disagrees with “Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear”, which is also the statement’s first part. He says that nature has made pain either endurable or short, and he tells Pain to its face that it is slight if he can bear it and short if he cannot: so a pain I cannot bear may come, and what he promises is only that it will not last. Marcus’s own 10.3 allows the same case (“it will perish once it has used you up”). Seneca is inconsistent with himself here: in Letter 91 he says that none of these things, pain among them, is beyond my power to bear (Ep. 91.19), and in Letter 96 that he will not endure himself on the day he finds anything unendurable (Ep. 96.1).

support.quote: No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.
support.follows: No one suffers both severely and for long: nature has made pain either endurable or short.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius who is ill: of the three hard things in disease Seneca takes up bodily pain, and says that extreme pain must come to an end.

support.quote: Slight thou art, if I can bear thee; short thou art if I cannot bear thee!
support.follows: Pain is slight if I can bear it and short if I cannot.
support.context: Letter 24, on fears: Seneca strips the masks from Death and Pain and speaks to each. “Thou” is Pain, which the gouty man scorns and the woman in labour bears bravely.

amend.t: ; but a pain I cannot bear may still come, and then it is short
; but until my virtue is complete my mind wavers, and at times I slip back

searches: unbearable, intolerable, endurable, cannot be borne
cannot be harmed, no harm, no injury
worse (with make, and mind, soul or man)
door, way out, exit, leave life
body, soul or mind, calm, pain or torture
born to, fitted, equal to (with bear, burden, endure)
judge (with evil, harm, the thing itself)
reservation, if nothing prevents, harm to the city or state

rejected.why: Toughen the spirit against mishaps. About being reconciled to the loss of goods; nothing on where harm lies.
The mind is to endure its lot and not cry out, since fortune spares no city. Acceptance of what happens, which is Article 3’s subject.
Nature says hardships are the same for all and whoever wishes makes them easier by equanimity. Its next section, 91.19, says the claim more directly and is used.
Hardships become goods once virtue has made them honourable. An argument that only the honourable is good; 85.40 says the use of hardship more plainly.
The sage stands erect under any load and was born to carry burdens. Said of the sage only, so not used to back the first claim; its neighbours 71.27 and 71.28 give the limit.
A sturdy young man will call more fortunate the one who bears adversity. Near 4.41, but it is a comparison whose other term lies outside the passage.
Every pain stops or slackens. Same point as 78.7, which is quoted.
“A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is.” Same point as 78.13 and 96.1; only its sentence on past and future suffering is used.
If we yield, trouble attacks harder (Article 6 has this from 78.15); and either the illness ends or I do, which is what 10.3 says in a said-once item.
The brave man under torture feels pain and has no fear. Same point as 71.29, which is quoted.

The school’s syllogism that what harms makes a man worse. Seneca reports it, then gives a different answer of his own (the pilot is harmed as a passenger, not as a pilot); too tangled to back claim 5.
The wise man is not harmed by poverty or pain, because he is never shut off from action. Article 2 already quotes this letter (85.38) for the blocked action.
“The present alone can make no man wretched.” Close to claim 6, but 8.34 says the present does weigh; 78.14 says the shared part, dropping past and future, more exactly.
We suffer more often in imagination than in reality. About dangers that have not come; the next two sections, which name the faults and give the question, are used.
A rule for telling real from imaginary sufferings: today nothing is wrong. About a person in health who fears the future, not about bearing a present hardship.
Fortune’s missiles rebound from the happy man like hail from a roof. A portrait inside a letter against logical puzzles; no claim of its own.
One entrance into life, many exits. Says what 8.45 says in a said-once item; Seneca’s own check on leaving life, in 78.2, is used.
Life keeps no one against his will. Same as 70.14.
Epicurus called a day of extreme pain his happiest. The same example as 9.41, which is a said-once item and takes no backing.
Hard matter does not make virtue worse. About the equality of virtues, not about harm to me.
Hardships are easy to endure after long rehearsal. About practising hardship in advance, a different exercise from the ones in this section.
The wise man is not distressed by the loss of children or friends. About grief.

articles.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

claims.t: I hold myself to a few things, the names I have given myself, among them good, dignified, just, affectionate and without pretence. I keep myself in them, I take care never to bear other names, and I struggle to remain this kind of person.
claims.shared: All three passages give a short list of qualities and tell the reader to keep to it. 2.2 and 6.27 both name dignity, affection and justice, and both rule out pretence (“unfeigned”, “unpretentious”); 6.27 and 10.8 both say “good” and “keep yourself”; 2.2 and 10.8 both say “few” and “take care”.
claims.changed: The claim names only the qualities that two lists share, and says “among them” because each list has more. Left out are freedom (2.2); simple, unspoiled, reverent, kindly, strong for fitting work (6.27); modest, truthful and the three names ending in “minded” (10.8), which have an item of their own. 2.2 speaks of “things” and 6.27 of a “kind of person”; the claim calls them names, 10.8’s word. “Unpretentious” in 6.27 stands for a Greek word meaning “without polish”, so its match with 2.2’s “unfeigned” is closer in the English than in the Greek.

support.quote: At every hour take firm care
gives: I take care
support.follows: Care is to be taken at every hour, and firmly.

support.quote: to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice
gives: dignified
just
affectionate
without pretence
support.follows: What is in hand is to be done with dignity, affection, freedom and justice, exactly and without feigning.

support.quote: You see how few the things are
gives: a few things
support.follows: The things that have to be mastered are few.

support.quote: keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent toward the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate
gives: I keep myself in them
good
dignified
just
affectionate
without pretence
support.follows: I should keep myself simple, good, dignified, unpretentious, just, reverent, kindly and affectionate.

support.quote: Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you.
gives: I struggle to remain this kind of person
support.follows: Remaining the person philosophy meant to make me takes a struggle.

support.quote: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names
gives: the names I have given myself
good
I take care
never to bear other names
support.follows: Marcus has given himself six names and must take care that he does not end up bearing others.

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names
gives: I keep myself in them
support.follows: The names are something a person keeps himself in.

support.quote: So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay
gives: a few things
I keep myself in them
support.follows: The names are few; I should put myself aboard them and stay on them if I can.

claims.t: Keeping to these few things lets me live a different life, one that flows smoothly. The gods ask nothing more of me. What they want is not to be flattered, but for rational beings to become like them and for a human being to do the work of a human being.
claims.shared: Both passages say that keeping to the few things leads to a life: in 2.2 the few things, once mastered, “let a person live a life that flows smoothly”; in 10.8 whoever keeps himself in the names “will enter a different life”. Both then say what the gods ask of a person: 2.2 that they demand nothing more, 10.8 what it is they want.
claims.changed: The claim takes the weaker verb, 2.2’s “let a person live”; 10.8 says outright “you will enter”. 2.2 adds that the life is god-fearing, and 10.8 that the person becomes a different person; the claim leaves both out. 10.8 lists the fig tree, the dog and the bee before the human being; the claim keeps the human being.

support.quote: once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing
gives: Keeping to these few things lets me live
one that flows smoothly
support.follows: The few things, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing.

support.quote: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these
gives: The gods ask nothing more of me
support.follows: The gods will demand nothing more of anyone who keeps to these few things.

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life
gives: Keeping to these few things lets me live
a different life
support.follows: Whoever keeps himself in these names becomes a different person and enters a different life.

support.quote: what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being
gives: What they want is not to be flattered
for rational beings to become like them
for a human being to do the work of a human being
support.follows: The gods do not want flattery; they want rational beings to become like them and each thing, the human being included, to do its own work.

claims.t: I keep these names without craving that others call me by them. I need neither show nor any human being as witness.
claims.shared: 1.14 and 3.5 both say “need neither … nor”: at a court one need have no bodyguards, marked clothes or similar show, and the man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness. 3.5 and 10.8 both do without other people’s word: no human being to witness for me, no craving that others use the names of me.
claims.changed: The words two passages share here are only the frame “need neither”; what is not needed differs. 1.14 lists bodyguards, clothes that mark one out, torches and statues; the claim keeps its summing word, “show”. 1.14 says this is possible at a court and reports it as a thought Marcus was brought to; the claim states it of myself. 3.5’s oath is dropped; standing beside an oath, its witness is someone who vouches for a man, not an audience.

support.quote: it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and similar show
gives: I need neither
show
support.follows: The ruler and father Marcus was placed under brought him to think that one can live at a court without guards, marked clothes or similar show.

support.quote: needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness
gives: I need neither
any human being as witness
support.follows: The man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness.

support.quote: without craving to have others call you by them
gives: without craving that others call me by them
support.follows: The names are to be kept without craving that other people use them of me.

claims.t: I want my last hour to come upon me with a good conscience. As a Roman and a man, I set myself in order and do each thing as someone about to leave life, waiting for the signal to withdraw. I carry out each action as the last of my life.
claims.shared: 2.2 and 3.5 both name who is acting, “a Roman” and a man (3.5: “male”), and both set him at the edge of life: 2.2 has each action done “as the last of your life”, 3.5 has him waiting for the signal “to withdraw from life”. 2.2 and 6.28 share the word “last”.
claims.changed: 3.5 adds that the man is old, engaged in public affairs and a ruler; the claim keeps what 2.2 also says. In 6.28 the good conscience at the last hour is the aim of following Antoninus; the claim states the aim without its model, who has an item of his own.

support.quote: so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his
gives: I want my last hour to come upon me with a good conscience
support.follows: Following Antoninus is meant to bring me to my last hour with a conscience as good as his.

support.quote: as a Roman and a man
gives: As a Roman and a man
support.follows: The care over what is in hand is to be taken as a Roman and a man.

support.quote: a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order
gives: As a Roman and a man
set myself in order
support.follows: The god within is to guard a being that is male, old, in public life, a Roman and a ruler, and that has set himself in order.

support.quote: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released
gives: as someone about to leave life
waiting for the signal to withdraw
support.follows: The man described is to be like someone who waits for the signal to withdraw from life and is easily released.

support.quote: carry out each action as the last of your life
gives: as someone about to leave life
each action as the last of my life
support.follows: Each action is to be carried out as if it were the last of my life.

claims.t: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now toward my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me, and whether I have done nothing wrong to any of them.
claims.shared: Both passages go through the same people (parents, teachers, friends, those close to me) and both speak of wrong done to them: 5.25 asks whether I have “done nothing wrong to anyone”, and 1.14 gives thanks that I was “not carried away into any offence against any of them”.
claims.changed: 5.25 asks the question; 1.14 answers it for the past and thanks the gods. The claim keeps the question. It drops the gods, brothers, wife, children, those who brought me up and household slaves of 5.25, and the grandfathers, sister and relatives of 1.14, which the other list does not have.

support.quote: How have you behaved up to now toward the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves?
gives: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now
my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
support.follows: Marcus asks himself how he has behaved up to now toward the gods, his family, teachers, friends, those close to him and his household.

support.quote: Does this hold of you up to now, toward all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”?
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them
support.follows: Marcus asks whether, toward all the people he has listed, he has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong.

support.quote: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them
gives: my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
support.follows: Marcus thanks the gods that nearly all his family, teachers, friends and those close to him were good.

support.quote: I was not carried away into any offence against any of them
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them
support.follows: Marcus was not carried away into any offence against his family, teachers, friends or those close to him.

claims.t: These names can be lost. It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar, made over by the office he holds. I fall short by my own fault. When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly.
claims.shared: 10.8 and 1.14 both admit a falling: “falling away and not prevailing” from the names, and “I still fall short” of the life according to nature. 6.27 and 10.8 both warn of becoming something else than what was to be kept: being turned into a Caesar “happens”, and the names can be lost.
claims.changed: In 1.14 what Marcus falls short of is living according to nature; in 10.8 it is the names. The claim treats them as one falling short. The word “fall” is shared only in the English: 10.8’s verb is “fall out” (ἐκπίπτεις) and 1.14’s is “be left behind” (ἀπολείπεσθαι). 6.27 says that being turned into a Caesar happens; it does not say that names are lost. “Made over by the office he holds” is the editor’s gloss: Caesar is Marcus’s own title as emperor.

support.quote: if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly
gives: These names can be lost
When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly
support.follows: The names can be lost; if they are, I should go back to them quickly.

support.quote: Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens.
gives: It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar
support.follows: Being turned into a Caesar is something that happens, and care must be taken against it.

support.quote: if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing
gives: I fall short
support.follows: A person can sense that he is falling away from the names and not prevailing.

support.quote: that I still fall short of this is by my own fault and by not keeping to the reminders from the gods
gives: I fall short
by my own fault
support.follows: That Marcus still falls short of living according to nature is his own fault: he has not kept to the gods’ reminders.

single.label: The one fruit
single.t: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions, that is, actions done for the community.
single.quote: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.why: Only this passage says that life has a single fruit. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused. “Actions done for the community” is the translators’ gloss of “social actions”.
single.follows: Life is short, and the one thing to be had from it is a pious disposition and actions done for the community.

single.label: Leading without the show
single.t: I can draw myself in until I am very nearly a private person, and be no lowlier and no slacker for it in what I have to do as a leader for the common good.
single.quote: one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good
single.why: Only this passage says it, as a thought Marcus was brought to by the ruler and father he was placed under. Its words on needing no show are fused in the claim on show and witness.
single.follows: Marcus’s ruler and father showed him that one can live almost as a private person and be no lowlier or slacker in a leader’s work for the common good.

single.label: The trade I learned
single.t: I love the little trade I have learned, and I rest in it. For what is left of my life I entrust everything that is mine to the gods with my whole soul, and I make myself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.quote: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of a trade to love, and of being neither tyrant nor slave. It does not say which trade, so it is not fused with the names.
single.follows: I should love the trade I learned and rest in it, entrust what is mine to the gods, and be neither tyrant nor slave to anyone.

single.label: How not to act
single.t: I do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. I do not let elegance dress up my thought, and I am not a person of many words or a busybody.
single.quote: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody.
single.why: Only this passage gives this list. 2.2 has its own list of what each action should be rid of, but the two lists share no words.
single.follows: Acting unwillingly, unsocially, unexamined or divided is ruled out, and so are dressed-up thought, many words and meddling.

single.label: Three further names
single.t: Three further names I have given myself are clear-minded, like-minded and high-minded, and I remember what each was to mean. Clear-minded: a discerning attention to each thing, letting nothing go unheeded. Like-minded: willingly accepting what the common nature assigns. High-minded: lifting the part of me that has mind above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, that is, pleasure and pain, above petty reputation, and above death.
single.quote: Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.why: Only this passage has these three names and defines them. No other list in the section has them, so they are not among the names of the first claim; the definitions are kept as something to recall. “Pleasure and pain” is the translators’ gloss of the movement of the flesh.
single.follows: The three names mean attention to each thing, willing acceptance of what nature assigns, and a mind lifted above the flesh, reputation and death.

single.label: A model
single.t: I do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, the emperor who adopted me. I recall his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity and his ambition to grasp matters.
single.quote: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters
single.why: Only this passage sets up a person as the model. Its long list describes Antoninus and is not the list of names, so it is not fused. That Antoninus is Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus, is the translators’ note.
single.follows: Marcus is to do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, whose traits he lists, beginning with these seven.

single.label: What I have come through
single.t: I call to mind what I have passed through and have been strong enough to endure; that the story of my life is now full and my service complete; how many fine things I have seen; how many pleasures and pains I have looked down on, how many honours I have looked past; and to how many inconsiderate people I have been considerate.
single.quote: Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
single.why: Only this passage looks back on what was endured and calls the life full. The question about wrongdoing in the same passage is fused in the review of my conduct.
single.follows: Marcus is to recall what he has endured, seen and looked past, and that his life’s story is full and his service complete.

single.label: A rider to the review
single.t: I remember that my clean record toward those close to me is partly the gods’ kindness: I had a disposition from which I might well have offended them, and no circumstances came about that would have shown me up.
single.quote: although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up
single.why: Only this passage says it. It sits under Practice as a rider to the review of my conduct: what I recall when the review comes out clean, that the record is partly good fortune.
single.follows: Marcus had it in him to offend those close to him, and thanks the gods that no circumstances arose to bring it out.

single.label: The soul giving out
single.t: It is shameful if my soul gives out in a life in which my body has not yet given out.
single.quote: It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names the failure as a giving out of the soul; the other passages speak of losing names or falling short.
single.follows: It is shameful for the soul to give out before the body does.

single.label: What failing looks like
single.t: To go on being as I have been up to now, torn and soiled in a life like this, is senseless clinging to life. It is like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown to the same claws and bites.
single.quote: For to go on being such as you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.why: Only this passage gives a picture of what not changing is like.
single.follows: Going on unchanged in a life that tears and soils me is senseless clinging to life, like a mauled beast-fighter begging for one more day.

single.label: If I am not prevailing
single.t: If I am not prevailing in keeping these names where I am, I go away with a good heart to some corner where I will prevail.
single.quote: go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail
single.why: Only this passage says where to go when the names cannot be kept. It goes on to a second way out, leaving life altogether, which the article does not turn into a rule (see the editor’s decisions).
single.follows: Someone who is not prevailing should withdraw, in good heart, to a corner where he will prevail.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 2.2 is 2.5, 6.27 is 6.29 with the first part of 6.30, 6.28 is the rest of 6.30, 3.5 is the first part of 3.5, 5.25 is 5.31, 4.26 is 4.31 and 1.14 is 1.17; 10.8 is the same.

Reads the qualities of 2.2, the list of 6.27 and the names of 10.8 as one short list. The first claim names only the qualities that two of the three lists have, and says “among them”; three of 10.8’s own names (clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded) stand in an item of their own with their meanings. Calling the qualities of 2.2 and 6.27 “names” is 10.8’s word, extended by the editor.

Leaves the second way out of 10.8 out of the first-person text. After “go away to some corner where you will prevail” Marcus adds “or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly”. The article does not write “I leave life” as a rule of life; the words stay in the passage for the reader to see.

Reads the last sentence of 10.8 as saying what the gods want (the fig tree doing a fig tree’s work, the human being a human being’s). The translators note that it can also depend on “remember”, as a statement of what makes each thing what it is.

Uses 1.14, a list of thanks to the gods, only where it states something Marcus holds or admits: no offence against those close to him, a court without show, falling short by his own fault. The rest of its thanks are not turned into rules.

Words the third part of the statement after 3.5 (“nor any human being as witness”). 10.8 backs its sense, not its words: it says “without craving to have others call you by them” and has neither “need” nor “witness”.
articles.limit: The article leans on 10.8, which feeds four of the six claims, and three of its joins are loose: “without pretence” rests partly on the English of 6.27, the claim on show and witness shares only the frame “need neither”, and the claim on falling short shares the word “fall” only in the English. Much of it is said in other articles: Article 5 has the human being’s own work, Article 3 accepting what is allotted, Articles 10 and 17 doing each thing as if it were the last (Article 10 on the same Ep. 101.7, Article 17 also without pretence), and Article 11 the good life in very few things, no show and no witness (on the same Ep. 113.32) and coming back after a failure. What this section adds is a short list of names I have given myself, kept without wanting others to call me by them, and each act done as a Roman and a man who waits for the signal to withdraw and wants a good conscience at the last hour.

statement.t: I keep to the few names I have given myself, do each thing as someone about to leave life, and need no one as witness.

parts.words: I keep to the few names I have given myself
do each thing as someone about to leave life
need no one as witness

statement.kind: A rule, the way it is carried out, and what it does not need
statement.form: Claim 1 is the rule: a few names, kept. Claim 4 says how each act is done under it and claim 3 what it does not need; they give the statement its second and third parts. Claim 2 is the ground, claim 5 a check on the past, and claim 6 what happens when the rule is lost. The third part takes its words from 3.5, where the witness stands beside an oath and is someone who vouches for a man; 10.8 backs its sense, not its words. The statement joins its parts with “and” only, so it holds no inference of the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if keeping these names is not enough, or if the gods ask something else.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second author; only the review of my conduct does not. Practice gains a daily review with a test of steadiness, action gains a warning against making a show of plainness, and the side on what failing looks like gains what Seneca says of those who are not yet one person. He limits two claims: until I respect myself I keep a witness in mind, and a day is lived as one that might be my last, not snatched at as the last. The side on doubt stays empty.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for the one who has not yet arrived: though more of the road to wisdom remains than lies behind me, the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.

items.quote: it is more important for you to keep the resolutions you have already made than to go on and make noble ones
gives: I keep myself in them
items.follows: Keeping the resolutions already made matters more than making new and noble ones.
items.context: Letter 16 opens: no happy life without wisdom, an idea to deepen by daily reflection. The “resolutions” are those Lucilius has already made, to be held until they become settled purpose.

items.quote: You should therefore force yourself to maintain to the very end of life’s drama the character which you assumed at the beginning.
gives: I struggle to remain this kind of person
items.follows: I should force myself to keep, to the end of my life, the character I took up at its beginning.
items.context: The close of Letter 120, on how we learn what virtue is: its mark is being always the same. The “character” is the one part a person has taken up, set against changing masks.

items.quote: Would you win over the gods? Then be a good man. Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently.
gives: for rational beings to become like them
items.follows: The way to win the gods is to be good; whoever imitates them worships them enough.
items.context: Letter 95 turns from rules of ritual to the right idea of the gods, who need no servants and do good by nature. “Them” are the gods; to imitate them is to be a good man.

items.quote: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown.
gives: without craving that others call me by them
items.follows: Whoever wants his virtue made known is after renown, not virtue.
items.context: The end of Letter 113, where Seneca says justice should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation. “Advertised” means made known to other people.

items.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
gives: any human being as witness
items.follows: How many people know that I am upright makes no difference.
items.context: Seneca’s closing charge to Lucilius in Letter 113, after saying one must be just without reward. “Your uprightness” is your being just, whether or not anyone knows of it.

items.quote: let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end
gives: as someone about to leave life
set myself in order
items.follows: I should put my mind in order as if I had reached the end of my life.
items.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning far ahead: death stands at our side and no one knows how near his fixed limit is. “The very end” is the end of life.

items.quote: I have looked upon every day as if it were my last
gives: as someone about to leave life
items.follows: Seneca has treated every day as if it were his last.
items.context: Letter 93, on a man whose life was short but complete: a life is measured by what is done in it. Seneca speaks of himself; he never counted on the days he hoped for.

items.quote: That which is short of perfection must necessarily be unsteady, at one time progressing, at another slipping or growing faint; and it will surely slip back unless it keeps struggling ahead
gives: I fall short
items.follows: Whatever is short of perfection is unsteady and slips back unless it keeps struggling forward.
items.context: Letter 71, on those who follow wisdom but have not reached it. “That which is short of perfection” is their progress, which goes backward as soon as effort slackens.

items.label: breaks
items.t: Nobody but the wise man can be one person; the rest of us often change masks. A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always travel the same path. More of the road remains than lies behind me, and the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
items.why: Marcus says what to do when the names are lost: go back to them quickly, or go to a corner where I will prevail (10.8). Seneca adds what Marcus does not say here: that not being one person is the common case, his own included; that the path can be kept at an uneven pace; and that wanting to progress is most of progress. The three sentences come from three letters, and setting them side by side is the editor’s.

support.quote: But nobody can be one person except the wise man; the rest of us often shift our masks.
gives: Nobody but the wise man can be one person; the rest of us often change masks
support.follows: Only the wise man can be one person; everyone else, Seneca included, often changes masks.
support.context: The close of Letter 120: the foolish mind is never like itself. To “be one person” is to keep one character; “the rest of us” counts Seneca among those who change.

support.quote: I do not say that the philosopher can always keep the same pace. But he can always travel the same path.
gives: A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always travel the same path
support.follows: A philosopher may not always keep the same pace, but he can always keep to the same path.
support.context: Letter 20 asks that deed and word agree and that a man be always the same. Asked who can keep this standard, Seneca answers that very few can, and then says this of the philosopher.

support.quote: There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
gives: More of the road remains than lies behind me
the greater part of progress is the desire to progress
support.follows: More of the road lies ahead than behind, but wanting to progress is the greater part of progressing.
support.context: Letter 71, just after Seneca says that progress slips back unless one struggles ahead. The “road” is the way to wisdom, which he says he desires with all his heart.

items.label: practice
items.role: A daily review, and a test
items.t: I watch myself continually and review each day. To find out whether I have accomplished anything, I ask whether I want the same things today that I wanted yesterday.
items.why: Marcus looks back once over his whole conduct up to now (5.25). Seneca makes the review a habit of every day, and gives a test of whether I am holding steady that Marcus does not give here.

support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day.
gives: I watch myself continually and review each day
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself continually and review each day, which he calls a most useful habit.
support.context: In Letter 83 Lucilius has asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, and says that what makes people wicked is that no one looks back over his own life.

support.quote: when you would find out whether you have accomplished anything, consider whether you desire the same things to-day that you desired yesterday
gives: To find out whether I have accomplished anything
I ask whether I want the same things today that I wanted yesterday
support.follows: To see whether I have achieved anything, I should ask whether I want today what I wanted yesterday.
support.context: In Letter 35 Seneca urges Lucilius to make progress and above all to be consistent with himself. This is the test he gives: a will that shifts shows a mind adrift.

items.label: action
items.t: I make no show of plainness either: rough dress, an unkempt beard, open scorn of silver and a bed on the bare earth are another kind of self-display. Inwardly I am different in every respect, and outwardly I live as the people around me do.
items.why: Marcus drops the show of a court and draws himself in toward a private person’s life (1.14). Seneca warns of the opposite show, which Marcus does not mention here: plainness worn in order to be noticed.

support.quote: Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided.
gives: I make no show of plainness either
rough dress, an unkempt beard, open scorn of silver and a bed on the bare earth are another kind of self-display
support.follows: Rough dress, unkempt hair and beard, scorn of silver and sleeping on the ground are self-display and should be avoided.
support.context: Letter 5 warns Lucilius, who studies philosophy, against those who want to be conspicuous rather than to improve. The list is of ways of flaunting an austere life.

support.quote: Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.
gives: Inwardly I am different in every respect, and outwardly I live as the people around me do
support.follows: We should differ from others inwardly in everything, while our outward life conforms to theirs.
support.context: From Letter 5, on not parading philosophy in dress or habits. “We” are those who pursue philosophy; “society” is the people among whom they live.

items.t: Seneca does not send the witness away so soon. Until I have come to respect myself, he has me set the authority of some man over myself as a guard; only after that may I dismiss him. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus’s man who needs no human witness has already set himself in order (3.5), and Marcus keeps a model of his own, Antoninus (6.28). Seneca’s witness is a person I picture for my own correction, not an audience whose praise I want.

support.quote: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man
support.follows: Until I have come to respect myself I should keep some man’s authority over me as a guard; after that I may dismiss him.
support.context: Letter 25 passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if a great man were watching. The “attendant” is that imagined guardian, a Cato, a Scipio or a Laelius, kept in mind.

support.quote: We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong.
support.follows: Most wrongdoing can be got rid of if a witness stands by when we are likely to go wrong.
