support.context: Letter 11 ends with Epicurus’s advice to keep a man of high character before one’s eyes. The “witness” is that man, pictured as present; he is not an actual onlooker.

items.t: Seneca draws a line that Marcus does not draw. He lives each day as a complete life and regards it as one that might be his last, but he says he does not snatch at it as if it were his last. The difference is small, and he does not always keep to it himself: in Letter 93 he says he has looked upon every day as if it were his last (Ep. 93.6).

support.quote: I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.
support.follows: Seneca does not seize a day as if it were his last; he regards it as one that might be.
support.context: In Letter 61 Seneca, now old, writes that his one task is to end his long-standing faults. “It” is each day, which he tries to live as a complete life.

support.quote: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
support.follows: Seneca tries to live every day as if it were a whole life.
support.context: The opening of Letter 61, on meeting death gladly. Seneca describes his own practice in old age; the letter itself, he says next, is written as if death might call him away.

amend.t: ; and though more of the road to wisdom remains than lies behind me, the greater part of progress is the desire to progress
; but until I have come to respect myself, I set the authority of some man over myself as a guard
, though I do not snatch at a day as if it were my last: I regard it as one that might even be my last

searches: last day, last hour, as if it were my last
play the part, one man, same man, consistent
slip back, relapse, fall back, lose ground
review, examine (with day, conduct, myself, yourself)
mask, character (with assume, play, part, wear)
good conscience, ready to depart, balance the account, complete life
imitate, like the gods, flatter (with god)
Cato, Laelius, pattern, model (with choose, guard, before your eyes)

rejected.why: Its sentence after the one quoted, “See to it that men be able to praise you; if not, let them at least identify you”, was weighed as a limit on keeping the names without craving that others use them. Not used: it asks that I be the same man from day to day so that others can tell who I am, not that I want their praise, and Ep. 113.32 says outright that how many know makes no difference.
“Pretence accomplishes nothing” and being “always the same”. It gives a reason, that pretence fails to deceive, and promises virtue’s reward; it is not the resolve to be without pretence.
Dressed-up style shows a flawed mind. It matches 3.5’s line on elegance, which is a said-once item and takes no backing; the letter is about writing.
“We are not merely defiled; we are dyed” by vices. The same image as 6.27, but the dye is vice in general, not an office that changes the person.
One’s own knowledge of one’s deeds as a witness. Apt to the limit on needing no witness, but the sentence is about base deeds done in secret; 25.6 and 11.9 say the point directly.
Live as if in plain sight of all; God is witness of our souls. A divine witness, where the claim is about a human one; the next section, 83.2, is used.
“Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you.” The same advice as 25.6, which states the condition (until you respect yourself) and is quoted.
Choose a Cato or a Laelius as pattern. Close to Marcus’s Antoninus (6.28), a said-once item that takes no backing.
God seeks no servants and is not worshipped by morning salutations. Near “not to be flattered”, but it needs the letter’s account of Roman ritual to see the match; 95.50 is plain.
Examine yourself and do not trust yourself too quickly. About judging one’s progress in philosophy, not about conduct toward others; 83.2 gives the review.
Philosophy is not devised for show. About what philosophy is for, not about needing no witness.
Lay hold of a single norm and regulate the whole life by it. One norm, where Marcus has a list of names; 20.2, on pace and path, is used.
People slip back to conduct they had abjured because they do not persist. Says what 71.35 says, which is quoted.
One who daily puts the finishing touches to his life is never short of time. Continues 101.7, which is quoted.
“I am ready to depart”; the letter written as if death were about to call him. Would back the same words as 93.6 and 101.7; its neighbour 61.1 is used for the limit.
He will not be frightened when the last hour comes. About fearlessness at death, not about how each act is done.
A man who fulfilled the duties of citizen, friend and son had a complete life. Near 5.25’s “your service complete”, a said-once item; said of another man, not as a review.
Its last sentence, “No one can resume his progress at the point where he left off”, could limit going back quickly, but Seneca does not deny the return. Only its first sentence is quoted.
A class of those making progress who can still slip back. A classification of grades; 71.35 says the slipping more directly.
The wise man cannot slip back. About the sage’s security, not about the one who falls and returns.
A portrait of the man who is always the same in all his actions. A description of how we form the idea of virtue; 120.22 gives the instruction.
An upright, good and great soul is a god dwelling in a human body, in knight or slave alike. Near 3.5’s “god in you”, which the article does not use as a claim.
Base for one who has held the highest honours to keep importuning the gods. About vows and prayer, not about what the gods ask.
The good man endures what happens as divine law. About enduring; Article 3’s subject.
A soul in love with what is upright vouches for Lucilius. Encouragement to go on as begun; no words of a claim.
A prayer that the mind come to rest and need no added years. About self-sufficiency and time.
A list of sayings to repeat (no man is good by chance, glory is empty). A different list, about indifferents.
Philosophy makes you prefer to please yourself rather than the populace. About the crowd’s judgment; 113.32 is closer to needing no witness.
The real good comes from a good conscience and a way of living that treads one path. About the source of joy.
Vices need onlookers and a stage; retire and they sink. About luxury and ambition, and a reason for retirement, not for keeping names unseen.
The wise man sets himself free when life troubles his peace. Bears on the second way out in 10.8, which the article leaves out of its text; not used.
Live among men as if God beheld you. Used in Article 6 for prayer; here it would repeat the divine witness of 83.1.

articles.title: Living now as one about to die

claims.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, as those before me already are, and forgotten by all. All that I live is the present, an instant.
claims.shared: 8.4 and 12.15 say the same words, “you will be no one and nowhere”, one “in a little while” and the other “before long”. 8.4 and 7.16 both point to named men who are already gone. 3.10 and 12.19 both say that each person “lives only” the present.
claims.changed: The passages say “you” and “each person”; the claim says “I”. Hadrian and Augustus (8.4) and Chrysippus, Socrates and Epictetus (7.16) become “those before me”. 12.19 adds that the present is all a person loses; the claim leaves that out.

support.quote: in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
as those before me already are
support.follows: In a little while I shall be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian and Augustus are not.

support.quote: before long you will be no one and nowhere, nor will any of the things you now see be, nor any of the people now living
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
support.follows: Before long neither I, nor anything I now see, nor anyone now living will exist.

support.quote: How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down.
gives: as those before me already are
support.follows: Eternity has already swallowed many a Chrysippus, many a Socrates and many an Epictetus.

support.quote: Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.
gives: forgotten by all
support.follows: Soon I shall have forgotten everything, and soon everyone will have forgotten me.

support.quote: each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain.
gives: All that I live is the present
an instant
support.follows: A person lives only the present instant; the rest is either already lived or uncertain.

support.quote: each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose
gives: All that I live is the present
support.follows: A person lives only the present, and the present is what a person loses.

claims.t: I live what is left as someone already at the end of life, and I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment. I no longer let what rules in me be pulled about on strings, whether by unsocial impulse or by what produces the passions; I have in me something stronger and more divine than whatever pulls me so.
claims.shared: 7.31 and 1.16 both open with the same turn, “as someone who has died” and “as one already dying”, and 1.16 adds “you are old”. 1.16 and 12.15 share the image of being pulled about on strings, in 1.16 by unsocial impulse and in 12.15 by what produces the passions.
claims.changed: 7.31 says “has died”, 1.16 says “already dying” and “old”; the claim says “at the end of life” to cover both. 2.8 does not use the figure: it says only that leaving life is possible at this moment. 7.31 calls what is left “a surplus”, which the claim drops. The claim keeps each passage’s own name for what pulls: unsocial impulse (1.16), what produces the passions (12.15). It does not say that I am stronger than impulse as such; “whatever pulls me so” is 12.15’s “the things that … pull you about on strings”.

support.quote: As someone who has died and whose life has been lived up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.
gives: I live what is left
as someone already at the end of life
support.follows: I must count my life as lived and over, and live what remains as an extra, according to nature.

support.quote: as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh
gives: as someone already at the end of life
support.follows: I am to despise my flesh, taking the stance of someone who is already dying.

support.quote: Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse
gives: as someone already at the end of life
I no longer let what rules in me be
pulled about on strings
by unsocial impulse
support.follows: I am old: I should no longer let my ruling part be a slave or be pulled about by unsocial impulse.

support.quote: To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment.
gives: I do, say and think each thing
knowing that I may leave life at this very moment
support.follows: Everything I do, say and think should be done knowing that I could leave life right now.

support.quote: you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings
gives: pulled about on strings
by what produces the passions
I have in me something stronger and more divine than whatever pulls me so
support.follows: There is something in me stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and pull me about.

claims.t: Until the end comes, this is enough, and how long I do it does not matter: I steer the present toward two things, justice in what I do and being at peace with what is allotted to me. I leave the past behind and hand the future over to providence.
claims.shared: 12.1 and 4.21 both name “the present” as the thing to be steered or turned to profit, and both name justice. 12.1, 4.21 and 9.29 each set the same two things side by side: justice in what I do, and a good mind toward what is allotted or happens from outside. 5.27 and 6.21 both say “enough”; 4.21’s “content with” is the same Greek word, and it is said of exactly this pair.
claims.changed: Toward what is allotted, 12.1 says “love”, 4.21 “pleased” and 9.29 “freedom from disturbance”; the claim says “being at peace”, the least of the three. What 5.27 calls enough is its own list: to revere the gods, do good to people and bear with them. What 6.21 calls enough is hours spent treating people socially and calling on the gods.

support.quote: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present toward piety and justice
gives: I steer the present toward
justice in what I do
I leave the past behind and hand the future over to providence
support.follows: I am to leave the past behind, entrust the future to providence, and steer only the present toward piety and justice.

support.quote: Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it.
gives: being at peace with what is allotted to me
support.follows: Piety here means loving what is allotted to me, since nature brought it and me together.

support.quote: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind
gives: this is enough
justice in what I do
being at peace with what is allotted to me
support.follows: The good person is pleased with what the whole allots and content if their own action is just and their disposition kind.

support.quote: In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice.
gives: I steer the present toward
justice in what I do
support.follows: Life is short; the present has to be put to good use, with good reasoning and justice.

support.quote: Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you.
gives: justice in what I do
being at peace with what is allotted to me
support.follows: Two things are named: not being disturbed by what happens from outside, and justice in what comes from me.

support.quote: And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back
gives: Until the end comes
this is enough
support.follows: Until the time of death comes, it is enough to revere the gods, do good to people, bear with them and hold back.

support.quote: do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough
gives: this is enough
how long I do it does not matter
support.follows: How long I go on acting this way should not worry me; even three hours of it are enough.

claims.t: I take death as nothing but a dissolving of the elements I am put together from; it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad. I wait for it cheerfully, whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere, and do not chafe at the delay.
claims.shared: 5.27 and 2.15 both say “wait” and “cheerful”: “You wait cheerfully” and “waiting for death with a cheerful mind”. 2.15 and 5.10 both call death a dissolving, and both tie it to nature: “according to nature” and “the natural dissolution”.
claims.changed: 5.27 leaves open what death is, an extinguishing or a move elsewhere; 2.15 and 5.10 call it a dissolution. The claim keeps both: it says how I take death, as 2.15 does (“as nothing other than”), and does not rule on what death is. 5.10 does not say “cheerfully”: it says to comfort oneself and not to chafe.

support.quote: waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together
gives: I take death as nothing but
a dissolving
of the elements I am put together from
I wait for it
cheerfully
support.follows: Philosophy includes waiting for death cheerfully, as nothing other than the coming apart of the elements a living thing is made of.

support.quote: For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad.
gives: it is according to nature
nothing that is according to nature is bad
support.follows: The change and dissolution of all is according to nature, and nothing according to nature is bad.

support.quote: One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay
gives: a dissolving
it is according to nature
I wait for it
do not chafe at the delay
support.follows: I should comfort myself, wait for the dissolution that nature brings, and not be impatient that it is slow to come.

support.quote: You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere.
gives: I wait for it
cheerfully
whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere
support.follows: I wait cheerfully for death, whichever it is: a going out like a flame or a move to another place.

claims.t: I look down on human affairs as if from high above, and among them I stand kindly, without sneering at them. The things people prize are small and empty, and they do not last; being remembered is of no account, a name is a noise, and many will very quickly forget mine.
claims.shared: 9.29 and 12.18 both say to look down from above on human life. 5.27 and 7.3 both call what people take seriously “empty” and both use the picture of “little dogs”. 12.18 alone adds that it is all alike and short-lived.
claims.changed: 12.18 says that from above I “will despise” human affairs; 7.3 says to stand among them “kindly and without snorting at them”, which the claim puts as “without sneering at them”. The claim keeps the smallness of the things and the kindness toward the people, and leaves out the word “despise”. “They do not last” is 12.18’s “short-lived”.

support.quote: To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms
gives: I look down on human affairs as if from high above
support.follows: The exercise is to look down from above on the herds, rites and voyages of human life.

support.quote: if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them
gives: I look down on human affairs as if from high above
support.follows: Lifted high into the air and looking down on human affairs, I would despise them.

support.quote: Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.
gives: among them I stand kindly, without sneering at them
support.follows: I must stand among these things kindly and without contempt, and remember that people are worth what they take seriously.

support.quote: The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying.
gives: The things people prize are small and empty
support.follows: What is highly prized in life is empty, rotten and small, like puppies biting or children quarrelling.

support.quote: The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs
gives: The things people prize are small and empty
support.follows: A procession’s empty seriousness, plays and spear fights are listed beside a little bone thrown to little dogs.

support.quote: you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived
gives: they do not last
support.follows: However often I look from above, I see the same things, all alike and all short-lived.

support.quote: neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all
gives: being remembered is of no account
support.follows: Being remembered is worth nothing, and neither is reputation or anything else.

support.quote: the name is a noise and an echo
gives: a name is a noise
support.follows: A name left behind is only a noise and an echo.

support.quote: how many will very quickly forget it
gives: many will very quickly forget mine
support.follows: Many of those who know my name will very quickly forget it.

claims.t: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living. My one fear is of living against nature: of never beginning to live according to it, or of doing what the makeup of a human being does not want.
claims.shared: Both passages narrow fear to one thing, and in both it is my own way of living measured against nature: 12.1 names “never beginning to live according to nature”, 7.16 “only one thing”, doing what “the constitution of a human being does not want”.
claims.changed: 12.1 says “fear” and 7.16 says “troubles me”; the claim says “fear” for both. “Living against nature” is the editor’s summary of the two. The translation’s “constitution” means how a human being is built; the claim says “makeup” so that it is not taken for this page’s own title. 7.16 adds doing a thing in the wrong way or at the wrong time, which the claim leaves out; it says nothing of death.

support.quote: what you fear is not that you will some day stop living but rather never beginning to live according to nature
gives: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living
My one fear is of living against nature
of never beginning to live according to it
support.follows: The thing to fear is not that life will stop one day, but never beginning to live according to nature.

support.quote: Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.
gives: My one fear is of living against nature
of doing what the makeup of a human being does not want
support.follows: One thing alone troubles Marcus: doing what a human being’s makeup does not want, or doing it in the wrong way or at the wrong time.

single.label: Neither good nor bad
single.t: Death and life happen alike to good people and to bad, and they are neither honorable nor shameful. So death is neither good nor bad.
single.quote: Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.
single.why: Only this passage argues from the fact that death comes to good and bad people alike. Other passages call death natural; none of them says that it is neither good nor bad.
single.follows: What happens alike to good and bad people is neither honorable nor shameful, so death and life are neither good nor bad.

single.label: Those who stumble
single.t: I love even those who stumble. At the moment they do, I remember that they are my kin, that they go wrong through ignorance, and that in a little while both of us will be dead.
single.quote: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead
single.why: Only this passage uses the nearness of death as a reason to love the person who wrongs me.
single.follows: I can love those who go wrong if I recall at that moment that they are kin, that they err unwillingly, and that we shall both soon be dead.

single.label: Those who complained
single.t: At each thing that happens, I picture the people to whom the same thing happened and who were vexed and complained. They are nowhere now, and I do not want to be like them.
single.quote: At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them?
single.why: Only this passage makes the dead into an exercise for the moment something happens. 8.4 and 7.16 name the dead and give no exercise.
single.follows: When something happens I should picture those who complained of the same thing, who are now nowhere, and not wish to be like them.

single.label: Coming back to life
single.t: I can come back to life, and the way is to see things again as I used to see them.
single.quote: You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of coming back to life. The 1634 passage leaves out the first half of the chapter, which is about principles dying when the impressions behind them go out; reading “life” here as the life of those principles leans on that half.
single.follows: Coming back to life is possible, and it consists in seeing things again as I used to see them.

single.label: Clinging to life
single.t: When I ask what it is I want, to breathe, to have sensation and impulse, to use my voice, to think, I ask whether any of these is worth longing for. If each of them is easy to despise, I go on to the one thing left, following reason and god. To value breathing, sensing and thinking, and to be vexed that death will take them from me, conflicts with following reason and god.
single.quote: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.
single.why: Only this passage lists what death takes away and asks whether any of it is worth longing for. It shows what failing looks like: valuing these things and being vexed at losing them. “Conflicts with that” follows the translation, which supplies “with that” (following reason and god); the translators’ note gives another construction.
single.follows: If breathing, sensing, speaking and thinking are each easy to despise, being vexed that death takes them conflicts with following reason and god.

single.label: With gods or without
single.t: If there are gods, leaving human life is nothing to fear, for they would not throw me into anything bad. If there are none, or they do not care about human affairs, then living on in a universe empty of gods and of providence is worth nothing to me.
single.quote: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.why: Only this passage sets out both cases, gods or none. Marcus goes on to say that the gods do exist and do care; the two cases are kept here as what holds if I doubt it.
single.follows: Leaving life is nothing to fear if gods exist; and if they do not, or do not care, there is nothing in such a universe to stay for.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 9.29 is 9.30–31, 7.31 is 7.56–59, 5.27 is 5.33, 2.8 is 2.11, 7.16 is 7.19–22, 12.15 is 12.19–21, 12.18 is 12.24, 4.21 is 4.25–26, 3.10 is 3.9–10, 8.4 is 8.4–5, 2.15 is 2.17, 7.3 is 7.2b–3, 6.21 is 6.22–23, 1.16 is 2.2, 5.10 is the second half of 5.10, 12.19 is 12.25–26 and 12.24 is 12.31; 12.1 is the same.

Says “at the end of life” in claim 2 for three different expressions: “someone who has died” (7.31), “one already dying” and “you are old” (1.16). 2.8 says only that leaving life is possible at this moment.

Takes the two things that are enough (claim 3) from 12.1, 4.21 and 9.29, which share them. The word “enough” is in 5.27 and 6.21, whose own lists are different: reverence for the gods, doing good to people, bearing with them, treating people socially. 4.21 says it of this pair, but in the translation as “content with”; the article follows the Greek, where the word is the same.

Folds what the section says about fame into the view from above (claim 5): 9.29 joins the view from above with fame, and 5.27 joins fame with the emptiness of what is prized. The lines on fame in 3.10 and 2.15 are not quoted. The puppet image shared by 1.16 and 12.15 is kept inside claim 2 and not made a claim of its own.

Leaves the word “despise” (12.18, and 1.16 of the flesh) out of the article’s own sentences and keeps 7.3’s kindness, putting its “without snorting at them” as “without sneering at them”. A reader may think the section is harsher than the article.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one. Article 3 already says that I accept what happens, and Article 2 that my work is to act well toward others; the two things named in claim 3 say both again. Article 17’s section says claim 3 too (10.12, 4.30, 6.2, 10.28), and Article 17 leaves that claim to this article; its statement (any moment now I may die; I live without pretence, here as anywhere, and I am ready to go) shares this one’s nearness of death and readiness for it, and adds the refusal of pretence and the indifference of place. The first half of claim 2 is Article 9’s fourth claim (I do each thing as someone about to leave life), on the same words of Seneca (Ep. 101.7), and its second half repeats Article 2’s second claim, that reason is not to be overpowered by impulse; what claim 2 adds is the “no longer”, said to someone old and already dying. Claim 4 is near Article 33’s fourth claim (nothing terrible in my coming apart) and Article 36’s third (nature, not I, fixes the time of my death, and my death is not bad); Article 36 leaves 9.3’s waiting for death to this article. Two said-once items come near others: “With gods or without” (2.8) is close to Article 4’s question why I should wish to stay in a world of confusion (6.8), and “Those who complained” (7.31) to Article 3’s fourth claim. What this article adds is the time: soon I shall be no one and nowhere and forgotten by all, I live only the present, an instant, and I live it as one already at the end. Several of these 1634 passages join separate chapters of the modern text, so a thought about death and a rule of conduct sometimes stand next to each other without Marcus joining them; the “so” in the statement is the editor’s. 5.27 feeds three claims and the statement, 12.1 two claims and the statement, and in claim 6 the words the two passages share are the editor’s summary.

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

parts.words: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
I live the present justly
as one already at the end
wait for death cheerfully

inferences.why: No passage says that I live justly because I shall soon be gone; 4.21 only sets “life is short” beside turning the present to profit.

statement.kind: A ground, the conduct that answers it, and the stance toward the end
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: I shall soon be gone and I live only the present. Claims 2 and 3 are the conduct: living as one already at the end, and what is enough meanwhile. Claim 4 is the stance toward death itself; claim 5 is the exercise that keeps the ground in view, and claim 6 says what failing would be.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, living as one already at the end gains three witnesses, waiting for death gains three, and what is enough and the view from above gain one each. Practice gains a nightly exercise and the reminder that a cheerful death is long prepared; When it breaks gains a name for the failure, a life always postponed. He limits leaving the past behind, and he challenges the claim that being remembered is of no account. His allowance for ending one’s own life, which differs from waiting for the natural end, is left out of this article.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a daily exercise: each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a bonus. He limits one claim, on leaving the past behind, and disagrees with another, on being remembered. A third difference is left out of this article: he allows a wise man to end his own life (Ep. 70.5), where claim 4 waits for the natural end.

items.quote: let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end
gives: as someone already at the end of life
items.follows: I should set my mind in order as if I had already reached the end of my life.
items.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio amid his plans: a limit is fixed for each of us and none knows how near it is. “The very end” is that limit.

items.quote: he has won his honourable discharge and is free,—who still lives after his life has been completed
gives: I live what is left
as someone already at the end of life
items.follows: The person who goes on living after his life is complete has his discharge and is free.
items.context: Seneca’s prayer for Lucilius: a mind at rest that has no need of added years. A “completed” life is one that already has what is truly good, however long it then lasts.

items.quote: The present letter is written to you with this in mind,—as if death were about to call me away in the very act of writing.
gives: knowing that I may leave life at this very moment
items.follows: Seneca writes this letter as if death might call him away while he is writing it.
items.context: Seneca, now old, has just said that he tries to live every day as a complete life and to regard it as possibly his last. “This” is that thought.

items.quote: To have lived long enough depends neither upon our years nor upon our days, but upon our minds.
gives: how long I do it does not matter
items.follows: Whether I have lived long enough is settled by my mind, not by the number of my years or days.
items.context: The end of Letter 61, on being ready to die: life is well enough furnished, but we are greedy and always find something lacking in it.

items.quote: she but resolves that which she has compounded, and compounds again that which she has resolved
gives: a dissolving
it is according to nature
items.follows: Nature only takes apart what she put together, and puts together again what she took apart.
items.context: From the letter on the old and dying Bassus: death’s rule is fixed and equal for everyone. “She” is Nature, whose law for us is the same as her own.

items.quote: I have lived, my dear friend Lucilius, long enough. I have had my fill; I await death.
gives: I wait for it
items.follows: Seneca says he has lived long enough, has had his fill, and now awaits death.
items.context: The last words of Letter 61, written in old age, where Seneca has said that dying well means dying gladly and that one should reflect on one’s end without sadness.

items.quote: And what is death? It is either the end, or a process of change.
gives: whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere
items.follows: Death is one of two things: the end, or a change into another state.
items.context: The close of Letter 65: the soul should rule the body as God rules matter, so we should be brave. Seneca goes on to say he fears neither ceasing to exist nor changing state.

items.quote: you will indeed look down from above upon all that men regard as most lofty
gives: I look down on human affairs as if from high above
The things people prize
items.follows: Whoever reaches the height of wisdom looks down from above on everything people consider most lofty.
items.context: The end of Letter 84: what is conspicuous in human affairs is really petty. The height is wisdom once reached, a peak above Fortune; it is a place arrived at, not an exercise.

items.label: practice
items.t: I order each day as if it completed my life. I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”; then every morning I wake to is a bonus.
items.why: 7.31 tells me to live what is left as a surplus and gives no way of doing it day by day. Seneca gives one: close each day as a finished life, so that the next day comes as a bonus.

support.quote: every day ought to be regulated as if it closed the series, as if it rounded out and completed our existence
gives: I order each day as if it completed my life
support.follows: Each day should be ordered as if it were the last of the series and completed my life.
support.context: Letter 12 is on old age. Seneca goes on to Pacuvius, who held his own funeral feast every evening. “The series” is the series of one’s days.

support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
gives: I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”
support.follows: At bedtime I should say, gladly, that I have lived and that the course Fortune set me is finished.
support.context: Pacuvius had himself carried from dinner to bed each night as if to burial. Seneca says to do from a good motive what he did from a bad one; the words to say are a line of verse.

support.quote: When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
gives: every morning I wake to is a bonus
support.follows: Whoever has said “I have lived” receives each new morning as a bonus.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s point in Letter 12 about ending each day as a finished life: if God adds another day, it is welcomed gladly. The “bonus” is that added day.

items.label: practice
items.t: Leaving life calmly when the hour comes is something I can learn only by long practice. I shall welcome death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long since composed myself for it.
items.why: Marcus says to wait for death cheerfully and gives the reasons. He does not say here that this has to be learned, or how long it takes. Seneca says it needs long practice.

support.quote: This is a great accomplishment, Lucilius, and one which needs long practice to learn,—to depart calmly when the inevitable hour arrives.
gives: Leaving life calmly when the hour comes is something I can learn only by long practice
support.follows: Departing calmly at the inevitable hour is a great thing, and it takes long practice to learn.
support.context: Seneca describes his old friend Bassus, who is dying of age and looks on his own end with courage. “This” is what Bassus is doing: facing his death calmly.

support.quote: when death comes to meet him, no one welcomes it cheerfully, except the man who has long since composed himself for death
gives: I shall welcome death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long since composed myself for it
support.follows: Only someone long prepared for death welcomes it cheerfully when it comes.
support.context: From the letter on the dying Bassus. Seneca contrasts men who rush at death in a fit of rage with those who meet it calmly; “him” is anyone to whom death comes unsought.

items.label: breaks
items.t: The great flaw is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off. Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun. I postpone nothing and settle life’s account every day.
items.why: 12.1 names the fear of never beginning to live according to nature and does not say how that comes about. Seneca says how: by postponing, so that the life is always unfinished. He also gives the way back, which is to settle the account daily.

support.quote: The greatest flaw in life is that it is always imperfect, and that a certain part of it is postponed.
gives: The great flaw is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off
support.follows: The worst fault in a life is that it is never complete, because part of it is always put off.
support.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio in the middle of his plans. “Imperfect” here means unfinished: part of the life is left for later.

support.quote: Some men, indeed, only begin to live when it is time for them to leave off living. And if this seems surprising to you, I shall add that which will surprise you still more: Some men have left off living before they have begun.
gives: Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun
support.follows: Some people start living only when it is time to stop, and some stop living before they have started.
support.context: Seneca comments on Epicurus’s saying that they live ill who are always beginning to live: such a life is always incomplete, and cannot be ready for death.

support.quote: Let us postpone nothing. Let us balance life’s account every day.
gives: I postpone nothing and settle life’s account every day
support.follows: I should put nothing off and settle the account of my life each day.
support.context: From Letter 101: a limit is fixed for each of us and no one knows how near it is. To “balance life’s account” is to leave nothing of one’s life owing at the end of the day.

items.t: Seneca does not hold that being remembered is of no account. He agrees that time will roll over everyone and that the dead do not feel what posterity says, but he promises Lucilius a name among later generations (Ep. 21.5) and tells him to have regard to the thousands of years to come (Ep. 79.17). He is not consistent: his good man, told that his deed will soon be forgotten, answers that this lies outside his task (Ep. 76.29).

support.quote: some few great men will raise their heads above it, and, though destined at the last to depart into the same realms of silence, will battle against oblivion and maintain their ground for long
support.follows: Time covers everyone, but a few great men hold out against oblivion for a long while before they too fall silent.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius that his name will last through these letters, as Epicurus’s letters kept the name of Idomeneus alive. “It” is the deep flood of time that rolls over us.

support.quote: I shall find favour among later generations; I can take with me names that will endure as long as mine.
support.follows: Seneca expects to be read by later generations and to make the names he writes down last as long as his own.
support.context: Seneca promises Lucilius what Epicurus promised his friend Idomeneus: a name preserved by being written into letters that later generations will read.

support.quote: Many thousands of years and many thousands of peoples will come after you; it is to these that you should have regard.
support.follows: I should have regard to the many peoples and years that come after me, not only to my own generation.
support.context: On virtue that goes unrecognised in its own time, as with Epicurus: a day will reveal it. “These” are the later peoples, who will judge without malice or favour.

support.quote: We ourselves, indeed, shall not be affected by the talk of posterity; nevertheless, posterity will cherish and celebrate us even though we are not conscious thereof.
support.follows: The dead are not touched by what posterity says, yet posterity will honour them all the same.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s argument in Letter 79 that virtue is never lost to view. “We” are those who followed virtue without recognition in their own lifetime.

support.quote: you may say: “Your deed will speedily be forgotten,” or “Your fellow-citizens will offer you scant thanks.” He will answer: “All these matters lie outside my task. My thoughts are on the deed itself.
support.follows: Told that his deed will soon be forgotten, the good man answers that this is outside his task and that he thinks only of the deed.
support.context: Seneca argues that the honourable is the only good. “He” is the good man who goes to his death rightly and dutifully, with no reward and no joy in prospect.

items.t: Seneca does not leave all the past behind. Consoling a mourner, he calls the past ours and the most secure thing we have, and says that people narrow their enjoyments if they take pleasure only in the present (Ep. 99.4–5). This limits the claim and does not overturn it: he means good things once had, and elsewhere he says that we torment ourselves over what is past and that the present alone makes no one wretched (Ep. 5.9).

support.quote: The past is ours, and there is nothing more secure for us than that which has been.
support.follows: The past belongs to us, and nothing we have is safer than what has already been.
support.context: A letter of consolation quoted in Letter 99: grief forgets how much was gained. “The past” is the years already had with the one who has died.

support.quote: People set a narrow limit to their enjoyments if they take pleasure only in the present; both the future and the past serve for our delight
support.follows: Whoever takes pleasure only in the present narrows his enjoyment; the past and the future give delight as well.
support.context: Seneca, consoling a mourner, says we are ungrateful for past gains because we hope for the future. The delight the past gives is memory, which is certain.

support.quote: The present alone can make no man wretched.
support.follows: Nothing in the present moment alone makes a person wretched.
support.context: The close of Letter 5: animals fear only the danger they see, while people are tormented by memory of the past and by anticipation of the future.

amend.t: ; each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a bonus
; but what has been is still mine, and nothing I have is more secure
; yet a few names hold out long against oblivion, and I should have regard to the thousands of years after me

searches: cheerful, gladly, glad heart (with death, die, dying)
as if (with the very end, my last, complete life)
begin to live, begun to live, beginning to live
annihilate, either the end, strips us
how long (with how well, how nobly, how good)
from above, lofty height, from on high, look down
oblivion, forgotten, forget (with name, memory, men)
old man, old age (with boy, child, learn, begin)

rejected.why: A real difference from 5.10, which says to wait for the natural dissolution: the wise man may end his own life when Fortune turns. Not written into a first-person rule; the strip sentence says it is left out, and the audit reports it to the owner.
Seneca’s own caution against a hasty exit and the lust for death. It belongs with Ep. 70.5 and is left out with it.
“Live in it as if you were about to leave it”, said of the body. From the letter on ending one’s own life; Ep. 101.7 and 32.5 say the same outside that argument.
Whether to hasten the end in extreme old age. Seen only in the search result; the same question as Ep. 70.5, and left out with it.
The time we live is a point. Said of the whole of life, as 2.15 says; in claim 1 “an instant” is the present, so the words do not match.
Death either annihilates us or strips us bare. The same two cases as Ep. 65.24, which is shorter and goes on to say he fears neither.
“I have looked upon every day as if it were my last.” Says what Ep. 61.2 and 101.7 say; a further witness was not needed.
Living every day as a complete life, possibly the last. It is about the day, not each act; the next section, 61.2, is quoted for one act done so.
Strive not to live long but to live rightly. Quoted in part in Article 6; Ep. 61.4 says of “enough” that it does not depend on years.
Life is like a play: what matters is how good the acting is, not how long. Seen only in the search result; Ep. 61.4 is used for the same point.
Not how long you live but how nobly. Seen only in the search result, not read in context; the same point as Ep. 61.4.
Men care how long they live, not how nobly. Seen only in the search result; an observation about others, not a rule.
We die daily, and the years behind us are in death’s hands. About saving time; it does not say that only the present is lived.
Whoever has learned to die has unlearned slavery. Near claim 2, but the claim does not say “slave”, and the passage is about freedom from outside power.
“Pain he endures, death he awaits”, said of a friend in pain. It has “awaits” without the cheer; Ep. 61.4 is used for the same word.
Philosophy makes us joyful in the very sight of death. A description of Bassus; Ep. 30.4 and 30.12, from that letter, say what it takes.
Bassus living almost as if he had survived his own death. A portrait of one man; Ep. 32.5 says it as a general rule.
Round out your life before death comes, then await the rest in peace. The same thought as Ep. 32.5, which is quoted.
A man cannot be ready for death if he has just begun to live. The next section, 23.11, is quoted for the same thought.
The soul looks out from lofty heights and laughs at the succession of the ages. It looks at time, not at human affairs; Ep. 84.13 is used.
Set human life beside the abyss of time and see how scant it is. A consolation for an early death; it does not look at what people prize.
Renown after death is a good, a belief of the school. Seen only in the search result; Ep. 21.5 and 79.17 say it plainly.
Fame is the shadow of virtue. From Letter 79, whose conclusion in 79.17 is quoted.
“Glory is an empty and fleeting thing”, one item in a list of maxims to learn by heart. Ep. 76.29 shows the same side of Seneca with an argument.
Nearest by vectors. Fortune has power over empires and cities, and we must not cry out. About enduring one’s lot, which is Article 3’s subject.
Near by vectors. Our bodies are mortal and frail. Said to calm a man’s petty anxieties, not as a way of living each day.
Near by vectors. Accept the inevitable calmly; nothing that happens is new. A consolation, and Article 3’s point.
Near by vectors. Banish worry about life by being reconciled to loss. About possessions and mishaps, not about the present or the end.

articles.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

claims.t: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants: the good life lies in very few things, in doing what nature asks of me, and that is a simple and modest work. It does not need to be seen: I make no show of it, I let go of reputation, and I do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
claims.shared: All four passages speak of what nature wants or asks: 5.9 and 8.1 both have “your nature wants”, 8.1 has “what human nature asks for” and 9.28 “what nature now demands”. Each of them also sets being seen aside: “no show” (5.9), “reputation” (8.1), “whether anyone will know” (9.28), “recognised by no one” (7.38).
claims.changed: “It does not need to be seen” is the editor’s summary: 7.38 says that one can become godlike and be recognised by no one, and 9.28 says not to look whether anyone will know. 9.28 says “simple and modest” of “the work of philosophy”; the claim says it of doing what nature asks, which the same passage names a few lines earlier, and that step is the editor’s. 8.1 says “human nature” and 9.28 “nature”; the claim says “nature”. 7.38 says “living happily” and 8.1 “the good life”; the claim uses one phrase for both.

support.quote: philosophy wants only what your nature wants
gives: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants
support.follows: Philosophy asks for nothing beyond what my own nature asks for.

support.quote: living happily lies in very few things
gives: the good life lies in very few things
support.follows: Very few things are needed for living happily.

support.quote: nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for.
gives: in doing what nature asks of me
support.follows: The good life is not in argument, wealth, reputation or enjoyment; it is in doing what human nature asks for.

support.quote: Do what nature now demands.
gives: in doing what nature asks of me
support.follows: The thing to do is what nature demands at this moment.

support.quote: The work of philosophy is simple and modest
gives: a simple and modest work
support.follows: What philosophy has to do is simple and modest.

support.quote: it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one
gives: It does not need to be seen
support.follows: A man can become godlike without anyone recognising it.

support.quote: Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
gives: It does not need to be seen
I do not look around to see whether anyone will know
support.follows: I should start if I am given the chance, and not look around to see whether anyone will know of it.

support.quote: For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it.
gives: I make no show of it
support.follows: Coming to philosophy in the right way, I shall not display my obedience to reason; I shall rest in it.

support.quote: let go of what reputation you will have
gives: I let go of reputation
support.follows: I should let go of the question of what reputation I shall have.

claims.t: The situation I am in now may fight against a philosopher’s reputation, but no other is so suited to philosophy. It is material for my reason, and I do not run away from it: I stay until I have made it my own.
claims.shared: 8.1 and 11.6 both speak of my “situation”: in 8.1 it fights against the reputation of a philosopher, in 11.6 none is so suited to philosophy. 10.32 calls what I would run from “material” and “a subject”; the Greek word behind “subject” is the one translated “situation” in the other two, though its sense there is a subject set before me to work on.
claims.changed: The “but” that sets 8.1 against 11.6 is the editor’s way of joining them; neither passage mentions the other’s point. 10.32 speaks of “all these things”, whose reference lies before the passage; the claim reads them as the things of my life, as 10.32’s own words “the things in life” allow, and so lets “Stay” be said of my situation. No passage says what the situation is.

support.quote: winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too
gives: The situation I am in now
may fight against a philosopher’s reputation
support.follows: Being known as a philosopher is no longer easy for Marcus, and his situation works against it as well.

support.quote: there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be
gives: The situation I am in now
no other is so suited to philosophy
support.follows: No situation in life is better suited to philosophy than the one I happen to be in now.

support.quote: What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has looked exactly, and as a student of nature, at the things in life?
gives: It is material for my reason
I do not run away from it
support.follows: What I am running away from is material: exercises for a reason that has looked exactly at the things in life.

support.quote: Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.
gives: I stay until I have made it my own
support.follows: I should stay until I have made these things my own, as a strong stomach does with food and a bright fire with whatever is thrown into it.

claims.t: Being good is my craft, and doing it well comes from principles. I keep them always at hand, as a doctor has his instruments ready, and as the fighter whose weapon is his own hand, which he never puts down and needs only to clench.
claims.shared: 3.14 and 12.6 both say “principles” and both say “always”: doctors “always have their instruments and blades at hand”, the fighter “always has his hand”. 11.4 wants one thought that “always comes to hand”. 8.1 and 11.4 both say where acting well comes from: “principles from which your impulses and actions come”, “from points of theory”.
claims.changed: 11.4 says “points of theory”; the claim says “principles”, the word of 8.1, 3.14 and 12.6. 11.4 wants one thought kept at hand (that a social act is its own benefit); the claim says it of the principles in general. 12.6’s “all-in fighter”, who fights with his hands, is given as “the fighter whose weapon is his own hand”; the gladiator, who puts his sword down and picks it up, is left out.

support.quote: What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory
gives: Being good is my craft
doing it well comes from principles
support.follows: My craft is to be good, and it is done well only from points of theory.

support.quote: How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come.
gives: doing it well comes from principles
support.follows: I shall do what is asked of me if I have principles from which my impulses and actions come.

support.quote: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready
gives: I keep them always at hand
as a doctor has his instruments ready
support.follows: I should have my principles ready in the way doctors always keep their instruments at hand for emergencies.

support.quote: in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.
gives: I keep them always at hand
as the fighter whose weapon is his own hand, which he never puts down and needs only to clench
support.follows: Principles should be used like a fighter’s own hand, which is always there, and not like a sword that is put down and picked up.

support.quote: I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.
gives: I keep them always at hand
support.follows: The thought that acting as a social being is itself my benefit should always be at hand.

claims.t: Whatever comes up in my life, I look at it stripped bare: what it is in its substance, what it is put together from, what it will change into, how long it lasts and what it is worth. Nothing does more for greatness of mind, and what seemed very trustworthy turns out cheap.
claims.shared: 3.11, 6.11 and 12.6 all say “bare”. 3.11 and 10.9 both ask what a thing is “in its substance” and what it is “put together from”. 3.11 and 10.11 have the same sentence, “nothing so produces greatness of mind”, and both speak of what things turn into.
claims.changed: In 12.6 what is looked at bare is “what is causal”; the claim says it of each thing. 3.11 says “into which it will be broken up”; the claim says “what it will change into”, which is nearer to 10.11’s “change into one another”. In 3.11 greatness of mind comes from testing each thing, in 10.11 from contemplating how things change; the claim joins the two. The meals, the wine, the robe and sex in 6.11 are dropped.

support.quote: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things it was put together from and into which it will be broken up
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
I look at it stripped bare
what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
what it will change into
support.follows: I should define each thing that comes up, see it bare and in its parts, and name what it was made from and what it will break up into.

support.quote: the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from
gives: what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
how long it lasts
support.follows: Marcus asks when he will enjoy recognising, case by case, what a thing is, how long it lasts and what it is made of.

support.quote: so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
I look at it stripped bare
what seemed very trustworthy turns out cheap
support.follows: All through life, where things look very trustworthy, I should strip them bare, see how cheap they are and take away their story.

support.quote: To look at what is causal, bare of its husks.
gives: I look at it stripped bare
support.follows: One thing to keep in mind is to look at what is causal with its husks taken off.
support.note: The passage is a list of headings. What is seen bare here is the causal element in things, not each thing as a whole.

support.quote: How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.
gives: what it will change into
Nothing does more for greatness of mind
support.follows: I should get a method for contemplating how all things change into one another and train in it; nothing does more for greatness of mind.

support.quote: nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
Nothing does more for greatness of mind
support.follows: Nothing makes the mind greater than being able to test, by method and truly, each thing that comes up in life.

support.quote: what worth it has in relation to the whole, and what in relation to the human being
gives: what it is worth
support.follows: Of each thing I should ask what it is worth to the whole and what it is worth to a human being.

claims.t: When I fail to act from my principles, or I see what I can no longer be, I do not give up. I come back, and I am content if most of what I do befits a human being, if I live at least the rest of my life as my nature wants, if even the smallest thing goes forward in what I do.
claims.shared: 8.1 and 9.28 both say “be content if”, and 5.9 says “be glad if”. 5.9 and 7.38 both say “give up”. In each passage the full measure is out of reach (acting rightly every time, a whole life as a philosopher, a logician’s knowledge, Plato’s republic) and a part of it is declared enough.
claims.changed: 5.9 says “be glad”; the claim says “content”, the word of 8.1 and 9.28. “Most of what I do befits a human being” rests on words the translation supplies: the Greek of 5.9 has only “if the greater part more human”, which can also mean “human enough”, and the claim drops the comparative. 9.28 is about public affairs: the smallest thing that goes forward there is a result among other people; “in what I do” is the editor’s, and so is “even”. 5.9’s “disgusted” and “lose patience” are dropped.

support.quote: Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time
gives: When I fail to act from my principles
I do not give up
support.follows: If I do not manage to act from right principles every time, that is no reason for disgust, for giving up or for impatience.

support.quote: you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy
gives: I see what I can no longer be
support.follows: Marcus can no longer have lived his whole life as a philosopher, and he and many others can see that he is far from philosophy.

support.quote: do not, because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god
gives: I see what I can no longer be
I do not give up
support.follows: Having lost hope of being a logician or a student of nature is no reason to give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.

support.quote: when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being
gives: I come back
I am content if
most of what I do befits a human being
support.follows: Knocked aside, I should come back, and be glad if most of what I do is more as a human being should be.

support.quote: be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants
gives: I am content if
I live at least the rest of my life as my nature wants
support.follows: It is enough to live what is left of my life, however much that is, as my nature wants.

support.quote: Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward
gives: I am content if
the smallest thing goes forward
support.follows: I should not hope for a perfect state, and should be content if the smallest thing moves forward.

single.label: What the principles say
single.t: My principles are about what is good and what is bad: nothing is good for a human being that does not make them just, self-controlled, brave and free, and nothing is bad that does not make them the opposite.
single.quote: What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.
single.why: Only 8.1 says what the principles are. 5.12 names nearly the same list as the true goods, but it does so inside a test of what most people call good, and it is set aside.
single.follows: The principles are about good and bad: only what makes a person just, self-controlled, brave and free is good, and only what does the opposite is bad.

single.label: As to a remedy
single.t: I love what I come back to. I do not come back to philosophy as a schoolboy to the slave who minds him, but as a person with sore eyes goes to the remedies for them, the sponge and the egg, or as another goes to a poultice.
single.quote: love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash.
single.why: Only this passage says in what spirit I come back. 3.14 also takes an image from medicine, but there the principles are the doctor’s instruments, not the patient’s remedy. That the sponge and the egg are remedies for sore eyes is from the translators’ note.
single.follows: I should love what I return to, and return to philosophy as a sick person goes to a remedy, not as a boy to the slave who keeps him in order.

single.label: How principles fade
single.t: Principles that I only picture, without studying nature, and then let pass are wiped out day by day, amid farce, war, panic, numbness and slavery.
single.quote: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by.
single.why: Only this passage says how principles are lost. The Greek opens with five bare nouns and does not say how they connect with the rest; “amid” is the editor’s reading of that link. The text of the last clause is doubted.
single.follows: After naming farce, war, panic, numbness and slavery, Marcus says that principles pictured without study of nature will be wiped out day by day.

single.label: Hard, not impossible
single.t: If something is hard for me to carry out, I do not judge it impossible for a human being. If it is possible for a human being and proper to them, I count it within my own reach too.
single.quote: Do not, if something is hard for you yourself to carry out, judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.
single.why: Only this passage answers the thought that I am not able to do it. It is also the passage farthest from the centre of the section.
single.follows: What is hard for me is not for that reason impossible for a human being, and what a human being can properly do is within my reach too.

single.label: If I cannot be sure
single.t: The Stoics themselves find the truth of things hard to grasp, and everything I agree to can shift, as it does for everyone. Then I pass on to the things themselves and see how short-lived and how cheap they are.
single.quote: to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap
single.why: Only this passage admits that what I hold to may be wrong. It stands under doubt because it says what I can still do then: look at the objects themselves. What Marcus goes on to rest in lies outside this passage.
single.follows: The Stoics themselves find things hard to grasp and no one’s assent is fixed; Marcus then turns to the objects and finds them short-lived and cheap.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 5.9 is 5.9 with the first part of 5.10, 12.6 is 12.7 to 12.9, 6.11 is 6.13, 9.28 is 9.29, 10.32 is 10.31, 7.38 is 7.67, 11.4 is 11.4 and 11.5, 11.6 is 11.7, 3.14 is 3.13 and 6.18 is 6.19; 8.1, 10.9, 3.11 and 10.11 keep their numbers.

Joins in claim 1 what philosophy asks with its not needing to be seen, because 5.9, 8.1, 9.28 and 7.38 each say both within a few lines. “It does not need to be seen” is the editor’s summary of 7.38 and 9.28, not words of either.

Reads “situation” (8.1, 11.6) and “subject” (10.32) as one thing in claim 2, because the Greek has the same word in all three. The translators note that its sense differs: in 8.1 and 11.6 it is the footing of a life, in 10.32 a subject set before one to work on. The contrast between a situation that fights against a philosopher’s reputation and one that suits philosophy is drawn by the editor, and no passage says what the situation is.
Uses 9.28 for my own progress although it is about public affairs and about other people, whose principles no one will change.
Puts the second paragraph of 5.9 under doubt. It says that every assent can shift and then turns to the objects; that this is what holds when I doubt is the editor’s reading.
articles.limit: The article leans on two passages: 8.1 feeds four of the five claims, and 5.9 feeds two claims and two said-once items. Much of it is said elsewhere: claim 1 comes near Article 2, claim 4 (doing my work is living by my nature) and Article 9, claims 2 and 3 (a few things are enough; I need no show and no witness); claim 2 near Article 8, claim 4 (what comes to hand is material for virtue) and Article 25, claim 1 (philosophy makes the court bearable), and Seneca’s Ep. 53.9, 62.1 and 72.3 limit claim 2 here and are marked as a challenge to Article 25’s claim 1; claim 3 near Article 8, claim 5 and Article 12’s said-once 4.3f (rules and truths kept ready), and Articles 23 and 24 (living as a craft); claim 4 is the exercise of Article 20, claims 1 and 2, and its 12.6 quote that of Article 4, claim 4; claim 5 and the said-once 5.9c come near Article 9, claim 6 and Article 25, claims 1 and 3 (I go back quickly, to philosophy as to a mother), and Seneca’s limit on claim 5 near Article 1’s warning that return grows harder. What this section adds is the rule for falling short of philosophy: it asks nothing beyond what my nature asks, failing is no reason to give up, a part is enough, and the principles I come back to are kept at hand.

aside.5.12: A test of what most people call good, made with a line of comedy. Its list of true goods is close to 8.1’s, but its subject is which things are good, not how I keep to philosophy or come back to it.
aside.10.38: Says that what moves a person is hidden inside and that the body is its tool. Nothing in it is about principles, their use or falling short; it belongs with the passages on the ruling part and the body.

statement.t: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up: I do what nature asks, keep my principles at hand and look at each thing stripped bare.

parts.words: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up
I do what nature asks
keep my principles at hand
look at each thing stripped bare

statement.kind: A rule for failure and the three things I come back to
statement.form: Claim 5 is the rule: falling short is no reason to give up. Claims 1, 3 and 4 say what I come back to: the simple work that nature asks, principles kept ready, and the habit of looking at each thing stripped. Claim 2 says where I do it. No passage lists these together; the order is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author: that the work needs no audience, that acting well comes from principles kept ready, that each thing is looked at bare, and that I do not give up. The article gains a measure for the learner, an image for what makes the teaching hold, a way to keep principles at hand, the same stripping used on what frightens, and what stands behind “I cannot”. He limits three claims: needing no one to see, since until I respect myself I picture a good man watching; coming back, since no one resumes where he left off; and the situation I am in, since affairs that engross me are to be put out of the way.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: the same demands are not made of a learner as of the wise man. He also warns that what I drop slips back, sets a pictured guard over the learner, and would put aside affairs that engross me.

items.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
gives: It does not need to be seen
items.follows: It makes no difference how many people know that I act rightly.
items.context: The end of Letter 113: justice should have nothing to do with ambition or reputation and is practised without reward. “Your uprightness” is one’s own just conduct.

items.quote: A man may be wise without parade and without arousing enmity.
gives: I make no show of it
items.follows: A person can be wise without making a display of it and without making enemies.
items.context: Seneca tells Lucilius to take refuge in philosophy but never to vaunt it or use it to condemn others. “Parade” is the display of one’s own philosophy.

items.quote: no one will do his duty as he ought, unless he has some principle to which he may refer his conduct
gives: doing it well comes from principles
items.follows: No one does his duty as he should without a principle to which he refers what he does.
items.context: Letter 95 argues that advice for particular cases is not enough. The “principle” here is the goal of the Supreme Good, the fixed point to which each act is referred, as sailors steer by a star.

items.quote: they should not be in storage, but ready for use
gives: I keep them always at hand
items.follows: What I know about how to act should not lie in storage; it should be ready for use.
items.context: Seneca defends advice that repeats the obvious: we know how to treat a friend or a wife and do not act on it. “They” are these known truths about how to act.

items.quote: Let us banish rumour and set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called.
gives: what it is worth
items.follows: I should set aside what people say, ask of each thing what it is and not what it is called, and value it by that.
items.context: From Letter 95, on how to make use of things: what opinion to hold of poverty, riches, renown, disgrace, exile. “Each thing” is each of these; “rumour” is what people say of them.

items.quote: to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom
gives: I look at it stripped bare
items.follows: I should take away from things whatever disturbs and confuses, and see what each one is underneath.
items.context: Lucilius is threatened by an enemy and fears the outcome. Seneca tells him to prepare for the worst; the “things” to be stripped are what he fears, such as pain and death.

items.quote: Therefore let us press on and persevere. There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us
gives: I do not give up
items.follows: Seneca urges himself and Lucilius to press on and persevere, and adds that more of the road remains than lies behind them.
items.context: Seneca has just said that whoever is short of perfection is unsteady and slips back when he slackens. “The road” is progress toward wisdom; “us” is Seneca and Lucilius.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is a mistake to ask of a learner what is asked of the wise man. I still urge on myself what I know I should do, and I do not yet do it; and even the lowest rank of those who are making progress is not to be despised.
items.why: Marcus tells himself to be content with a part and does not say by what measure a part is enough. Seneca separates the learner from the wise man, says that the same demands are not to be made of both, and counts himself among the learners. Seneca says this as a teacher of what he recommends to Lucilius; the article puts it as what I know I should do.

support.quote: it is a mistake on our part to make the same demands upon the wise man and upon the learner
gives: It is a mistake to ask of a learner what is asked of the wise man
support.follows: The same demands should not be made of a learner as of a wise man.
support.context: Seneca has said that the wise man overcomes Fortune while many who profess wisdom are frightened by slight threats. The “learner” is anyone still on the way, himself included.

support.quote: I still exhort myself to do that which I recommend; but my exhortations are not yet followed.
gives: I still urge on myself what I know I should do, and I do not yet do it
support.follows: Seneca still urges himself to do what he recommends, and does not yet do it.
support.context: Seneca speaks of himself, straight after saying that learner and wise man are not to be judged alike. “That which I recommend” is what he urges on Lucilius in Letter 71.

support.quote: But not even the third type is to be despised.
gives: even the lowest rank of those who are making progress is not to be despised
support.follows: Even the third and lowest class of those making progress is worth belonging to.
support.context: Seneca sorts those who are making progress into three classes. “The third type” is the lowest: free of the great vices but not of all, still giving way to some fears.

items.label: breaks
items.t: The teaching I follow does not keep its promises if it has only coloured my mind. It has to go deep and sink in for a long time, as wool takes some dyes only when it is soaked in them many times.
items.why: 10.9 says that principles pictured without study of nature are wiped out day by day, and it points to that study and to keeping the contemplative side at work. Seneca adds an image for what holding takes: depth, and soaking repeated over a long time. He says it of the Stoic teaching in particular, in contrast with systems that can be applied at once.

support.quote: this system of which I speak, unless it has gone deep and has sunk in for a long time, and has not merely coloured but thoroughly permeated the soul, does not fulfil any of its promises
gives: The teaching I follow does not keep its promises if it has only coloured my mind
It has to go deep and sink in for a long time
support.follows: The Stoic teaching keeps none of its promises unless it has gone deep and soaked through the soul over a long time.
