support.context: “This system” is the Stoic teaching that virtue is the only good, stated in the next lines of Letter 71. Seneca sets it against other systems, which can be applied at once.

support.quote: there are others which it will not absorb unless it is soaked and steeped in them many times
gives: as wool takes some dyes only when it is soaked in them many times
support.follows: Some dyes take only after the wool has been soaked in them many times.
support.context: Seneca compares doctrines to dyes in a letter on the supreme good. “It” is wool, which takes some colours at once and “others” only after repeated soaking.

items.label: practice
items.role: How they come to be at hand
items.t: What is wholesome I discuss often and bring before my mind often, so that it is not only familiar to me but ready to hand.
items.why: Marcus says to keep principles at hand and compares them to a doctor’s instruments and a fighter’s hand; he does not say in this section how they come to be there. Seneca names the means: going over them often.

support.quote: whatever is wholesome should be often discussed and often brought before the mind, so that it may be not only familiar to us, but also ready to hand
gives: What is wholesome I discuss often and bring before my mind often, so that it is not only familiar to me but ready to hand
support.follows: What is wholesome should be discussed and recalled often, so that it is both familiar and ready to hand.
support.context: Seneca defends advice that repeats what we already know, such as how to treat a friend or a wife. “Whatever is wholesome” is any such sound truth about conduct, however obvious.

items.label: practice
items.t: I strip the mask from things as well as from people. Then I see that what I feared holds nothing fearful except the fear itself.
items.why: Marcus strips what attracts and impresses: the dishes, the wine, the purple robe, whatever seems very trustworthy. Seneca uses the same stripping on the other side, on what frightens.

support.quote: We should strip the mask, not only from men, but from things, and restore to each object its own aspect.
gives: I strip the mask from things as well as from people
support.follows: The mask should be taken off things as well as off people, so that each thing shows its own face.
support.context: Seneca compares us to boys frightened by friends who wear masks. The “mask” on things is the alarming show around what we fear, such as the swords and fire around death.

support.quote: they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear
gives: what I feared holds nothing fearful except the fear itself
support.follows: Seen stripped, the things I fear contain nothing fearful except the fear.
support.context: Seneca tells Lucilius, who is threatened by an enemy, to look at what he fears with everything confusing removed. “They” are those feared things, such as pain and death.

items.t: Seneca narrows “It does not need to be seen” for the learner. He agrees that being known makes no difference (Ep. 113.32), but until I have come to respect myself he would have me set a good man over myself as a guard and live as I would under his eyes. The guard is pictured, a model to correct me, not an audience, and he is sent away once I respect myself. Article 9 marks the same letter as a limit on its claim that I need no human witness.

support.quote: when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man
support.follows: Until I respect myself, I should set the authority of some man over me as a guard; after that I may let him go.
support.context: Seneca passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if a respected man were watching. The “attendant” is that imagined guard, a Cato or a Laelius, kept until one respects oneself.

support.quote: It is, indeed, nobler by far to live as you would live under the eyes of some good man, always at your side
support.follows: It is nobler to live as I would under the eyes of a good man who is always beside me.
support.context: Seneca comments on the saying “Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you”. The “good man” is an imagined witness of one’s acts and thoughts, since solitude prompts to evil.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I say that I am not able, the reason is that I am unwilling, and inability is my excuse. Nature has given me strength enough if I use it, and the difficulty comes from my lack of confidence.
items.why: 6.18 says only that what is hard for me is not impossible for a human being. Seneca goes further and names what stands behind “I cannot”: unwillingness and lack of confidence.

support.quote: The reason is unwillingness, the excuse, inability.
gives: the reason is that I am unwilling, and inability is my excuse
support.follows: We fail because we are unwilling, and we plead that we are unable.
support.context: The last words of Letter 116, on why people say the Stoic ideal is beyond them. “The reason” is the reason we do not attain it; “inability” is what we plead.

support.quote: We mortals have been endowed with sufficient strength by nature, if only we use this strength
gives: Nature has given me strength enough if I use it
support.follows: Nature has given us strength enough, provided we use it.
support.context: Seneca answers the complaint that Stoic counsels are too hard for mere human beings. “This strength” is the power to do what the Stoics ask, here to be rid of the passions.

support.quote: Our lack of confidence is not the result of difficulty; the difficulty comes from our lack of confidence.
gives: the difficulty comes from my lack of confidence
support.follows: Things are not too hard for us to be confident; they are hard because we lack confidence.
support.context: Seneca speaks of people who think that what they cannot do is impossible and that Stoic words are too big for human nature. The “difficulty” is that of bearing toil and death.

items.t: Seneca agrees that I must not stop, but he does not let coming back be free of cost. Whoever slackens goes backward, and no one resumes at the point where he left off (Ep. 71.35); philosophy studied with breaks goes back to where it was at the beginning (Ep. 72.3). This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus says to come back and to be content with a part, and he does not say that nothing was lost.

support.quote: No one can resume his progress at the point where he left off.
support.follows: After a break, no one takes up his progress at the point he had reached.
support.context: Seneca describes anyone short of perfection as unsteady, now advancing and now slipping. “Progress” is progress toward wisdom; to leave off is to slacken in zeal and application.

support.quote: it will surely slip back unless it keeps struggling ahead
support.follows: What is short of perfection slips back unless it keeps struggling forward.
support.context: From Letter 71, on those who follow wisdom without having reached it. “It” is whatever is short of perfection: the state of a person who is still on the way.

support.quote: it does not stay as it was when you dropped it, but, because its continuity has been broken, it goes back to the position in which it was at the beginning
support.follows: Philosophy that is dropped does not stay where it was; with its continuity broken it goes back to where it began.
support.context: Letter 72 says that philosophy must not wait for leisure. “It” is philosophy studied with interruptions, which Seneca compares to things stretched taut that fly apart.

items.t: Seneca narrows the claim. Marcus says that no situation suits philosophy better than the one he is in (11.6), and no passage says what that situation is. Seneca names one that does not suit it: being engrossed in affairs. He tells Lucilius to throw such hindrances aside and put them out of the way, because no one attains a sound mind while engrossed in other matters (Ep. 53.9, 72.3). If Marcus’s situation is read as the affairs that occupy him, the two disagree outright; that reading is the editor’s, so this is marked as a limit and not as a challenge. Seneca is not consistent: in the same section of Letter 72 he says that no time is unsuitable for study, and in Ep. 62.1 that a multitude of affairs does not block study. Both are quoted below.

support.quote: Throw aside all hindrances and give up your time to getting a sound mind; for no man can attain it if he is engrossed in other matters.
support.follows: I should throw aside every hindrance and give my time to getting a sound mind, which no one gets while engrossed in other matters.
support.context: Seneca argues that a sick man drops his business to get well, and that the mind deserves the same. “It” is a sound mind; the “hindrances” are business duties and other concerns.

support.quote: We must resist the affairs which occupy our time; they must not be untangled, but rather put out of the way.
support.follows: The affairs that take up my time are to be resisted and put out of the way, not untangled one by one.
support.context: Seneca writes on a day full of business and says that new employments always spring up. The “affairs” are these occupations, which he would clear away, not settle one by one.

support.quote: there is no time that is unsuitable for helpful studies; and yet many a man fails to study amid the very circumstances which make study necessary
support.follows: No time is unsuitable for helpful study, yet many fail to study in the very circumstances that make it necessary.
support.context: Letter 72 says affairs must be put out of the way to make room for philosophy; then Seneca adds this. The “circumstances” are those in which a person is pressed and most needs it.

support.quote: We are deceived by those who would have us believe that a multitude of affairs blocks their pursuit of liberal studies
support.follows: People who say that their many affairs keep them from study are deceiving us.
support.context: The opening of Letter 62, where Seneca says his own time is free wherever he is, since he lends himself to his affairs and does not surrender to them. “Liberal studies” include philosophy.

amend.t: ; and I do not make the same demands on a learner as on the wise man
; but I do not resume at the point where I left off, and what I drop slips back
; but within it, affairs that engross me I put out of the way, for no one gains a sound mind while engrossed in other matters
; but until I respect myself, I live as I would under the eyes of a good man set over me as a guard

searches: nearest by vectors to the section (30)
progress (with wise man, perfect, not yet, far from)
at hand, ready to hand, in readiness
philosophy (with display, parade, boast, conspicuous, show)
philosophy (with leisure, business, retire, withdraw; postpone, hinder, odd times, excuse)
witness, watching, guardian, attendant (with sin, alone, respect)
principles, doctrines, dogmas (with action, conduct, duty)
remedy, medicine, physician, cure (with philosophy, wisdom, study)
do not dare, unwillingness, cannot do
uncertain, hard to grasp, cannot know (with truth, know)
Academic, Sceptic, nothing can be known
mask, strip, bare, naked (with thing, object, fear, value)

rejected.why: Nearest by vectors. About repeating “Heaven decreed it otherwise” at every mishap: a defence against Fortune, not about principles or falling short.
Reason’s voice telling me to abandon riches, pleasure and office. A list of things to give up; says nothing of coming back or of keeping principles ready.
Prove by the result whether what you have heard is true. About deeds against words in the face of death; Ep. 24.12 and 24.13 from the same letter are quoted.
Philosophy makes you prefer to please yourself rather than the populace. About popularity; Ep. 113.32 says more plainly that being known makes no difference.
Leave off the word-play of philosophers. Near 8.1’s “not in syllogisms”, but no claim of the article carries that point.
Against splitting hairs while Fortune sets real problems. The same point as Ep. 71.6, and no claim carries it.
Philosophy offers counsel, not puzzles. Again against logic-chopping; no claim to attach it to.

The philosopher cannot always keep the same pace but can always travel the same path. Said of the philosopher, one of the very few who keep deed and word in accord; using it for the learner would be the editor’s step.
Philosophy is not devised for show. It means that philosophy is deeds and not entertainment; Ep. 103.5 is plainer on not displaying it.
An idea must be strengthened by daily reflection. The same means as Ep. 94.26, which is quoted and uses the article’s own words, “ready to hand”.
Avoid repellent dress and other forms of self-display. About outward eccentricity in a philosopher, not about doing the work unseen.
Do not placard yourself “Philosopher and Quietist”. About hiding one’s retirement, which Marcus does not have.
Reason demands the easiest thing, to live by one’s own nature. Already used in Article 2, and it speaks of reason, not of philosophy.
Doctrines support precepts as elements support members. Says what Ep. 95.45 says less plainly; 95.45 is quoted.
As our belief is, so will our acts be. A good second witness for claim 3, left out because Ep. 95.45, the next section, says it in terms of duty done well.
Weaker spirits are helped by the accepted principles of philosophy. About who needs doctrines, not about keeping them ready.
Virtue needs the art of understanding things human and divine. Near 3.14’s phrase, but about what perfect virtue requires.
The second class of those making progress can still slip back. A description of one class; Ep. 71.35 states the rule directly.
The convalescent relapses; the wise man cannot slip back. About the difference between the wise and the progressing, in an image of illness.
Critics think that what they cannot do is not done. Close to 6.18, but said in an argument that goods are equal; Ep. 104.26 and 116.8 are quoted instead.
Men who think that what they are unable to do is impossible. Sets up Ep. 104.26, which is the part quoted.
A draught of philosophy is at once wholesome and pleasant. Says what 5.9 already says of philosophy as a remedy, and that item takes no backing.
Seneca and Lucilius lie ill in the same hospital. A confession about his standing to give advice; adds no rule for falling short.
“My progress is still insufficient”: he is still bothered by what other travellers think. An anecdote of his own failure, not a statement to quote.
We must digest what we read and make it our own. The stomach image of 10.32, but about reading, where 10.32 is about what life puts before me.
A witness standing near prevents most sins. The same advice as Ep. 25.5 and 25.6, which also say when the witness may be sent away.
Withdraw from all the business of which you speak. The same advice as Ep. 53.9 and 72.3, which give the reason.
Do not put philosophy off until you have enough; learn while you are acquiring it. About poverty as an excuse; Ep. 72.3 and 62.1 are quoted for Seneca’s other side.
Do not study philosophy merely during your spare time. The next section, Ep. 53.9, says it with its reason and is quoted.
Against the schools that deny knowledge. Seneca is vexed at them and does not say what holds if they are right, so it gives nothing under doubt.
Studying philosophy while applying it. About learning courage from one who shows it in pain; not about my own situation as material.
“We hasten towards virtue while hampered by vices.” A confession that follows Ep. 75.15, which is quoted for the lowest class.

articles.title: The retreat within

claims.t: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain: where I am is just like them, and at any hour I can retreat into myself. No place is quieter than my own mind; there it can be at ease, that is, in good order, and when it acts justly it has calm.
claims.shared: 4.3 and 10.24 both name the country place, the seashore and the mountain, and both say I need none of them: 4.3 calls the longing for them untrained, 10.24 says the place where I am is just like them. 4.3 and 7.20 both send me into myself (“retreat into yourself”, “Draw in upon yourself”) and both say what I find there: ease that is good order (4.3), and calm when the ruling part acts justly (7.20).
claims.changed: 4.3 says the ease belongs above all to someone who has the right things within; the claim keeps only that ease means good order. 10.24 goes on to Plato’s herdsman in his sheepfold, which the claim leaves out.

support.quote: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
at any hour
I can retreat into myself
support.follows: Longing for a retreat in the country, by the sea or in the mountains is untrained, since I can retreat into myself whenever I wish.

support.quote: Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
where I am is just like them
support.follows: The place where I am is no different from a country place, a mountain top or a seashore.

support.quote: Draw in upon yourself.
gives: I can retreat into myself
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to draw in upon himself.

support.quote: nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul
gives: No place is quieter than my own mind
support.follows: No place a person can retreat to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul.

support.quote: they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order
gives: at ease, that is, in good order
support.follows: Looking within, such a person is at once at ease, and Marcus means by ease nothing but good order.

support.quote: It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.
gives: when it acts justly it has calm
support.follows: When the rational ruling part acts justly, it is content with itself and, by that very fact, calm.

claims.t: Unless it serves the common good, I do not spend my life guessing what other people are saying, doing or thinking; I look at what I am doing and keep watch over what is within me. And I set no store by the praise of the many.
claims.shared: 3.4 and 4.15 both name the same three things not to look at: what another is saying, doing and thinking (3.4: “what they are saying, and what they have in mind”; 4.15: “what their neighbour said or did or thought”). 3.4 and 2.11 both set against this the care of what is within: “watching over your own ruling part” (3.4), “keep only to the guardian spirit within them” (2.11). 3.4 and 6.15 both set no value on praise.
claims.changed: 3.4 keeps the good opinion of those who live in agreement with nature and sets no store only by the praise of the others; 6.15 speaks of “the many”, and the claim follows 6.15. The guardian spirit of 2.11 and the ruling part of 3.4 are both called “what is within me”.

support.quote: Do not wear away the part of your life that is left in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit
gives: Unless it serves the common good, I do not spend my life
support.follows: I should not use up what is left of my life on impressions of other people, unless they serve some common benefit.

support.quote: forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part
gives: what other people are saying, doing or thinking
keep watch over what is within me
support.follows: Picturing what others do, say, mean and plot draws me away from watching over my own ruling part.

support.quote: looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly
gives: guessing
keep watch over what is within me
support.follows: Guessing at what is in other people’s souls is wretched; it is enough to keep to the guardian spirit within me and serve it.

support.quote: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing
gives: what other people are saying, doing or thinking
I look at what I am doing
support.follows: Whoever looks only at what they are doing, not at what a neighbour said, did or thought, gains much leisure.

support.quote: So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.
gives: I set no store by the praise
support.follows: The good man sets no store by praise from people who do not live by nature and are not even pleased with themselves.

support.quote: Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well.
gives: I set no store by the praise of the many
support.follows: Applause has no value, and the praise of the many is only applause by tongues, so petty fame has no value either.

claims.t: The things I chase and run from do not come to me: they stay outside, unmoving, and my turmoil comes from my own judgment about them. When I let that judgment be quiet, I neither chase them nor run from them.
claims.shared: Both passages say that the things which disturb me do not reach me (4.3: “things do not touch the soul”; 11.10: they “do not come to you”), and both put what matters in my judgment about them. Both call the things “unmoving”: 4.3 as a standing fact, 11.10 as what follows when my judgment is quiet.
claims.changed: 11.10 adds that “in a way you yourself go to them”; the claim keeps only that they do not come to me. 4.3 speaks of “disturbances”, 11.10 of “turmoil”; the claim uses “turmoil”. 4.3 says the disturbance comes “only” from the judgment; the claim says “from my own judgment about them”. Only 4.3 says “unmoving” as a standing fact; in 11.10 the things stay unmoving as a consequence, when my judgment about them is quiet.

support.quote: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them.
gives: The things I chase and run from
do not come to me
support.follows: The things I chase or flee do not come to me; in a way I go to them.

support.quote: things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within
gives: do not come to me
they stay outside
unmoving
my turmoil comes from my own judgment about them
support.follows: Things stay outside the soul and do not touch it; every disturbance comes from the judgment within.

support.quote: At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay unmoving, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
gives: unmoving
When I let that judgment be quiet, I neither chase them nor run from them
support.follows: If my judgment about these things is quiet, they stay where they are, and I neither pursue nor avoid them.

claims.t: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine; the other two are mine to take care of. I keep my mind apart from them: once it has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, and it is not to be fused with my body so that it is swayed whichever way my body is swayed.
claims.shared: All three passages set the mind apart from the body and its breath: 4.3 says the mind “does not mix with the breath”, 12.2 tells me to separate from my thought what comes from “the little body” and “the little breath”, and 10.24 asks with misgiving whether the ruling part has been “melted into the bit of flesh”.
claims.changed: 10.24 is a question; the claim turns it into what the question hopes for. 12.2 puts the separating as an “if” that leads to an untroubled life; the claim states it as what I do. 10.24’s image of melting into the flesh is given in plain words: fused with my body and swayed as it is swayed.

support.quote: There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours.
gives: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine; the other two are mine to take care of
support.follows: Of body, breath and mind, only the mind is properly mine; body and breath are mine to care for.

support.quote: So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that belongs to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you
gives: I keep my mind apart from them
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to separate from his thought, among other things, all that comes to him unchosen from his body and breath.

support.quote: the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power
gives: I keep my mind apart from them
once it has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath
support.follows: Once the mind has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly.

support.quote: Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?
gives: it is not to be fused with my body so that it is swayed whichever way my body is swayed
support.follows: Marcus asks, with misgiving, whether his ruling part has been melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.

claims.t: I keep to what is present: I practise living only the present, I do not think of absent things as if they were already mine but count up the best of what I have, and I am content with my present state and take pleasure in it.
claims.shared: All three passages turn me to what is present: 12.2 to living “only what you are living, that is, the present”, 7.20 to “the best of the things that are present” instead of absent things, and 10.1 to being “content with your present state”.
claims.changed: 10.1 is a question Marcus puts to his soul (“Will you ever …?”); the claim states what the question longs for. 7.20 says “already there”; the claim says “already mine”, the other reading the translators give.

support.quote: practise living only what you are living, that is, the present
gives: I keep to what is present
I practise living only the present
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to practise living only what he is living now, the present.

support.quote: Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present
gives: I keep to what is present
I do not think of absent things as if they were already mine but count up the best of what I have
support.follows: I should not treat absent things as already there, but count up the best of what is present.

support.quote: But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present
gives: I keep to what is present
I am content with my present state and take pleasure in it
support.follows: Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.

claims.t: I give my impulses a target and go straight toward it: I look at what has to be done and, when I see it clearly, go that way without turning back, not drifting and not thrown this way and that.
claims.shared: 4.15 and 10.13 both say to go straight on: “run straight along the line” (4.15), go “that way with good will and without turning back” (10.13). 2.4 and 4.15 both name the opposite: “drifting” (2.4), being “thrown this way and that” (4.15).
claims.changed: 10.13 adds what to do when I do not see clearly: hold off and use the best advisers. 4.15 says the aim is that what I do be just and holy. Both are left out. 2.4’s “drifting” and 4.15’s “not thrown this way and that” are near-synonyms, joined into one phrase that both passages back; each passage says one half of it.

support.quote: But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too, those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
gives: I give my impulses a target
not drifting and not thrown this way and that
support.follows: People with no target for their impulses play the fool in what they do, and this drifting has to be guarded against.

support.quote: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back
gives: go straight toward it
I look at what has to be done and, when I see it clearly, go that way without turning back
support.follows: Instead of guessing, I can look at what has to be done and, if I see it clearly, go that way without turning back.

support.quote: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that
gives: go straight toward it
not drifting and not thrown this way and that
support.follows: I should not look round at a bad character but run straight along my line, not thrown from side to side.

single.label: Renewing the retreat
single.t: I give myself this retreat again and again and renew myself there. I keep a few short, basic truths ready, enough to wash away all distress and to send me back without resentment to what I return to.
single.quote: So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to.
single.why: Only 4.3 says to make the retreat a habit and to carry short truths into it. The other passages that send me inward give no such store of truths.
single.follows: The retreat should be taken continually, with a few short truths that wash away distress and send me back without resentment.

single.label: A test for my thoughts
single.t: I make a habit of having only such thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking, I could answer at once and frankly.
single.quote: And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”
single.why: Only 3.4 gives this test of answering frankly at once. 10.24 also checks the mind, but with different questions.
single.follows: I should form only impressions I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking.

single.label: Three questions
single.t: I ask myself what my mind, the part of me that rules, is to me, what I am making it into now, and what I am using it for now.
single.quote: What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?
single.why: Only 10.24 puts these questions. They are kept as a practice I can repeat.
single.follows: Marcus asks himself what his ruling part is to him, what he is making of it now and what he is using it for.

single.label: Serving what is within
single.t: I serve the guardian spirit within me by keeping it clean of passion, of aimlessness, and of discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.quote: To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.why: 12.2 also calls the freed mind clean, but only 2.11 says what serving the spirit within consists of, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Serving the guardian spirit within means keeping it free of passion, aimlessness and discontent with what gods and people send.

single.label: Valuing other things
single.t: If I go on valuing many things outside my mind, I am not free or sufficient to myself: I envy and suspect those who can take them away. Respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.
single.quote: Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and what is more to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself
single.why: Only 6.15 says what valuing outside things does to me and that respect for my own mind is the way back.
single.follows: Valuing many outside things leaves me unfree, envious and confused; respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.

single.label: A caution
single.t: Glad as I am of what I have now, I take care not to prize it so much that I would be troubled if it were ever gone.
single.quote: be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.
single.why: Only 7.20 warns that taking pleasure in what is present can become a dependence on it.
single.follows: Being glad of what I have, I should not get used to prizing it so much that losing it would trouble me.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 2.11 is 2.12–13, 7.20 is 7.27–28, 10.24 is 10.23–24, 6.15 is 6.16, 2.4 is 2.7, 10.13 is 10.12, 11.10 is 11.11, 4.15 is 4.18 and 12.2 is 12.2–3; 4.3, 3.4 and 10.1 are the same.

Reads the soul (4.3), the ruling part (3.4, 7.20, 10.24), the guardian spirit within (2.11) and the mind (4.3, 12.2) as one thing, called “my mind” or “what is within me”. This section does not say that the guardian spirit is the mind; the identification is the editor’s.

Puts praise into claim 2 with not watching other people. 3.4 sets no store only by the praise of those who do not live by nature; the claim follows 6.15’s “the many”. 4.3’s own reasons against petty fame (forgetting, the earth a point) are not quoted.

Keeps claim 6, acting with an aim, though its passages do not speak of retreat. 2.4 begins with distraction from outside and 4.15 with the leisure gained by not watching a neighbour; the editor reads them as where the retreat sends me back to.
articles.limit: The section holds together less well than its title: 2.4, 10.13 and 4.15 are about aim rather than retreat, and 4.3 feeds three claims, so much rests on one long passage. Much of it is said elsewhere: going back into myself, and doing it continually (claim 1 and the item from 4.3), is in Article 25’s claims 1 and 3; that the place makes no difference is Article 17’s claim 4 and Article 18’s claim 1; claim 3 repeats Articles 7 and 8; claim 4 comes near Article 2’s claim on the body; claim 5 comes near Articles 10 and 16; and asking what my mind is being used for (10.24) and going straight toward a target (claim 6) are in Article 31’s claims 3 and 6, with holding to one aim and going straight on in Articles 1 and 2. Articles 22, 26 and 27 turn my attention to other people’s minds for a purpose, which claim 2’s exception for the common good may allow, though no passage here says so; what this article adds is the retreat as a place I can reach at any hour, keeping to my own mind instead of to what others say and do, and, in claim 6, seeing clearly what has to be done and not being thrown about.

statement.t: At any hour I can retreat into myself, and I keep to my own mind rather than to what others say and do.

parts.words: At any hour I can retreat into myself
I keep to my own mind
rather than to what others say and do

statement.kind: A place, how I keep to it, and the way back
statement.form: Claims 1 and 4 say where the retreat is and why the mind is mine. Claims 2, 5 and 6 say how I keep to it: away from other people’s doings and praise, in the present, and with an aim when I act. Claim 3 says what being disturbed is and how it stops.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if I cannot retreat into myself, or if my mind is not my own.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the retreat of claim 1 gains a second author for its hour and its place, the praise of claim 2 and the target of claim 6 gain one each; the practice gains a way to keep my mind within amid noise, and what failing looks like gains two signs: travelling to escape my own gloom, and starting at every sound. He sets two limits on the retreat: one goes into the statement (it is right only for someone already good), and one into claim 1 (a mind not yet sound is harmed by some places).
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands with a condition: retreating into myself is right only if I am already good, calm and self-controlled; otherwise, alone, I am too close to a rascal.

items.quote: the mere place avails little for this purpose, unless the mind is fully master of itself, and can, at its pleasure, find seclusion even in the midst of business
gives: at any hour
I can retreat into myself
items.follows: A place does little for the mind unless the mind can find seclusion in itself whenever it wishes, even amid business.
items.context: Letter 104, written from Seneca’s country house where his health has mended: the place itself does little for peace of mind; the mind must find its own seclusion.

items.quote: The place where one lives, however, can contribute little towards tranquillity; it is the mind which must make everything agreeable to itself.
gives: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain
items.follows: Where I live does little for my calm; my mind has to make every place agreeable to itself.
items.context: Letter 55: Seneca passes the seaside villa where the rich Vatia hid in leisure, and says the villa could not give calm; only the mind can.

items.quote: Lay these words to heart, Lucilius, that you may scorn the pleasure which comes from the applause of the majority.
gives: I set no store by the praise of the many
items.follows: I should scorn the pleasure that comes from the applause of the majority.
items.context: End of Letter 7, on avoiding crowds. “These words” are three sayings he has just quoted, each content with an audience of one or none.

items.quote: Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
gives: I give my impulses a target
items.follows: Plans go wrong when they have no aim; if I do not know where I am heading, no wind helps me.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: everything we do should be set by one chief purpose of life, as an archer must know what he is trying to hit.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I am troubled, going somewhere else does not help, because I always take myself with me. What I need is a change of soul, not a change of climate.
items.why: Marcus says the place where I am is just like a country place, but not what happens to someone who keeps going elsewhere. Seneca says it: the trouble travels with me, and only a change in me ends it.

support.quote: Why do you wonder that globe-trotting does not help you, seeing that you always take yourself with you?
gives: going somewhere else does not help, because I always take myself with me
support.follows: Travelling cannot help me, because I take myself wherever I go.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel as a cure for discontent: Seneca repeats Socrates’s answer to a man who complained that his travels had not cured his gloom.

support.quote: You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate.
gives: What I need is a change of soul, not a change of climate
support.follows: What a gloomy mind needs is a change in itself, not a change of country.
support.context: Opening of Letter 28: Lucilius has travelled far and changed scene often, and still cannot shake off the gloom and heaviness of his mind.

items.label: practice
items.t: When there is noise all around me, I make my mind concentrate and keep it from straying to things outside itself. Outside may be bedlam, so long as there is no disturbance within: a quiet neighbourhood is no use if my feelings are in an uproar.
items.why: 4.3 says no place is quieter than my own soul, but gives no exercise for a noisy place. Seneca, lodging over a bath house, trains himself to keep his mind on its work through the noise.

support.quote: For I force my mind to concentrate, and keep it from straying to things outside itself; all outdoors may be bedlam, provided that there is no disturbance within
gives: I make my mind concentrate and keep it from straying to things outside itself
Outside may be bedlam, so long as there is no disturbance within
support.follows: Seneca makes his mind concentrate and keeps it on itself; the noise outside does not matter if nothing is in turmoil within.
support.context: Letter 56: Seneca lodges over a public bath and lists its noises. Here he says how he studies through them by holding his mind to itself.

support.quote: For of what benefit is a quiet neighbourhood, if our emotions are in an uproar?
gives: a quiet neighbourhood is no use if my feelings are in an uproar
support.follows: A quiet place is no use to someone whose feelings are in an uproar.
support.context: Letter 56, after listing the noises of the bath house below his lodgings: the uproar that matters is fear and desire fighting within, not the noise outside.

items.label: breaks
items.t: If a word or a chance sound makes me start, my mind has not yet withdrawn into itself. I know I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no word, of flattery or of threat, shakes me out of myself.
items.why: Marcus tells me to retreat into myself and does not say how I can tell whether I have. Seneca gives the sign of failing and the sign of success.

support.quote: The mind which starts at words or at chance sounds is unstable and has not yet withdrawn into itself
gives: If a word or a chance sound makes me start, my mind has not yet withdrawn into itself
support.follows: A mind that starts at words or chance sounds is unsteady and has not yet withdrawn into itself.
support.context: Letter 56, on quiet and study: Seneca says that a mind shaken by noises still holds fear within it, and so has not truly retired.

support.quote: You may therefore be sure that you are at peace with yourself, when no noise reaches you, when no word shakes you out of yourself, whether it be of flattery or of threat
gives: I know I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no word, of flattery or of threat, shakes me out of myself
support.follows: I am at peace with myself when no noise reaches me and no flattering or threatening word shakes me out of myself.
support.context: Letter 56: after Virgil’s hero who fears every sound for the load he carries, Seneca gives the test of a mind that has really withdrawn into itself.

items.t: Seneca allows the retreat into oneself only to someone already good, calm and self-controlled. Until then he gives the opposite advice: almost any company is better than one’s own, for alone one is too close to a rascal. Marcus comes near this in 4.3, where the ease within belongs above all to someone with the right things within; Seneca makes it a condition and says what to do before it is met. This limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.quote: Yes, provided that you are a good, tranquil, and self-restrained man; otherwise, you had better withdraw into a crowd in order to get away from your self. Alone, you are too close to a rascal.
support.follows: Withdrawing into myself is right only if I am good, calm and self-controlled; otherwise I am better off in company, away from myself.
support.context: End of Letter 25: Seneca grants Epicurus’s saying “withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd”, and here sets its condition.

support.quote: while it is not yet safe to withdraw into solitude, seek out certain individuals; for everyone is better off in the company of somebody or other,—no matter who,—than in his own company alone.
support.follows: Until it is safe to be alone, I should seek out some people, since almost any company is better than my own.
support.context: Letter 25, on reforming oneself: Lucilius is still making himself into someone in whose company he would not dare to do wrong.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the person matters more than the place, but not that every place is alike. A mind that is recovering but not yet sound is harmed by some places; and he himself, having tested himself against the noise of a bath house, decides that it is simpler to move. Marcus says the place where I am is just like a country place; Seneca keeps that for a mind already sound, and moves when he can. This limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.quote: For just as pestilential places assail even the strongest constitution, so there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment.
support.follows: Some places harm a mind that is recovering but not yet quite sound, as unhealthy places harm even a strong body.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel: Seneca has said one can live quietly even in the Forum if one must, but that he would keep far from it if he could choose.

support.quote: “What then?” you say, “is it not sometimes a simpler matter just to avoid the uproar?” I admit this. Accordingly, I shall change from my present quarters.
support.follows: It is sometimes simpler just to avoid the noise, and Seneca will move from his lodgings.
support.context: End of Letter 56: Seneca has shown he can study over the noise of a bath house; he says he only wanted to test himself, and will now move.

amend.t: ; the retreat is right only if I am good, calm and self-controlled, for otherwise, alone, I am too close to a rascal
; yet some places harm a mind not yet sound, and it is sometimes simpler just to move away from a noisy place

searches: withdraw into yourself, retire into, retreat
change of scene, place or climate; travel

rejected.why: The sage, friendless in prison or on a lonely shore, retreats into himself. About living without friends; 104.7 backs the claim more directly.
“Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can”, beside advice to seek better company. The limit “as far as you can” is said fully in 25.7, which is used.
Avoid crowds while you cannot yet trust yourself among them. About crowds, not places; 28.6 gives the same limit for places.
The person matters more than the place; the whole world is my country. Same point as 55.8, which is used.
You need not another place but another personality. Same point as 28.1, which is used.
Stop the body’s restless moving before the spirit can grow into unity. Close to the limit in 28.6; kept out so that the limit rests on two pieces.
Once truly retired, no outward thing distracts us. Says what 56.14 says, which is used as the test.
A life withdrawn into itself, with no reaching forward; anxiety comes to one whom the present does not profit. About planning ahead; matching it to claim 5 would need explaining.
We do not adapt ourselves to the present. About hope and fear of the future, not about living the present as a practice.
Philosophy makes you prefer to please yourself rather than the populace. 7.12 says the claim’s words more closely.
Why take pleasure in praise from men you cannot praise? About applause in the lecture hall; 7.12 is used.
A shifting will is a mind at sea heading every way. About consistency of the will; 71.3 is closer to having a target.
The countryside does not of itself teach plain living. About faults that ripen in public view, not about retreat into oneself.
Vatia hid from the world out of fear and was not living for himself. A portrait of false leisure; 55.8 from the same letter is used.
Abandon riches and pleasures at reason’s bidding. About what to give up, not about retreat.
Rejoice only in what comes from your own store, your best part. About where the true good lies, nearer the article on virtue.
Come back to the good that is really yours, a clear mind. About the good of a reasoning being, not about retreat.
Useless flesh is fastened to the higher parts. An argument about whether quiet adds to virtue; does not back claim 4 without explaining.
An upright soul is a god dwelling as a guest in a body. About what to seek, not about keeping the mind apart from the body.
In retirement, talk with yourself and speak ill of yourself. Letter 68 is about not advertising one’s retirement.

articles.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

claims.t: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. That is the good that is my own. Everything else is small beside it, and I chase after none of it and run from none of it.
claims.shared: Both 3.7 and 3.8 put the spirit within first: in 3.7 nothing appears better than “the spirit itself that is seated in you”, in 3.8 the good person “has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue”. 3.7 and 5.28 both name a good that is one’s own (“that good which is proper to you and is yours”; “to have its good in a just disposition and just action”), and 3.8 and 3.13 both say the person flees nothing (“neither pursuing nor fleeing”; “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”).
claims.changed: 3.7 puts it as a test, “if nothing appears better”; the claim states the answer that 3.7 expects. 3.8 says “neither pursuing nor fleeing” and 3.13 “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”, with no object; the claim limits both to the things set below the spirit, so it does not forbid choosing the better and holding on to it. 5.28 speaks of every rational being; the claim says “me”.

support.quote: But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else
support.follows: If nothing appears better than the spirit seated within me, that spirit is the best thing I have.

support.quote: whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else
support.follows: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.

support.quote: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage
gives: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage
support.follows: Justice, truth, self-control and courage are the standard that anything better in human life would have to beat.

support.quote: that good which is proper to you and is yours
gives: That is the good that is my own
support.follows: There is a good that belongs to me as my own, and I am to honour it above everything else.

support.quote: to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there
gives: That is the good that is my own
support.follows: A rational being’s good lies in being just and acting justly, and its desire should go no further than that.

support.quote: if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else
gives: Everything else is small beside it
support.follows: If everything else looks smaller and cheaper than the spirit within, nothing else should be given room.

support.quote: Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
gives: I chase after none of it and run from none of it
run from none of it
support.follows: Whoever prefers their own mind and spirit lives without chasing things and without running from them.

support.quote: waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing
gives: run from none of it
support.follows: Living well requires, among other things, waiting for nothing and running from nothing.

claims.t: No one can prevent me from living well, or from doing and saying what is according to nature. Nothing from outside stands in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and good sense.
claims.shared: Four passages say that no one can prevent it: “there is no one who can prevent this” (3.13), “there is no one who prevents you” (2.6), “No one will prevent you” (6.53), “no one at all can prevent you” (8.30). 3.13 and 11.15 both speak of living well and say it is in my power; 2.6 and 6.53 both say what is unpreventable is what accords with nature.
claims.changed: The four passages name different things that no one can prevent: living well (3.13), doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole (2.6), living by the reason of my own nature (6.53), each action doing its part (8.30). The claim puts living well first and names doing and saying after it. 2.6 speaks of the nature of which I am a part, 6.53 of my own nature; the claim says “according to nature” and does not choose between them. 8.30 says “at least” of acting justly, with self-control and good sense, and grants that some other activity may be prevented; the claim keeps that second sentence to those three.

support.quote: you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
gives: No one can prevent me
living well
support.follows: Whoever does the present work by right reason and keeps their spirit pure will live well, and no one can prevent it.

support.quote: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul
gives: living well
support.follows: The power to live in the finest way lies in the soul itself.

support.quote: there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part
gives: No one can prevent me
doing and saying
what is according to nature
support.follows: No one can stop me from always doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole I am part of.

support.quote: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature.
gives: No one can prevent me
what is according to nature
support.follows: No one can stop me from living by the reason of my own nature.

support.quote: And no one at all can prevent you from having it do its own part.
gives: No one can prevent me
support.follows: No one can stop each of my actions from doing its own part as far as it can.

support.quote: “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
gives: Nothing from outside stands in the way
acting justly, with self-control and good sense
support.follows: Nothing outside me can stop me from acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.

claims.t: In all I say and do, I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens, and I strip away the rest, needless impressions as well as needless acts. Keeping to it is taking the short road, the one according to nature, and it spares me toil and trouble.
claims.shared: Both passages are about everything one says and does (4.20: “most of what we say and do”; 4.43: “say and do everything in the soundest way”), and both say that keeping to the right course frees one from burden: 4.20 “more leisure and be less troubled”, 4.43 “frees you from toil”.
claims.changed: 4.20 puts this as a cautious question (“Might it not be better…?”) that suggests its answer; the claim states the answer. 4.20 says doing only what is necessary leaves one “less troubled”; 4.43 says the short road “frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation”. The claim says “spares me toil and trouble” for both, and drops hanging back, contriving and affectation. That the necessary road and the short road are the same road is the editor’s reading.

support.quote: For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled.
gives: In all I say and do
I strip away the rest
spares me toil and trouble
support.follows: Most of what we say and do is unnecessary, and stripping it away gives more leisure and less trouble.

support.quote: Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires?
gives: I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens
support.follows: Doing what is necessary, as reason requires of a being made for civic life, may be better than simply doing few things.

support.quote: And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too
gives: needless impressions as well as needless acts
support.follows: Needless impressions should be stripped away as well as needless actions.

support.quote: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way.
gives: In all I say and do
taking the short road, the one according to nature
support.follows: The short road is the road of nature, and taking it lets me say and do everything in the soundest way.

support.quote: For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
gives: spares me toil and trouble
support.follows: Keeping to that road frees one from toil, from hanging back, and from contriving and affectation.

claims.t: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal. If as an animal, I admit plainly that it is only an animal’s benefit, and I take what my animal nature asks for only if it does not make me worse as a rational being. What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens.
claims.shared: Both passages tell apart what I am as an animal and what I am as a rational being, and both put the rational first: 3.7 “If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so”; 10.2 “unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state”. Both also join the rational to the civic: 3.7 “the rational and civic good”, 10.2 “what is rational is by that very fact also civic”.
claims.changed: 10.2 speaks of what my animal nature asks for, not of a benefit, and asks no question; that the two passages speak of one thing is the editor’s reading. 10.2 begins one step lower, with what I need simply as a growing body, and climbs to the animal and then to the rational; the claim keeps only the last step. 3.7 answers a speaker who says “the better is what benefits”; the claim makes the question my own. “Civic” in both passages is put as “made for life among fellow citizens”.

support.quote: “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so
gives: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me
as a rational being or as an animal
If as an animal, I admit plainly that it is only an animal’s benefit
support.follows: If something benefits me as a rational being I should keep to it; if only as an animal, I should admit that.

support.quote: Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and all of this is to be taken up, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state.
gives: as a rational being or as an animal
I take what my animal nature asks for only if it does not make me worse as a rational being
support.follows: What my animal nature asks for is to be taken up, unless it would make my rational nature worse.

support.quote: should take up a position against the rational and civic good
gives: What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens
support.follows: The good of a rational being is also a civic good, and nothing of another kind may be set against it.

support.quote: And what is rational is by that very fact also civic.
gives: What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens
support.follows: Whatever is rational is, for that very reason, also civic.

claims.t: I put my life together one action at a time. I carry through what lies before me step by step, as I would spell out a name letter by letter, and I join one good to the next without leaving a gap.
claims.shared: 5.28 and 6.24 both say “step by step”: to “judge and act step by step, as along a road” (5.28) and to “carry through step by step what lies before you” (6.24). 8.30 says something near it of a whole life: “put your life together one action at a time”.
claims.changed: 6.24 speaks of each duty, 8.30 of a life, 5.28 of the road a life travels; the claim speaks of my life. The link between “step by step” and 8.30’s “one action at a time” leans on the translation: in 5.28 and 6.24 the Greek is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”, rendered “step by step”. 12.22 adds the joining of one good to the next.

support.quote: You must put your life together one action at a time
gives: I put my life together one action at a time
support.follows: A life is to be built one action at a time.

support.quote: if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road
gives: step by step
support.follows: Life goes well for whoever can judge and act step by step, as one goes along a road.

support.quote: carry through step by step what lies before you
gives: I carry through what lies before me
step by step
support.follows: Whatever lies before me is to be carried through step by step.

support.quote: Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?
gives: as I would spell out a name letter by letter
support.follows: Asked how a name is written, one calmly counts off its letters one by one.

support.quote: joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap
gives: I join one good to the next without leaving a gap
support.follows: Once I do what is just and say what is true, what is left is to enjoy living, linking one good to the next.

claims.t: If I lean toward anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me, such as praise, office, wealth or pleasure, it pulls me about, takes control of me and carries me off course. I count nothing as a benefit that will force me to break faith, to hate or to play a part. The way back is to choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
claims.shared: Both passages warn against giving weight to what is not my own good: 3.7 against having “tipped and turned aside toward anything else”, 3.8 against valuing “as a benefit to yourself” what will one day harm me.
claims.changed: 3.8 does not say that praise or wealth forces anyone to break faith; it forbids counting as a benefit whatever will. The claim keeps that as a rule of its own. 3.8 lists seven things such a benefit forces: to break faith, abandon self-respect, hate, suspect, curse, play a part, and want what must be hidden behind walls and curtains; the claim keeps three. “The way back” is the editor’s name for 3.7’s command to choose the better.

support.quote: Once you have tipped and turned aside toward anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honor above all else
gives: If I lean toward anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me
it pulls me about
support.follows: Once I lean toward anything else, I can no longer honour my own good above all without being pulled about.

support.quote: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
gives: If I lean toward anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me
I count nothing as a benefit that will force me to break faith, to hate or to play a part
support.follows: Nothing that will one day force me to break faith, hate, suspect or pretend should count as a benefit to me.

support.quote: such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures
gives: such as praise, office, wealth or pleasure
support.follows: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and pleasures are things of another kind than the rational and civic good.

support.quote: All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course.
gives: takes control of me and carries me off course
support.follows: Such things may seem to fit for a while, but then they suddenly take control and carry one off course.

support.quote: But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it.
gives: choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it
support.follows: I should choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.

single.label: If I find better
single.t: If I ever see anything better than this, I shall turn to it with my whole soul and enjoy what I have found to be best.
single.quote: if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best
single.why: Only 3.7 allows that something might be better than justice and the spirit within, and says what to do then. No other passage of the section considers it.
single.follows: If something better than justice and a mind content with itself is ever seen, one should turn to it wholeheartedly.

single.label: Keeping it pure
single.t: I keep my own spirit pure, as if I had to give it back this very moment.
single.quote: keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment
single.why: Only 3.13 speaks of keeping the spirit pure and of giving it back. 3.8 shares the readiness (“even if they have to depart this moment”) but not the purity or the giving back, so it is not fused.
single.follows: I should keep my spirit pure as though I had to hand it back right now.

single.label: Wiping out a verdict
single.t: Things do not put judgments about themselves into me; I write the verdicts myself. I need not write them, and if one gets written without my noticing, I can wipe it out at once.
single.quote: none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one somehow escapes notice, to wipe it out at once
single.why: Only 11.15 says where my verdicts about things come from and that I can wipe one out. It is kept as a way back when a wrong verdict has been written.
single.follows: Things do not judge themselves in me; I write the verdicts, and I can refuse to write them or wipe one out at once.

single.label: When things go against nature
single.t: When what I meet is contrary to nature, I look for what there is for me that is according to my own nature and hurry toward it, even if it brings me no reputation.
single.quote: if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry toward that, even if it brings no reputation
single.why: Only 11.15 says what to do when things are contrary to nature. In 11.15 “they” are the indifferent things just named, and the translators note that the sentence before is obscure.
single.follows: When things are contrary to nature, I should seek what accords with my own nature and go for it, even if it brings no fame.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 3.7 is 3.6, 3.8 is 3.7, 3.13 is 3.12, 11.15 is 11.16, 12.22 is 12.29, 2.6 is 2.9, 8.30 is 8.32, 4.20 is 4.24, 4.43 is 4.51, 5.28 is 5.34, 6.53 is 6.58, 6.24 is 6.26; 10.2 and 10.6 are the same.

Reads 3.7’s “if nothing appears better than the spirit” as the answer Marcus expects, and states it in claim 1 as my view; 3.7’s open side is the said-once item under doubt. Under “Why” the section gives the statement’s two halves at length (claims 1 and 2), not an argument for them.

Claim 2 gathers four passages that each say “no one can prevent”, though each names a different thing that cannot be prevented: living well, doing and saying what fits nature, living by my own nature’s reason, each action doing its part. The claim puts living well first and names the others after it; only “No one can prevent me” is said by all four.

Claim 4 pairs 3.7’s question (does it benefit me as a rational being or as an animal?) with 10.2’s ladder of natures, and places it under “In action”, not under doubt, though in 3.7 it answers an objection.
articles.limit: Article 8’s claim 4 already says that nothing that happens prevents me from being good and just, and Article 2 that reason leads my work; what this article adds is the ranking, that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue. Article 17’s claim 4 allows that the people around me may not let me live according to nature, so “no one can prevent me” in claim 2 is read here as holding of the inner act, not of my outward life; the said-once item on verdicts (11.15) repeats Article 7’s claims 2 and 3 and Article 8’s claim 2. 3.7 carries much of the article, which asserts that nothing is better and does not argue it; Seneca’s item under “Why” and the statement clause come close to Article 5, which already quotes Ep. 76.8 and has an item on 76.10 and 41.8, and what they add here is 76.9’s comparison with animals.

aside.10.6: Its subject is that I am a part of the whole and kin to those of my own kind, and so welcome what the whole allots and do nothing unsocial; Articles 1 and 3 say this, and it does not speak of what is best or of what no one can prevent.

statement.t: Nothing is better than the spirit within me and its virtue, and no one can prevent me from living by it.

parts.words: Nothing is better than the spirit within me and its virtue
no one can prevent me from living by it

statement.kind: What is best, and why it is safe
statement.form: Claim 1 says what is best: the spirit within and its virtue, beside which everything else is small. Claim 2 says that no one can prevent me from living by it. The other claims say what follows for what I do, how I practise it, and how it fails.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: the good that is my own, keeping to what is necessary, and what pulls me away from it. “Why” gains his argument that reason is a human being’s own good, and “In action” gains where the good in a choice lies. He limits the claim that no one can prevent me from living well: nothing can break the happiness of the wise, but mine can be broken off while I am short of perfection, and old age can shatter the mind.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: each thing is judged by its own good, and a human being’s own good is reason brought to perfection. Its second half is narrowed in the second claim: he grants it fully only to the wise.

items.quote: come back to the Good that is really yours
gives: That is the good that is my own
items.follows: There is a good that is truly my own, and I should come back to it.
items.context: Letter 124, on the good grasped by reason. Seneca tells Lucilius to stop rivalling animals in strength and looks; “the Good” is a clear, flawless mind: perfect reason.

items.quote: how pleasant and unimpeded life is for those who follow these laws, but how bitter and perplexed it is for those who have put their trust in opinion rather than in nature
gives: spares me toil and trouble
items.follows: Life is easy and unhindered for those who follow nature’s laws, and bitter and confused for those who trust opinion.
items.context: Letter 48, against logic games. Philosophy should show people what nature makes necessary and what superfluous; “these laws” are nature’s simple laws on that.

items.quote: Abandon those pursuits which heretofore have caused you to run hither and thither.
gives: it pulls me about
items.follows: The pursuits that have kept me running here and there are to be given up.
items.context: Letter 84: reason’s voice, as Seneca imagines it, on making the mind one whole. “Those pursuits” are the riches, pleasures and office she tells one to give up next.

items.label: why
items.role: Why reason is my own good
items.t: Everything is judged by its own good, as a vine is valued for its wine and a stag for its speed. Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals; reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being.
items.why: Marcus says that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue, and does not say why. Seneca argues it: each thing is judged by what is its own, and what is a human being’s own is reason, which no animal shares.

support.quote: Everything is estimated by the standard of its own good. The vine is valued for its productiveness and the flavour of its wine, the stag for his speed.
gives: Everything is judged by its own good
as a vine is valued for its wine and a stag for its speed
support.follows: Each thing is valued by the good that is its own, as a vine for its wine and a stag for its speed.
support.context: Letter 76 sets out to prove that there is only one good. Each thing, vine, stag or dog, is valued for the quality it was brought into being for.

support.quote: Man is strong; so is the lion. Man is comely; so is the peacock. Man is swift; so is the horse.
gives: Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals
support.follows: Strength, beauty and speed a human being shares with the lion, the peacock and the horse.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: qualities a human being shares with animals, which therefore cannot be his own good.

support.quote: Perfect reason is therefore the good peculiar to man; all other qualities he shares in some degree with animals and plants.
gives: reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being
support.follows: Perfect reason is the good peculiar to a human being; every other quality animals or plants share.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: what is best in a human being is reason, by which he surpasses the animals.

items.label: action
items.role: Where the good lies in a choice
items.t: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain, not because they are goods but because they are according to nature. What is good is not the thing I choose but the quality of my choice.
items.why: 10.2 says I am to take up what my animal nature asks for unless it makes me worse as a rational being, and 3.7 says to admit it when a benefit is only an animal’s. Neither says what is good in such a choice. Seneca says: not the thing chosen but the choosing.

support.quote: Of course I shall seek them, but not because they are goods,—I shall seek them because they are according to nature
gives: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain
not because they are goods but because they are according to nature
support.follows: Health, rest and freedom from pain may be sought because they are according to nature, not because they are goods.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. An objector asks whether health, rest and freedom from pain, which do not hinder virtue, should be sought; “them” are those three.

support.quote: the good is not in the thing selected, but in the quality of the selection
gives: What is good is not the thing I choose but the quality of my choice
support.follows: The good lies not in what is chosen but in how well it is chosen.
support.context: Letter 92, on choosing neat clothing: the choice of it is a good, the clothing is not. “The thing selected” is whatever is chosen, clothing or health.

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing from outside can break the happiness of the wise man (Ep. 72.4), but he grants this only to the wise: the happiness of anyone still short of perfection can be broken off. He also names a case Marcus does not name here, old age shattering the mind (Ep. 58.35). He gives it as the premise of his rule on when to leave life, not as an objection, and old age is not plainly a thing from outside. This narrows the claim; it does not deny it.

support.quote: It is those who are still short of perfection whose happiness can be broken off; the joy of a wise man, on the other hand, is a woven fabric, rent by no chance happening and by no change of fortune
support.follows: The happiness of one not yet perfect can be broken off; the wise man’s joy no chance can tear.
support.context: Letter 72, on business crowding out philosophy. Someone says that something will hinder him; Seneca answers that only the happiness of the imperfect can be broken off.

support.quote: if old age begins to shatter my mind, and to pull its various faculties to pieces
support.follows: Old age can begin to shatter the mind and pull its faculties apart.
support.context: Letter 58 ends on when one may leave life. Seneca will keep his old age while it leaves his mind intact; what may shatter the mind is old age.

amend.t: ; each thing is judged by its own good, and mine is reason brought to perfection
; but while I am short of perfection my happiness can be broken off, and old age can shatter my mind

searches: only good, sole good, one good
step by step, one by one, little by little, one thing at a time
one path, short road, shortest, straight road
neither … flee, nor flee, flee from nothing
no one can, nobody can, none can
own store, best part of you
as an animal, dumb animal, benefit with animal
give back, restore, lent, on loan

rejected.why: Virtue as man’s sole good, all else in between. Spoken in the voice of an opponent of precepts whom Seneca goes on to answer; not his own claim in context.
Rejoice only in what comes from your own store, the best part of you. Says what 124.23 says; 124.23 names the good as reason and is clearer.
Reason is man’s one peculiar good, worth all the rest. The same argument as 76.8 and 76.9, which are used.
The happy life depends on perfect reason alone. Repeats 124.23 without naming it as one’s own good.
Straying from Nature makes one crave, fear and serve chance. About straying from nature in general, not about counting a thing as a benefit; 84.11 names riches, pleasure and office.
Decide what you wish and abide by it. A settled choice, not a choice of the better; the match to 3.7 would need explaining.
Study loses its continuity when broken off. About the study of philosophy, not about joining one good act to the next.
Philosophy should proceed step by step. About speaking slowly, not about acting one step at a time.
One straight path to wisdom. About reaching freedom through wisdom, not about the short road of doing what is necessary.
Men sweat for superfluous things; enough is at hand. About wealth and poverty, not about all one says and does.
A good man will not be busy for the sake of being busy. Said of withdrawing from a public career; 48.9 states the point more generally.
