Indulge the body only as far as health needs. About the body’s needs; the claim is about all that I say and do.
The wise man leaves when many events disturb his peace. About the time to end one’s life; 58.35 states the narrower case plainly.
Will not flee an illness that is curable and does not impede the soul. Same limit as 58.35; one quote was enough for the clause.
That pain hinders the work of virtue is an opponent’s argument, which Seneca rejects; not his view.
Only the wise man can be one person; the rest shift masks. Near 3.8’s “play a part”, but about consistency, not about a false benefit.
Without philosophy no one can live fearlessly. About philosophy as a guide, not about what no one can prevent.
Riches, beauty and titles are “middle” things. Part of an argument about death as indifferent.
Health, rest and freedom from pain do not hinder virtue. Only the answer is quoted; the objection is context.
“What then is peculiar to man? Reason.” Already an added item in Article 5; here 76.8 and 76.9 are used for the comparison with animals, which Article 5 does not make.

articles.title: Living with the gods

claims.role: With the gods at every moment
claims.t: I live with the gods and experience their power all the time. I constantly show them my own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that is wanted by the spirit Zeus gave me as protector and leader, a fragment of himself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of dealings with the gods that never stop. In 12.21 Marcus experiences their power “on every occasion”; in 5.21 the one who lives with the gods shows them their own soul “constantly”. “All the time” stands for both. Only 5.21 calls this living with the gods.
claims.changed: 12.21 gives this experience as the way Marcus knows that the gods exist; the claim takes from it only that the experience comes on every occasion, and sets it beside living with the gods without making it a part of that life. 5.21 says “each person” and “their own soul”; the claim says “me” and “my own soul”.

support.quote: the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself
gives: I live with the gods
all the time
I constantly show them my own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that is wanted by the spirit Zeus gave me as protector and leader, a fragment of himself
support.follows: To live with the gods is to show them, constantly, a soul content with its lot that does all that the spirit given by Zeus wants.

support.quote: from what I experience of their power on every occasion
gives: experience their power
all the time
support.follows: Marcus experiences the power of the gods on every occasion.

claims.t: I revere the gods and reason, and I honour my own soul, though I have never seen it.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of reverence, with words from one Greek root: in 12.21 Marcus is asked why he should “revere” the gods, and 4.13 calls for “reverence for reason”. 12.21 adds a third thing that is honoured, the soul that he has never seen.
claims.changed: In 12.21 the word “revere” is spoken by those who question Marcus; his answer accepts it and ends with his awe of the gods. 4.13 does not say whether the reason to be revered is a person’s own or the reason of the whole, and the claim leaves that open as well.

support.quote: that you revere them as you do
gives: I revere
the gods
support.follows: Those who question Marcus take it as a fact that he reveres the gods.

support.quote: reverence for reason
gives: I revere
reason
support.follows: Reason is something to be revered.

support.quote: I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it
gives: I honour my own soul, though I have never seen it
support.follows: Marcus has never seen his own soul, and he honours it all the same.

claims.t: I give myself reminders, by rules taken from schools of philosophy. At dawn I turn my eyes to the sky and am reminded of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way; and I constantly remind myself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
claims.shared: Both passages give a rule for reminding oneself, and both use the same verb: 11.25 “so that we are reminded”, 11.24 “to remind oneself”. Both name the school the rule comes from: “The Pythagoreans” in 11.25, “the writings of the Epicureans” in 11.24. Each names something to be reminded of that does its part well: those in the sky that always complete their own work, and a person of old who practised virtue.
claims.changed: The claim takes both rules as my own and says “schools of philosophy” for the Pythagoreans and the Epicureans. 11.25 says “we” and 11.24 “oneself”; the claim says “I”. Only 11.24 uses the word “rule”; 11.25 gives the Pythagoreans’ instruction without a verb. 11.25 says “those”; the claim says “those in the sky”, since the passage has just named the sky.

support.quote: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way
gives: I give myself reminders
by rules taken from schools of philosophy
At dawn I turn my eyes to the sky and am reminded of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way
support.follows: The Pythagoreans’ instruction is to look at the sky at dawn, as a reminder of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way.

support.quote: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue
gives: I give myself reminders
by rules taken from schools of philosophy
I constantly remind myself of one of the people of old who practised virtue
support.follows: The Epicureans had a written rule: keep reminding yourself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.

single.label: What the spirit is
single.t: The spirit that Zeus gave me as my leader is my own mind and reason.
single.quote: this spirit is each person’s mind and reason
single.why: Only this passage says what the spirit is. 4.13 names reason and does not connect it with a spirit or with Zeus, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: The spirit that the passage has just described is each person’s own mind and reason.

single.label: Seen with the eye
single.t: The gods can be seen, even with the eye.
single.quote: they are visible even to the eye
single.why: Only this passage says that the gods are visible, and it does not say which gods. 11.25 looks at the sky but does not call what is seen there gods, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Marcus’s first answer to those who ask where he has seen the gods is that they can be seen with the eye.

single.label: Known by their power
single.t: It is from my experience of their power that I grasp that the gods exist, and I stand in awe of them.
single.quote: from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them
single.why: Only this passage says how I know that the gods exist. No other passage of the section argues for it.
single.follows: Marcus’s ground for holding that the gods exist, and for his awe of them, is what he has just named: his experience of their power.

single.label: What the sky shows
single.t: The sky at dawn also reminds me of order, of purity and of nakedness: a star has no veil in front of it.
single.quote: and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.why: Only this passage names order, purity and nakedness. 5.21 speaks of showing the gods my soul, but it does not say that the soul is shown uncovered, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Those in the sky are also a reminder of order, purity and nakedness, since a star has nothing hung in front of it.

single.label: From beast to god
single.t: To the very people to whom I now seem a beast and an ape, I shall seem a god within ten days, if I turn back to the principles.
single.quote: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles
single.why: Only this passage says what it looks like to have left the principles, and that there is a way back. It speaks of how I seem to people, not of living with the gods, so it is not fused with 5.21. Its last words, “reverence for reason”, are counted in claim 2.
single.follows: Whoever turns back to the principles will soon seem a god to the same people who now take him for a beast and an ape.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.21 is 12.28, 5.21 is 5.27, 4.13 is 4.16, 11.25 is 11.27 and 11.24 is 11.26.

Sets living with the gods (5.21) and experiencing their power (12.21) side by side, in claim 1 and in the first part of the statement, joined by the one thing both say: that it goes on all the time. Only 5.21 speaks of living with the gods, and 12.21 mentions the experience to explain how Marcus knows that the gods exist. Claim 1 is headed “With the gods at every moment”, not as a definition, and neither it nor the statement says that the experience is part of living with them.

Takes “I revere the gods” from words that 12.21 gives to Marcus’s questioners (“that you revere them as you do”), because they share a Greek root with “reverence for reason” in 4.13. Marcus’s own verbs in 12.21 are “honour”, of his soul, and “stand in awe”, of the gods.

Does not say that the reason I revere is the reason that leads me. 4.13 says “reverence for reason”, and its Greek leaves open whether a person’s own reason or the reason of the whole is meant; 5.21 says that the spirit leads and is mind and reason, but not that it is revered. The two stand side by side: the reverence in claim 2 and in the statement, the leading spirit in claim 1 and in the said-once item from 5.21.

Reads “those that always complete their own work” (11.25) as the stars, as the passage’s last sentence suggests, but writes “those in the sky” in the claim and does not name them. Does not join them to the gods who are “visible even to the eye” in 12.21: neither passage says that the stars are gods.

Says in claim 3 that both rules come from schools of philosophy. For 11.24 this follows the edition’s text, “Epicureans”; the translators’ note says, from memory and unchecked, that the manuscripts read “Ephesians” and that “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction.
articles.limit: Article 4 already says that what rules in me is of one kind with the reason that governs the world, and that I honour what is supreme in myself (5.18); Article 3 already says that I accept what happens, which here is “content with what is allotted”. What this article adds is that life with the gods goes on all the time, that it consists in what I show them, and two exercises of reminding. Of Seneca’s additions, the one on what I come back from (w4) comes near Article 5’s Seneca item from Ep. 76.10, that reason is what is peculiar to me; what it adds here is the turning back from what is not my own. It is weakest where it joins its parts: the section holds three passages on the gods and reason and two on reminders, and no passage connects the two groups; the statement only sets them side by side.

statement.t: I live with the gods and meet their power always, revere both them and reason, and keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old.

parts.words: I live with the gods and meet their power always
revere both them and reason
keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old

statement.kind: A way of living with the gods, what I revere, and two exercises of reminding
statement.form: Claim 1 says that I live with the gods and experience their power all the time, and what living with them consists in. Claim 2 names what is revered: the gods, reason and the unseen soul. Claim 3 gives two exercises of reminding, and the statement names what each keeps before me: the dawn sky I look at (11.25) and the good person I am reminded of (11.24). No passage joins the three, so the statement lists them with “and” and draws no conclusion from one to another. Its first part sets what 5.21 says (living with the gods) beside what 12.21 says (meeting their power), joined by what both say: “always”, which stands for 12.21’s “on every occasion” and 5.21’s “constantly”. It closes the first part so that it covers that part only: 11.25 is an exercise at dawn, and 4.13 gives no frequency.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if there are no gods; 12.21 answers those who ask where Marcus has seen them with grounds for revering them, which stand under Why.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 1 gains a second author for calling the spirit, which is reason, a fragment of the divine, and claim 3 a second author for keeping one good person in mind. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: God as a witness within me, what worship consists in, the chosen person as a watcher, an example of what I turn back from when I return to reason, and what holds if no guardian was given to me. He limits claim 3: I need the person as a guard over me only until I respect myself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains two watchers: God, who is a witness of my soul, and the good person of old, whom I treat as if he were watching me. He sets a term to the second: once I have come to respect myself, I need no longer keep that person over me as a guard.

items.quote: Reason, however, is nothing else than a portion of the divine spirit set in a human body
gives: a fragment of himself
items.follows: Human reason is a portion of the divine spirit, placed in a human body.
items.context: Letter 66 argues that all goods are equal, since the divine is of one nature. “Reason” is human reason; it matches claim 1 through 5.21, where the spirit is each person’s mind and reason.

items.quote: Cherish some man of high character, and keep him ever before your eyes
gives: I constantly remind myself of one
who practised virtue
items.follows: The counsel is to pick one man of high character, hold him dear and keep him always in view.
items.context: The closing motto of Letter 11, which Seneca gives as the counsel of Epicurus. “Some man of high character” is a man one chooses; the motto does not say that he must be of old.

items.label: why
items.t: God is near me, with me and within me. A holy spirit lives within me that marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian, and as I treat this spirit, so it treats me. Nothing is shut off from the sight of God: he is a witness of my soul and comes into the midst of my thoughts.
items.why: Marcus says that I show the gods my soul and that the spirit is my protector and leader. He does not say that the spirit marks what I do, that it treats me as I treat it, or that nothing in me can be kept from the sight of God.

support.quote: God is near you, he is with you, he is within you.
gives: God is near me, with me and within me
support.follows: God is near a person, with that person and within that person.
support.context: The opening of Letter 41: Lucilius need not pray at a temple for sound understanding, since he can get it from himself. “You” is Lucilius, and through him anyone.

support.quote: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it.
gives: A holy spirit lives within me that marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian
as I treat this spirit, so it treats me
support.follows: A holy spirit within us notes our good and bad deeds and guards us, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41, just after “God is within you”. “This spirit” is the holy spirit dwelling in each person; no one, Seneca adds, is good without God’s help.

support.quote: Nothing is shut off from the sight of God. He is witness of our souls, and he comes into the very midst of our thoughts
gives: Nothing is shut off from the sight of God: he is a witness of my soul and comes into the midst of my thoughts
support.follows: God sees everything, is a witness of our souls and enters into our thoughts.
support.context: The opening of Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of Seneca’s whole day. One should live and think as if seen, since God sees into our souls and thoughts.

items.label: action
items.t: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to acknowledge their majesty and their goodness. God is worshipped by those who truly know him.
items.why: Marcus says that he reveres the gods and stands in awe of them; in this section he does not say what worship consists in. Seneca does, and he begins where the questioners of 12.21 begin: with holding that the gods exist.

support.quote: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; the next to acknowledge their majesty, to acknowledge their goodness without which there is no majesty.
gives: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to acknowledge their majesty and their goodness
support.follows: Worship of the gods begins with believing in them and goes on to acknowledging their majesty and their goodness.
support.context: Letter 95 holds that rules for ritual are useless without a right idea of God. This sentence begins Seneca’s own account of what worshipping the gods is.

support.quote: God is worshipped by those who truly know Him
gives: God is worshipped by those who truly know him
support.follows: The people who worship God are those who truly know him.
support.context: Letter 95, on worship: Seneca would forbid lamps, morning calls at temples and gifts to Jupiter’s and Juno’s statues, and sets knowing God against these rites.

items.label: practice
items.t: I choose a Cato, or, if Cato seems too severe a model, a gentler Laelius. I live as if he were watching me and order all my actions as if he saw them. With a witness standing near when I am likely to go wrong, I can get rid of most of my faults.
items.why: 11.24 gives the Epicurean rule in one line: remind yourself of a person of old. Seneca gives a similar counsel, which he quotes from Epicurus and comments on. In it the person is more than a reminder: he is a witness, and I act as if he saw me. Seneca also names whom to choose.

support.quote: Choose therefore a Cato; or, if Cato seems too severe a model, choose some Laelius, a gentler spirit.
gives: I choose a Cato, or, if Cato seems too severe a model, a gentler Laelius
support.follows: The person to choose is a Cato, or, for someone who finds Cato too severe, the gentler Laelius.
support.context: Letter 11: Seneca applies Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man always before one’s eyes. Cato and Laelius are Romans of earlier centuries, offered as that man.

support.quote: living as if he were watching you, and ordering all your actions as if he beheld them
gives: I live as if he were watching me and order all my actions as if he saw them
support.follows: One should live and arrange every action as if the chosen man were looking on.
support.context: The second half of a motto that Seneca quotes from Epicurus at the end of Letter 11. “He” is the man of high character whom one is to keep before one’s eyes.

support.quote: We can get rid of most sins, if we have a witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong.
gives: With a witness standing near when I am likely to go wrong, I can get rid of most of my faults
support.follows: Having a witness close by at the moment of going wrong removes most wrongdoing.
support.context: Letter 11, Seneca’s comment on Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man before one’s eyes. The “witness” is here the man one pictures watching, as in the motto.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I have been striving for what is not my own, such as bodily strength, which nature has given in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts, I come back to the good that is really mine. I am a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within me is perfect reason. The greatest service my teacher can do me is to show me that good, to take me out of the class of dumb animals and place me on a level with God.
items.why: 4.13 says that I pass from seeming a beast to seeming a god if I turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason; it does not say what I had turned to instead. Seneca gives an example: bodily strength, which cattle and wild beasts have in greater degree. He speaks of what I am, where 4.13 speaks of how I seem to others.

support.quote: Why, pray, do you foster and practise your bodily strength? Nature has granted strength in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts.
gives: such as bodily strength, which nature has given in greater degree to cattle and wild beasts
support.follows: Seneca asks why anyone cultivates bodily strength, when nature has given more of it to cattle and wild beasts.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 124, on the Good as grasped by reason. Seneca asks Lucilius why he cultivates strength, beauty, hair and speed, in each of which some animal surpasses him.

support.quote: striving as you are for something that is not your own—and come back to the Good that is really yours
gives: When I have been striving for what is not my own
I come back to the good that is really mine
support.follows: Whoever is striving for something not his own is asked to come back to the good that really is his.
support.context: Letter 124: Seneca has asked why Lucilius trains strength, beauty and speed, in which animals surpass him. Those are the things “not your own”; the Good is a clear mind.

support.quote: You are a reasoning animal. What Good, then, lies within you? Perfect reason.
gives: I am a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within me is perfect reason
support.follows: A human being is a reasoning animal, and the good that lies within one is perfect reason.
support.context: The close of Letter 124. “You” is Lucilius as a human being; Seneca’s answer to his own question is that a human’s good is reason brought to perfection.

support.quote: I can be of no greater benefit to you than by revealing the Good that is rightly yours, by taking you out of the class of dumb animals, and by placing you on a level with God
gives: The greatest service my teacher can do me is to show me that good, to take me out of the class of dumb animals and place me on a level with God
support.follows: Seneca’s greatest service to Lucilius is to show him his own good, take him out of the class of animals and set him level with God.
support.context: The end of Letter 124, which argues that the Good is grasped by reason and not by the senses. Seneca says what use the argument is to Lucilius, the “you”.

items.label: doubt
items.t: I can set aside for the present the belief that a god is assigned to each of us as an attendant. Whether I have been allotted a guardian or am neglected and left to Fortune, the heaviest curse on me would be to be at enmity with myself.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if no spirit was given to me. Seneca sets that belief aside and says what holds either way: the worst thing is to be at enmity with myself. He doubts only the guardian assigned to each person, not the gods; and in Letter 41 he himself says that a holy spirit within us is our guardian.

support.quote: Lay aside for the present the belief of certain persons—that a god is assigned to each one of us as a sort of attendant
gives: I can set aside for the present the belief that a god is assigned to each of us as an attendant
support.follows: The belief that each person has a god assigned as an attendant can be left aside for now.
support.context: The opening of Letter 110, just after the greeting. Seneca sets aside, for the moment, the popular belief in a lesser god attached to each person, which Roman ancestors held.

support.quote: whether we are allotted to special guardians, or whether we are neglected and consigned to Fortune, you can curse a man with no heavier curse than to pray that he may be at enmity with himself
gives: Whether I have been allotted a guardian or am neglected and left to Fortune, the heaviest curse on me would be to be at enmity with myself
support.follows: With guardians or without them, no curse on a person is heavier than enmity with himself.
support.context: Letter 110: Seneca leaves open whether gods attend to individuals. “Special guardians” are gods assigned to each person; either way enmity with oneself is the worst curse.

items.t: Claim 3 says that I constantly remind myself of a person of old, by a rule from the writings of the Epicureans. Seneca gives a similar Epicurean practice an end: the man is a guard set over me until I have come to respect myself, and then I may send him away (Ep. 25.6). This limits the claim and does not contradict it; he does not say that the reminding ever does harm. Letter 11 sets no such term: at its end he says to picture the chosen man always.

support.quote: when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant; but until then, set as a guard over yourself the authority of some man
support.follows: The imagined guard is to be kept until one respects oneself; after that he may be dismissed.
support.context: Letter 25, on Epicurus’s saying “Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you”. The “attendant” is the good man one imagines as a guard over oneself.

support.quote: picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern
support.follows: The chosen man is to be pictured always, as a protector or as a pattern; no end to this is named.
support.context: The last lines of Letter 11, after the advice to choose a Cato or a Laelius. “Him” is that chosen man, by whom one regulates one’s character as by a ruler.

amend.t: ; God is a witness of my soul, and I live as if the good person of old were watching me
; but once I have come to respect myself, I need no longer keep this person over me as a guard

searches: live with the gods, with the gods, company of the gods, associate of the gods
stars, heaven, sky (with look, gaze, eyes, behold and with order, course)
portion, fragment, part of God, spark
example, pattern, model (with Cato, Socrates, Laelius)
unseen, invisible, cannot be seen, not seen
sight of God, God beheld, gods see or watch, in the presence of
heavenly bodies, constellations, stars (with unchanging, regular, fixed, same, constant)

rejected.why: “Something of divinity exists in one who is a part of God.” Says less directly what Ep. 66.12 says, in a passage on the soul striving back to the heights.
The upright soul is “a god dwelling as a guest in a human body”. Calls the good soul itself a god, to show that rank and birth do not matter; not a spirit given to each person.
“God comes to men; nay, he comes into men.” The same point as Ep. 41.1, at the end of a letter on philosophers and rulers; a further witness was not needed.
“The way to the stars” by thrift and courage. The stars are a destination there, not something looked at as a reminder.
“The gods are witnesses of everything”, said of what thoughts of immortality teach. Ep. 83.1 says it directly and in Seneca’s own voice.
“Live among men as if God beheld you.” Already used in Article 6, where it is about prayer.
“Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you.” The same counsel as Ep. 11.8, which is quoted; the next section, 25.6, is used for the limit.
Keeping statues of great men and celebrating their birthdays. A way of remembering people of old, but the passage is about honouring the founders of philosophy as teachers.
“Live with the Catos, with Laelius.” About leaving bad company in order to lose one’s faults; it names the men Ep. 11.10 names.
Nature raised our gaze to the sky. Part of an argument that nature set the heavens before us and hid gold; it does not make the stars a reminder of anything.
A grove or a cave gives “a certain intimation of the existence of God”. Near 12.21, but there the power is met on every occasion, here at rare places; and 12.21’s ground stands as a said-once item.
Reverence for the unshaken man on whom “a divine power has descended”. Near 4.13’s “seem a god”, but it describes a sage and not a return.
The gods exist because every people believes in some. A ground Marcus does not give, but Seneca offers it as an example in passing, in a dispute about logic.
The wise man “lives on a plane with the gods”. A portrait of the sage’s joy and equality with the gods, not of dealings with them.
“The associate of the gods, and not their suppliant”, reached through knowledge of things human and divine. About rank with the gods.
Reason is common to gods and men. Article 4’s subject.
By reason man surpasses the animals and is surpassed only by the gods. About the good peculiar to man, Article 5’s subject; Letter 124 makes the same contrast and adds the return, and is quoted.
The pleasure-seeker should “herd with the dumb brutes”. Only the beast half of 4.13; Ep. 124.21 to 124.23 have both halves.

Article 4 quotes two of its sentences: “Whoever imitates them, is worshipping them sufficiently” (S95.50a) and the gods as guardians of the human race (S95.50b). Only its first sentence, on believing in the gods, is used here.
The good man’s duty toward the gods makes him endure whatever happens. About accepting what happens, Article 3’s subject.
The wise man taught us “not merely to know the gods, but to follow them”. One item in a list of what philosophy found.

Two of its sentences are left out. That whoever is a blessing to himself is assured of the gods’ favour comes before Seneca sets the guardian belief aside, so it is not said under that doubt. The remark on Genius and Juno is history of belief.

articles.title: Blaming no one for what is not up to me

claims.role: What counts as good or bad
claims.t: I count only what is up to me as good or bad for me. I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me: letting it would be slavery, and doing so leads me into many wrongs.
claims.shared: Both passages set what is up to me against what is not, and both name the same mistake in the same words: letting what is not up to me “make a difference” (6.36: “the difference these things make to us”; 9.40: “make a difference to you”).
claims.changed: 6.36 says “we” and 9.40 says “you”; the claim says “I”. 6.36 calls the other things “not yours to choose”, 9.40 “not up to you”; the claim uses 9.40’s phrase for both. 9.40 asks a question (“is it not better…?”); the claim states its answer. 6.36 gives a condition (“if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad”); the claim states it as a rule I keep: I count only these things as good or bad.

support.quote: if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad
gives: I count only what is up to me as good or bad for me
support.follows: Marcus proposes that we count only the things that are up to us as good or bad.

support.quote: And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us.
gives: make a difference to me
doing so leads me into many wrongs
support.follows: When things outside our choice make a difference to us, that leads us into many wrongs.

support.quote: is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation?
gives: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me
make a difference to me
letting it would be slavery
support.follows: It is better to use freely what is up to me than to let what is not up to me make a difference to me, which is slavery.

claims.t: No one is to be blamed: not the gods, not people, and not things. I do not accuse a god, I do not take an enemy’s stand against a person, and I am not angry with things, which do not care at all.
claims.shared: 8.15 and 12.9 both contain the same words, “no one is to be blamed”. 12.9 and 6.36 both name the gods and people together. 8.15’s “no one” is equally “nothing” in the Greek, and 7.25 says the same of things: they are not to be raged at.
claims.changed: 6.36 says there is no cause left for accusing a god or taking an enemy’s stand, once only what is up to us counts as good or bad; the claim states the conduct without the condition, which claim c1 gives. 7.25 speaks of anger at things, not of blame; the claim puts both under “not to be blamed”.

support.quote: No one is to be blamed.
gives: No one is to be blamed
not things
support.follows: No one, and nothing, is to be blamed for what goes wrong.

support.quote: The gods are not to be blamed
gives: not the gods
I do not accuse a god
support.follows: The gods are not to be blamed.

support.quote: Nor are people, for they go wrong in nothing except unwillingly.
gives: not people
support.follows: People are not to be blamed either, since whatever they go wrong in, they go wrong in unwillingly.

support.quote: So no one is to be blamed.
gives: No one is to be blamed
support.follows: Since neither the gods nor people are to be blamed, no one is.

support.quote: no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person
gives: not the gods
not people
I do not accuse a god
I do not take an enemy’s stand against a person
support.follows: Once only what is up to us counts as good or bad, there is no cause to accuse a god or to stand against a person as an enemy.

support.quote: For one must not be angry with things, for they do not care at all.
gives: not things
I am not angry with things, which do not care at all
support.follows: One must not be angry with things, because they do not care at all.

claims.role: When the gods seem to neglect
claims.t: The gods go wrong in nothing. If they have neglected me and my children, or seem to have overlooked very good people, who once dead do not come to be again, this too has its reason: they would not let anything be neglected unjustly and against reason, and if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise.
claims.shared: 7.25 and 12.4 both face a neglect by the gods and both answer with reason: in 7.25, if I and my two children have been “neglected by the gods, this too has its reason”; in 12.4 the gods, who seem to have “overlooked” very good people, would not let anything be “neglected unjustly and against reason”. 12.9 gives the ground both rest on: the gods go wrong in nothing.
claims.changed: 7.25 grants the neglect as a condition and gives it a reason. 12.4 asks how the gods could have overlooked the very good and answers that nothing is neglected unjustly; “seem” is said of 12.4’s case only. 12.4’s case is particular: very good people who, once dead, may not come to be again.

support.quote: for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly
gives: The gods go wrong in nothing
support.follows: The gods go wrong in nothing, neither on purpose nor against their will.

support.quote: But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.
gives: If they have neglected me and my children
this too has its reason
support.follows: Even if the gods have neglected me and my children, there is a reason for that too.

support.quote: overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones
gives: seem to have overlooked very good people
support.follows: It looks as if the gods, who arranged everything well, overlooked one thing: what becomes of very good people after death.

support.quote: they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason
gives: this too has its reason
they would not let anything be neglected unjustly and against reason
support.follows: If the gods are best and most just, nothing in the order of things has been neglected unjustly or against reason.

support.quote: be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise
gives: if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise
support.follows: If things ought to have been otherwise, the gods would have made them otherwise.

claims.t: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it. Another person’s wrong is up to them, and I cannot escape it. What I can do is set that person right if I can, or else at least put the situation right; and if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
claims.shared: 8.15 and 7.41 both split a wrong into mine and another’s, and both say that mine is the one I can deal with: 8.15 “If it is up to you, why do you do it? If it is up to another …”; 7.41 “one’s own vice, which is in fact possible” to flee, and “that of others, which is impossible”.
claims.changed: 8.15 asks questions; the claim states their answers. 8.15 does not say what “it” is; the claim takes it to be a wrong, as 7.41’s “vice” is. 7.41’s “flee” is rendered “escape”: I cannot rid myself of other people’s vice as I can of my own. 8.15’s “the thing itself” is rendered “the situation”.

support.quote: If it is up to you, why do you do it?
gives: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to me, I have no reason to go on doing it.

support.quote: It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.
gives: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it
Another person’s wrong
I cannot escape it
support.follows: I can get clear of my own vice and cannot get clear of other people’s, so it is ridiculous to try the second and not the first.

support.quote: If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame?
gives: Another person’s wrong
is up to them
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to someone else, there is no one and nothing for me to blame.

support.quote: For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you?
gives: set that person right if I can, or else at least put the situation right; and if I can do neither, blaming serves no end
support.follows: I should correct the other person if I can, or else the thing itself; if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.

claims.t: When I let what is not up to me count as good or bad, I make a case against the gods: I blame them for what I met with or missed, or I argue with them about what is just; and I hate the people who caused it. The way back is to stop grumbling and become simpler and better toward the gods.
claims.shared: 6.36 and 12.4 both describe a charge brought against the gods: 6.36 “you blame the gods”, 12.4 “you are arguing a case of justice with god”. 9.35 names the grumbling and turns it back: “toward the gods too … become simpler and better”.
claims.changed: In 12.4 the prying is part of an argument: that we argue a case of justice with god shows we hold the gods to be just. The claim keeps only the prying, which the word itself marks as going beyond what is proper. 9.35 does not say what the grumbling is about. Joining 12.4’s arguing with god to 6.36’s condition (letting what is not up to me count as good or bad) is the editor’s reading: 12.4 pries into the fate of the very good after death and does not give that cause. 12.4 says “god” in the singular; the claim says “them”, the gods named in the same sentence.

support.quote: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause
gives: When I let what is not up to me count as good or bad
I make a case against the gods
I blame them for what I met with or missed
I hate the people who caused it
support.follows: Whoever counts things outside their choice as good or bad will blame the gods and hate people when they meet or miss those things.

support.quote: For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god.
gives: I make a case against the gods
I argue with them about what is just
support.follows: Prying into why the good do not come to be again after death is arguing a case of justice with god.

support.quote: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping.
gives: stop grumbling
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to have done with a wretched life of grumbling and putting on an act.

support.quote: But toward the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.
gives: and become simpler and better toward the gods
support.follows: It is time to become simpler and better toward the gods as well.

single.label: Turning prayers round
single.t: I turn my prayers round. Instead of praying not to lose my child, I pray not to be afraid of losing it.
single.quote: Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It is kept as the article’s practice: a way of asking for what is up to me.
single.follows: I should pray not to be afraid of losing my child, instead of praying not to lose it, and see what happens.

single.label: Looking at it
single.t: When I am troubled, I ask what is new in it, and I look at its cause and at what it is made of. There is nothing more to it than these.
single.quote: Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.why: Only this passage gives questions to put to whatever troubles me. Article 4 asks about causes in general; here it is done at the moment of trouble.
single.follows: When something troubles me, I should look at its cause and at what it is made of, since there is nothing more to it.

single.label: Not joining in
single.t: When others lament, I do not join in the wailing, and I do not let my pulse race.
single.quote: No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of others’ lamenting and of my own agitation. Its two instructions are kept as a practice.
single.follows: I should not join others in lamenting, and I should not let myself grow agitated.

single.label: Giving up on bad people
single.t: When I give up on bad people, I remember that the gods, who are immortal, put up with them and care for them. I am about to come to an end, and I am one of the bad ones myself.
single.quote: The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people, such as they are and so many. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the gods’ patience with bad people. It names a failure, giving up on them, and sets the gods’ care against it.
single.follows: If the immortal gods bear with bad people and care for them, I, who will soon die and am bad myself, have no ground to give up on them.

single.label: Either way
single.t: Whether what happens comes from the atoms or from the gods, blaming either is madness.
single.quote: The atoms or the gods? Both are madness.
single.why: Only this passage argues by cases: blame is mad whichever account of the world is true, chance or the gods. It is kept as what still holds if I doubt that the gods govern.
single.follows: Whether things come about by the atoms or by the gods, blaming either is madness.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 6.36 is 6.41, 12.4 is 12.5, 8.15 is 8.17, 7.25 is 7.38 to 7.43, 7.41 is 7.70 to 7.71, 9.40 is 9.40, 9.35 is 9.37a and 12.9 is 12.11b to 12.12.

Changes the title from “What is not in my power” to “Blaming no one for what is not up to me”. Five of the eight passages are about blame or anger at gods, people or things; what is up to me is the ground they give for it.

Reads the “prying” of 12.4 as a failure, as the Greek word marks it (going beyond what is proper). In 12.4 the same sentence is also a step of an argument that the gods are just; the article does not quote that step and mentions it only in `limit`.

Takes “make a difference” as the translators render the idiom shared by 6.36 (διαφορά) and 9.40 (διαφέρεσθαι πρός). Their notes give another reading, “quarrels over” or “be at odds with”; on either reading the two passages use the same idiom, so claim c1 holds.

Reads 8.15’s “No one is to be blamed” as also “nothing”, as the Greek allows (Οὐδενί), so that 8.15 and 7.25 meet on “not things” in claim c2. 8.15’s two cases, the atoms or the gods, are kept apart under “If I doubt it”.

Reads 7.41’s “do you give up” as giving up on bad people, from the gods’ patience with them in the sentence before. The Greek verb (ἀπαυδᾷς) has no object and could mean giving up from weariness in general.

Every line of 7.25 but the last is a quoted verse, which the translators (from memory) take to be from lost plays; the two used here, “one must not be angry with things” (7.25a) and “if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods” (7.25b), are verses Marcus copied out and keeps as his own maxims. Leaves out three of the other lines: the wish for joys to the gods, the line on reaping life like grain, and “what is right is with me”; none says anything about blame. Also leaves out 12.9’s fragment “What follows in order on nature.” and most of the question that opens 12.4; claim c3 quotes only its words on the very good being overlooked.
articles.limit: Articles 3, 4, 7 and 8 already say that I do not complain of what happens, that the reason governing the world has no cause to do evil, that my judgment is up to me, and that only my judgment makes a thing harm me; Article 19 says that I teach or bear with whoever wrongs me and that the gods too are kind to such people (close to claim c4 and the said-once 7.41a), Article 28 that I leave another person’s wrong with them, and Article 4 already quotes Seneca’s Ep. 95.50 (S95.50b). What this article adds is blame: since I count only what is up to me as good or bad, I have no one to blame, the gods, people or things, and my own wrongdoing is the one thing I can stop. Its weak point is claim c3: the gods’ justice is asserted, not argued, apart from 12.4’s step that we would not argue a case of justice with gods who were not just.

statement.t: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me, and I blame no one for it, neither the gods nor people.

parts.words: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me
I blame no one for it
neither the gods nor people

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Claims c1 and c3 are the ground: I count only what is up to me as good or bad, and the gods go wrong in nothing. Claims c2 and c4 are the conduct that follows: no one is to be blamed, and my own wrong is what I can stop. 6.36 itself draws the line from the ground to the conduct, so the “and” of the statement needs no inference of the editor’s. Claim c5 is the failure and the way back.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the slavery of claim c1 and the case against the gods in claim c5 gain a second author; what I do gains philosophy turned on my own faults, the practice gains happiness without vows, and “If I doubt it” gains a second answer to the gods’ neglect. He limits two claims: the gods are sometimes unmindful of the individual, and for the harm we bring on ourselves we can complain of ourselves.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, and he adds what holds if the gods do neglect me: the worst would be to be at odds with myself.

items.quote: It means not being a slave to any circumstance, to any constraint, to any chance
gives: letting it would be slavery
items.follows: To be free is to be no slave to any circumstance, constraint or chance.
items.context: Letter 51, written from the pleasure resort of Baiae: Seneca resolves not to yield to Fortune or to pleasure. “It” is freedom, which he has set before his eyes.

items.quote: For if he regards anything else as good, he is, in the first place, passing an unfavourable judgment upon Providence
gives: I make a case against the gods
items.follows: Whoever counts anything but the honourable as good ends by judging Providence unfavourably.
items.context: Letter 74 says that whoever wants to be happy must hold that only the honourable is good. “He” is that person; the next words give his grievance: upright men suffer misfortunes.

items.label: action
items.t: I use philosophy to strip off my own faults, not to decry the faults of others, and I do not use it to condemn every way of living that I do not follow myself.
items.why: 7.41 and 8.15 say that my own wrong is the one I can deal with. Seneca says what that means for what I have learned: it is for my own faults, not a means of finding fault with other people.

support.quote: Let her strip off your faults, rather than assist you to decry the faults of others.
gives: I use philosophy to strip off my own faults, not to decry the faults of others
support.follows: Philosophy should be used to remove my own faults, not to help me decry other people’s.
support.context: The end of Letter 103, on the dangers that come from other people. “Her” is philosophy, in which Seneca has just told Lucilius to take refuge, without vaunting it.

support.quote: Let her not hold aloof from the customs of mankind, nor make it her business to condemn whatever she herself does not do.
gives: I do not use it to condemn every way of living that I do not follow myself
support.follows: Philosophy should not stand apart from ordinary life or condemn whatever it does not itself do.
support.context: Letter 103, on the dangers that come from other people, ends by warning that philosophy must not be vaunted. “She” is philosophy, which must not set itself against everyone else’s ways.

items.label: practice
items.t: I do not pick and choose by prayer what fortune should fall to me. I make myself happy through my own efforts, knowing that whatever is joined to virtue is good and whatever is joined to vice is bad.
items.why: 9.40 keeps praying and turns the prayer toward what is up to me. Seneca asks what need there is of vows at all: the happiness I would pray for is made by my own efforts. This is a difference: 9.40 answers that very objection (“who told you that the gods do not also lend a hand with the things that are up to us?”), and Seneca himself elsewhere tells Lucilius to pray for a sound mind (Ep. 10.4).

support.quote: There is, then, no reason why, in accordance with that old vow of your parents, you should pick and choose what fortune you wish should fall to your lot, or what you should pray for
gives: I do not pick and choose by prayer what fortune should fall to me
support.follows: Lucilius has no reason to choose by prayer what fortune he wants, as his parents once prayed for him.
support.context: Letter 31 tells Lucilius to be deaf to the wishes of those who love him. The “old vow” is his parents’ prayer for his success, which Seneca says he no longer needs.

support.quote: What need is there of vows? Make yourself happy through your own efforts; you can do this, if once you comprehend that whatever is blended with virtue is good, and that whatever is joined to vice is bad.
gives: I make myself happy through my own efforts
whatever is joined to virtue is good and whatever is joined to vice is bad
support.follows: No vows are needed: I can make myself happy by my own efforts once I see that only what goes with virtue is good.
support.context: Letter 31, on not heeding the prayers of those who love us. Seneca says a man who has held the highest offices should stop importuning the gods; “this” is being happy.

items.label: doubt
items.t: Whether a guardian has been set over me or I have been neglected and left to Fortune, nothing worse can be wished on me than to be at odds with myself.
items.why: Marcus’s answer in 7.25 to being neglected by the gods is that this too has its reason. Seneca adds a second answer that does not depend on the gods: whether I am guarded or neglected, the worst that can happen to me is to be at odds with myself.

support.quote: whether we are allotted to special guardians, or whether we are neglected and consigned to Fortune, you can curse a man with no heavier curse than to pray that he may be at enmity with himself
gives: Whether a guardian has been set over me or I have been neglected and left to Fortune
nothing worse can be wished on me than to be at odds with myself
support.follows: Whether or not the gods look after us, the heaviest curse on anyone is to be at enmity with himself.
support.context: Letter 110 opens on whether each of us has a guardian god. Seneca puts off asking whether the gods care for individuals; “a man” is anyone one might wish harm on.

items.t: Marcus says that if the gods have neglected me, this too has its reason (7.25), and that they would not let anything be neglected unjustly (12.4). Seneca states as a fact that the gods are sometimes unmindful of the individual, and gives no reason for it: they are guardians of the human race (Ep. 95.50). In Ep. 110.2 he leaves open whether the gods care for individuals at all, which sits uneasily with stating it here. This limits the claim; Ep. 95.50 itself affirms the gods’ goodness.

support.quote: acting as guardians of the human race, even though they are sometimes unmindful of the individual
support.follows: The gods guard the human race, though they sometimes do not attend to the individual.
support.context: Letter 95 says how to worship the gods: believe in them and acknowledge their goodness. “Acting as guardians” is said of the gods, who rule the universe.

items.t: Seneca does not blame God, but he does not say that no one is to blame: for the harm humankind has brought on itself by digging up what Nature hid, we can complain of nothing but ourselves (Ep. 110.10). Marcus excuses people because they go wrong only unwillingly; Seneca keeps one complaint, against ourselves. This limits the claim; the complaint he keeps is not against the gods.

support.quote: We can complain of nothing but ourselves; for we have brought to light the materials for our destruction, against the will of Nature, who hid them from us.
support.follows: For the harm we suffer from what we dug up against Nature’s will, we can complain only of ourselves.
support.context: Letter 110, on true and false riches: God put good things within reach and buried what harms. “We” are humankind, who dug up gold and the like out of greed.

amend.t: ; whether or not the gods watch over me, the worst for me is to be at odds with myself
; but they guard the human race and are sometimes unmindful of the individual
; but for the harm we bring on ourselves, we can complain of no one but ourselves

searches: in our power, within our power, in your power
complain (with god, heaven, providence, fortune, nature)
vices of others, faults of others
err (with ignorance, unwillingly, against his will)

rejected.why: The good man endures what happens and does not blaze out in anger at misfortune. About enduring fate, near Article 3; it does not speak of blaming people.
Straying from Nature makes one a slave to the things of chance. Says what 51.9 says; 51.9 defines the freedom directly and is quoted.
The gods cannot do harm. About harm, not about going wrong; the match to “the gods go wrong in nothing” needs explaining.
Do not rail at Nature; endure what you cannot reform. Already in Article 3; about enduring, not about blame.
Pray for a sound mind and for health of soul. Says what to pray for, as 9.40 does, and adds nothing to it; Article 6 already uses Letter 10.
We complain about the gifts of heaven because they are few and fleeting. Continues 74.10, which carries the point and is quoted.
Mourners lament louder for being seen. About grief put on show; it matches only the said-once 7.25 line, which takes no backing.
What you run from is within you; reform yourself. “Run away” means travel, which cannot escape one’s vices: another sense of “flee” from 7.41.
Seneca will not cure his fellow men while ill himself. About his standing to give advice, not about whose fault is whose.
Lucilius mourns Metronax as dead too soon. About the time of a death; Article 6 uses Letter 93.
Be content with goods that spring from yourself; commit other prayers to God. Near 31.5, which says it more directly.
Entreat the gods that the fond wishes of those who love you not come true. A turned prayer like 9.40, but about others’ wishes for me; 31.5 is used.
Whatever Chance holds sway over is a chattel. About the worth of virtue under fortune, not about blame.
The prayers of our own family are hostile to us. About what others pray for on our behalf.
The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue. About an act and its outcome; Article 2 uses it.
Take refuge in philosophy from the harm other people do. The refuge, not the use of philosophy on oneself; 103.5 is used.

articles.title: Happiness and unhappiness are my own doing

claims.t: Whether I am happy or unhappy is decided in my own soul. Happiness is a good ruling part. If I do not keep track of what moves in my own soul, I am bound to be unhappy; not attending to what goes on in someone else’s soul hardly ever makes anyone unhappy.
claims.shared: The two passages speak of one thing from its two sides: 7.14 says what “happiness” is, 2.5 who is “unhappy” (in Greek the two words are built on the same root). Both look for it inside the person: 7.14 in the “ruling part”, 2.5 in “their own soul”.
claims.changed: “Is decided in my own soul” is the editor’s summary of the two; it takes the ruling part to be the leading part of my own soul. 7.14 says “a good spirit, or a good ruling part”, and the claim keeps the second name. 2.5 says “hardly anyone has been seen”; the claim says “hardly ever”.

support.quote: Happiness is a good spirit, or a good ruling part.
gives: Whether I am happy or unhappy
is decided in my own soul
Happiness is a good ruling part
support.follows: Happiness is having a good spirit, or a good ruling part.

support.quote: But those who do not keep track of the movements of their own soul are bound to be unhappy.
gives: Whether I am happy or unhappy
is decided in my own soul
If I do not keep track of what moves in my own soul, I am bound to be unhappy
support.follows: People who do not keep track of what moves in their own soul are certain to be unhappy.

support.quote: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy through not attending to what goes on in another person’s soul.
gives: not attending to what goes on in someone else’s soul hardly ever makes anyone unhappy
support.follows: Hardly anyone has been seen to be unhappy because they did not attend to what goes on in another person’s soul.

claims.t: I am content with my ruling part doing what it is made to do; when I was not content with it, I had countless things to endure. What I have in myself is enough: it gives me everything useful for my life, and I need nothing besides.
claims.shared: 9.24 and 4.24 both blame a person for not finding enough in themselves: “not content with your ruling part”, “does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life”. In the English, 4.24 and 7.14 share the word “need”, which stands for two different Greek words: the beggar is “in need of another”, and Marcus tells an impression “I do not need you”.
claims.changed: 9.24 and 4.24 describe the failure (“you were not content”, “a beggar”); the claim states the rule and keeps 9.24’s failure beside it. “Everything useful for my life” is 4.24’s alone; 9.24 speaks only of the ruling part. 7.14 says “I do not need you” to one impression and 4.24 says “another”; the claim says “nothing besides” for both. The Greek verb in 7.14 can also mean “want” (“I do not want you”); on that reading “I need nothing besides”, here and in the statement, would rest on 4.24 alone. 9.24 says “because”; the claim says “when”.

support.quote: You have endured countless things because you were not content with your ruling part doing the kind of things it is made to do.
gives: I am content with my ruling part doing what it is made to do
when I was not content with it, I had countless things to endure
What I have in myself is enough
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he endured countless things because he was not content with his ruling part doing what it is made to do.

support.quote: A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life.
gives: What I have in myself is enough
it gives me everything useful for my life
I need nothing besides
support.follows: Whoever needs another and does not have from themselves everything useful for life is a beggar.

support.quote: So what are you doing here, impression? Go away, by the gods, as you came: for I do not need you.
gives: I need nothing besides
support.follows: Marcus asks an impression what it is doing here and tells it to go away as it came, because he does not need it.

claims.t: When I do not want what happens, I desert the very thing that sends it. Displeased with it, I stand apart and separate myself from the common nature, which brings it and brought me forth too. Distressed, angry or afraid, I am a runaway slave: I flee from my master, the law, which governs all things and deals out to each what falls to them.
claims.shared: Both passages name a person who is against what happens: “displeased with what happens” (4.24), “does not want one of the things appointed” (10.25). Both say that this person is the one who leaves: in 4.24 whoever “stands apart and separates themselves”, in 10.25 the slave who “flees”. And both say that what is left is what sends the event: the nature that “brings this forth”, the law that “deals out all that falls to each”.
claims.changed: “The very thing that sends it” joins 4.24’s common nature and 10.25’s governor of all things, who is law. “I desert” stands for standing apart and separating in 4.24 and for fleeing in 10.25; the word is the editor’s, chosen because both passages blame the one who leaves (an abscess, a runaway slave). The statement names the two for a reader who meets it alone: “nature and the law that send it”. 4.24 says “the reason of the common nature”; the claim shortens it to “the common nature”. 4.24’s image of the abscess is left to the quote. Its exile leaves a different thing, the reason that belongs to citizens, and stands as a said-once item.

support.quote: An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens
gives: When I do not want what happens
I desert
Displeased with it, I stand apart and separate myself from the common nature
support.follows: Whoever is displeased with what happens separates themselves from the reason of the common nature, as an abscess stands apart.

support.quote: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too
gives: the very thing that sends it
which brings it and brought me forth too
support.follows: The nature that brings this event is the same nature that brought you into being.

support.quote: Whoever flees from their master is a runaway slave. And the law is master
gives: I desert
I am a runaway slave
I flee from my master, the law
support.follows: Someone who flees from their master is a runaway slave, and the law is master.

support.quote: But whoever is distressed or angry or afraid, too, does not want one of the things appointed by the one who governs all things to have happened, or to be happening, or to be going to happen
gives: When I do not want what happens
Distressed, angry or afraid
support.follows: Whoever is distressed, angry or afraid does not want something that the one who governs all things appointed, past, present or to come.

support.quote: and the one who governs all things is law, as the one who deals out all that falls to each
gives: the very thing that sends it
which governs all things and deals out to each what falls to them
support.follows: The one who governs all things is law: the one who deals out all that falls to each.

support.quote: So whoever is afraid or distressed or angry is a runaway slave.
gives: Distressed, angry or afraid
I am a runaway slave
support.follows: Whoever is afraid, distressed or angry is therefore a runaway slave.

single.label: A practice
single.t: When an impression comes out of old habit, I am not angry with it. I only tell it to go away.
single.quote: But you have come out of old habit. I am not angry with you. Only go away.
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say. It adds two things no other passage has: the impression comes out of old habit, and it is sent away without anger.
single.follows: The impression has come out of old habit; Marcus is not angry with it and only tells it to go away.

single.label: An exile by my own act
single.t: I am an exile when I exile myself from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.quote: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of exile. “The reason that belongs to citizens” is, by the translators’ note, the reason of those who live together as citizens of the one city that all rational beings share. The passage does not say that the exile is against what happens, so the exile is not joined to claim 3.
single.follows: A person becomes an exile by exiling themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens.

single.label: Blind by my own act
single.t: I am blind when I shut the eye of my own mind.
single.quote: Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of sight. It does not say what the eye of the mind should be looking at, so it is not joined to 2.5 on keeping track of my own soul.
single.follows: To be blind, in the sense meant here, is to shut the eye of the mind.

single.label: Breaking off
single.t: When I catch myself going over all I endured because I was not content with my ruling part, I stop: enough.
single.quote: But enough.
single.why: Only this passage ends with an order to stop, the nearest thing in the section to a way back. The first half of the line comes from the sentence of 9.24 just before these words, which is quoted under the claim on being content. The Greek does not say what there has been enough of. The line takes it as enough of going over what was endured; it could also be enough of the enduring itself.
single.follows: Marcus breaks off with two words: but enough.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 4.24 is 4.29 without its first sentence, 2.5 is 2.8, 7.14 is 7.17 and 9.24 is 9.26; 10.25 is the same.

Keeps “a good ruling part” and leaves “a good spirit” (7.14) to the quote. The Greek word for happiness contains the word for spirit, which English cannot show, and the “or” between the two names can also mean “that is”.

Turns two descriptions of a failure into a rule: 9.24’s “you were not content” becomes “I am content”, and 4.24’s beggar, who is “in need of another”, becomes “I need nothing besides”. Neither passage states the rule in the positive.

Reads the common nature that “brings this forth” (4.24) and the one who governs all things, who is law (10.25), as what sends what happens; “the very thing that sends it” (claim 3), “nature and the law that send it” (the statement) and “I desert” are the editor’s words for what the two say. Keeps 4.24’s exile out of that claim, because the exile leaves the reason that belongs to citizens and is not said to be against what happens.

Leaves out two sentences of quoted passages. The last sentence of 4.24, on splitting one’s own soul off from the one soul of rational beings, is about my tie to other people, which Article 1 states. The step in 10.25 about whoever breaks the law is the middle of the argument and is not about what happens to me; the conclusion it leads to is quoted.
articles.limit: Article 1 already says that resenting what happens cuts me off from the whole, and Article 3 that I accept what happens and do not complain. Claim 3’s “Displeased with it, I stand apart and separate myself from the common nature” is close to Article 3’s item from 5.8, that each time I am displeased with what happens I cut through the connection of the whole, and its “brought me forth too” is close to Article 3’s first claim, that what happens comes from the same causes that produced me. Claim 2 is close to Article 2, whose fourth claim says that doing my work makes me content and whose item from 7.30 says that my mind then has all that belongs to it, and it is nearly the same as Article 18’s first claim, that a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me. The same words of Seneca’s Ep. 98.2 back that claim and this article’s claim 1. Claims 1 and 2 are also near Article 12, which says that I keep watch over what is within me rather than guess what others think, and that I am content with my present state. What this article adds is that my happiness or unhappiness is decided in my own soul, and that distress, anger and fear are a flight from a master. The section has two strands that no passage joins: 2.5, 7.14 and 9.24 are about my own soul, 10.25 is about the law of the whole, and only 4.24 touches both, so it feeds two claims. Claim 1 rests on two short passages, each of which gives one side of it.

statement.t: My happiness is decided in my own soul, and I need nothing besides; not wanting what happens, I desert nature and the law that send it.

parts.words: My happiness is decided in my own soul
I need nothing besides
not wanting what happens
I desert nature and the law that send it

statement.kind: A ground, what follows from it, and the failure named
statement.form: Claim 1 says where happiness and unhappiness are decided; “is decided in my own soul” is the editor’s summary of 7.14’s “ruling part” and 2.5’s “their own soul”. Claim 2 draws what follows for me: what I have in myself is enough (9.24, 4.24, 7.14). Claim 3 names the failure: whoever does not want what happens deserts what sends it, the common nature in 4.24 and the law in 10.25. No passage joins the first two claims to the third; setting them in one statement is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section considers what would still hold if my happiness were not decided in my own soul, so Marcus gives nothing under this label.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first claim gains two witnesses and the second one. The article gains a sentence that the editor reads as joining its two halves (being under orders does not make me unhappy; acting against my will does), the spirit within, a daily review, a way back, and an answer to an objection. He limits the second claim: the wise man is enough for a happy life, not for staying alive.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a sentence that the editor reads as joining its two halves: being under orders does not make me unhappy; acting against my will does. “I need nothing besides” holds for a happy life, not for staying alive.

items.quote: the soul is more powerful than any sort of Fortune; by its own agency it guides its affairs in either direction, and of its own power it can produce a happy life, or a wretched one
gives: Whether I am happy or unhappy
is decided in my own soul
items.follows: The soul is stronger than Fortune, and by its own power it can make a life happy or wretched.
items.context: Letter 98, on not leaning on Fortune’s gifts: Fortune hands us only the raw material of goods and ills. “Its affairs” are the soul’s own, turned by it to good or ill.

items.quote: the happy life depends upon this and this alone: our attainment of perfect reason
gives: Happiness is a good ruling part
items.follows: The happy life depends on one thing only: reaching perfect reason.
items.context: Opening of Letter 92, on the happy life: the soul has a primary part whose rational side commands the rest. “This” is perfect reason in that commanding part.

items.quote: he keeps to the heights, leaning upon none but himself; for one who sustains himself by any prop may fall
gives: I need nothing besides
items.follows: The happy man leans on no one and nothing but himself, because whoever is held up by a prop may fall.
items.context: Letter 92, on the happy life: Seneca calls happy the man whom nothing makes weaker than he is. “He” is that man; a “prop” is anything outside himself that he leans on.

items.label: why
items.t: Being under orders does not make me unhappy; doing a thing against my will does. If I take my orders gladly, I escape the bitterest part of slavery, which is doing what I do not want to do.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section joins its two halves: happiness in my own soul, and the runaway who does not want what happens. Seneca ties unhappiness to unwillingness, with the same picture of orders and slavery; he does not speak here of where happiness is decided. The editor reads his sentence as joining the two halves: what makes me unhappy is not the order but my unwillingness. His slave does not run; he stays and takes the order gladly.

support.quote: The man who does something under orders is not unhappy; he is unhappy who does something against his will.
gives: Being under orders does not make me unhappy; doing a thing against my will does
support.follows: Acting under orders does not make a person unhappy; acting against one’s own will does.
support.context: Letter 61, on meeting death gladly. Seneca explains why a necessity stops being one if I want it; the orders are those of circumstances, not of a human master.

support.quote: he who takes his orders gladly, escapes the bitterest part of slavery,—doing what one does not want to do
gives: If I take my orders gladly, I escape the bitterest part of slavery, which is doing what I do not want to do
support.follows: Whoever takes his orders gladly escapes the worst of slavery, which is doing what one does not want to do.
support.context: Letter 61: Seneca, now old, says that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. The “orders” are what necessity demands, death above all.

items.label: why
items.t: A holy spirit lives within me. It marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian, and as I treat it, so it treats me.
items.why: 7.14 calls happiness “a good spirit” and says nothing more about it; the claim keeps its other name, a good ruling part. Seneca says what the spirit within does: it watches and guards me, and it treats me as I treat it. He does not call it my happiness.

support.quote: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it.
gives: A holy spirit lives within me
It marks my good and bad deeds and is my guardian
as I treat it, so it treats me
support.follows: A holy spirit lives in us, watches what we do and guards us, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41: Lucilius need not pray for a sound mind, because God is near him, with him and within him. The “holy spirit” is that god within each person.

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep watching myself and review each day. I question myself: am I ever downcast, is my mind harassed by fear of what is to come, does my soul keep its even course day and night, content with itself?
items.why: 2.5 says that I am bound to be unhappy if I do not keep track of my own soul, and gives no way of doing it. Seneca gives two: a review of each day, and questions to put to myself. In Letter 83 he says that not looking back over one’s life makes people wicked, where Marcus says unhappy.

support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day. For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life.
gives: I keep watching myself and review each day
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself and review each day, because not looking back over one’s own life is what makes people wicked.
support.context: Letter 83: Lucilius has asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, having said that God is witness of our souls. “Us” is people in general.

support.quote: Now go, question yourself; if you are never downcast, if your mind is not harassed by any apprehension, through anticipation of what is to come, if day and night your soul keeps on its even and unswerving course, upright and content with itself, then you have attained to the greatest good that mortals can possess.
gives: I question myself: am I ever downcast, is my mind harassed by fear of what is to come, does my soul keep its even course day and night, content with itself
support.follows: If I am never downcast or harassed by fear of the future, and my soul keeps an even course, content with itself, I have the greatest human good.
support.context: Letter 59, on joy: Seneca shows Lucilius how to tell that he is not yet wise, since the wise man is joyful, happy and calm. “Yourself” is Lucilius, testing his own soul.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I stray from nature I am forced to crave and to fear, and to be a slave to the things of chance. I can return to the true path and be restored to my proper state.
items.why: Marcus names the exile and the runaway and, in this section, gives no return; 9.24 only says “enough”. Seneca says the return is open. His order also differs: for Marcus the fear is itself the flight from the master; for Seneca the straying comes first and brings the fear, and with it another master, chance.

support.quote: when one strays away from Nature one is compelled to crave, and fear, and be a slave to the things of chance
gives: When I stray from nature I am forced to crave and to fear, and to be a slave to the things of chance
support.follows: Whoever strays from Nature is forced to crave, to fear and to be a slave to the things of chance.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune: after naming men who scorned riches and bore pain, Seneca asks why we lose heart. “Nature” is what we are to follow; “things of chance” are Fortune’s gifts.

support.quote: We may return to the true path; we may be restored to our proper state
gives: I can return to the true path and be restored to my proper state
support.follows: We can go back to the true path and be restored to the state that is proper to us.
support.context: Letter 98: Seneca has just said that straying from Nature brings craving, fear and slavery to chance. The “true path” is following Nature; “we” are he and Lucilius.

items.label: doubt
items.t: If my own opinion made me happy, a man who grew rich by base means would be happy as soon as he called himself so. What matters is not what I say but what I feel, and not on one day but at all times; and only the wise are pleased with what is their own.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section meets an objection. Seneca meets the nearest one: cannot anyone then decide that he is happy? He raises it against a poet’s line, that a man is unblest if he thinks himself so, and the line keeps his terms: happiness by one’s own opinion. Placing it beside this article’s statement, which says my happiness is decided in my own soul, is the editor’s step; Seneca does not speak of the soul here.
