This is an objection answered, not the case in which the statement is false; Seneca does not consider that case here. His answer is that what counts is what I feel at all times, and that only the wise are pleased with what is theirs.

support.quote: If yonder man, rich by base means, and yonder man, lord of many but slave of more, shall call themselves happy, will their own opinion make them happy?
gives: If my own opinion made me happy
a man who grew rich by base means would be happy as soon as he called himself so
support.follows: Seneca puts the objection: if base and enslaved men call themselves happy, does their own opinion make them so?
support.context: End of Letter 9, on the wise man’s self-sufficiency. Seneca has quoted the line “Unblest is he who thinks himself unblest” and lets Lucilius object to it.

support.quote: It matters not what one says, but what one feels; also, not how one feels on one particular day, but how one feels at all times.
gives: What matters is not what I say but what I feel, and not on one day but at all times
support.follows: What counts is what a person feels, not what he says, and what he feels at all times, not on one day.
support.context: End of Letter 9, on the wise man’s self-sufficiency. Seneca answers the objection that a man rich by base means could make himself happy merely by calling himself happy.

support.quote: only the wise man is pleased with his own. Folly is ever troubled with weariness of itself.
gives: only the wise are pleased with what is their own
support.follows: Only the wise man is pleased with what is his; folly is always weary of itself.
support.context: End of Letter 9: Seneca tells Lucilius not to fear that happiness by one’s own judgment will fall to the unworthy. “His own” is what the wise man has and is.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the wise man is enough for himself, and says how far that reaches: for a happy life, not for mere existence, for which he needs many helps (Ep. 9.13). He adds Chrysippus’s distinction: the wise man needs hands, eyes and many things for daily use, and yet is in want of nothing (Ep. 9.14). And the wise man still wants friends, though he would live happily without them (Ep. 9.15). Marcus’s beggar is whoever is “in need of another” for what is useful for life; Seneca’s wise man needs many things and is in want of none. This limits the claim and does not contradict it on two readings, both the editor’s: that 4.24’s “useful for life” means useful for living well, not for staying alive, and that “I do not need you” (7.14), said just after Marcus defines happiness, is about happiness. Seneca says all this of the wise man, and tells Lucilius that he is not yet one (Ep. 59.14); the clause on the claim says “I”, as Marcus’s claims do. Seneca also warns against reading the saying so that the wise man is taken out of the world.

support.quote: the wise man is sufficient unto himself for a happy existence, but not for mere existence. For he needs many helps towards mere existence; but for a happy existence he needs only a sound and upright soul, one that despises Fortune.
support.follows: The wise man is enough for himself for a happy life, not for staying alive; for happiness he needs only a sound and upright soul.
support.context: Letter 9, on friendship: Seneca explains the saying “The wise man is self-sufficient”, which many, he says, read so as to withdraw the wise man from the world.

support.quote: The wise man needs hands, eyes, and many things that are necessary for his daily use; but he is in want of nothing.
support.follows: The wise man needs hands, eyes and much else for daily use, and yet he is in want of nothing.
support.context: Letter 9: Seneca reports Chrysippus’s distinction between needing a thing and being in want of it. Want implies necessity, and nothing is necessary to the wise man.

support.quote: Therefore, although he is self-sufficient, yet he has need of friends. He craves as many friends as possible, not, however, that he may live happily; for he will live happily even without friends.
support.follows: Though self-sufficient, the wise man wants as many friends as possible, but not in order to be happy; he is happy without them.
support.context: Letter 9, answering whether the self-sufficient wise man needs friendship. “He” is the wise man; the sentence draws on the distinction between needing and being in want.

amend.t: ; being under orders does not make me unhappy, acting against my will does
; nothing, that is, for a happy life: to stay alive I need many things, and I still want friends

searches: nearest sections by vectors to c3.s10 (20)
self-sufficient, sufficient unto, content with itself
happy, happiness (with within, own soul, in the mind)
beggar, in need of, needs nothing
examine, scrutinize, watch over, observe yourself
rebel, resist, rail (with nature, law, fate, god)
unhappy, wretched, miserable (with own fault, himself, yourself)
master (with law, nature, fortune; obey, flee, escape)
another man’s, neighbour (with affairs, soul, own)

rejected.why: “Happiness has its abode in one place only, namely, in the mind itself.” Says what Ep. 98.2 says of the soul; 98.2 gives both the happy and the wretched side, so it was preferred.
The wise man’s happiness is “something within himself”. A third witness for the same words of claim 1; not needed.
“Unblest is he who thinks himself unblest.” A comic poet’s line that Seneca quotes; it is named in the context of Ep. 9.22, which is used.
The friendless sage retreats into himself as Jupiter does. A picture of the limiting case; Ep. 9.13 to 9.15 state the limit directly.
Rejoice only in what comes from your own store, the best part of you. About where joy comes from; Article 5 already quotes this section.
The happy man is he “whose possessions are all in his soul”. One clause in a long portrait, in a letter against logical quibbles.
“Under such laws do we live. If you like it, obey; if not, depart whithersoever you wish.” The law here is that cities and people perish; it is not the law that deals out what falls to each.
“No man is unhappy except by his own fault”, but the ground is that anyone may leave life. A letter on suicide; not about where happiness is decided.
“A man is as wretched as he has convinced himself that he is.” About not dwelling on past pain in illness; close, but 98.2 says it more generally.
Travel does not help, because you bring your own character along. About changing place, not about what my soul needs.
“You are your own stumbling-block.” About Lucilius’s hesitation to leave his present life.
Virtue needs nothing because it is pleased with what it has. Said of virtue, not of me; Ep. 92.2 says it of the happy man.
No one can be happy who yields to fears at a neighbour’s misfortune. About fear of sudden evils, not about another person’s soul.
“Fear means slavery.” An argument that honourable acts are voluntary; a slave, but not one who runs from a master.
“Look into your own soul”: to value a man, strip off his trappings. About judging worth, not about keeping track of what moves in the soul.
Mentions the Genius assigned to each person, and tells Lucilius to lay that belief aside for the present. Ep. 41.2 states the spirit within outright.
A mind in blind panic “runs away” from danger. Flight from danger, not from a master or a law.
Do not rail at Nature; a bad soldier grumbles at his commander. Already in Article 3, and about enduring.
“All vices rebel against Nature.” About luxury and turning night into day.
The man banished to seclusion by his own desires. Near 4.24 by vectors, but about a false retirement; Article 5 quotes it.

articles.title: Ready to leave

claims.t: My time is short: very soon I will leave all this behind, and any moment now I will be dead. What is left now is little.
claims.shared: All three say that the end is close, each in its own words: “very soon” (10.12), “any moment now” (4.30), “what is left now is little” (10.17).
claims.changed: 10.12 speaks of “such a person” and 4.30 speaks to “you”; the claim says “I”. 10.17 does not say what is left; the claim takes it to be time.

support.quote: having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people
gives: My time is short
very soon I will leave all this behind
support.follows: The person described has understood that very soon they must leave all this behind and go from among people.

support.quote: Any moment now you will be dead
gives: My time is short
any moment now I will be dead
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he will be dead any moment now.

support.quote: What is left now is little.
gives: My time is short
What is left now is little
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that little is left now.

claims.t: I am ready to go, and I go as one who suffers nothing bad: dying is nothing much, one of the acts of my life. If my mind has been disciplined and cleaned out, then whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished.
claims.shared: 5.23 and 6.2 both say that dying matters little: “Why do you think it anything much?” (5.23) and “Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting … whether dying” (6.2). 5.23 and 3.9 both describe someone ready to leave: “There is smoke, and I leave” (5.23), a life that fate does not overtake unfinished (3.9).
claims.changed: 5.23 says that one should go out of life as one who suffers nothing bad; the claim keeps this as the manner of going, and takes for any death the calm that 5.23 speaks of when others do not allow one to live rightly. 6.2 says only that dying should make no difference to doing what is fitting; “dying is nothing much” is wider. “I am ready to go” is said without 3.9’s condition; the claim’s last sentence keeps it.

support.quote: as one who is suffering nothing bad
gives: I go as one who suffers nothing bad
support.follows: If one has to go out of life, one goes as someone who is suffering nothing bad.

support.quote: There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much?
gives: I am ready to go
dying is nothing much
support.follows: When there is smoke, Marcus leaves, and he asks why one should think leaving any great matter.

support.quote: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act.
gives: dying is nothing much
support.follows: Whether I am dying or doing something else, as with cold or praise, it should make no difference to doing what is fitting.

support.quote: For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die.
gives: one of the acts of my life
support.follows: Dying is one of the acts of life.

support.quote: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus
gives: If my mind has been disciplined and cleaned out
support.follows: A mind that has been disciplined and cleansed has nothing festering in it.

support.quote: Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the play through.
gives: I am ready to go
whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished
support.follows: Whenever death comes to such a person, their life is not left unfinished, like a play an actor walks out of.

claims.t: I do not pretend or play a part. The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence, with nothing affected or hidden in me.
claims.shared: 9.2 and 7.40 both refuse pretence: “any pretence” (9.2) and “nor to play a part” (7.40). In the Greek the two are one word, the noun ὑπόκρισις and its verb.
claims.changed: 9.2 says that going without having tasted pretence would have been the finer course, one already missed; the claim names it as the finer thing, and says “leave this life” for 9.2’s “go from among people”, and does not say that I can still have it. 9.2 names lying, luxury and vanity beside pretence; the claim keeps pretence. From 3.9’s longer list the claim keeps “affected” and, as “hidden”, “lurking in a hole”.

support.quote: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part
The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence
support.follows: It would have been finer to leave life without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity.

support.quote: nor to play a part
gives: I do not pretend or play a part
support.follows: A perfect character does not play a part.

support.quote: nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole
gives: with nothing affected or hidden in me
support.follows: In a cleansed mind there is nothing slavish, affected or hidden, and nothing that has to answer for itself.

claims.t: The place makes no difference: I can live here the way I mean to live, according to nature, wherever I am. If the people around me do not allow it, I would rather die than live another way.
claims.shared: Both say that the life one means to live can be lived where one is: “you can live that way here” (5.23), “it makes no difference whether there or here” (10.17). Both call it a life by nature, and both say what to do if others will not have it: “if they do not allow it, then go out of life” (5.23), “If they do not bear it, let them kill that person” (10.17).
claims.changed: 5.23 speaks of going out of life oneself, 10.17 of being killed by others; the claim says only “die”. In 10.17 “that way” is open: it may mean living as those people live. 10.17 says that the place makes no difference if a person lives in the universe as in a city; the claim does not repeat that condition.

support.quote: The way you have in mind to live once you have gone out, you can live that way here.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live
support.follows: The life one plans to live after leaving can be lived here already.

support.quote: Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live
wherever I am
support.follows: One can live as on a mountain anywhere, since the place makes no difference to someone whose city is the universe.

support.quote: Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature.
gives: according to nature
support.follows: Marcus asks that people see and study a true human being living according to nature.

support.quote: And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living creature.
gives: according to nature
support.follows: What Marcus wants is what fits the nature of a rational and social creature.

support.quote: But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die
support.follows: If others do not let one live that way, one should go out of life.

support.quote: If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die
than live another way
support.follows: If people cannot bear a person who lives by nature, being killed by them is better than living that way.

single.label: Free while I stay
single.t: As long as nothing leads me out of life, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.quote: But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.why: Only 5.23 says that staying is free. “Of that kind” in the quote refers to the smoke just before it: something that makes staying impossible. 10.23’s first case, living here and being used to it, is about staying too, but it does not say that staying is free.
single.follows: Until something like the smoke leads Marcus out, he stays, free, and no one stops him from doing what he wants.

single.label: Every day as the last
single.t: I live through every day as if it were my last, neither feverish nor numb.
single.quote: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb
single.why: Only 7.40 in this section gives an exercise for each day. Its last words, on playing no part, feed claim 3.
single.follows: A perfect character lives each day as the last, without agitation and without numbness.

single.label: The next best course
single.t: If I have tasted lying and pretence, the next best thing is at least to be sick of them when I die. I do not stay sitting beside vice: a corrupt mind is a worse plague than any sickness of the air.
single.quote: But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around.
single.why: Only 9.2 gives a way back for someone who has already failed: to grow sick of these things before the end and to flee the plague.
single.follows: Having tasted these vices, the next best course is to die sick of them, since staying with vice is staying with a worse plague.

single.label: The piglet at the sacrifice
single.t: When I am pained or displeased at anything, I am like the piglet at the sacrifice that kicks and squeals, and no less so when I lament alone on my bed, in silence.
single.quote: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence.
single.why: Only 10.28 pictures what failing looks like. Its last sentence, on following what happens willingly, is left to Article 10.
single.follows: Whoever is pained or displeased at what happens is like a sacrificial piglet kicking, even when they lament in silence.

single.label: Three cases
single.t: Either I go on living here, and I am used to it by now; or I go away from here, as I wanted; or I die, and my service is complete. There is no other case, so I can be of good heart.
single.quote: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be of good heart.
single.why: Only 10.23 argues by cases, and it holds whether or not death comes soon, so it stands under doubt. Its “completed your service” is close to 3.9, but it is kept whole here. Its “so” is Marcus’s own.
single.follows: Whether one lives on here, goes away or dies, there is no fourth case, and in each one can be of good heart.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.12 is 10.11b, 4.30 is 4.37, 3.9 is 3.8, 10.23 is 10.22, 10.17 is 10.15, 7.40 is 7.69 and 5.23 is 5.28b–29; 9.2, 6.2 and 10.28 are the same.

Joins 5.23 and 10.17 in claim 4 although one speaks of going out of life oneself and the other of being killed; both say that dying is the answer when others will not allow a life by nature. In 10.17 “that way” is open, and the claim’s “another way” keeps it open.

Takes 9.2’s “pretence” and 7.40’s “play a part” as one thing, because the Greek uses one word for both. 3.9’s “affected” is a different word, smart or showy in a bad sense, and backs only its own part of claim 3.

Leaves to Article 10 the claim that acting justly now and taking what is allotted are enough, though 10.12 (“content with these two things”), 4.30 (“wisdom only in acting justly”), 6.2 (“it is enough to manage well what is at hand”) and 10.28 (“follow willingly what happens”) say it here too. Leaves out as well: 5.23’s opening “Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute”, which closes a part of the chapter on anger and has no verb; 10.12’s “What anyone will say or think about them … they do not even let into their mind” and the rest of 4.30’s list, which concern what others do and belong with Articles 8 and 12; 9.2’s last sentence, which only explains the two plagues; and 10.28’s “Picture also how we are bound”, whose Greek does not construe as it stands.
articles.limit: Much of this section is said elsewhere: Article 10 already says that death is near and that justice in what I do and peace with what is allotted are enough, Article 3 that I accept what happens, and Article 6 that nothing comes too early; 7.40’s every day as the last is Article 9’s claim 4 and Article 10’s claim 2, the refusal of pretence is in Article 9’s claim 1, a life complete whenever it ends is Article 31’s claim 5 (without this article’s condition), and Articles 12 and 18 already say that where I am makes no difference. What this article adds is the readiness to go, the refusal of pretence set beside death, and the indifference of place joined to a willingness to die rather than live otherwise. In claim 4, “do not allow” means the outward conditions of a life, where and among whom I live, not the power to act justly, which Article 13 (claim 2) and Article 8 (claim 4) say no one can take from me; and the article states that dying is nothing much without arguing for it beyond calling it one of the acts of life.

statement.t: Any moment now I may die; I live without pretence, here as anywhere, and I am ready to go.

parts.words: Any moment now I may die
I live without pretence
here as anywhere
I am ready to go

statement.kind: A fact faced, and how to live under it
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the ground: death is near, and dying is nothing much. Claims 3 and 4 say how to live meanwhile: without pretence, and here as anywhere. The said-once items give a way to stay free, a daily exercise, two pictures of failing and the way back, and an argument by cases that holds whether or not death comes.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that death is near, that I am ready to go, that I do not pretend, and, in claim 4, both “wherever I am” and preferring death to living another way. He adds what can serve as a reason for the article, though he does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were felt or a pretence. He adds words to say each night, and he limits the readiness to die: not in haste, and not from a longing for death.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what can serve as a reason, though Seneca does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence.

items.quote: But who is not near death? It is ready for us in all places and at all times.
gives: any moment now I will be dead
items.follows: Everyone is near death, since death is ready for us everywhere and always.
items.context: Letter 30: Seneca reports the old, failing Bassus on the fear of death. The words say that death, “it”, is near to everyone, in all places and at all times.

items.quote: I shall never be frightened when the last hour comes; I am already prepared
gives: I am ready to go
items.follows: Seneca will not be afraid when his last hour comes, because he is already prepared for it.
items.context: Letter 54: Seneca has just come through an attack of asthma, which doctors call rehearsing death. “The last hour” is the hour of his own death.

items.quote: Surely you are aware that dying is also one of life’s duties?
gives: one of the acts of my life
items.follows: Dying is one of the duties of life.
items.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: someone says he wants to live on because of the honourable duties he is fulfilling. Seneca answers that dying is a duty too.

items.quote: At whatever point you leave off living, provided you leave off nobly, your life is a whole.
gives: whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished
items.follows: A life that ends nobly is whole, wherever it ends.
items.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: a journey stopped halfway is incomplete, Seneca says, but a life is not incomplete if it is honourable.

items.quote: Never shall this flesh drive me to feel fear, or to assume any pretence that is unworthy of a good man.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part
items.follows: Seneca will never let his body drive him into fear or into a pretence unworthy of a good man.
items.context: Letter 65: Seneca calls his body a chain on his freedom. “This flesh” is his body, and the pretence is one he might put on to protect it.

items.quote: I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.
gives: wherever I am
items.follows: Seneca is not born for one corner of the universe; the whole world is his country.
items.context: Letter 28: Lucilius travels to shake off his gloom, and Seneca says it goes with him. This is the belief he tells him to live by instead.

items.quote: It is not a question of dying earlier or later, but of dying well or ill. And dying well means escape from the danger of living ill.
gives: I would rather die
than live another way
items.follows: What matters is dying well, and dying well is escaping the danger of living badly.
items.context: Letter 70, on the proper time to end one’s life: the wise man lives as long as he ought; Seneca then blames a captive who chose to live on in a tyrant’s cage.

items.label: why
items.t: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing. I leave it to death to judge what progress I have made: on that day, without stage paint, I will see whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence.
items.why: In this section Marcus sets the nearness of death beside a life without pretence and does not say why the two belong together. Seneca says that death will test whether his brave words against fortune were felt or a pretence; reading that as the reason is the editor’s link.

support.quote: The showing which we have made up to the present time, in word or deed, counts for nothing.
gives: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing
support.follows: Nothing we have shown so far, in words or deeds, proves anything.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the old Seneca speaks to himself as if the day that judges all his years had come. “The showing” is what he has said and done.

support.quote: I shall leave it to Death to determine what progress I have made.
gives: I leave it to death to judge what progress I have made
support.follows: Seneca leaves it to death to decide how far he has progressed.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the progress is Seneca’s progress in philosophy, which, he says, his words so far cannot prove.

support.quote: putting aside all stage artifice and actor’s rouge, I am to pass judgment upon myself,—whether I am merely declaiming brave sentiments, or whether I really feel them; whether all the bold threats I have uttered against fortune are a pretence and a farce.
gives: on that day, without stage paint, I will see whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence
support.follows: On that day, with the stage paint off, Seneca will judge whether his brave words were felt or a pretence.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the day Seneca is making ready for is the day of his death, when he judges himself without the actor’s make-up.

items.label: practice
items.t: When I go to sleep, I go gladly and say: “I have lived; the course that fortune set for me is finished.” If God adds another day, I welcome it gladly.
items.why: 7.40 says to live through every day as the last, and gives no words for it. Seneca gives words to say when each day ends, and a way to take the next morning.

support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
gives: When I go to sleep, I go gladly and say
I have lived; the course that fortune set for me is finished
support.follows: We should go to sleep glad and say that we have lived and that the course fortune set us is finished.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: Pacuvius held his own funeral feast every evening; Seneca turns the custom to a good use. The course is the course of one’s life.

support.quote: And if God is pleased to add another day, we should welcome it with glad hearts.
gives: If God adds another day, I welcome it gladly
support.follows: If God adds another day, we should welcome it gladly.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: said right after the bedtime words “I have lived”. The added day is the next morning, taken as a gift.

items.t: Seneca agrees that leaving life can be right, but he limits it. The brave and wise man does not beat a hasty retreat from life, and above all he avoids the lust for death that seizes even noble spirits. Marcus says to leave if others will not allow a life by nature; Seneca adds that the leaving must not be hasty or come from a longing to die. The limit concerns going to death rather than waiting for it; it limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.quote: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life; he should make a becoming exit.
support.follows: A brave and wise man does not leave life in haste; he leaves it in a fitting way.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: having argued against fearing death, Seneca warns that even when reason advises ending life, one must not act headlong.

support.quote: And above all, he should avoid the weakness which has taken possession of so many,—the lust for death.
support.follows: Above all, a brave and wise man avoids the longing to die that has seized so many.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: “the lust for death” is an unreflecting pull toward dying, which Seneca says seizes the noble and the craven alike.

amend.t: ; death will show whether my brave words were really felt or a pretence
; but I do not go to death in haste, and I keep clear of a longing to die

searches: last day, each day, every day
desire for death, longing for death, lust

rejected.why: The wise man marks where and how he lives and frees himself when fortune turns. About choosing the time of death; 70.6 says the point more plainly and is quoted.
The wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can. Close to claim 4, but it is about troubles from fortune, not others refusing a life by nature.
Live in the body as if about to leave it. Near 10.12’s stripped-off body, which the article does not quote.
Stay alive for those dear to me even at great cost. A possible limit on claim 4, but it is about illness and old age, not about others refusing a life by nature.
One may leave if one can no longer be of service to anyone. About pain and old age; not the case of claim 4.
Do not love or hate life overmuch. Says what 24.25 says, less directly.
Life is like a play: what matters is how good the acting is, not how long. Close to 3.9’s actor, but 77.4 says the claim’s words more plainly.
His age may have been incomplete, but his life was complete. Same point as 77.4; Letter 93 is already used in Article 6.
One cannot be prepared for death if one has just begun to live. About beginning to live late; 54.7 says “prepared” of oneself.
You do not know where death awaits you; be ready for it everywhere. Close to 30.16, which is fuller and is quoted.
One is not even owner of the morrow. About foolish plans, in a letter on a sudden death; 30.16 says the nearness itself.
We die daily, most of death is behind us; and lay hold of today’s task. Neither says that death is near or that acting justly now is enough.
Every day should be ordered as if it closed the series. Says what 7.40 says, which is a said-once item; 12.9 adds words to say and is used.
Rehearse this thought every day, that you may leave life contentedly. A general exhortation; 12.9 gives the words themselves.
The wise man regards his lifetime as a term of service. Near 10.23’s completed service, which is a said-once item; Seneca backs only claims.
A great role, to play one man; the rest of us shift masks. About being consistent, not about refusing pretence.
Pretence accomplishes nothing; few are deceived by a mask. About true and false fame.
The rich wear their happiness like an actor’s mask. About others’ show, not my own pretence.
Strip the mask from men and things. About fear of what looks terrible, not about pretending.
What you seek, to live well, is found everywhere. Same letter as 28.4, which says it in words closer to claim 4.

Some places are unwholesome even for a healthy mind not yet strong. Says the place can matter while one is still weak; 28.4’s “whole world is my country” is used for “wherever I am” only, not for “the place makes no difference”.
Those who let death in without loathing life weigh more with Seneca. Close to claim 2 but about other men; 54.7 speaks for himself.
First half only: “the person you are matters more than the place” compares the two and does not say the place makes no difference. The next sentence is quoted.

articles.title: Content wherever I am put

claims.t: Wherever I am put, my lot can be good and I can be content there. A good lot is one I assign myself: a good state of soul and good actions. These are enough for me.
claims.shared: 8.43 and 5.30 both say “wherever”, and both say that I am well off there: in 8.43 the divinity within me is gracious, in 5.30 my lot is good. Both then name what that rests on, and both name how the soul is and how it acts (8.43: “the state it is in and the way it acts”; 5.30: “good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions”). 8.43’s “content” and 9.5’s “It is enough” are the same verb in the Greek.
claims.changed: The claim says “soul” where 8.43 says “the divinity within me” and 5.30 says “the soul”. 8.43 does not call the state good; it says the state and the way of acting “follow from its own make-up”. 5.30 lists three things; the claim drops “good impulses”, which stand between the soul’s turnings and its actions. In 8.43 it is the divinity within me that is content, and the claim says that I am, and that these are enough for me. The span quoted from 9.5 names only the judgment; in the passage the same “It is enough” also governs the social action and the well-pleased disposition, which are quoted in claim 2. 5.30 says “yourself”; the claim says “myself”.

support.quote: For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious
gives: Wherever I am put
I can be content there
support.follows: Even in the place I am thrown to, the divinity within me will be gracious.

support.quote: wherever caught, a person whose lot is good
gives: Wherever I am put
my lot can be good
support.follows: The words describe a person whose lot is good wherever that person is caught.

support.quote: “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot
gives: A good lot is one I assign myself
support.follows: To have a good lot is to have assigned a good lot to yourself.

support.quote: good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions
gives: a good state of soul
good actions
support.follows: A good lot consists of good turnings of the soul, good impulses and good actions.

support.quote: content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up
gives: I can be content there
a good state of soul
good actions
These are enough for me
support.follows: The divinity within me is content if its state and its way of acting follow from the way it is made.

support.quote: It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there
gives: These are enough for me
support.follows: Three present things are enough, and the first is a judgment with a firm grasp of what is there.

claims.t: What I do, I do for the good of other people. What happens to me, I accept, whatever it is, as something that comes from the gods.
claims.shared: All three passages set what I do beside what happens to me and give one rule for each. For what happens, 8.22 and 12.8 both say “accept” and both name the gods or god; 12.8 and 9.5 both say “everything”. For what I do, 8.22 says “the doing of good to human beings” where 9.5 says “social”.
claims.changed: 9.5 says “well pleased”, which is warmer than “accept”; the claim keeps the word that 12.8 and 8.22 share. 9.5 names “the external cause” and not the gods. 12.8 measures what I do by god’s praise, not by the good of other people; that half of 12.8 stands alone under “Why”.

support.quote: Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings.
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people
support.follows: Whatever I am doing, I do it with the good of other people as its aim.

support.quote: the present action should be social
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people
support.follows: What I am doing at this moment should be a social action.

support.quote: Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.
gives: What happens to me, I accept
as something that comes from the gods
support.follows: When something happens to me, I accept it and trace it back to the gods and to the one source of everything that comes about.

support.quote: to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is
as something that comes from the gods
support.follows: A human being is able to accept everything god assigns, whatever it turns out to be.

support.quote: the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is
support.follows: My disposition at this moment should be well pleased with everything that comes from the cause outside me.

claims.role: Words that hand over the choice
claims.t: I hand the choice over: to nature I say “Give what you want, take back what you want”, and about where I am put I say “Pick me up and throw me wherever you want”. The words to nature I say in obedience to it and good will toward it, not in bold defiance.
claims.shared: Both passages are spoken to a “you”, and both leave the choice to it in nearly the same words: “what you want” (10.16) and “wherever you want” (8.43). The Greek verb is the same in both.
claims.changed: 10.16 is about things given and taken back, 8.43 about the place I am thrown to; the claim keeps the two sayings apart. 8.43 does not say who is addressed, and the claim does not make it nature. Only 10.16 says in what spirit its words are said, so the last sentence speaks of the words to nature alone and rests on that passage alone. 8.43 names no spirit; its next words state a confidence, that the divinity within will be gracious there too.

support.quote: To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back
gives: to nature
support.follows: Nature gives everything and takes everything back.

support.quote: “Give what you want. Take back what you want.”
gives: I hand the choice over
I say “Give what you want, take back what you want”
support.follows: The educated and modest person tells nature to give what it wants and to take back what it wants.

support.quote: Pick me up and throw me wherever you want.
gives: I hand the choice over
about where I am put I say “Pick me up and throw me wherever you want”
support.follows: The speaker tells someone unnamed to pick him up and throw him wherever they want.

support.quote: not in bold defiance, but only in obedience to it and good will toward it
gives: The words to nature I say in obedience to it and good will toward it, not in bold defiance
support.follows: The words are said in obedience to nature and good will toward it, not to defy it.

single.label: A great power
single.t: To do nothing but what god is going to praise is in my power, as it is in every human being’s, and it is a great power.
single.quote: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise
single.why: Only this passage calls the rule a power, and only it measures what I do by god’s praise; 8.22 and 9.5 measure it by the good of other people. The same sentence goes on to accepting what god assigns, which is quoted under “In action”.
single.follows: A human being has the power to do only what god is going to praise, and it is a great power.

single.label: Taking, letting go
single.t: I take without conceit, and I let go readily.
single.quote: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of how I take and how I let go. It does not say what is taken, so it is not fused with 10.16, where it is nature that gives and takes back.
single.follows: Whatever is taken should be taken without conceit and let go readily.

single.label: When I am troubled
single.t: When an impression troubles me or is out of place, I can push it away and wipe it out, and at once be completely calm. This is easy.
single.quote: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of an impression that troubles me and of calm. It is kept as what losing my contentment looks like, with the way back.
single.follows: A troublesome or out-of-place impression is easy to push away and wipe out, and complete calm follows at once.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.8 is the first part of 12.11, 8.43 is the first part of 8.45, 9.5 is 9.6, 10.16 is 10.14, 8.22 is 8.23, 5.30 is the end of 5.36 and 8.31 is 8.33; 5.2 is the same.

Says “a good state of soul” for two different things: the state of the divinity within me, when it follows from its own make-up (8.43), and good turnings of the soul (5.30). Only 5.30 uses the word “good”. The translators note that Marcus elsewhere treats the divinity within as one’s own mind and reason.

Reads 8.43’s “content if …” as naming what the divinity within is content with: its state and its way of acting. The translators give another reading, “content, provided that …”, which makes the clause a condition on the whole promise. “These are enough for me” leans on the first reading; 9.5’s “It is enough” backs the same words independently.

Reads 5.30 from where the 1634 edition cuts it, in the middle of a sentence. The opening words, “Once I was”, stand in the passage before, so “wherever caught, a person whose lot is good” has no verb here. The claim takes it with the definition that follows, which is complete, and says only that my lot “can be” good.

Joins 8.43 to 10.16 because both hand the choice to a “you”. The Greek of 8.43 does not say who that is, and the article does not make it nature. The obedience and good will of 10.16 are kept to the words spoken to nature.
Places the calm of 5.2 under “When it breaks”. The passage does not mention place or lot; it is read as the way back when an impression disturbs my contentment.

Keeps the translators’ reading of 12.8, ὃ ἂν νέμῃ (“whatever he assigns”), for the transmitted ὃν, which does not construe. Their note says the edition’s text was given from memory and is unchecked, and no printed edition could be consulted for this article; the English of 1634 (“whatsoever God doth send”) reads it the same way. Claim 2’s “whatever it is” does not rest on 12.8 alone: 9.5’s “everything that happens” backs the same words.
articles.limit: Much of this article is said elsewhere. Claim 2 repeats Article 3 (I accept whatever happens) and Articles 1 and 2 (what I do aims at the common good), and adds only that the two stand side by side as one rule. Claim 1’s “wherever” is already Article 17’s claim 4 (I can live as I mean to wherever I am) and Article 12’s claim 1 (where I am is like any retreat); its “enough” is Article 16’s claim 2 (what I have in myself is enough), and Article 2 says that doing my own work makes me content. Claim 3 stands near Article 6, which already takes the universe’s side; and the said-once 5.2a is Article 7’s claim 3 (when I take away the judgment there is calm) and Article 21’s claim 3 (I keep wiping out impressions). What this article adds is that a good lot is one I assign myself, and that the same measure holds for whatever is given or taken back as for the place; claim 3 adds the spoken words that hand over gifts, losses and place. That part rests mainly on 5.30, a fragment cut from a sentence in the past tense, and on 10.16. No passage joins “wherever I am put” to “whatever is given or taken back” in one sentence; the statement does, and its “equally” is marked as the editor’s. In the statement, “taken back” is said by 10.16 alone; 12.8 backs only “whatever is given me”.

statement.t: Wherever I am put, and equally whatever is given me or taken back, a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me.

parts.words: Wherever I am put
whatever is given me or taken back
a good state of soul and good actions
are enough for me

inferences.why: No passage joins the place I am put in to what is given and taken back; setting 8.43 and 5.30 beside 10.16 under one “enough” is the editor’s step.

statement.kind: A ground, the rule it supports, and words to say
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: wherever I am, a good lot is one I assign myself, and a good state of soul and good actions are enough. Claim 2 is the rule for those two things: what I do is for other people, and what happens I accept. Claim 3 gives words that hand the choice of gifts, losses and place to another. The statement joins the “wherever” of 8.43 and 5.30 to the giving and taking back of 10.16; that joining is the editor’s.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if a good state of soul and good actions are not enough for me, or if nothing gives and takes back.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all three claims gain a second author. For the first: any land I am driven to can be a hospitable home, the soul by its own power makes a life happy or wretched, and the real good comes from a good conscience, honourable purposes and right actions. For the second: a good man bears whatever happens to him as the result of divine law. For the third: a prayer hands to Jupiter the choice of where I am led. The article gains two grounds (the person matters more than the place; a spirit within treats me as I treat it), two things under “In action” (how to hold what is given; making something of whatever fortune I find) and a rehearsal of poverty and exile. Nothing is added under “If I doubt it”. He limits the first claim: some places harm a mind still recovering, and where he may choose he avoids them.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: the person I am matters more than the place I go to. His limit on the first claim touches the statement’s “wherever” too: for a mind not yet sound some places are harmful, and where I may choose I avoid them.

items.quote: though you may be driven to the uttermost ends of the earth, in whatever corner of a savage land you may find yourself, that place, however forbidding, will be to you a hospitable abode
gives: Wherever I am put
I can be content there
items.follows: Once the mind’s trouble is removed, even the most forbidding place I am driven to will be a hospitable home to me.
items.context: Letter 28, on travel that does not cure a gloomy mind: Lucilius needs a change of soul, not of scene. “That place” is any land, once the mind’s trouble is removed.

items.quote: For the soul is more powerful than any sort of Fortune; by its own agency it guides its affairs in either direction, and of its own power it can produce a happy life, or a wretched one.
gives: A good lot is one I assign myself
items.follows: The soul is stronger than Fortune and by its own power makes a life happy or wretched.
items.context: Letter 98, on not depending on Fortune’s gifts. Seneca has just said that Fortune hands us only the raw material of goods and ills; the soul turns it to good or ill.

items.quote: it comes from a good conscience, from honourable purposes, from right actions
gives: a good state of soul
good actions
items.follows: The real good comes from a good conscience, honourable purposes and right actions.
items.context: Letter 23, on true joy: rejoice only in what comes from your own store. “It” is the real good; these are the first three of the five sources Seneca names for it.

items.quote: he will endure with an unruffled spirit whatever happens to him; for he will know that it has happened as a result of the divine law
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is
as something that comes from the gods
items.follows: A good man bears calmly whatever happens to him, because he knows it happened by the divine law.
items.context: Letter 76, on the honourable as the only good. “He” is the good man, who owes the gods the highest duty; the divine law is the one that moves all creation.

items.quote: Lead me, O Master of the lofty heavens, My Father, whithersoever thou shalt wish. I shall not falter, but obey with speed.
gives: I hand the choice over
items.follows: The speaker asks Jupiter to lead him wherever Jupiter wishes, and promises to obey at once.
items.context: Letter 107, on obeying the order of the universe, ends with lines of the Stoic Cleanthes that Seneca has put into Latin. They are spoken to Jupiter.

items.label: why
items.t: The person I am matters more than the place I go to, and for that reason I do not bind my mind to any one place. I am not born for one corner of the universe: the whole world is my country.
items.why: Marcus says that he will be content wherever he is thrown and gives as the ground the state of the divinity within him. He does not say in this section, as Seneca does, that the person counts for more than the place, or that the whole world is my country.

support.quote: The person you are matters more than the place to which you go; for that reason we should not make the mind a bondsman to any one place.
gives: The person I am matters more than the place I go to
for that reason I do not bind my mind to any one place
support.follows: Who I am counts for more than where I go, so the mind should not be tied to any one place.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel that fails to cure a gloomy mind. Seneca has just said that, once the mind’s trouble is gone, any land is hospitable; “you” is Lucilius.

support.quote: I am not born for any one corner of the universe; this whole world is my country.
gives: I am not born for one corner of the universe
the whole world is my country
support.follows: I should live in the belief that I was not born for one corner of the universe and that the whole world is my country.
support.context: Words Seneca gives Lucilius to live by, in a letter saying that a restless traveller needs a change of soul. “This whole world” is set against any one place.

items.label: why
items.t: A holy spirit dwells within me as my guardian and marks what I do well and badly. As I treat this spirit, so it treats me.
items.why: 8.43 says that wherever I am thrown the divinity within me will be gracious, and that it is content if its state and its actions follow from its make-up; the fused claim keeps the state and the actions and leaves the divinity out. Seneca too speaks of a spirit within, and says what Marcus does not say here: it marks what I do, and how it treats me depends on how I treat it.

support.quote: a holy spirit indwells within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our guardian. As we treat this spirit, so are we treated by it.
gives: A holy spirit dwells within me as my guardian and marks what I do well and badly
As I treat this spirit, so it treats me
support.follows: A holy spirit lives in each of us as guardian and witness of our deeds, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41 opens by telling Lucilius not to pray to heaven for a sound mind: God is near him, with him, within him. “This spirit” is that god within each person.

items.label: action
items.t: What I am given I use but do not boast of, as something left with me for safe-keeping that will be withdrawn. I do not let it stick fast to me, so that when it is withdrawn it tears no part of me away.
items.why: 8.31 says to take without conceit and to let go readily, and does not say what is taken. 10.16 says that nature gives and takes back. Seneca names the things, the advantages that opinion calls goods, and says how to hold them between the giving and the taking back.

support.quote: Let us use these things, but not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as if they were given for safe-keeping and will be withdrawn.
gives: What I am given I use but do not boast of
as something left with me for safe-keeping that will be withdrawn
support.follows: I should use such things sparingly and without boasting, as things given into my keeping that will be withdrawn.
support.context: From Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. “These things” are the advantages that opinion calls goods, which Seneca says are in our possession but outside ourselves.

support.quote: Let everything of this nature be added to us, and not stick fast to us, so that, if it is withdrawn, it may come away without tearing off any part of us.
gives: I do not let it stick fast to me
when it is withdrawn it tears no part of me away
support.follows: Such things should be added to me without sticking fast, so that losing them tears no part of me away.
support.context: Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. Seneca has just said that what opinion calls goods are only “advantages”, our chattels and not parts of us; “everything of this nature” means these.

items.label: action
items.t: I develop virtue in my own country if that is possible and in exile if it is not, in sound health if that is possible and enfeebled if it is not. Whatever fortune I find, I make something noteworthy of it, as Phidias would have made the best statue that his material permitted.
items.why: Marcus says here that I act for the good of others and accept what happens; he does not say what I do with the place or the fortune I am handed. Seneca does: I work with it as a sculptor works with the material he is given. He grants with his “if possible” that one fortune is preferable to another, which no passage of Marcus in this section does.

support.quote: So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. Whatever fortune he finds, he will accomplish therefrom something noteworthy.
gives: I develop virtue in my own country if that is possible and in exile if it is not, in sound health if that is possible and enfeebled if it is not
Whatever fortune I find, I make something noteworthy of it
support.follows: The wise man develops virtue at home if he can and in exile if he cannot, and makes something noteworthy of whatever fortune he finds.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: what Seneca draws from Phidias, who made the best statue each material allowed. Poverty, exile and illness are the poorer materials.

support.quote: If you had given him marble, or a still meaner material, he would have made of it the best statue that the material would permit.
gives: as Phidias would have made the best statue that his material permitted
support.follows: Given marble or something meaner, Phidias would have made the best statue that the material allowed.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: he is not weighed down by evils but makes use of them. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in bronze as well as ivory.

items.label: practice
items.t: I think of everything that can happen as something that will happen. If I become poor, I shall be one among many; if I am exiled, I shall regard myself as born in the place I am sent to.
items.why: Marcus’s words are said to whoever throws him, and they leave the place open. Seneca thinks of each thing that can happen before it does, and for poverty and exile he gives the answer to have ready; his answer to exile is to regard the new place as my birthplace.

support.quote: Let us think of everything that can happen as something which will happen.
gives: I think of everything that can happen as something that will happen
support.follows: Whatever can happen should be thought of as something that is going to happen.
support.context: Letter 24, on the fear of a lawsuit. Seneca reminds Lucilius that death, exile and grief have hung over him since birth, and that he was born to these perils.

support.quote: I may become a poor man; I shall then be one among many. I may be exiled; I shall then regard myself as born in the place to which I shall be sent.
gives: If I become poor, I shall be one among many
if I am exiled, I shall regard myself as born in the place I am sent to
support.follows: If I become poor I shall be one among many, and if I am exiled I shall treat the place I am sent to as my birthplace.
support.context: Letter 24, to Lucilius, who fears losing a case in court. Seneca has told him to turn from his own case to what can befall anyone; “I” is anyone saying this.

items.t: Seneca agrees that any land can be a home once the mind is at peace (Ep. 28.4), but he does not treat all places alike. Some places are unwholesome for a mind that is recovering and not yet sound, and he says we ought to choose where we live with our character in mind. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. The harm he names does not depend on choosing: some places are unwholesome for a mind not yet sound, whether or not it chose them. His remedy does depend on it: where he may arrange things himself he keeps away from such places, and where he may not, he says that one can live quietly even in the Forum if necessary.

support.quote: there are some places which are also unwholesome for a healthy mind which is not yet quite sound, though recovering from its ailment
support.follows: Some places are bad for a mind that is recovering but is not yet fully sound.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca likens such places to pestilential regions that attack even the strongest body; the mind meant is one still mending from its faults, not yet sound.

support.quote: Of course, if one were allowed to make one’s own arrangements, I should flee far from the very sight and neighbourhood of the Forum.
support.follows: Given the choice, Seneca would keep far away from the Forum.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca has just said that one can live quietly even in the Forum, the most confused of places, if necessary; this is what he adds at once.

support.quote: We ought to select abodes which are wholesome not only for the body but also for the character.
support.follows: I should choose where I live with my character in mind as well as my body.
support.context: Letter 51, on Baiae, which Seneca left the day after he came because luxury has claimed it. He says the wise man avoids such places without hating any place as such.

amend.t: ; the person I am matters more than the place I go to
; but some places harm a mind still recovering, and where I may choose I pick a place that is wholesome for my character

searches: nearest letter sections to c3.s12 by vectors (25)
take back, give back, restore, loan, lent
safe-keeping, deposit, borrowed, withdrawn, she gave, has given
whithersoever, my country, native land, any land
tranquil, calm (with impression, fancy, opinion, thought)
praise, approve (with god and act, deed)
spirit within, god within, holy spirit, guardian

rejected.why: “Pleased with whatever has pleased God”. It would back claim 2, but Articles 3 and 6 already quote it; Ep. 76.23 says the same and names the divine law.
Agreeing with God’s decisions and paying the tax of life. Already quoted in Articles 3 and 6.
Obey the law of nature and do not rail at it. Already in Article 3; about enduring, with nothing on place or on what is enough.
The perfect man accepts whatever happens as his assigned duty. A further witness for claim 2 that Ep. 76.23 makes unnecessary; his “lot” here is a hardship, not a lot I assign myself.
The mind should learn to endure its lot, since Fortune has the same power over cities as over their citizens. About enduring calamity, not about being content.
The one road to safety is to be contented with what is honourable. Near “enough”, but it does not name what the honourable consists of; Ep. 23.7 does.
“Heaven decreed better”. Words for a setback, already used in Article 6.

Be content with yourself and the goods that spring from yourself, and leave other prayers to God. Close to claims 1 and 3, but it leads into advice to practise poverty; Ep. 98.2 and 23.7 are more direct.
A spirit that feels neither loss nor gain. Said of wealth, about a friend’s retirement; Ep. 74.18 says how to hold such things and is quoted.
The true philosopher is equal to himself under all conditions. A portrait in a letter against logical puzzles; it gives no ground and names no place.
The wise man thrown into prison or cast on a lonely shore retreats into himself. About being without friends, in a letter on friendship, not about the place.
Stilbo, his city and family lost: “I have all my goods with me”. A story about the loss of people, in a letter on whether the sage needs friends.
“Wherever I am, I am master of myself.” About keeping one’s time free from business, not about one’s lot or place.
The place where one lives contributes little to tranquillity. Says what Ep. 28.4 says, as an aside on a villa; Ep. 28.4 is fuller and is quoted.
“Fortune has taken away, but Fortune has given.” Said of dead friends, in a letter on grief; it does not hand over the choice as 10.16 does.
What Fortune has not given she cannot take away. About the lasting joy of the wise; seen only as the closing line of its letter.
The wise man accepts what falls to him carelessly and lays it aside. Close to 8.31, but Ep. 74.18 says the same more fully and is quoted.
“Make yourself happy through your own efforts.” Close to assigning myself a good lot, but in an argument about work and virtue; Ep. 98.2 is quoted.
He has the gods’ favour who has become a blessing to himself. Close to 5.30, but it is a greeting that turns at once to whether each person has a guardian god.
The wise man will endure a stormy life but will not choose it. About a way of life, not a place; Ep. 28.6, just before it, is quoted for the limit.
There are places the wise man will avoid as foreign to good morals. Same letter and point as Ep. 51.4, which states it as a rule and is quoted.
Exile and prison are tamed when they meet the wise man. Follows Ep. 85.40, which is quoted and says more.
Desire whatever circumstances demand. Already quoted in Article 6, where it is said of dying gladly.
Ranked near by the vectors. About what Seneca owes to old age and what to wisdom; nothing on place or lot.
Ranked near by the vectors. Goods met in pleasure and goods met in hardship are equal; an argument about the equality of goods.
No good thing makes its owner happy unless he is reconciled to losing it. About worry and loss; Ep. 74.18 covers how to hold what is given.
The good that is really mine is a clear and flawless mind. Would back “a good state of soul”, but it says nothing of actions; Ep. 23.7 names both.

articles.title: When someone offends me

claims.t: Whoever wrongs me does it against their will, out of ignorance of what is good and bad, and with a disposition like theirs they can do nothing else. To require that bad people do no wrong is to demand the impossible.
claims.shared: 7.34 and 11.16 both say it is done against the will (“against its will”, “against their will”), and 11.16 repeats the saying 7.34 quotes. 1.15 and 11.16 both say it comes from ignorance (“through ignorance”, “in ignorance”). 9.43 and 11.16 both call the demand that there be no such people, or that they do no wrong, a demand for “the impossible”.
claims.changed: 1.15 names kinds of people (a meddler, an ungrateful person and others); the claim says “whoever wrongs me”. 12.12 asks “what are they to do?”; the claim states the answer the question implies. 12.12 speaks of not wanting the bad person to do wrong, 11.16 of requiring it; the claim uses 11.16’s word.

support.quote: “Every soul,” he says, “is deprived of truth against its will.” So too, then, of justice and self-control and kindness and everything of that kind. It is most necessary to remember this continually, for you will be gentler toward everyone.
gives: against their will
support.follows: No soul loses truth, justice, self-control or kindness willingly, and keeping this in mind makes me gentler toward everyone.

support.quote: and if not rightly, then plainly they do them against their will and in ignorance.
gives: against their will
out of ignorance
support.follows: If what they do is not right, they do it against their will and without knowing better.

support.quote: All these things have come upon them through ignorance of what is good and bad.
gives: out of ignorance
of what is good and bad
support.follows: The faults of the people I will meet come from not knowing what is good and what is bad.

support.quote: For what are they to do, having a disposition like that?
gives: with a disposition like theirs they can do nothing else
support.follows: Someone with that disposition cannot be expected to act otherwise.

support.quote: whoever does not want the bad person to do wrong is like someone who does not want the fig tree to bear sap in its figs, or babies to cry, or the horse to neigh, or any of the other things that have to be.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong
support.follows: Wanting a bad person not to do wrong is like wanting a fig tree to have no sap: it wants what has to be not to be.

support.quote: that to require bad people not to do wrong is madness, for it aims at the impossible.
gives: To require that bad people do no wrong
to demand the impossible
support.follows: Requiring bad people not to do wrong is madness, because it asks for the impossible.

support.quote: “Is it possible, then, for there to be no shameless people in the universe?” It is not possible. Then do not demand the impossible.
gives: to demand the impossible
support.follows: There cannot be a world without shameless people, so I should not demand one.

claims.t: No one who wrongs me can harm me, for what is bad for me can exist only in my own mind. The one who does the wrong is the one harmed.
claims.shared: 1.15, 9.43 and 11.16 all say that the one who wrongs me does me no harm: “can neither be harmed by any of them”, “what harm have you in fact suffered?”, “I shall certainly not be harmed”. 11.16 and 12.12 both put the harm on the one who does the wrong: “it is you who are being harmed”; “like tearing one’s own face”.
claims.changed: 1.15 gives as its reason that no one can wrap me in what is shameful; the claim gives 9.43’s reason, that what is bad for me exists only in my mind. 12.12 says the wrongdoer has condemned themselves; the claim says “harmed”, as 11.16 does.

support.quote: can neither be harmed by any of them, for no one will wrap me in what is shameful
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
support.follows: None of the people I will meet can harm me, because none of them can wrap me in what is shameful.

support.quote: And what harm have you in fact suffered? For you will find that none of those you are provoked at has done anything of a kind that was going to make your mind worse; and it is there that what is bad for you, and what harms you, has its whole existence.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
what is bad for me can exist only in my own mind
support.follows: No one who provokes me has made my mind worse, and only there can anything be bad for me or harm me.

support.quote: I shall certainly not be harmed; it is you who are being harmed, child.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
The one who does the wrong is the one harmed
support.follows: To someone trying to hurt me I can say: I will not be harmed; you are the one being harmed.

support.quote: And if they did do wrong, that they have condemned themselves, and so this is like tearing one’s own face.
gives: The one who does the wrong is the one harmed
support.follows: If they did wrong, they have condemned themselves, and the wrong tears at the one who did it.

claims.t: I wish them well, for by nature they are friends. The gods too are kind to such people and help them toward the things they care about (health, wealth, reputation); I am free to be as kind.
claims.shared: Both passages say that the gods too help the very people who offend: “the gods too help them” (9.25), “The gods too are kind to such people … they even work with them” (9.9), and both send that help toward particular things. Only 9.25 marks those things as what the people themselves care about; 9.9 names them: health, wealth, reputation.
claims.changed: “Kind” is 9.9’s word; 9.25 says the gods help them in every kind of way. 9.25 lists the means (dreams, oracles) and 9.9 the ends (health, wealth, reputation); the claim keeps the ends. 9.9 presents the help as the gods’ goodness; the claim does not say whether it is limited. 9.9 asks “who is stopping you?”; the claim says I am free.

support.quote: You must wish them well, however; for by nature they are friends, and the gods too help them in every kind of way, through dreams, through oracles, yet toward the things those people care about.
gives: I wish them well, for by nature they are friends
The gods too
help them toward
the things they care about
support.follows: I should wish them well, since they are friends by nature and the gods too help them toward what they care about.

support.quote: The gods too are kind to such people, and toward some things they even work with them, toward health, toward wealth, toward reputation: so good are they. You may be so too; or tell me, who is stopping you?
gives: The gods too
are kind to such people
help them toward
health, wealth, reputation
I am free to be as kind
support.follows: The gods are kind even to such people and help them toward health, wealth and reputation, and nothing stops me being kind too.

claims.role: Teaching them, or bearing with them
claims.t: I teach them kindly and show them what they fail to see, without reproach. If I cannot, I bear with them: kindness and gentleness were given to me for this.
claims.shared: 10.4, 9.9, 8.56 and 9.43 all say to teach them (“teach them kindly”, “teach them otherwise”, “teach them”, “teach … to think otherwise”). 10.4 and 11.12 both say “show” them “what they are failing to see”. 10.4 and 9.9 both go on to the case where I cannot (“if you cannot”, “if not”). 9.9 and 9.43 both say that what I need for it was given to me: “kindness has been given to you”, nature “has given … gentleness”.
claims.changed: 8.56 offers teaching and bearing as two choices; 10.4 and 9.9 put teaching first and the other way only if it fails, and the claim follows them. 10.4 then says to blame myself, or not even myself; the claim leaves that out. 9.43 says gentleness is given to every human being; the claim says “to me”.

support.quote: If someone is mistaken, teach them kindly and show them what they are failing to see.
gives: I teach them
kindly
show them what they fail to see
support.follows: When someone is mistaken, I should teach them kindly and show them what they are missing.

support.quote: But I am kind and well-disposed to everyone, and ready to show this very person what they are failing to see, not with reproach, nor as if making a show of putting up with them, but genuinely and good-heartedly
gives: kindly
show them what they fail to see
without reproach
support.follows: I am ready to show this person what they are missing, sincerely, without reproach and without making a show of my patience.

support.quote: If you can, teach them otherwise; and if not, remember that kindness has been given to you for this.
gives: I teach them
If I cannot
kindness and gentleness were given to me for this
support.follows: I should teach them if I can, and if I cannot, remember that I was given kindness for just this case.

support.quote: But if you cannot, blame yourself, or not even yourself.
gives: If I cannot
support.follows: If I cannot teach them, the blame is mine, or perhaps not even mine.

support.quote: Human beings have come into being for one another’s sake. So either teach them or bear with them.
gives: I teach them
I bear with them
support.follows: Since people exist for one another’s sake, I either teach them or put up with them.

support.quote: It is useful too to think at once of this: what virtue nature has given to a human being to meet this wrong. For it has given, as an antidote, gentleness against the unfeeling person, and against another some other power. And in general you are free to teach the one who has gone astray to think otherwise
gives: I teach them
kindness and gentleness were given to me for this
support.follows: Nature gave people gentleness and other powers as antidotes to wrongs, and I am free to teach whoever has gone astray.

claims.t: If someone despises me or hates me, that is for them to see to, and I do not need their good opinion. My part is to do and say nothing that deserves contempt.
claims.shared: 9.25 and 7.34 both say I do not need what these people think of me (“you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you”; “nor need their testimony”), and both reach it by looking inside them. 11.12 and 9.25 both begin from someone who hates me.
claims.changed: 9.25 speaks of being blamed and hated, 11.12 of being despised and hated; the claim keeps “despises” from 11.12 and “hates” from both. 7.34 speaks of the testimony I want in my favour; the claim calls it their good opinion.

support.quote: Will someone despise me? That is for them to see to. But I will see to it that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves to be despised. Will they hate me? That is for them to see to.
gives: If someone despises me
hates me
that is for them to see to
My part is to do and say nothing that deserves contempt
support.follows: Whether others despise or hate me is their concern; mine is not to deserve contempt by what I do or say.

support.quote: When someone else blames you or hates you, or people voice things of that kind
gives: hates me
support.follows: Others will at times blame me, hate me or speak against me.

support.quote: You will see that you need not be torn apart so that these people may think this or that of you.
gives: I do not need their good opinion
support.follows: Once I see what such people are like, I need not torment myself over what they think of me.

support.quote: Keep turning your attention to who these people are whose testimony in your favour you want, and what ruling parts they have. For you will neither blame those who stumble against their will nor need their testimony, if you look into the springs of their judgment and impulse.
gives: I do not need their good opinion
support.follows: If I look at the minds of those whose praise I want, I stop needing their praise and stop blaming them.

claims.role: Looking into them, then into myself
claims.t: When someone wrongs me, I at once look into them, at what they took to be good or bad and at what sort of people they are, and turn to myself to count the wrongs of the same kind that I do; then my anger goes.
claims.shared: 7.19, 10.30 and 11.16 all turn from the other’s wrong to my own of “the same kind” (7.19, 11.16) or “a similar kind” (10.30). 9.25 and 11.16 both ask “what sort of people they are”. Both 7.19 and 10.30 make the response immediate (“at once”): 7.19 for looking at what they judged good, 10.30 for turning to myself. Both end with the anger gone: “neither surprised nor angry”, “you will quickly forget your anger”.
claims.changed: 10.30 begins from a wrong that offends me, not necessarily one done to me; the claim, and the statement’s “Whoever wrongs me”, take it as a wrong done to me. 9.25 begins from someone who blames or hates me; the claim takes only its looking inside. 7.19 counts judgments of the same kind (“judge the same thing to be good”); 10.30 counts such judgments as wrongs (“judging money to be a good”), and the claim follows 10.30. 7.19 also says “you will pity them”; the claim leaves pity out.

support.quote: Whenever someone does you some wrong, consider at once what they judged to be good or bad when they did the wrong. For once you have seen this you will pity them, and will be neither surprised nor angry.
gives: When someone wrongs me
at once
look into them
what they took to be good or bad
my anger goes
support.follows: When someone wrongs me, seeing what they took to be good or bad turns my anger and surprise into pity.

support.quote: go to their little souls, pass inside and see what sort of people they are.
gives: look into them
what sort of people they are
support.follows: I should go inside the minds of those who blame or hate me and see what they are like.

support.quote: Second: what sort of people they are at table, in bed, and so on; and above all, what compulsions their principles have laid on them
gives: what sort of people they are
support.follows: I should keep in mind what these people are like in daily life and what their principles force on them.

support.quote: Whenever you take offence at someone’s wrongdoing, turn at once to yourself and reckon up what wrong of a similar kind you do: for example, judging money to be a good, or pleasure, or a scrap of reputation, and so on, kind by kind. For when you put your mind to this you will quickly forget your anger
gives: When someone wrongs me
at once
turn to myself to count
the wrongs of the same kind that I do
my anger goes
support.follows: When someone’s wrong offends me, counting my own wrongs of the same kind soon makes me forget my anger.

support.quote: For either you yourself still judge the same thing to be good as they do, or another thing of the same kind; so you must forgive.
gives: the wrongs of the same kind that I do
support.follows: If I still judge the same thing, or a thing of the same kind, to be good, I must forgive them.

support.quote: Fourth: that you yourself also do many wrongs and are another of the same kind
gives: the wrongs of the same kind that I do
support.follows: I too do many wrongs and am one of the same kind as those who wrong me.

claims.t: Being indignant and turning away from them is against nature, and so is a scowl on my face. Anger and harshness toward them are weakness: in anger I have given in, and in harshness I desert my post as surely as if I had fled my work in fright.
claims.shared: 1.15 and 7.18 both say it “is against nature”: being indignant and turning away (1.15), the scowl (7.18). 11.16 and 11.8 both call it weakness (“a weak person”, “weakness”). 11.16 says the angry person has “given in”; 11.8 sets harshness beside giving in from fright as an equal weakness and calls both “deserters from their post”.
