claims.changed: 11.16 speaks of anger, 11.8 of being harsh with those who stand in my way and of becoming estranged from them; the claim joins them as anger and harshness toward people who wrong me. 7.18 does not say whose scowl it is or why; its Greek word means a grudging, wrathful look, and the claim takes it as my own angry face.

support.quote: So to work against one another is against nature; and to be indignant and to turn away is working against.
gives: Being indignant and turning away from them
is against nature
support.follows: Working against one another is against nature, and being indignant and turning away is a way of working against.

support.quote: A scowl on the face is very much against nature.
gives: is against nature
a scowl on my face
support.follows: An angry look on the face goes against nature.

support.quote: And just as distress belongs to a weak person, so does anger; for both have been wounded and have given in.
gives: Anger
are weakness
in anger I have given in
support.follows: Anger, like distress, belongs to the weak: the angry person has been wounded and has given in.

support.quote: For this too is weakness, to be harsh with them, just as it is to abandon the action and give in from fright. For both are equally deserters from their post: the one who has flinched, and the one who has become estranged from a person who is by nature kin and friend.
gives: harshness toward them
are weakness
in harshness I desert my post as surely as if I had fled my work in fright
support.follows: Being harsh with those who block me is as weak as abandoning my action in fright: both desert their post.

claims.t: I may not even know whether it was a wrong, for much is done for a purpose I cannot see. And if it was done rightly, there is nothing to be annoyed at.
claims.shared: Both passages question the wrong itself: “how do I know whether this is a wrong?” (12.12); “you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong” (11.16).
claims.changed: Only 11.16 gives the reason (a purpose not seen) and the case in which it was done rightly.

support.quote: In the case of someone who has given the impression of having done wrong: “But how do I know whether this is a wrong?”
gives: I may not even know whether it was a wrong
support.follows: When someone seems to have done wrong, I should first ask how I know that it was a wrong.

support.quote: Fifth: that you have not even grasped for certain whether they are doing wrong; for many things are done with some further purpose in view
gives: I may not even know whether it was a wrong
much is done for a purpose I cannot see
support.follows: I often do not know for certain that they did wrong, since many acts serve a purpose I cannot see.

support.quote: Third: that if they do these things rightly, one should not be annoyed
gives: if it was done rightly, there is nothing to be annoyed at
support.follows: If what they did was right, there is no cause for annoyance.

single.label: A false belief is strong
single.t: To someone with jaundice honey tastes bitter. A false belief has no less power over a person than that illness has over the body, so I have no cause to be angry.
single.quote: To people with jaundice honey appears bitter, and to those bitten by a mad dog water appears frightening, and to small children their little ball appears beautiful. Why, then, am I angry? Or do you think that a false belief has less power than the bile has over the person with jaundice and the poison over the one bitten by a mad dog?
single.why: Claim 1 says that wrongs come from ignorance. Only this passage says how strong a false belief is, by setting it beside an illness of the body.
single.follows: A false belief rules a person as bile rules the jaundiced, so it makes no sense for me to be angry at them.

single.label: Reason answering reason
single.t: If they have reason, so do I: I use my reason on theirs, show them and remind them. If they listen, I cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.quote: Well then, you have reason too: stir a rational disposition with a rational disposition; show them, remind them. For if they listen, you will cure them, and there is no need of anger.
single.why: Its “show them” is the teaching of claim 4, which already rests on five passages, the most one claim can carry on the page. It stands apart for what it alone says: that my reason is what I use on theirs, and that a cure leaves no need of anger.
single.follows: I have reason as they do, so I can show and remind them; if they listen, they are cured and anger is not needed.

single.label: Each morning
single.t: At dawn I tell myself beforehand that I will meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one and an unsocial one.
single.quote: At dawn, say to yourself beforehand: I shall meet a meddler, an ungrateful person, an insolent one, a deceitful one, an envious one, an unsocial one.
single.why: Only this passage prepares for the day before anyone has done anything. The others answer a wrong once it is done.
single.follows: Each morning I should expect to meet difficult people, naming beforehand the kinds I will meet.

single.label: Taking away the verdict
single.t: What troubles me is not what they do but my own judgment of it. If I take away the verdict that it is something terrible, and am willing to let it go, the anger is gone.
single.quote: Seventh: that it is not their actions that trouble us, for those are in their ruling parts, but our own judgments. At any rate, take away the verdict that this is something terrible, and be willing to let it go, and the anger is gone.
single.why: Claim 2 says that what is bad for me exists only in my mind. Only this heading turns that into an exercise: remove the verdict and the anger goes.
single.follows: My anger comes from my judgment, not from their act; when I drop the verdict that it is terrible, the anger goes.

single.label: Training partners
single.t: I treat the people around me as training partners. When one of them hurts me, I do not mark them down or suspect them; I am on my guard, but I step aside kindly and let many things pass.
single.quote: In the gymnasium someone has scratched us with their nails, and butted us with their head and landed a blow; but we do not mark them down, nor take offence, nor suspect them afterwards of plotting against us. We are on our guard, certainly, yet not as against an enemy, nor with suspicion, but with a kindly stepping aside. Let something like this happen in the other parts of life too: let us overlook many things in those who are, as it were, our training partners.
single.why: Only this passage gives the image of training, and only it says to step aside and overlook. That is neither teaching nor bearing, the two ways of claim 4.
single.follows: As in the gymnasium, I should be careful without being suspicious, step aside kindly, and let many things pass.

single.label: Indignation is cruel
single.t: When I am indignant that people do wrong, I am in a way refusing to let them go after what seems good to them, and that is cruel.
single.quote: How cruel it is not to let people go after the things that appear to them to suit them and to be good for them. And yet in a way you do not allow them to do this, whenever you are indignant that they do wrong.
single.why: Only this passage calls indignation cruel. It goes on to say “teach them and show them”, as claim 4 does; those words are not quoted, since claim 4 already rests on five passages.
single.follows: Being indignant at people’s wrongs is cruel, because it refuses them the pursuit of what looks good to them.

single.label: Blaming the ungrateful
single.t: When I blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, the mistake is mine: I trusted such a person to keep faith, or I did them a favour and looked for something back, as if the act were not complete in itself.
single.quote: Above all, whenever you blame someone as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For plainly the wrong is yours, whether you trusted that a person with such a disposition would keep faith, or whether, in doing a favour, you did not do it as something finished in itself, nor so as to have received the whole fruit at once from the act itself.
single.why: 10.30 also says to turn to myself, but there to count my own wrongs of the same kind. Here it is to find that my expectation was the mistake, and no other passage says that a favour is complete when it is done.
single.follows: If I blame someone for ingratitude, the fault is mine, for trusting them or for wanting a return for a favour.

single.label: Not becoming like them
single.t: I never let myself feel toward inhuman people anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.
single.quote: See that you never come to feel toward the inhuman anything like what the inhuman feel toward human beings.
single.why: Only this passage warns that meeting inhumanity can make me answer it in kind.
single.follows: However inhuman someone is, I must not come to feel toward them what they feel toward others.

single.label: Life is short
single.t: Whenever I am deeply indignant or take something hard, I remember that a human life lasts a moment, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.quote: Sixth: that, whenever you are extremely indignant or even take it hard, human life is a moment long, and in a little while we are all laid out.
single.why: Only this heading brings in death. It holds even if they did wrong willingly and did harm me.
single.follows: However indignant I am, a human life lasts a moment, and soon we will all be dead.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 9.43 is 9.42, 7.34 is 7.62–63, 11.16 is 11.17–18, 7.19 is 7.26, 1.15 is 2.1, 12.12 is 12.16, 9.25 is 9.27, 11.12 is 11.13, 6.19 is 6.20, 6.25 is 6.27, 7.18 is 7.24–25, 9.9 is 9.11, 11.8 is 11.8b–9, 5.22 is 5.28a, 7.36 is 7.65, 6.52 is 6.57 and 8.56 is 8.59; 10.30 and 10.4 are the same.

Keeps eight fused claims, more than the three to five of a smaller section. The section has twenty passages, and each claim rests on words that two of them say; merging any two would join things the passages keep apart, such as being wronged and being despised.

Keeps claim 4 at five passages, the most one claim can carry on the page. 5.22 and 6.25 also say to show or teach them; they are quoted as said-once items for what each says alone, and their words on teaching are not counted.

Reads the scowl of 7.18 as an angry face, from its Greek word for a grudging look. Its next sentence is reconstructed from Greek that does not construe and is not quoted. Claim 3’s “the things they care about” rests on a reading of 9.25 (9.27 in modern editions) that the translators mark as unchecked; their other reading, “the things those people quarrel over”, would not support it.
articles.limit: 11.16, Marcus’s nine headings against anger, feeds five of the eight claims and two said-once items, so the article leans on one passage, and in the statement “bear with them” is 8.56’s word alone. Much of it is said elsewhere: Article 28 (claim 1, and 9.37) that a wrong harms only the one who does it and that perhaps no wrong was done, Article 8 (claim 2) that harm lies in my judgment, Article 7 that taking the judgment away removes the trouble (this article’s 11.16 heading), Article 15 (claim 4, and 7.41) that I set them right if I can and that the gods bear with bad people, Article 26 (claim 5) that I ask what they hold good and bad and begin with myself, Article 29 that I must not become like them (this article’s 7.36), Article 10’s 7.16 that they go wrong through ignorance and we will both soon be dead, Article 22 (claim 1) that blame does not pull me away, Articles 1 and 5 that we are kin and made for one another, and Article 2 (claim 1) that I mean well by my own kind, to which claim 3 here adds that the gods too are kind to those who offend; what this article adds is the moment of being wronged, gathered in one place: why they act as they do, the exercise of looking into them and into myself, what failing looks like, and the doubt whether it was a wrong at all. It disagrees with Article 28, which holds that the wrongdoer can be rid of the wrong as soon as they wish and that a wrong done from desire comes from one’s own impulse (2.7), while claim 1 here says they act against their will and can do nothing else; this section never considers the willing wrongdoer, so the two articles are not reconciled.

aside.11.14: About counterfeit frankness, a “wolf’s friendship”, and how real goodness shows in the eyes. It does not speak of meeting someone who wrongs me.

statement.t: Whoever wrongs me does it against their will and cannot harm me, and I teach them or bear with them.

parts.words: Whoever wrongs me
does it against their will
cannot harm me
I teach them or bear with them

statement.kind: Grounds, a practice and the answer they lead to
statement.form: Claims 1 to 3 are the grounds: why people do wrong, why it cannot harm me, and that the gods are kind to them as well. Claims 4 and 5 say what I do, and claim 6 is the exercise of looking into them and into myself. Claim 7 is what failing looks like, and claim 8 what holds if there was no wrong at all.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 2, 5 and 6 gain a second author. The practice gains a habit of reading words and looks generously, and the side of failing gains three things: going on giving after ingratitude, that how far anger goes depends on the soul a provocation reaches, and not copying bad people because they are many. He challenges claim 1, holding that people know what evil is and do not care, and claim 2, holding that the least part of a wrong does reach the one wronged; he limits claim 4 to those willing to listen.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, except that two of its grounds are disputed: he holds that people who do wrong know what evil is and are indifferent to it, and that the least part of a wrong reaches the one it is done to. It gains a habit for doubtful cases, leaning toward the better reading, and he would teach only those willing to listen.

items.quote: Allow any man who so desires to insult you and work you wrong; but if only virtue dwells with you, you will suffer nothing.
gives: No one who wrongs me can harm me
items.follows: Whoever insults or wrongs me, I suffer nothing so long as virtue dwells in me.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: Seneca quotes Socrates, who put the highest wisdom in telling good from evil. “You” is anyone following his rules; the wrong is insult and injury from others.

items.quote: Let her strip off your faults, rather than assist you to decry the faults of others.
gives: turn to myself
items.follows: Philosophy should strip away my own faults, not help me condemn other people’s.
items.context: Letter 103, on the dangers of mixing with people, closes by warning against vaunting philosophy. “Her” is philosophy, which is to be used on my own faults.

items.quote: If you wish to be happy, if you would be in good faith a good man, let one person or another despise you.
gives: If someone despises me
that is for them to see to
items.follows: To be happy and truly good, I should let this person or that despise me.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: Seneca quotes Socrates on being happy and good, letting others insult you, think you a fool and despise you. “You” is the one following his rules.

items.quote: one should listen in an unruffled spirit to the railings of the ignorant; when one is marching toward the goal of honour, one should scorn scorn itself.
gives: I do not need their good opinion
items.follows: I should hear the mockery of the ignorant calmly and, on the way to what is honourable, disregard their contempt.
items.context: Letter 76, on learning wisdom in old age: the crowd mocks the few who attend lectures on how to be a good man as idlers. “The railings of the ignorant” are that mockery.

items.label: practice
items.t: I do not put a wrong construction on a word or a look; I read what happens generously, and in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading. The wrongs done to me I forget, and on purpose.
items.why: Marcus asks whether it was a wrong at all (claim 8), looks into the person who did it (claim 6), and in 6.19 says to overlook many things. Seneca adds two habits: deliberate forgetting of wrongs, and reading a doubtful word or look toward the better interpretation. Article 28 adds the same habit from the same letter.

support.quote: He will not misinterpret a word or a look; he makes light of all mishaps by interpreting them in a generous way.
gives: I do not put a wrong construction on a word or a look
I read what happens generously
support.follows: The wise man does not misread a word or a look, and he makes light of mishaps by reading them generously.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca’s portrait of the wise man weighing a person’s kindnesses against their injuries. “He” is the wise man; the words and looks are other people’s.

support.quote: the spirit of kindliness always tries to bend every doubtful case toward the better interpretation
gives: in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading
support.follows: Kindliness always tries to turn every doubtful case toward the better reading.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: weighing a person’s good deeds against their bad, as a tied vote acquits a defendant, kindliness settles a doubtful case in that person’s favour.

support.quote: He despises the wrongs done him; he forgets them, not accidentally, but voluntarily.
gives: The wrongs done to me I forget, and on purpose
support.follows: The wise man disregards the wrongs done to him and forgets them deliberately.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: unlike evil men, the wise man keeps a lasting joy from benefits received. “He” is the wise man; “them” are the wrongs done to him.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When someone proves ungrateful, I do not stop doing good. It is better to get no return than to confer no benefits; after a poor crop, one sows again.
items.why: 9.43 says that if I blame someone as ungrateful, the mistake was mine for looking for a return, and that the good done is complete in itself. Marcus does not say that I go on giving to the one who proved ungrateful; Seneca says to sow again.

support.quote: It is better, however, to get no return than to confer no benefits. Even after a poor crop one should sow again
gives: It is better to get no return than to confer no benefits
after a poor crop, one sows again
support.follows: Getting nothing back is better than giving nothing, and after a bad harvest one sows again.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Lucilius complains of an ungrateful person, and Seneca answers that caution would only make him ungenerous. The “benefits” are favours done for others.

items.label: breaks
items.t: What matters is not how great the provocation is but what kind of soul it reaches. Great anger ends in madness, so I avoid anger, to keep my mind healthy.
items.why: Marcus calls anger weakness and against nature (claim 7). Seneca adds that the state of the soul, not the size of the offence, decides how far anger goes, and that great anger ends in madness.

support.quote: And it makes no difference how important the provocation may be, but into what kind of soul it penetrates.
gives: What matters is not how great the provocation is but what kind of soul it reaches
support.follows: The size of the provocation makes no difference; what decides is the kind of soul it reaches.
support.context: Letter 18, on festivals and fasting, ends on anger: “it” is the provocation, which, like a flame, does little to solid timber and sets dry stuff ablaze.

support.quote: the outcome of a mighty anger is madness, and hence anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind.
gives: Great anger ends in madness
I avoid anger, to keep my mind healthy
support.follows: Great anger ends in madness, so anger should be avoided for the sake of a healthy mind.
support.context: Letter 18, on festivals and fasting: the end of Seneca’s comparison of anger with fire, where what burns depends on what the flame falls upon.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I do not copy bad people because there are many of them.
items.why: Marcus warns against hating them (1.15, 6.19) and against feeling toward the inhuman what they feel (7.36). Seneca names the other way to fail among bad people: copying them because they are many. The other half of his sentence, not hating the many, is already Seneca’s addition to Article 1.

support.quote: you should not copy the bad simply because they are many
gives: I do not copy bad people because there are many of them
support.follows: I should not imitate bad people just because there are many of them.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: the world’s vices rub off on us, so that we either imitate it or loathe it, and Seneca rejects both. “The bad” are that crowd.

items.t: Seneca disagrees that people do wrong out of ignorance. Men, he says, are not ignorant of what evil is but indifferent to it, and each enjoys his own crimes; the proof is that all of them hide their sins. He grants that an idea of good conduct remains even in depraved souls, and elsewhere he says that all men suffer from ignorance of the truth (Ep. 118.7), so he is not consistent on this.

support.quote: but on the other hand every man enjoys his own crimes.
support.follows: Unlike a craftsman who regrets his failures, everyone enjoys his own crimes.
support.context: Letter 97, on the degeneracy of the age: the pilot, the physician and the orator are not glad of failure, but each man delights in his own wrongdoing.

support.quote: there is an idea of good conduct present subconsciously in souls which have been led even into the most depraved ways, and that men are not ignorant of what evil is but indifferent
support.follows: Even depraved people keep some idea of good conduct; they know what evil is and do not care.
support.context: Letter 97, on the degeneracy of the age: the proof follows at once, that all men hide their sins. “Men” are wrongdoers, who show by hiding it that they know it is evil.

support.quote: Now all men suffer from ignorance of the truth; deceived by common report, they make for these ends as if they were good
support.follows: Misled by common opinion, everyone pursues certain things as good without knowing the truth about them.
support.context: Letter 118, on the vanity of place-seeking: “these ends” are riches, honours and power, which men chase as goods and later find evil or empty.

items.t: Seneca limits the teaching to those willing to listen. One must not talk to a man who is unwilling to hear; wisdom chooses those who will make progress and withdraws from the hopeless, though not too soon. This narrows the claim and does not contradict it. He is not consistent: to readers who resent his remedies he says he will speak words that help men even against their will (Ep. 89.19).

support.quote: for one must not talk to a man unless he is willing to listen.
support.follows: Advice should be given only to someone willing to hear it.
support.context: Letter 29, on Marcellinus, who avoids Seneca for fear of hearing the truth. The “man” is anyone being advised; Seneca goes on to question the Cynics, who advised everyone.

support.quote: choosing only those who will make progress, but withdrawing from those whom it has come to regard as hopeless,—yet not abandoning them too soon
support.follows: Wisdom should advise those who will make progress and withdraw from the hopeless, but not give up on them too early.
support.context: Letter 29, on whether to advise everyone: “it” is wisdom, which Seneca calls an art that aims its advice instead of scattering it by the handful.

support.quote: I shall utter words that will help men even against their will.
support.follows: Seneca will say what helps people even when they do not want to hear it.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy, ends with Seneca turning on readers who resent his remedies for their vices and saying he will keep on talking.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the worst of a wrong stays with the one who does it, and quotes Attalus: evil drinks the largest portion of its own poison. But he does not say that none of it reaches the other person: the least and lightest portion flows back on the one wronged (Ep. 81.22). Marcus says the one wronged is not harmed at all. Article 28 reads the same letter the same way. He is not consistent on this point: in Ep. 71.7, quoted here as backing claim 2, he gives Socrates’s word that whoever has virtue suffers nothing from those who wrong him.

support.quote: When we do wrong, only the least and lightest portion of it flows back upon our neighbour; the worst and, if I may use the term, the densest portion of it stays at home and troubles the owner.
support.follows: Of a wrong we do, only the least part falls on our neighbour; the worst part stays with us and troubles us.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca says to avoid ingratitude for our own sake. “It” is the wrong we do; the “neighbour” is the one it is done to.

support.quote: Evil herself drinks the largest portion of her own poison.
support.follows: Wickedness harms the one who has it more than it harms anyone else.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca quotes his teacher Attalus. “Evil” is the wrongdoer’s own wickedness, whose poison stays mostly with its owner.

amend.t: ; yet people do not do wrong in ignorance: they know what evil is and are indifferent to it, and each enjoys his own crimes
; but I teach only someone willing to listen, and I withdraw from the hopeless, though not too soon
; and in a doubtful case I lean toward the better reading
; yet the least and lightest part of a wrong does reach the one it is done to

rejected.why: “Harm not, in order that you be not harmed”: prudence about harm to body and goods, not about harm to the mind.
A good life brings “not necessarily freedom from harm at their hands”. Harm here is worldly harm; Marcus’s claim 2 is about the mind, so there is no real disagreement.
Contempt “works you injury” but passes on. A letter on living safely; injury means danger to one’s person, not to the mind.
Avoid hatred by never provoking anyone. Prudence about safety; claim 5 already says to give no cause for contempt.
What annoys us does not necessarily injure us; luxury makes us angry. About masters raging at slaves, and “not necessarily” is weaker than claim 2.
Kings claim injuries in order to inflict them. A portrait of the powerful, not of one who is wronged.
Nothing need provoke anger if one does not add to one’s troubles. Said of a late dinner and missing bread, not of people.
Epicurus’s “Ungoverned anger begets madness”. Its point is used through 18.15, which explains it.
Little help in casting out your own faults if you quarrel with those of others. About choosing a quiet place to live, not about a person who wrongs me.
A fool’s fault in returning favours is lack of knowledge, not of will. Near claim 1, but about gratitude, and the match needs explaining.
Try many ungrateful people to find one grateful. Repeats 81.1, which is quoted.
More wretched to commit than to suffer injury. A comparison within a passage on what nature owes among people, Article 1’s subject; 81.22 says it of the wrong itself and is used.
The gods do kindness by nature and cannot do harm. About worship; does not say they help the wicked, as claim 3 does.
The sun and moon do not rise for me alone. About gratitude to rulers and the seasons, not about the gods helping bad people.
Every age produces a Clodius. Says bad men will always exist, but not that demanding otherwise is impossible; and it is the letter used for the challenge.
All men suffer from ignorance of the truth. Could back claim 1, but its ends are riches and office; it is used only to show Seneca is not consistent.
Seneca will be bold enough to show Marcellinus his faults. About a friend sliding into vice, not someone who wronged him.
“Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.” About choosing company; only the first sentence is used.
Precepts to check hatred in an enemy. Named only as an example of precepts with reasons; no context of its own.
A man kind to friends and restrained toward enemies. One trait in a sketch of how we form the idea of virtue.
Kindliness is gentle and courteous to all men. An argument that liberal studies do not teach virtue.
Demetrius: the talk of ignorant men is like rumblings of the belly. Said against the fear of death and gossip.
The angry prayers of enemies instil false fears. About what words do to us, not about meeting a wrong.
The mind fancies a grudge more serious than it is. About imagined fears.
The wise man never provokes the anger of those in power. Prudence toward the powerful.
Force sick friends to submit to things against their will. About curing a friend’s chronic faults, not someone who wronged me.
No man confesses his faults while still in their grip. About self-knowledge in general.

articles.title: Taking a thing apart: material, cause, purpose and time

claims.t: I take each thing apart into its material and its cause, the active element that shapes the material into this thing. I ask what it is for and what it does in the universe, and how long it lasts before it is over.
claims.shared: 12.14 and 12.7 both say “dividing” and name the same heads: the material (12.7: “matter”), the cause and the purpose. 8.10 asks for the same heads as questions, “what in it is substance and material, and what is cause?”, and, like 12.14, it asks about the time: how long the thing lasts.
claims.changed: “The active element that shapes the material into this thing” is the editor’s gloss on “cause”, taken from the translators’ note: in Stoic use the cause is not an earlier event. 12.14’s “open it out” is folded into “take apart”. 12.7 has no time. 8.10 asks what the thing does in the universe where the other two say “purpose”; the claim keeps both.

support.quote: open it out, dividing it into the cause, into the material, into the purpose, into the time within which it will have to be over
gives: I take each thing apart
its material
its cause
what it is for
how long it lasts
before it is over
support.follows: I should open a thing out by dividing it into its cause, its material, its purpose and the time by which it will be over.

support.quote: dividing them into matter, cause, purpose
gives: I take each thing apart
its material
its cause
what it is for
support.follows: I should divide things into their matter, their cause and their purpose.

support.quote: What in it is substance and material, and what is cause?
gives: its material
its cause
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask what in it is its material and what is its cause.

support.quote: What does it do in the universe?
gives: what it does in the universe
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask what it does in the universe.

support.quote: And how long does it last?
gives: how long it lasts
support.follows: Of a thing I can ask how long it lasts.

claims.t: When something makes an impression on me, I always look to see in full what the thing itself is: its own make-up, its own quality and its worth. I look inside it and do not let its quality or its worth run past me.
claims.shared: 12.14 and 8.10 both ask what the thing itself is (12.14: “what that thing itself is”; 8.10: “what is it in itself”). 8.10 and 6.3 both point to what is the thing’s own (“its own make-up”, “its own quality”; the Greek has the same word for “own” in both).
claims.changed: 12.14 speaks of the thing that produces the impression; 8.10 and 6.3 do not mention impressions. 6.3’s “Look inside” could also mean inside myself; the claim reads it, with the translation, as inside the thing. “See in full” follows the translation of εἰς τὸ πᾶν; the Greek could also mean “look to the whole”.

support.quote: Always see in full what that thing itself is which produces the impression in you
gives: When something makes an impression on me
I always look to see in full
what the thing itself is
support.follows: Each time something makes an impression on me, I should see in full what the thing itself is.

support.quote: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own make-up?
gives: what the thing itself is
its own make-up
support.follows: Of a thing before me I can ask what it is in itself, in the way it is made up.

support.quote: Look inside. With any thing, do not let either its own quality or its worth run past you.
gives: its own quality and its worth
I look inside it
do not let its quality or its worth run past me
support.follows: I should look inside, and not let the quality or the worth of any thing go by me unnoticed.

single.label: Three studies
single.t: Continually, and with every impression if I can, I reason about nature, I reason about the passions, and I practise dialectic, the art of reasoning correctly.
single.quote: Continually, and with every impression if possible, reason about nature, reason about the passions, practise dialectic.
single.why: Only this passage names these three studies. 12.14 also says “always” and speaks of an impression, but it asks for a different act, seeing what the thing is, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: With every impression I can, I should keep reasoning about nature and about the passions, and keep practising dialectic.

single.label: Four things to attend to
single.t: I pay attention to the thing before me, or to the principle involved, or to the activity going on, or to what the words mean.
single.quote: Pay attention to the thing before you, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.
single.why: Only this passage names these four. Its first, the thing before me, is near 12.14’s “that thing itself”, but no other passage names the other three, and its “or” offers a choice among four rather than a division of one thing.
single.follows: I should attend to the thing before me, or to the principle, or to the activity, or to what is meant.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s: 12.14 is 12.17b in modern editions, 12.7 is 12.10, 8.10 is 8.11, 8.12 is 8.13 and 8.20 is 8.22a; 6.3 is 6.3 in both.

Explains “cause” in claim 1 as the active element that shapes the material, following the translators’ note. No quote of Marcus is mapped to these words; Seneca’s Ep. 65.2 backs them when his voice is on.
Keeps 8.10’s question “What does it do in the universe?” beside “purpose” as its own item. The translators read the two as the same head of the list; the claim does not merge them.
Reads 6.3’s “Look inside” as looking inside the thing, as the translation leans. The Greek could also mean looking inside oneself.
Follows the translation’s “see in full” in 12.14 (claim 2). The Greek εἰς τὸ πᾶν could also mean “look to the whole”, the whole of the thing or the universe.

Adds the editor’s glosses to two said-once items, from the translators’ notes: in 8.12 “the art of reasoning correctly” for dialectic; in 8.20 “involved”, “going on” and “what the words mean” for Marcus’s bare “the principle”, “the activity” and “what is meant”.
Leaves out 12.7’s first words, “See things as being of this kind”: “of this kind” points to nothing in the passage, and the translators’ note leaves it open.
articles.limit: Article 4, claim 4 already says that I ask what causes each thing, the power at work in it apart from its matter. Article 11, claim 4 is the same exercise: I look at whatever comes up stripped bare, what it is in its substance, what it is put together from, how long it lasts and what it is worth; and Article 7, claim 5 says I see things as they are. This article adds Marcus’s full division into material, cause, purpose and time, and the rule to look past the impression to the thing itself. No passage of the section says why I should do this, or what failing at it looks like. The two fused claims both lean on 12.14 and 8.10.

statement.t: I look at what each thing itself is, I take it apart into its material, its cause and its purpose, and I ask how long it lasts.

parts.words: I look at what each thing itself is
I take it apart into its material, its cause and its purpose
I ask how long it lasts

statement.kind: What I look at, then how I take it apart
statement.form: Claim 2 says what I look at: the thing itself behind the impression, and what is its own. Claim 1 gives the method: 12.14, 12.7 and 8.10 divide a thing under the same heads. The statement puts the two in that order.

empty.why: No passage in this section says why I should take things apart; the section gives the method and not its reason.
empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes what failing at this looks like or the way back.
empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what would remain if things could not be taken apart in this way.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the division into material and cause gains a second author, and so does asking what each thing is and what it is worth. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: why to look, since what I fear, seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing but my fear; what failing looks like; a rule that the parts must not be countless and tiny; and what holds if I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is true.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a reason: what I fear, stripped of what disturbs and confuses and seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing fearful except my fear.

items.quote: there must be, in the case of each thing, that from which it is made, and, next, an agent by which it is made. The former is its material, the latter its cause.
gives: its material
its cause
items.follows: Every thing has something it is made from, its material, and an agent that makes it, its cause.
items.context: Letter 65, on the first cause, sets out the Stoic view that everything comes from cause and matter. “Each thing” is any thing that is made.

items.quote: Cause, however, by which we mean reason, moulds matter and turns it in whatever direction it will, producing thereby various concrete results.
gives: the active element that shapes the material into this thing
items.follows: The cause, which is reason, shapes matter as it wills and so produces particular things.
items.context: Letter 65 gives the Stoic account of cause and matter: matter lies idle until something moves it, and the cause, reason, is what moves and shapes it.

items.quote: set a value upon each thing, asking what it is and not what it is called
gives: what the thing itself is
its worth
items.follows: I should give each thing its value by asking what it is, not what it is called.
items.context: Letter 95, on why precepts need principles: before using things, decide what to think of each, such as poverty, riches, renown, disgrace and exile.

items.label: why
items.t: When I strip what I fear of all that disturbs and confuses and see what it is at bottom, I find nothing fearful in it except my fear.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section says why I should look at the thing itself. Seneca gives a reason for the things I fear: seen as they are, they hold nothing fearful but the fear.

support.quote: strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom
gives: I strip what I fear of all that disturbs and confuses
see what it is at bottom
support.follows: I should strip things of whatever disturbs and confuses, and see what each one is at bottom.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Lucilius fears a lawsuit an angry opponent threatens. The “things” are what he fears: losing the case and, as the letter goes on, pain and death.

support.quote: you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.
gives: I find nothing fearful in it except my fear
support.follows: Once seen as they are, the things I fear turn out to hold nothing fearful except the fear.
support.context: Letter 24, advice to Lucilius under threat of a lawsuit. “They” are the feared things once stripped of what disturbs and seen as they are at bottom.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I fail when I agree too quickly with what people say and do not examine what I fear; then I retreat like soldiers who leave their camp because cattle raised a cloud of dust. The way back is to strip the mask from things and give each its own face again.
items.why: Marcus says in this section what to look at and how to take it apart, but not what it looks like when I fail to. Seneca names the failure in Letter 13, believing report instead of testing what I fear, and the unmasking in Letter 24. Joining the second to the first as the way back is the editor’s step; Seneca does not offer it as the cure for rumour.

support.quote: we agree too quickly with what people say. We do not put to the test those things which cause our fear; we do not examine into them; we blench and retreat just like soldiers who are forced to abandon their camp because of a dust-cloud raised by stampeding cattle
gives: I agree too quickly with what people say
do not examine what I fear
I retreat like soldiers who leave their camp because cattle raised a cloud of dust
support.follows: We agree too quickly with what people say, we do not test what we fear, and we retreat like soldiers from a dust cloud raised by cattle.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: Lucilius fears trouble to come, and Seneca tells him to test whether the signs of it are sure, since rumour misleads us.

support.quote: We should strip the mask, not only from men, but from things, and restore to each object its own aspect.
gives: strip the mask from things
give each its own face again
support.follows: We should take the mask off things as well as people, and let each be seen as it is.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: children are terrified by people they love wearing masks, and adults are the same with the things they fear, such as pain and death.

items.label: doubt
items.t: I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is absolutely true; I can still judge which seems truest.
items.why: No passage of Marcus here asks what holds if taking a thing apart does not reach the truth. Seneca, judging between the schools’ accounts of cause, says flatly that absolute truth is beyond us, and asks only for the account that seems truest. Placing his judgment on the schools’ accounts of the first cause beside Marcus’s method for taking a single thing apart is the editor’s step.

support.quote: state who seems to you to say what is truest, and not who says what is absolutely true. For to do that is as far beyond our ken as truth itself.
gives: I cannot be certain which account of what causes things is absolutely true
I can still judge which seems truest
support.follows: I can judge which account seems truest; which is absolutely true is beyond what we can know.
support.context: Letter 65, on the first cause: after setting out the Stoic, Aristotle’s and Plato’s accounts of what causes things, Seneca asks Lucilius to judge between them.

items.label: practice
items.t: When I break a large thing into parts to know it better, the parts must not be countless and tiny: a thing cut as fine as dust is as hard to grasp as one not divided at all.
items.why: Marcus divides a thing under four heads and says nothing of how far division should go. Seneca, before dividing philosophy, gives a rule for breaking any large thing into parts, such as a people or an army.

support.quote: Whatever has grown to greater size is more easily identified if it is broken up into parts; but the parts, as I have remarked, must not be countless in number and diminutive in size.
support.follows: A large thing is easier to know when divided into parts, but the parts must not be countless or tiny.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: before dividing philosophy for Lucilius, Seneca says how any large thing, like a people or an army, should be divided.
gives: When I break a large thing into parts to know it better
the parts must not be countless and tiny

support.quote: For over-analysis is faulty in precisely the same way as no analysis at all; whatever you cut so fine that it becomes dust is as good as blended into a mass again.
support.follows: Dividing too finely is as bad as not dividing: what is cut to dust becomes one mass again.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: Seneca will divide philosophy into parts but not into scraps, and says why too fine a division fails.
gives: a thing cut as fine as dust is as hard to grasp as one not divided at all

amend.t: ; what I fear, stripped of what disturbs and confuses and seen as it is at bottom, holds nothing fearful except my fear

searches: set a value, its proper or true value, real value
matter, purpose, divid, worth (counted only; read through the matter-with-cause and value searches)

rejected.why: Aristotle’s three or four senses of “cause”, reported to be argued against. Not Seneca’s own view and not about taking a thing apart.
Plato’s five causes, including the end in view. Reported, then criticised in 65.11 to 65.14; it would make Plato back Marcus.
Time and place must be counted among causes if Plato’s rule is followed. Part of an argument against Plato, not advice to ask how long a thing lasts.
The purpose of the maker is only an accessory cause. A point about the word “cause”; Marcus keeps purpose apart from cause too, so there is no disagreement.
The first part of ethics weighs the worth of each thing. Backs “its worth”, but 95.54 says it and also “what it is”; a second witness was not needed.
Impulse should match the worth of its object. A further step to action that no claim here takes.
The elements divided into matter and the cause that moves all things. Says less than 65.2.
Weigh things by their nature, not their reputation. Same point as 95.54, in a letter on benefits.
Judge a man naked, his soul’s quality and stature. About judging a person, not a thing.
A buyer has the bandage taken off to see the body. About judging people by their trappings.
To value yourself, look into your own soul. About oneself; 6.3 is read as about things.
Examine the causes of fear: some exist, some only seem to. Says what 24.12 says, less directly.
Measure the trouble you fear and estimate your fear. Near the reason in 24.12, which is quoted.
Idle report disturbs us most. Explains 13.8, which is quoted.
An external impression stirs impulse and assent confirms it. About how action begins; says nothing of examining the impression.
Dialecticians should teach how to help a friend, not the senses of “friend”. Bears on 8.12’s dialectic, a said-once item; no claim to qualify.
Give dialectic only a glance. Would limit 8.12, which is said once and takes no qualification.
Dialectic divided into words and their meanings. Near 8.20’s “what is meant”, a said-once item; a classification only.
Examine the parts as parts of the whole man. About reading a philosopher whole instead of in extracts.
Wisdom asks of the soul whence it comes and how long it abides. A list of what philosophy studies, not advice for each thing.
Consider each thing’s relation to the purpose of your whole life. About the purpose of my life, not the purpose of the thing.
Plato’s division of what exists into classes. A classification of being, not a way to look at a thing.
See what is necessary and what superfluous. About needs, not about what a thing is.
Lies are transparent if examined with care. About pretence in people.

articles.title: Wiping out impressions, checking impulses

claims.t: It is up to me what is in my soul: I keep my ruling part in my own power, and no one can rob me of the power to choose.
claims.shared: Two passages say that this is in my own hands: 8.27 that “it is up to me” that my soul be free of wickedness and craving, 9.6 that I am to keep the ruling part “in one’s own power”. In the Greek they use the same Stoic phrase for what is in a person’s own power. 11.31 adds that no one can rob me of the power to choose.
claims.changed: 9.6 is an instruction (“To keep the ruling part in one’s own power”); the claim says “I keep”. The translators allow “in its own power” as well. 11.31 is a saying of Epictetus that Marcus copied out; the claim makes it first person. 8.27 lists what is to be kept out of the soul (wickedness, craving, disturbance); the claim keeps only “what is in my soul”.

support.quote: Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all
gives: It is up to me
what is in my soul
support.follows: Keeping wickedness, craving and disturbance out of my soul is in my own power.

support.quote: To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.
gives: It is up to me
I keep my ruling part in my own power
support.follows: The ruling part can be kept in one’s own power, and one is to keep it there.

support.quote: There is no robber of the power to choose.
gives: no one can rob me of the power to choose
support.follows: No one can take a person’s power to choose away from them.

claims.t: Whatever others do, my mind cannot be harmed when it is gathered into itself and free of passions. It stays so while I take refuge in it and guard myself at every hour.
claims.shared: Both passages give the mind an image of something that cannot be harmed: in 8.46 a citadel that cannot be taken (“beyond capture”), in 8.50 a spring that washes out the mud thrown into it and “will in no way be stained”. Both also make it depend on me: in 8.46 I must flee to it, in 8.50 I must guard myself at every hour.
claims.changed: Each passage has its own image, a fortress and a spring; the claim keeps neither and says what they share. “Whatever others do” rests on 8.50 alone, which says “they kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses” without saying who; the claim says “others”.

support.quote: Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
when it is gathered into itself
support.follows: The ruling part cannot be conquered when it is gathered into itself and content with itself.

support.quote: This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
free of passions
while I take refuge in it
support.follows: A mind free of passions is a fortress: whoever flees to it cannot be captured.

support.quote: They kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses. What, then, is that to the mind staying clean, sane, self-controlled, just?
gives: Whatever others do
my mind cannot be harmed
support.follows: Killing, butchering and cursing have no bearing on whether the mind stays clean, sane, self-controlled and just.

support.quote: even if they throw in mud, even if dung, it will very quickly scatter these and wash them out, and will in no way be stained
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
support.follows: A clear spring quickly washes away mud or dung thrown into it and is not stained by them.

support.quote: If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free
gives: guard myself at every hour
support.follows: The mind stays an ever-flowing spring if I guard myself at every hour so as to be free.

claims.t: I keep wiping out impressions, and any turn my mind takes that I should guard against. As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it.
claims.shared: Three passages give the same command in the same words: “Wipe out the impression” (7.21), “Keep wiping out impressions” (8.27), “To wipe out an impression” (9.6). Two of them, 8.27 and 11.17, add that something is to be said while wiping: “saying to yourself continually” and “saying over each one”.
claims.changed: 11.17 wipes away four “turns” of the ruling part, not impressions; the first of them is an imagining, the others are a thought that dissolves community, words not my own, and giving way to the body. The claim names both impressions and turns, and does not say that every turn is an impression.

support.quote: Wipe out the impression.
gives: I keep wiping out impressions
support.follows: An impression can be wiped out, and Marcus tells himself to do it.

support.quote: Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually
gives: I keep wiping out impressions
As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it
support.follows: Wiping out impressions is to be done again and again, while saying something to oneself.

support.quote: To wipe out an impression.
gives: I keep wiping out impressions
support.follows: Wiping out an impression is one of the things a person can do.

support.quote: Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows:
gives: any turn my mind takes that I should guard against
As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it
support.follows: Four turns of the ruling part are to be watched for, wiped away when caught, and met each with a sentence said over it.

claims.t: I can stop an impulse, and each impulse I form is for the common good and has a reservation: if nothing prevents it. I go by the worth of each thing, with each impulse I give what is just, and I keep desire out altogether.
claims.shared: 11.31 asks that impulses be “according to worth”, and 8.27 that I use each thing “according to its worth”: both go by the worth of each thing. 9.6 and 11.31 both keep desire out: “To quench desire” and “keep away from desire altogether”.
claims.changed: “If nothing prevents it” is the editor’s gloss on “with a reservation”, the Stoic sense the translators give for the word; no passage spells it out. 6.45 shows it in use (claim 6): when I am blocked, I was not desiring what is impossible. 11.31 speaks of the worth of what an impulse aims at, 8.27 of the worth of the things I use; the claim says “each thing” to cover both. 11.31 gives Epictetus’s rule; the claim makes it mine. 6.45 speaks of “desiring” an impulse, which sits uneasily with keeping away from desire altogether; the claim follows 9.6 and 11.31 on desire.

support.quote: To stop an impulse.
gives: I can stop an impulse
support.follows: An impulse can be stopped, and one is to stop it.

support.quote: in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth
gives: each impulse I form is for the common good and has a reservation
I go by the worth of each thing
support.follows: Impulses must be watched so that each carries a reservation, serves the community and matches the worth of its object.

support.quote: seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth
gives: I go by the worth of each thing
support.follows: Once I see what kind of thing each thing is, I deal with each according to its worth.

support.quote: at every impulse to give what is just
gives: with each impulse I give what is just
support.follows: With every impulse I should give what is just.

support.quote: To quench desire.
gives: I keep desire out
support.follows: Desire can be put out, as a fire is put out.

support.quote: keep away from desire altogether
gives: I keep desire out
support.follows: Desire is to be kept away from entirely.

claims.t: Nothing I do is careless: I do no act at random, but by a rule of the art of living. I do not wander among my impressions, and with each one I keep the sure grasp: I hold to what is so clear that it cannot be false.
claims.shared: 4.2 and 8.49 both forbid carelessness in acts: “no act be done at random” and “Not to be slovenly in actions”. 4.18 and 8.49 both forbid wandering: “Not to roam away” and “not to wander in impressions”.
claims.changed: 4.2 says “the art” and does not name it; “of living” is the editor’s. 4.18 does not say where one roams; “among my impressions” is 8.49’s. 4.18’s “sure grasp” is a Stoic term: an impression that grasps its object so clearly that it cannot be false. The words after the colon are the editor’s explanation of it, from the translators’ note.

support.quote: Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.
gives: Nothing I do is careless
I do no act at random, but by a rule
support.follows: Every act should follow a rule that belongs to the art, and none should be done at random.

support.quote: Not to be slovenly in actions
gives: Nothing I do is careless
support.follows: My actions should not be slovenly.

support.quote: not to wander in impressions
gives: I do not wander
among my impressions
support.follows: I should not let myself wander from one impression to another.

support.quote: Not to roam away
gives: I do not wander
support.follows: I should not roam off course.

support.quote: at every impression to keep the sure grasp
gives: with each one I keep the sure grasp
support.follows: With every impression I should keep the sure grasp.

claims.role: When I am kept from something
claims.t: When I am kept from something, I am content and free of distress, and I turn the hindrance to another virtue: one that is still possible. My impulse had its reservation, and I was not desiring what is impossible.
claims.shared: Both passages begin from something that cannot be done: in 6.45 someone “stands in the way”, in 8.7 “It is not possible to read”. Both turn from it to a virtue that remains: 6.45 to “another virtue”, 8.7 to holding back insolence and mastering pleasures and pains.
claims.changed: 6.45 is about a just act blocked by force; 8.7 does not say what keeps Marcus from reading. The claim says only “kept from something”. Only 6.45 ties the block to the reservation of claim 4.

support.quote: If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue
gives: When I am kept from something
I am content and free of distress, and I turn the hindrance to another virtue
support.follows: When someone forcibly blocks what I set out to do, I should be content and use the hindrance to practise another virtue.

support.quote: remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible
gives: My impulse had its reservation, and I was not desiring what is impossible
support.follows: When blocked, I am to remember that my impulse had a reservation and that I was not desiring the impossible.

support.quote: It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains.
gives: When I am kept from something
one that is still possible
support.follows: Reading may not be possible, but holding back insolence and getting the better of pleasures and pains still are.

single.label: What is at stake
single.t: In governing my impressions, impulses and desires I am contending for no small matter: it is whether I am sane or mad.
single.quote: is not about just anything, but about being mad or not
single.why: Only this passage names what the struggle is about. 8.50 calls the mind “sane”, but it does not speak of a contest.
single.follows: Epictetus says the contest is about being mad or not, not about some ordinary matter.

single.label: Another’s wrong
single.t: When someone does wrong, I leave the wrong with them, where it came to be.
single.quote: The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.
single.why: Only this passage says where another person’s wrong belongs. 8.7 speaks of not being angry with the ungrateful, which is a different point.
single.follows: A wrong stays with the one who did it, and I should leave it there.

single.label: The ungrateful
single.t: I can keep from being angry with people who are insensitive or ungrateful, and more than that, I can care for them.
single.quote: But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of anger at other people and of caring for them instead.
single.follows: It is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and ungrateful, and even to care for them.

single.label: Three sentences
single.t: When I catch my mind taking a turn I should guard against, I say one of three sentences over it: that this imagining is not necessary, that this one dissolves community, or that what I am about to say is not from myself.
single.quote: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This that you are about to say is not from yourself.”
single.why: Only this passage gives these three sentences. 8.27 gives a different sentence, which this article quotes in claim 1.
single.follows: Each of three turns has its sentence: this imagining is not needed, this breaks community, these words are not my own.

single.label: Beaten by the body
single.t: When the body and its pains or pleasures get the better of me, the more divine part of me is beaten and lies down under the lesser, mortal part, and I reproach myself for it.
single.quote: The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.
single.why: Only this passage says what it looks like when the ruling part loses. 8.7 says it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains, but not what losing is.
single.follows: When the more divine part gives way to the body and its movements, it has been beaten, and that is a cause for self-reproach.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 7.21 is 7.29–31a, 11.17 is 11.19, 8.27 is 8.29, 6.45 is 6.50, 8.46 is 8.48, 8.49 is 8.51a, 11.31 is 11.36–38, 4.18 is 4.22, 8.50 is 8.51b, 8.7 is 8.8 and 9.6 is 9.7; 4.2 is the same.
Calls the section “Wiping out impressions, checking impulses” instead of “Clearing away opinion and impulse”. No passage speaks of opinion; seven speak of impressions or impulses.
Puts 11.17’s four “turns” of the ruling part beside impressions in claim 3. Only the first turn, an imagining, is a kind of impression; the claim names both.

Explains “with a reservation” as “on condition that nothing prevents it” in the statement and as “if nothing prevents it” in claim 4. That is the Stoic sense the translators give for the word; no passage says it in these words. 6.45 shows it in use: when blocked, I was not desiring what is impossible (claim 6).
Reads 11.31 as Marcus’s own rule, though he gives it as the words of Epictetus.

Takes 11.17’s “rough or smooth movements” as the body’s pains and pleasures, as the translators do, and says “pains or pleasures” in the article; the quote keeps Marcus’s words. The wording of the Greek there has been doubted.

Keeps “If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free” in 8.50 as the translators give it. They note, from memory and unchecked, that the verb has been doubted and “grow” proposed; with that reading, “guard myself at every hour” in claim 2 would lose its backing.

Leaves out, as repeats or as off this section’s topic: most of 7.21’s other commands (the puppet strings, drawing a line around the present time, the last hour, taking a thing apart into cause and matter, which is Article 4’s, and the closing words on simplicity and following god); 11.31’s “art for giving assent” and its rule on aversion; 8.27’s “Remember this power in accordance with nature”; and 8.7’s being above petty reputation.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one. Wiping out a judgment once it is made is Article 7’s claim 3 and Article 8’s claim 2, and 5.2 in Article 18 says the same of impressions; this article adds the daily habit and the sentence said over each one. Article 8 says that setting out without “if nothing prevents it” is already bad, and that nothing from outside touches my mind (8.39 and claim 3); here the reservation becomes a rule for every impulse, and the mind’s safety depends on my guarding it. Article 12 says I can retreat into myself at any hour, and Article 13 that no one can prevent me from living well, both near claims 1 and 2. Leaving another’s wrong with them (7.21) is Article 28’s statement. Article 2 already says that dealing with an obstacle becomes my next action (claim 6), that I do not accept what is uncertain (near claim 5), and that reason should not be overpowered by the body, the failing side of which is 11.17. Claim 4’s “for the common good” is close to Article 1’s claim 3. What this article adds is the exercise itself: wiping out impressions, making impulses with a reservation, keeping desire out. Many of its passages are bare commands with no reason given, and the six claims read more as a list of exercises than as one thought.

statement.t: It is up to me to keep wiping out impressions and to make every impulse with a reservation, on condition that nothing prevents it.

parts.words: It is up to me
to keep wiping out impressions
to make every impulse with a reservation

statement.kind: A power and its daily exercise
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the ground: what is in my soul is up to me, and the mind kept to itself cannot be harmed. Claims 3 to 6 exercise that power on impressions, impulses, desire and acts, including what to do when an act is blocked.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if wiping out impressions and checking impulses were not in my power.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 2 (my mind cannot be harmed) and claim 4 (impulse by worth, desire kept out) gain a second author, and the article gains how an impression leads to an act, worth, impulse and action as three steps in order, what being carried along by impulse looks like, and what to do if I leave open what is in my power. He limits claim 1: once a passion is let in, it is no longer in my power; and claim 4: keeping desire out still leaves me free to wish.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: my actions must then agree with my impulses.

items.quote: The soul stands on unassailable ground, if it has abandoned external things; it is independent in its own fortress; and every weapon that is hurled falls short of the mark.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
items.follows: A soul that has let go of external things stands where it cannot be attacked, and nothing thrown at it reaches it.
items.context: Letter 82, on the fear of death: no retreat keeps fear and pain out, so Seneca tells Lucilius to wall himself in with philosophy. “It” is the soul.

items.quote: For it is easier to keep a thing out than to keep it under after you have let it in.
gives: I keep desire out
items.follows: Keeping a thing out is easier than holding it down once it has been let in.
items.context: Letter 85 argues against keeping the passions moderate. The “thing” is a passion, such as the sadness, fear and desire named two sections before.

items.quote: impulse toward an object arises in each case from the worth of the object
gives: I go by the worth of each thing
items.follows: Each impulse toward an object arises from that object’s worth.
items.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy, after its three duties of worth, impulse and action: life agrees with itself when each impulse matches its object’s worth.

items.label: why
items.t: Nothing moves me to act until an impression stirs me; then an impulse comes, and my assent confirms it. I walk only after giving myself the order and approving it.
items.why: In this section Marcus tells me to wipe out impressions and to check impulses, but he does not say how the two lead to an act. Seneca gives the order: an impression, then an impulse, then my assent.

support.quote: Every living thing possessed of reason is inactive if it is not first stirred by some external impression; then the impulse comes, and finally assent confirms the impulse.
gives: Nothing moves me to act until an impression stirs me
then an impulse comes, and my assent confirms it
support.follows: A reasoning being does nothing until an impression stirs it; the impulse follows, and assent confirms the impulse.
support.context: Letter 113, arguing that the virtues are not living things. Seneca first sets out how any reasoning being comes to act.

support.quote: I do walk, but only after uttering the command to myself and approving this opinion of mine.
gives: I walk only after giving myself the order and approving it
support.follows: Seneca walks only after he has told himself to and has approved that judgment.
support.context: Letter 113, Seneca’s example of assent. “This opinion of mine” is his judgment that he ought to take a walk.

items.label: action
items.t: I first weigh what each thing is worth, then form an ordered impulse toward it, and then make my actions agree with my impulse.
items.why: Marcus says here that an impulse should be according to worth (11.31), but not that this is one of three steps in order. Seneca sets them out: settle what a thing is worth, then form the impulse, then make action agree with it. The last step is new.

support.quote: the first duty is to determine severally what things are worth; the second, to conceive with regard to them a regulated and ordered impulse; the third, to make your impulse and your actions harmonize
gives: I first weigh what each thing is worth
then form an ordered impulse toward it
then make my actions agree with my impulse
support.follows: First settle what each thing is worth, then form an ordered impulse toward it, then make impulse and action agree.
support.context: Letter 89, on the parts of philosophy: Seneca splits its moral part into three, the worth of things, impulse and action. “Them” are the things whose worth is set.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is a disgrace to be carried along by impulse instead of going forward, and then to ask, dazed, in the middle of events: “How did I get into this condition?”
items.why: Marcus shows failure here as the divine part beaten by the body (11.17). Seneca shows another failure: being driven by impulse without forethought, and waking up in the middle of events. Joining “driven by impulse” and “carried along” into one sentence is the editor’s; in the letter they are two sentences apart.

support.quote: He has not been led to that pass by forethought; he has been driven to it by impulse.
gives: by impulse
support.follows: Whoever craves something got there by impulse, not by thinking ahead.
support.context: Letter 37, on the oath a person takes to virtue. “He” is any man who craves something without knowing how he came to crave it.

support.quote: It is disgraceful, instead of proceeding ahead, to be carried along, and then suddenly, amid the whirlpool of events, to ask in a dazed way: “How did I get into this condition?”
gives: It is a disgrace to be carried along
instead of going forward
to ask, dazed, in the middle of events: “How did I get into this condition?”
support.follows: It is disgraceful to be swept along and then to ask, in a daze, how one came to be where one is.
support.context: The close of Letter 37: it is shameful to be swept along by events instead of advancing. The “condition” is the state a man finds himself in.

items.label: doubt
items.t: Even if I leave open what is in my own control, I do not let my eagerness for wisdom weaken: I hold fast to it until it becomes a habit of mind.
items.why: No passage of Marcus here asks what holds if the matter is not up to me. Seneca sets that question aside without answering it, and says what to do all the same.

support.quote: it is not my purpose now to be led into a discussion as to what is within our own control
gives: Even if I leave open what is in my own control
support.follows: Seneca declines, for now, to argue about what lies within our own control.
support.context: Letter 16, on philosophy as the guide of life. Seneca has asked whether fate, God or chance rules us; what lies in our control is the question he leaves aside.

support.quote: that you should not allow the impulse of your spirit to weaken and grow cold
gives: I do not let my eagerness for wisdom weaken
support.follows: Lucilius should not let the eager impulse of his spirit weaken and cool.
support.context: Letter 16 opens by urging Lucilius to keep up the study of wisdom; “the impulse of your spirit” is his eagerness for it.

support.quote: Hold fast to it and establish it firmly, in order that what is now impulse may become a habit of the mind.
gives: I hold fast to it until it becomes a habit of mind
support.follows: An impulse held fast and made firm can become a settled habit of the mind.
support.context: Letter 16, the same advice. “It” is Lucilius’s impulse toward philosophy, which Seneca wants turned into a settled habit.

items.t: Seneca limits the claim’s broad wording, that what is in my soul is up to me. What is in my power is to keep a passion out; once I let sadness, fear or desire in, it no longer lies within my power, because what stirs it is outside me. On keeping passions out, 8.27 and Seneca agree.

support.quote: if you grant any privileges to sadness, fear, desire, and all the other wrong impulses, they will cease to lie within our jurisdiction
support.follows: Passions given any room stop being under our control.
support.context: Letter 85, against the view that passions should be kept moderate. The “wrong impulses” are passions; “our jurisdiction” is what lies in our own power.

support.quote: Simply because the means of arousing them lie outside our own power.
support.follows: Passions once admitted are not ours to govern, because what stirs them is outside our power.
support.context: Letter 85, Seneca’s reason for that claim. “Them” are the passions; what arouses them is the outside things that cause fear or the hope of gain.

support.quote: How have I the power to bring something to a close, when I have not had the power to check it at the beginning?
support.follows: If I had no power to stop a thing at its start, I have none to bring it to an end.
support.context: Letter 85, closing the argument against moderate passions. “Something” is a passion that was let in.

items.t: Seneca limits keeping away from desire. He bans the desires, but still allows the wish to do the same things without fear and with better judgment. For him, keeping desire out does not mean wanting nothing.

support.quote: after I have issued my prohibition against the desires, I shall still allow you to wish that you may do the same things fearlessly and with greater accuracy of judgment
support.follows: Banning the desires still leaves room to wish to act without fear and with better judgment.
support.context: Letter 116, on self-control: should emotions be moderate or absent? Seneca says absent. “The same things” are what Lucilius strives for as necessary, useful or pleasant.

support.quote: I shall simply strip away the vice.
support.follows: Seneca takes away only the vice, not the things Lucilius strives for.
support.context: Letter 116: Seneca promises to be indulgent to what Lucilius strives for. “The vice” is the passion attached to those things.

amend.t: ; and my actions must then agree with my impulses
; but once I let a passion in, it no longer lies within my power
; but keeping desire out still leaves me free to wish to act without fear and with better judgment

searches: own control, own power, jurisdiction, in our power
crave nothing, desire nothing, no desire

rejected.why: The wise man barred from statecraft teaches how to bear poverty. It backs claim 6, but Article 2 already uses it for the same point.
The beginning is in our power, fortune decides the issue. Near the reservation of claim 4, but already used in Article 2.
Easier to stop passions at the start than to control them later. Says what 85.13, which is quoted, says.
Passions are more easily removed than controlled. Same argument as 85.13; one witness is enough.
Reason tames the madness of our desires. About knowledge of self and nature, not about keeping desire out.
Bravery as an impregnable fortress. About courage under siege, not the mind kept free of passions.
Freedom is power over oneself. Said of a height still to be reached, while claim 1 says it is in my power now; the text also has a misprint at that place.
A mind shaken by wandering thoughts. Thoughts, not impressions, and said as a prayer for Lucilius; does not back claim 5’s words.
What is settled does not wander from its place. About desires changing day to day, not wandering among impressions.
A true judgment clarifies every appearance that stirs our impulses. A definition of virtue; matching it to the sure grasp would need explaining.
What takes effect by chance is not an art; wisdom is an art. Said of when to give advice, not of doing each act by a rule.
Put yourself under the control of reason and you will rule many. About wisdom freeing us from passions in general; 37.5 is used.
Keeping the mind from straying outside itself amid noise. About concentration in a noisy lodging.
The worst part of a wrong stays with the wrongdoer. Near 7.21, but said of ingratitude, and 7.21 is a said-once item that takes no backing.
Checked impulses and desires in one’s control are useless without knowing the time for action. About timing; only its last sentence is used.
Whatever rules, philosophy is our defence. Already in Article 3; 16.6, which follows it, is used.
You must crave nothing to rival Jupiter. Attalus on riches and freedom from Fortune; 85.13 says keeping out more plainly.
Anger leads to madness. About anger, not about the contest of 11.31, which is a said-once item.

articles.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

claims.t: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good, as an emerald has its own color. When I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away.
claims.shared: 7.24 and 5.3 both speak of a good act that other people then speak against: in 7.24 it is “to act well and yet be spoken ill of”, in 5.3 a word or deed “that accords with nature” followed by “the blame or the talk” of some people. 7.12 backs “I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away” only as “whatever anyone says, I stay good”; blame and the pull are 5.3’s words.
claims.changed: 5.3 speaks of a word or deed that accords with nature; the claim calls it acting well, 7.24’s words. 7.12 names gold, emerald and purple; the claim keeps the emerald, the one that speaks.

support.quote: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own color.”
gives: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good, as an emerald has its own color
I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away
support.follows: Whatever anyone else does or says, I must still be good, as an emerald must still be an emerald and have its own color.

support.quote: “It is kingly to act well and yet be spoken ill of.”
gives: When I act well
am spoken ill of
support.follows: To act well and to be spoken ill of is the part of a king.

support.quote: Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterward from some people pull you away
gives: When I act well
