am spoken ill of
I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away
support.follows: When I say or do what accords with nature, the blame and talk of some people that follow should not pull me away from it.

claims.t: Like a headland that stands while the waves break against it, my mind must put itself in order by itself and stand upright, not set upright by anything else and needing no service or quiet from outside.
claims.shared: 3.6 and 7.24 both ask that the mind be right by its own doing and not by another’s: 3.6 “upright, not set upright”, 7.24 “shaped and put in order by itself”. 4.40 gives the image of the headland that stands while the waves break against it; it shares the standing, not the word “upright”.
claims.changed: 7.24 says it is shameful when the mind does not order itself; the claim turns this into what the mind must do. 3.6 and 4.40 speak of “one” and of being like a headland; the claim speaks of my mind. 3.6’s “cheerfulness within” is left out of the claim.

support.quote: while the mind itself is not shaped and put in order by itself
gives: put itself in order
by itself
support.follows: The mind ought to shape itself and put itself in order; it is shameful when it does not.

support.quote: So one must be upright, not set upright.
gives: by itself
stand upright, not set upright by anything else
support.follows: One must stand straight of oneself, not be straightened or propped up by something else.

support.quote: And let there be cheerfulness within, and no need of service from outside, and no need of the quiet that others provide.
gives: needing no service or quiet from outside
support.follows: Cheerfulness should come from within, without needing help from outside or a quiet that others provide.

support.quote: To be like the headland against which the waves break without pause; but it stands, and around it the water that had swelled up is put to sleep.
gives: Like a headland that stands while the waves break against it
support.follows: I should be like a headland: the waves break on it without pause, it stands, and the swell around it grows calm.

claims.role: Changing my mind for the truth
claims.t: When someone sets me right and makes it plain that I am judging or acting wrongly, I change my mind gladly, and it is still my own free act. I change only for what is just or of common benefit, not because a view is pleasant or well thought of; what I am looking for is the truth.
claims.shared: 4.10 and 8.14 both speak of changing one’s mind to follow “someone … who sets one right” (8.14: “the one who sets you right”); 6.20 says the same of anyone who can refute me: “I will gladly change”. 4.10 names what may move me, what is just or of common benefit; 6.20 names the truth.
claims.changed: 4.10 speaks of “one” and of two kinds of readiness; the claim keeps the second and says “I”. The three passages use one Greek verb for changing one’s position.

support.quote: The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion.
gives: When someone sets me right
I change my mind
support.follows: I should be ready to change my mind when someone is at hand to set me right and lead me away from a mistaken notion.

support.quote: But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.
gives: I change only for what is just or of common benefit, not because a view is pleasant or well thought of
support.follows: I should change only for a reason that persuades, as just or for the common good, never because the new view is pleasant or well regarded.

support.quote: Remember that to change your mind, too, and to follow the one who sets you right is no less free.
gives: When someone sets me right
I change my mind
it is still my own free act
support.follows: Changing my mind and following the one who sets me right is no less free.

support.quote: For the activity is yours, carried through according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.
gives: it is still my own free act
support.follows: When I follow someone who corrects me, the act is still mine, done by my own impulse, judgment and mind.

support.quote: If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change.
gives: makes it plain that I am judging or acting wrongly
I change my mind
gladly
support.follows: If anyone shows me plainly that I am judging or acting wrongly, I will change, and gladly.

support.quote: For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.
gives: what I am looking for is the truth
support.follows: What I want is the truth, which harms no one; the one harmed is the one who holds on to delusion and ignorance.

claims.t: I fail when I want to be approved of: when I flatter, try to please and show off, or want everyone to praise whatever I do, like a diseased eye that wants only the green things. I could have been rid of these faults long ago.
claims.shared: Both passages name wanting other people’s approval as a fault of the mind: 5.5 “to flatter”, “to try to please, to show off”; 10.35 the mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do”.
claims.changed: 5.5 lists approval-seeking among other faults (grumbling, stinginess, blaming the body); the claim keeps only those that seek approval. 10.35 also names the wish that “the little ones be kept safe”, which the claim leaves out.

support.quote: to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of
flatter, try to please and show off
support.follows: Flattering, trying to please and showing off are among the faults no lack of talent forces on me.

support.quote: you could have been rid of these long ago
gives: I could have been rid of these faults long ago
support.follows: I could have got rid of these faults long ago; nothing in my nature kept me from it.

support.quote: “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of
want everyone to praise whatever I do, like a diseased eye that wants only the green things
support.follows: A mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do” is like an eye that looks only for the green things.

support.quote: The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased.
gives: like a diseased eye that wants only the green things
support.follows: A healthy eye takes in everything there is to see; wanting only the green things is a sign of diseased eyes.

claims.t: I give my whole attention to what another person is saying, and as far as I can I enter into the soul of the one who speaks; and I let every other person enter into my own ruling part, the part of me that judges and decides.
claims.shared: Both passages ask me to go inside the other person: 6.48 “be in the soul of the one who speaks”, 8.58 “enter into each person’s ruling part”. 8.58 adds the other direction.
claims.changed: 6.48 says “soul”, 8.58 “ruling part”; the claim keeps each passage’s own word.

support.quote: Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.
gives: I give my whole attention to what another person is saying
I enter into
the soul of the one who speaks
support.follows: I should train myself to follow what another person says closely and, as far as I can, be inside the soul of the one speaking.

support.quote: To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.
gives: I enter into
let every other person enter into my own ruling part
support.follows: I should enter into each person’s ruling part and let every other person enter into mine.

single.label: Their impulse is their own
single.t: The people who blame me have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own, and I do not look round at those things.
single.quote: For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things
single.why: This is the one reason the section gives for not heeding blame. Only 5.3 says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Other people judge and act from their own minds and impulses, and I need not keep looking at what moves them.

single.label: One road
single.t: I go straight on, following my own nature and the common nature, and these two have one road.
single.quote: go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.
single.why: Only this passage joins my own nature to the common nature. No second passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: I should go straight on following my own nature and the common nature, and the two take one road.

single.label: Being, not discussing
single.t: I stop discussing at all what kind of man the good man is, and set myself to be one.
single.quote: No longer to discuss at all what kind of man the good man is, but to be such a man.
single.why: Only this passage sets being good against talking about it. It is kept as a rule for what I do.
single.follows: The time for discussing what a good man is has ended; what is left is to be one.

single.label: What is in my power
single.t: Much is wholly in my power, and no lack of natural gift excuses me from it: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, and more.
single.quote: Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which there is no excuse of want of natural gift or of unfitness, and yet you still stay down below of your own will?
single.why: Only this passage lists what is in my power whatever my talents. The list in the item is shortened: not loving pleasure, not complaining of my lot, no idle talk and greatness are in the quote but not in the sentence. Its faults of seeking approval feed claim 4.
single.follows: These qualities depend on no natural gift, so I can show them now and have no excuse for lacking them.

single.label: Fitting and true
single.t: If something is not fitting, I do not do it; if it is not true, I do not say it.
single.quote: If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.
single.why: Only this passage gives the test of fitting and true. Its next sentence breaks off in the Greek of this section.
single.follows: Before acting I ask whether the act is fitting, and before speaking whether the words are true.

single.label: A practice · speaking
single.t: When I speak, in the senate or to anyone at all, I speak with decorum, in a delivery that is not too careful or studied, and what I say is sound.
single.quote: To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.
single.why: Only this passage is about the manner of speaking. Its rare word for “over-distinctly” is not certain: it may mean a delivery that is too carefully distinct, or a voice that is too piercing.
single.follows: Whether in the senate or with anyone, I should speak with decorum, not with an over-careful delivery, and say what is sound.

single.label: A practice · bearing
single.t: As my mind keeps my face composed and graceful, I keep my whole body firm in the same way, in movement and at rest, and without affectation.
single.quote: The body too must be firmly set, and not thrown about, either in movement or in posture. For what the mind provides in the face, keeping it composed and graceful, something of that kind must be required in the whole body as well. But all this must be kept up without affectation.
single.why: Only this passage turns from the mind to the body. 7.24 also speaks of the mind ordering the face, but uses it to say the mind must order itself.
single.follows: My body should be steady and composed, as my face is when my mind governs it, and none of it should be put on.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.12 is 7.15, 4.10 is 4.12, 8.28 is 8.30, 6.48 is 6.53, 12.13 is 12.17, 7.32 is 7.60, 3.6 is 3.5, 8.14 is 8.16, 7.24 is 7.36 and 7.37, 4.40 is 4.49, 8.36 is 8.38, 10.18 is 10.16, 8.58 is 8.61 and 6.20 is 6.21; 5.3, 5.5 and 10.35 are the same.

Changes the title from “Being good for its own sake”. No passage speaks of a motive or of anything’s own sake; they speak of staying good whatever others say, and of changing my mind when someone sets me right.

Reads “a word or deed that accords with nature” (5.3) as acting well, 7.24’s words, and its “blame or talk” as being spoken ill of. 7.24’s first sentence is a saying Marcus quotes; it is taken as a rule he adopts.
Reads 3.6’s “upright, not set upright” as standing by oneself, and pairs it with 4.40’s headland that “stands” and with 7.24’s mind that should order itself “by itself”.
articles.limit: The statement joins two halves that the passages do not join: holding firm against talk, and giving way to someone who sets me right. The editor reads them as one rule, that only reasons move me, but no passage says so. The practices of speaking and bearing (8.28, 7.32) and of entering another mind (6.48, 8.58) are loosely tied to the statement. The Why column holds companion demands (my mind must stand by itself; I follow my own and the common nature) and one stated reason, 5.3’s that other people have their own ruling part. Article 27’s claim 4 (wanting others’ good opinion goes against myself) is near claim 4 here, and Article 19’s claim 5 (if someone despises me, that is for them to see to) is near claim 1. Article 23 says what claim 1 says, for the case of those I work for speaking ill of me; Article 29 says what claim 2 says, from 7.9 (I am upright on my own, not held upright). Article 12’s claim 2 says I do not spend my life guessing what others say or think unless it serves the common good; claim 5 here, attending to the one who speaks, is that exception at work. What this article adds is being set right: I change my mind for reasons, and only for them.

aside.8.36: Obscure: the speaker is not named, and the Greek as given does not settle whether it means judging together with the wisest men or by the wisest standards.

statement.t: Whatever others say of me, I act well, and I change my mind only when I am shown what is true, just or of common benefit.

parts.words: Whatever others say of me, I act well
I change my mind
only when I am shown what is true, just or of common benefit

statement.kind: Two kinds of firmness
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 hold the first half: talk does not move me, and my mind stands by itself. Claim 3 is the other half: a reason given by someone else does move me, and that too is my own act. Claim 4 shows the failure, wanting approval; claim 5 is a practice of openness to other minds.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if acting well whatever others say, or changing only for reasons, were wrong.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, acting well while spoken ill of and wanting approval as the failure gain a second author, the ground gains a reward that lies in the deed itself, the way back gains an answer for one who cannot stand alone, and the claim that my mind stands upright by itself is limited, since he holds that no one rises above his folly unaided.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a motive: I act well whatever others say, change my mind only for what is true, just or of common benefit, and look for no reward, since the wages of a good deed is to have done it.

items.quote: Nay, indeed you must often be just and be at the same time disgraced.
gives: When I act well
am spoken ill of
items.follows: Acting justly will often go together with being in disgrace, and a just person must accept that.
items.context: Letter 113 ends on justice that wants no reward and no renown. “Disgraced” is having a bad name while one is acting justly.

items.quote: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown.
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of
items.follows: Whoever wants his good conduct made known is striving for renown, not for goodness.
items.context: Letter 113, on justice: it makes no difference how many people know of one’s uprightness. “Their virtue” is the good conduct they want others to know of.

items.label: why
items.t: I am good without looking for a reward. The reward of every virtue lies in the virtue itself: the wages of a good deed is to have done it.
items.why: In this section Marcus says I must be good whatever others say; he does not say what I gain by it. Seneca says: nothing outside the good deed itself. 113.31 speaks of justice, 81.19 of all the virtues; the item’s “good” rests on the second.

support.quote: “I must be just without reward.”
gives: I am good without looking for a reward
support.follows: I must act justly without expecting anything in return.
support.context: Letter 113 ends on justice, which seeks nothing for itself. Seneca says each person should first convince himself of this sentence.

support.quote: the reward for all the virtues lies in the virtues themselves. For they are not practised with a view to recompense; the wages of a good deed is to have done it.
gives: The reward of every virtue lies in the virtue itself
the wages of a good deed is to have done it
support.follows: Virtues are not practised for payment; doing a good deed is its own payment.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: gratitude helps the grateful person, not because the favour comes back, but because a virtue is its own reward.

items.label: breaks
items.t: If I cannot find the way by myself, I can follow faithfully where someone else leads; that is the second rank, and it is still excellent. I need not despise myself for needing help: wanting to be saved means a great deal.
items.why: Marcus already allows that I follow the one who sets me right (claim 3). Seneca adds that needing a guide is a lower rank but still excellent, and nothing to despise. He speaks of “a man”; the item turns it to “I”.

support.quote: there are others who need outside help, who will not proceed unless someone leads the way, but who will follow faithfully. Of these, he says, Metrodorus was one; this type of man is also excellent, but belongs to the second grade.
gives: I can follow faithfully where someone else leads
that is the second rank, and it is still excellent
support.follows: Some people go forward only when someone leads them, and follow faithfully; such a person is excellent too, though of the second rank.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers: Epicurus ranks those who reach the truth alone above those who need a guide. Seneca says he would be glad to be admitted to the second.

support.quote: Nor need you despise a man who can gain salvation only with the assistance of another; the will to be saved means a great deal, too.
gives: I need not despise myself for needing help
wanting to be saved means a great deal
support.follows: Someone who can be saved only with another’s help is not to be despised; the will to be saved counts for much.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers. “Salvation” is being freed from folly, which Seneca has just said no one escapes unaided.

items.t: Seneca says that no man has the strength by himself to rise above his folly: he needs a helping hand and someone to pull him out. Marcus asks that my mind be upright by itself, not set upright. Reading the two as goal and route, a limit and not a contradiction, is the editor’s; Marcus too follows the one who sets him right (claim 3). Seneca is not consistent here: in the next section (Ep. 52.3) he reports Epicurus’s first class, men who worked their way to the truth without anyone’s help.

support.quote: No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it; he needs a helping hand, and some one to extricate him.
support.follows: No one is strong enough to rise above his folly alone; he needs someone to give him a hand and pull him out.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers, opens on how we veer from plan to plan. “It” is that folly, which Lucilius says belongs to the fool.

amend.t: ; and I look for no reward, since the wages of a good deed is to have done it
; yet to rise above my own folly I am not strong enough by myself, and I need a helping hand

searches: ill repute, evil report, spoken ill, slander
change my mind, changed my mind, correct me
convinced of error, admit a mistake, confess an error
ashamed to learn, willing to learn
own judgment, slave to a master or opinion
talking about, discussing virtue, instead of words
consistent, one and the same, like itself
into another’s mind or soul, inmost

rejected.why: Strives for what honour demands amid disgrace. Backs claim 1, but in a narrow case (gratitude that looks like ingratitude); Ep. 113.32 says it plainly.
Good character abides by its judgments; badness changes, not for the better. No real difference from 4.10, which also refuses change for its own sake.
Be consistent with yourself; a shifting will shows a mind at sea. About desires changing, not about being set right.
We must be admonished and have an advocate with an upright mind. About resisting false values of wealth; Ep. 52.2 makes the point about needing help more directly.
A guardian to pluck us by the ear against popular opinion. Near claim 3, but it is about rumours and crowds, not about being shown an error in argument.
The happy man is upright, unshaken, moved by force but not to distraction. A portrait of happiness; “upright” is moral, and the match with the headland needs explaining.
A less ostentatious gait and a restrained style of speech. Matches 7.32 and 8.28, which are said-once items and take no backing; Marcus already says both.
Our words should aim not to please but to help. About eloquence and style; near claim 4 but not about wanting approval for oneself.
Scorn the pleasure of the majority’s applause; your good qualities should face inwards. Close to claim 4, but Ep. 113.32 names the failure more directly; kept to one witness.
Why take pleasure in praise from those you cannot praise? About a lecture audience; a limit on whose praise counts would say more than the quote.
Renown as the favourable opinion of good men. Spoken by Seneca’s opponents, not his own view.
Philosophy teaches us to act, not to speak; an inner life of one hue. Near 10.18 and 7.12, which are said once or already backed; about word and deed agreeing.
Men prove their words their own by doing what they talk about. Near 10.18, a said-once item.
Seneca admits Lucilius to his inmost thoughts. Near claim 5, but he uses Lucilius as a pretext for arguing with himself.
Who that is pleased by virtue can please the crowd? Says what Ep. 113.32 says for claim 4.
A foolish mind is never like itself; play the role of one man. About consistency, not about others’ talk.
A witness who stands near us when we are likely to go wrong. About an imagined guardian, not about being set right by argument.
It makes no difference how many know of one’s uprightness. Repeats what the two quoted sentences of the same section say.
Hold nothing in oneself unfit for an enemy to know, but share one’s worries with a friend. Its main clause narrows openness to a friend; it does not back letting every other person in.

articles.title: Keeping to one’s craft

claims.t: I attend only to what I am doing now. If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me, I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating well.
claims.shared: 9.42 and 6.50 both shut everything else out of attention, and each has its word of exclusion: 9.42 “only” with what is being done now, 6.50 “anything other than” how I myself bring the work about. This is the one component of the claim that two passages say; the steering, the doctoring and the abuse are 6.50’s alone.
claims.changed: 9.42 is an instruction with no subject and 6.50 a question about an imagined case; the claim states both in the first person. 6.50’s “how I myself might bring about” is read as the act being done now. In 9.42 the word “only” covers the act and the instrument together; the claim takes the act, and the instrument stands as a said-once item. 6.32 is not in the claim: it shares the doctor with 6.50 but says nothing of attention, and in 6.50 nobody asks the helmsman or the doctor to give anything up.

support.quote: To be occupied only with what is being done now
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now
support.follows: My attention is to stay on what is being done now.

support.quote: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now
If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me
I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating well
support.follows: If the sailors or the sick spoke ill of me while I steered or treated them, I would still attend only to keeping those on board safe or making the sick well.

single.label: Up to a point
single.t: I look at how craftsmen work: they adapt to people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the rule the craft works by and will not give it up.
single.quote: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it?
single.why: Only this passage speaks of adapting to others and of where the adapting stops. It is the first half of 6.32’s argument and says what craftsmen do; the passage does not go on to say that I adapt to others up to a point. 6.50 has people who speak ill, but nobody there asks for anything to be given up, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Craftsmen fit in with people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the craft’s own rule and refuse to give it up.

single.label: My own reason
single.t: It would be shocking if a master builder or a doctor respected the reason of their craft, the rule their work is done by, more than I respect my own reason, which I share with the gods.
single.quote: Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
single.why: Only this passage gives a ground. It sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and uses one word, “reason”, for both; the line adds “the rule their work is done by” only to say what the reason of a craft is. It argues from the smaller thing to the greater and does not call reason a craft.
single.follows: A human being’s own reason, shared with the gods, deserves at least the respect a builder or a doctor has for the reason of a craft.

single.label: The instrument
single.t: In what I am doing now, I keep my mind also on the instrument through which I act.
single.quote: and with the instrument through which you act
single.why: Only this passage names an instrument, and it does not say which one: the body, the mind, or the tool in hand. It is kept as a point of attention I can return to at any moment.
single.follows: I am to be occupied also with the instrument through which I act.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition: 6.32 is 6.35 in modern editions and 6.50 is 6.55; 9.42 is the end of 9.41, the last words of one sentence and the sentence after it.

States in the first person what 6.32 only asks. No passage says “I keep to my own reason”: 6.32 sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and asks whether the second deserves less respect. It does not call reason a craft, and it does not say that I adapt to others as craftsmen do; the title’s “craft” is the picture, not an identification.

Reads 6.50 with “I” as the one who attends. The Greek quoted is Leopold’s edition of 1908 in its Perseus copy, which prints the first-person ἐνεργοίην, “I myself might bring about”; but even so ἂν προσεῖχον can be third person plural, “would they be attending”, with the sailors and the sick still the subject, and the translators’ notes give both that reading and a third-person form of the second verb. Taking ἂν προσεῖχον as first person is allowed by the printed Greek but not required; on the other reading 6.50 still backs “speak ill of me” but not “I attend only”, and the article would have no fused claim.

Lets two of the three parts of the statement rest on one passage each: the likeness on 6.32, the abuse on 6.50. This is an exception to rule 8, for the owner to approve: with three passages, of which only two say the same thing, no more is available. Does not quote the opening words of 9.42, “… is common to every school”, because their subject stands before the cut; places the instrument of 9.42 under Practice, although the Greek leaves open which instrument is meant.
articles.limit: The section’s three passages yield one fused claim, carried by two of them, and it rests on reading ἂν προσεῖχον in 6.50 as first person (“would I be attending”), which the printed Greek allows but does not require; on the third-person reading nothing here is fused. That claim, attending to my work alone when those I work for speak ill of me, is already Article 22’s claim 1 (when I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away), and Article 2 already says that my work is the act itself. What this article adds is only the likeness to a craft from 6.32, that I owe my own reason at least the respect a builder or a doctor gives the reason of the craft, which Article 24’s claim 1 (I treat living as a skill, learned by training) comes near from another side.

statement.t: I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft, and attend only to what I am doing now, even when those I work for speak ill of me.

parts.words: I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft
attend only to what I am doing now
even when those I work for speak ill of me

statement.kind: A likeness, and a rule of attention with its test
statement.form: 6.32 gives the likeness between a craft and a person’s own reason, in two said-once items under Why. The one fused claim is the rule of attention that 9.42 states and 6.50 tests in the case where the people the work is for speak ill of the one doing it. The statement joins the likeness and the rule with a plain “and”; no passage joins them.

empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes losing hold of my reason or my attention, or the way back; 6.32 only calls the first shocking.
empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if my reason deserves no more respect than a craft does.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: a ground, that what a pilot answers for is the work and not its success; how far to go along with other people, which 6.32 says only of craftsmen; and, under “When it breaks”, philosophy that courts applause. He backs nothing in the one claim, and he limits the picture it uses: a pilot’s or a physician’s skill is for the good of other people, and the wise person’s good is their own as well.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause on praise, which he says of philosophy only: my philosophy does not court applause. His limit falls on the claim that pictures steering and doctoring, not on the statement: the statement’s likeness to a doctor is about holding to a rule, and his limit is about whose good the skill serves.

items.label: why
items.t: What a pilot has promised me is a serviceable performance of the task, not a prosperous voyage. A storm interferes with the pilot’s success, not with the pilot’s work.
items.why: 6.50 fixes attention on what keeps those on board safe and says nothing of a voyage that ends badly. Seneca, with the same picture, says what the pilot answers for: the work, not its success. He says it of the pilot only; applying it to my own work is left to the reader. Article 2 says of every act that the work is the act itself.

support.quote: The pilot has promised you, not a prosperous voyage, but a serviceable performance of his task
gives: What a pilot has promised me is a serviceable performance of the task, not a prosperous voyage
support.follows: A pilot owes those who sail with him a competent performance of his task, not a good voyage.
support.context: Seneca answers the objection that a storm makes a pilot worse at his work, as pain might make a wise man worse. “You” is anyone who sails with the pilot.

support.quote: the storm does not interfere with the pilot’s work, but only with his success
gives: A storm interferes with the pilot’s success, not with the pilot’s work
support.follows: A storm gets in the way of the pilot’s success; it does not get in the way of his work.
support.context: Letter 85, on whether hardship harms the wise man as a storm harms a pilot. Seneca’s own answer: a pilot who keeps the ship on an even keel as it sinks has met his art’s demands.

items.label: action
items.t: Outwardly I conform to the customs of the people around me; inwardly I am different in every respect. I try to keep a higher standard of life than most people, but not a contrary one, or I would drive away the very people I am trying to improve.
items.why: 6.32 says that craftsmen adapt to laymen “up to a point”. It does not apply this to me, and it does not say where the point is or why they adapt at all. Seneca says it of those who practise philosophy: he draws the line between the outward life and the inward one, and gives a reason, that a contrary way of life repels the people one hopes to improve.

support.quote: Inwardly, we ought to be different in all respects, but our exterior should conform to society.
gives: Outwardly I conform to the customs of the people around me
inwardly I am different in every respect
support.follows: A person who practises philosophy should differ from others inwardly and conform to them outwardly.
support.context: Seneca warns Lucilius not to show off his philosophy by odd dress or habits. “We” are those who practise philosophy; “society” is the customs of the people they live among.

support.quote: Let us try to maintain a higher standard of life than that of the multitude, but not a contrary standard; otherwise, we shall frighten away and repel the very persons whom we are trying to improve.
gives: I try to keep a higher standard of life than most people, but not a contrary one
I would drive away the very people I am trying to improve
support.follows: The standard should be higher than the multitude’s but not contrary to it, or it repels the people one is trying to improve.
support.context: Letter 5, on living as a philosopher without making a display of it. “The multitude” are ordinary people, whom the philosopher hopes to improve and must not frighten off.

items.label: breaks
items.t: Nothing is baser than philosophy that courts applause: a sick man does not praise the surgeon during the operation. I take no pleasure in being praised by people whom I could not praise myself.
items.why: 6.50 speaks only of being spoken ill of. Seneca, with the same picture of a healer and the sick, takes the other case, being praised. He says it of philosophy, not of every kind of work, and it shows what failing looks like there: doing philosophy for the sake of the praise.

support.quote: For what is baser than philosophy courting applause? Does the sick man praise the surgeon while he is operating?
gives: Nothing is baser than philosophy that courts applause
a sick man does not praise the surgeon during the operation
support.follows: Philosophy that courts applause is as base as anything can be; a patient does not praise the surgeon in the middle of an operation.
support.context: On choosing teachers: Seneca allows public lecturers only if they aim to improve people. The surgeon is the philosopher who teaches; the sick man is his hearer.

support.quote: Why do you take pleasure in being praised by men whom you yourself cannot praise?
gives: I take no pleasure in being praised by people whom I could not praise myself
support.follows: There is no reason to enjoy praise from people one cannot praise oneself.
support.context: Letter 52, on philosophers who lecture in public. “You” is a lecturer who goes home happy because an audience of ignorant people applauded him.

items.t: Seneca takes the same two crafts as 6.50, the pilot’s and the physician’s, and marks where the likeness ends. Their art is for the good of other people, the passengers and the patients. The wise man’s good is common: it belongs to the people he lives among and to himself as well. The limit falls on the picture the claim uses, steering and doctoring, and not on its rule of attention, about which Ep. 85.36 says nothing. It does not contradict Marcus, whose 6.32 implies that a person’s own reason deserves no less respect than the reason of a craft. Seneca is not quite steady on the pilot: in Ep. 85.33 the storm does not interfere with the pilot’s work, and three sections later it hinders the services he has promised to others.

support.quote: the pilot’s art is another’s good—it concerns his passengers just as a physician’s art concerns his patients
support.follows: A pilot’s art, like a physician’s, is for the good of other people: the passengers and the patients.
support.context: Seneca argues that hardship harms the wise man less than a storm harms a pilot. “Another’s good”: the art serves the passengers or patients, not the one who practises it.

support.quote: But the wise man’s good is a common good—it belongs both to those in whose company he lives, and to himself also.
support.follows: The wise man’s good belongs to the people he lives with and to himself as well.
support.context: Letter 85, comparing the wise man with a pilot in a storm. The wise man’s good, set against the pilot’s art, is said in this sentence to belong to others and to himself.

amend.t: , and my philosophy does not court applause
; but unlike a pilot’s or a physician’s skill, which is for others’ good, my good, if I am wise, belongs to those I live among and to me

searches: physician, doctor, surgeon (with art, craft, skill)
speak ill, abuse, revile, slander, insult
conform, outward, exterior, crowd (with differ, inward, within)
applause, praise (with physician, surgeon, pilot, sick)
task in hand, at hand, what I am doing, the present, engrossed, intent on
please, approval, favour (with crowd, people, many, mob)
ignorant, uninitiated, unskilled, layman, inexperienced (with talk, opinion, judge, say)
art of living, art of life, handmaid, mistress
blame, censure, criticism, gossip, ill repute
thanks, ungrateful (with task, duty, deed, work)

rejected.why: “My thoughts are on the deed itself”: a good man about to die for his country sets the deed against later fame and thanks. The deed is still to come, so the words do not back attention to what is being done now. Used at first as a backing and withdrawn.

Says the pilot aims at the port and the wise man at doing all things rightly, and calls the arts handmaids. It is a reply Seneca reports and then sets aside for his own answer in 85.33, so it is not used as his view.
A storm harms the pilot as a voyager, not as a pilot. Repeats 85.33, which is quoted.
The pilot is also a passenger. Part of the same argument; adds nothing about keeping to the work.
The wise man is always in action, even when fortune has blocked his way. About the blocked act, which is Article 2’s subject.
“The very thing which engages his attention” is the hardship itself, which becomes his work. Quoted in Article 2; not about undivided attention.
“One must steer, not talk”: a sea-sick pilot as the picture of a teacher who does not live as he teaches. About matching words with deeds.
A sick man does not call in a physician for his eloquence. About style in philosophical writing, not about holding to the craft.
“There is other business at hand”: the patient wants to be treated, not entertained. A letter on style; the nearest by vectors, but its subject is words against things.

The other arts deal with the tools of life, the art of living with life as a whole. Another difference between a craft and wisdom, in an argument about whether precepts suffice; one limit, from 85.36, was enough.
In a craft an intended mistake is the lesser fault, in the art of living the greater. A further difference between the two; off the section’s point.
Philosophy is mistress and appoints her own time. About giving philosophy all one’s time, not about attention to the act in hand.
The theatre is full and the philosopher’s lecture hall empty. A complaint about what people value.
Illness hinders the artisan’s handiwork but not a practised soul. About illness.
The skilled workman handles his tools with ease. An illustration in an argument about animals; says nothing of attending to the instrument.
Philosophy teaches us to act, not to speak. About consistency of life and words.
Demetrius hears the talk of ignorant men as rumblings of the belly. Scorns the talkers; in 6.50 the people who speak ill are the ones the work is for.
Madness to fear disrepute among the disreputable. Used to argue that death’s bad name should not frighten; not about work.
Whoever is pleased by virtue cannot please the crowd; to win its approval one must become like it. About popularity; 5.2 and 5.3 say more exactly how far to conform.
Philosophy makes one prefer to please oneself rather than the populace. Same point as 52.11, without the picture of the healer.
Do what the crowd does, but in a different way. About keeping a festival; 5.2 states the rule generally.

“You will stick to your purpose, even though the crowd may surround and seek to distract you.” The advice around it is to keep away from such people, where 6.32’s craftsmen go along with them up to a point.
Socrates: let men think you a fool and insult you. About virtue as the only good; no work is being done for those who insult.
One must often be just and disgraced, and ill repute well won should be a delight. Goes further than 6.50, which only looks away from abuse; about justice without reward.
Reason is common to gods and men. Says what 6.32 says once under Why; a said-once item takes no backing.
Reason is the best in man, surpassed only by the gods. The same ground as 6.32’s, which is said once and takes no backing.
Fabianus wrote to say what pleased him, without any search for applause. Praise of a writer’s style.
Submit to the cure in silence. Addressed to the hearer, not to the one doing the work; 52.9 and 52.11 are quoted.
Applause belongs to the arts that aim to please the crowd. Repeats 52.9, and shows that Seneca’s point is about philosophy, not about every art.
We do not adapt ourselves to the present but send our thoughts ahead. About fretting over the future, not about attention to an act.
A musician’s instruments serve his performance, not his art itself. About what makes a musician, not about attending to the instrument while acting.
Those who seem busied with nothing are busied with the greater tasks. Seneca defending his withdrawal from public business.
“I do not surrender myself to my affairs, but loan myself to them.” About keeping time free for study; quoted in Article 2.

articles.title: Training, and the use of reason

claims.t: I treat living as a skill, and in a skill I am able only where I have been trained: in writing and reading I do not give the rules before I have been given them, and this holds still more in life.
claims.shared: 12.5 and 11.27 both make ability depend on training that came before it: the left hand holds the bridle firmly “because this is what it has had practice in”, and no one rules in writing and reading before having “been ruled”. The words they back together, “I am able only where I have been trained”, are the editor’s summary of “practice” and “been ruled”. 11.27 and 7.33 both set living beside a skill: 11.27 carries the rule of writing and reading over to life, and 7.33 speaks of “the art of living”.
claims.changed: 12.5 speaks of a hand and 11.27 of writing and reading; the claim puts both under “a skill”. 11.27’s “rule” and “been ruled” are written out as giving the rules and being given them: the master and the pupil of the translators’ note. 12.5 does not speak of living; only 11.27 says “in life”.

support.quote: the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in
gives: in a skill I am able only where I have been trained
support.follows: A hand that is no good at anything else is the stronger one at the single thing it has practised.

support.quote: In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.
gives: I treat living as a skill
in a skill I am able only where I have been trained
in writing and reading I do not give the rules before I have been given them, and this holds still more in life
support.follows: In writing and reading nobody gives the rules before having been given them, and this is even more true of life.

support.quote: The art of living
gives: I treat living as a skill
support.follows: Living is spoken of as an art, in the same words as the arts of wrestling and dancing.

claims.t: Using reason does not wait for anything else. I have it, so I use it, and when it is doing its own work I want nothing more; I hold to it without a tunic, without a book, without bread, and without the nourishment that learning gives.
claims.shared: Both passages turn on what a person has. In 4.11 the one thing he has is reason (“Do you have reason?” “I do.”), and once it is at work there is nothing else to want. In 4.25 the speakers “have no bread” and “do not have” learning’s nourishment, and they hold to reason all the same. Both say “reason”, and in both nothing else has to be there first.
claims.changed: 4.11 is a dialogue and 4.25 a row of philosophers; the claim speaks as “I” throughout. 4.11 says “use” and 4.25 says “hold to”; the claim keeps both verbs. “Does not wait for anything else” is the editor’s summary: 4.11 says there is nothing else to want when reason is doing its work, and 4.25 concedes each lack with “and yet”. Neither says that nothing else is needed. The “so” is 4.11’s “Then”. In 4.25 the first two people “practise philosophy”, one without a tunic and one without a book; only the man without bread and the last speaker “hold to reason”. The claim puts all four under “hold to reason”.

support.quote: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it?
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
I have it, so I use it
support.follows: Someone who agrees that he has reason is asked why, then, he does not use it.

support.quote: For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
when it is doing its own work I want nothing more
support.follows: Once reason is doing its own work, there is nothing else to want.

support.quote: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
gives: Using reason does not wait for anything else
I hold to it without a tunic, without a book, without bread, and without the nourishment that learning gives
support.follows: People practise philosophy and hold to reason while lacking a tunic, a book, bread, or what learning would feed them.

claims.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, and what it takes from wrestling is not throwing an opponent. It is to be disciplined in the face of what happens: to stand ready for what falls on me unforeseen, and not to fall.
claims.shared: Both passages take the wrestler as their figure, and both name the same thing to be good at: 7.28 being “disciplined in the face of what happens”, 7.33 standing ready for “the things that fall on it”. The words they back together are “in the face of what happens”.
claims.changed: 7.28 names throwing and 7.33 names standing; neither sets the one against the other. 7.28 does not say that discipline belongs to wrestling: its better thrower is precisely not better disciplined. The claim takes that discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, which is the editor’s reading. 7.33 speaks of the art of living as “it”; the claim says “me”.

inferences.words: what it takes from wrestling is not
inferences.why: 7.28 only denies that better throwing is better discipline; 7.33 only puts the likeness in standing ready. Setting one against the other is the editor’s step.
7.28 does not call discipline what living takes from wrestling; its better thrower lacks it. Equating it with 7.33’s standing ready is the editor’s step.

support.quote: The art of living is more like the art of wrestling than the art of dancing
gives: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing
support.follows: Living is an art, and it resembles wrestling more than it resembles dancing.

support.quote: Better at throwing an opponent
gives: throwing an opponent
support.follows: Someone can be better at throwing an opponent and no better in the ways the sentence goes on to list.

support.quote: nor better disciplined in the face of what happens
gives: to be disciplined
in the face of what happens
support.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent does not make a person better disciplined in the face of what happens.

support.quote: in that it stands ready for the things that fall on it and are not foreseen, and does not fall
gives: in the face of what happens
to stand ready for what falls on me unforeseen, and not to fall
support.follows: The likeness to wrestling is this: the art of living stands ready for what falls on it unforeseen, and does not fall.

single.label: A practice
single.t: I practise even the things I have given up on.
single.quote: Practise even the things you have given up on.
single.why: Only this passage gives the instruction. 11.27 says that training comes first; it does not say to go back to what I have written off.
single.follows: I should practise even what I have given up as hopeless.

single.label: Putting it off
single.t: If I would rather become good tomorrow than be good today, I deserve what is happening to me.
single.quote: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of delay. It shows what failing looks like here. The Greek sets the two halves side by side; the “if” that joins them is the editor’s reading.
single.follows: A person who prefers becoming good tomorrow to being good today is told that he deserves what is happening to him.

single.label: Winning without improving
single.t: I can become better at throwing an opponent and be no more social, no more modest, and no kinder toward the oversights of the people near me.
single.quote: but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder toward the oversights of those nearby
single.why: Only this passage lists what skill at winning leaves unimproved in my dealings with other people. Its one item about what happens is fused in the claim on what the skill is. The item’s opening words, “better at throwing an opponent”, come from the start of the same sentence (7.28a).
single.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent is not being more social, more modest, better disciplined, or kinder toward the oversights of those nearby.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay those of the 1634 edition. In modern editions 12.5 is 12.6, 11.27 is 11.29 and 11.30, 4.11 is 4.13, 4.25 is 4.30, 8.21 is the second half of 8.22, 7.28 is 7.52 and 7.33 is 7.61.

Reads “rule” and “been ruled” in 11.27 as the master and the pupil, and writes it out in the claim as giving the rules and being given them; the same Greek verb can also mean “lead” and “been led”. Leaves out the second half of 11.27, “You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.” It is a separate chapter in modern editions (11.30), it reads like a line quoted from a play, Marcus adds no comment, and its last word may mean “speech”.

“I treat living as a skill” is the editor’s wording for what two passages do. 11.27 applies the rule of writing and reading to life; 7.33 says “the art of living”. Neither says in so many words that living is learned as a skill is.

Reads 7.28, which has no subject and no verb, as a general remark: being better at throwing an opponent is not being better in the four ways listed. Setting that throwing against the standing of 7.33, and taking 7.28’s discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, are marked in the third claim as the editor’s steps.
Keeps “practise even the things I have given up on” (12.5) and the rebuke about tomorrow (8.21) as said once. No second passage says either, though both fit the statement.
articles.limit: Articles 2 and 5 already say that my work is to use reason; this article adds that living is trained like a skill, that using reason does not wait for anything else, and what the skill is used for. Article 6 already has one passage (8.54) about standing and not falling before an obstacle. The first claim is thin: 12.5 speaks of any ability and not of living, only 11.27 says “in life”, and 7.33 gives it three words. The last sentence of 4.25 has other readings. Seneca’s exercise of thinking troubles through in advance is already in Article 3, from other letters (Ep. 91.4, 76.34, 78.29); the item from Ep. 107.4 here repeats it. Claims 1 and 2 pull in different directions: 11.27 puts being given the rules before giving them, and 4.25 holds to reason even without the nourishment that learning gives. The article keeps both. Living as a craft is also in Article 11, claim 3 (being good is my craft, with principles kept ready as a doctor keeps his instruments), and in Article 23 (I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft); this article adds that the skill is learned by training and that it is used to face what happens. Article 35 already says, with the same Ep. 1.2, that I hurry to become good while it is possible and that I fail by putting things off (claims 3 and 4); here 8.21 is one said-once failure, and Seneca’s way back from delay repeats that ground.

statement.t: I treat living as a skill: I learn it by training, I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else, and I use it to face what happens.

parts.words: I treat living as a skill
I learn it by training
I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else
to face what happens

statement.kind: A likeness, with its means and its use
statement.form: Two passages set living beside a trained skill: writing and reading in 11.27, wrestling in 7.33. Claim 1 gives the rule of any skill, that ability comes from training; in the statement, “I learn it by training” rests on 11.27 for living, and on 12.5 only for the general rule. Claim 2 says that using reason does not wait for anything else. Claim 3 says, through the wrestler, what the skill is used for. The statement lists the three side by side, with one link of the editor’s: “I bring reason to it” makes reason something brought to the skill of living, which neither 4.11 nor 4.25 says.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if living cannot be trained like a skill, or if reason is not enough for it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first two claims gain a second author, the article gains two reasons under Why, an exercise of thinking ahead and three things for when it breaks, and claims 2 and 3 are limited: I need a helping hand, and I may fall so long as I rise again.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, with one restriction: “wait for nothing else” holds for things and not for people, since I need a helping hand. It also gains its reason: becoming good is an art, and nature does not give me virtue.

items.quote: Everyone approaches courageously a danger which he has prepared himself to meet long before, and withstands even hardships if he has previously practised how to meet them. But, contrariwise, the unprepared are panic-stricken even at the most trifling things.
gives: I am able only where I have been trained
items.follows: People stand up to dangers and hardships they have practised meeting, and the unprepared panic even at small things.
items.context: Letter 107, on what life is bound to bring: illness, loss, runaway slaves. To have “practised” is to have thought about such things often and in advance.

items.quote: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy,—no, nor even actual want.
gives: without bread
items.follows: Neither poverty nor outright want is a reason to leave philosophy.
items.context: Letter 17, on philosophy and riches: Lucilius wants an income first. Seneca answers that neither poverty nor “actual want”, meaning hunger, is a reason to wait.

items.label: why
items.role: Born for it, not with it
items.t: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art. I was born to attain it, not in possession of it, and no soul has it unless it has been trained and taught and brought to perfection by unremitting practice.
items.why: Marcus says that ability comes from training and that this holds in life. He does not say in this section why goodness has to be learned at all. Seneca does: nature does not give it.

support.quote: For nature does not bestow virtue; it is an art to become good.
gives: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art
support.follows: Virtue is not given by nature; becoming good is an art.
support.context: Letter 90, on the first human beings. Seneca says they were guileless and sturdy but not wise, and this sentence gives his reason.

support.quote: For the attainment of this boon, but not in the possession of it, were we born
gives: I was born to attain it, not in possession of it
support.follows: We are born to attain virtue, and we are not born having it.
support.context: The close of Letter 90, on the first humans, who were innocent out of ignorance. “This boon” is virtue, named in the sentence before.

support.quote: Virtue is not vouchsafed to a soul unless that soul has been trained and taught, and by unremitting practice brought to perfection.
gives: no soul has it unless it has been trained and taught and brought to perfection by unremitting practice
support.follows: A soul has virtue only after it has been trained, taught and perfected by constant practice.
support.context: The conclusion of Letter 90: the first humans did no wrong because they knew no wrong, and that is not virtue. Seneca then says what virtue requires.

items.label: why
items.t: The art of living is unlike the other arts. They deal with the tools of life and not with life as a whole; and in this one a mistake made on purpose is more shameful than one made by accident.
items.why: Marcus says that the rule of writing and reading holds “much more” in life, and stops there. Seneca also speaks of an art of living, and he says where its likeness to the other arts ends. He leaves untouched the rule that ability comes from training, so this adds to the first claim and does not limit it.

support.quote: Would you like to know how unlike its status is to the other arts?
gives: The art of living is unlike the other arts
support.follows: The art of life does not stand as the other arts stand.
support.context: Letter 95, on whether precepts are enough to teach wisdom. “Its status” is that of the art of life, which Seneca sets apart from the pilot’s and other crafts.

support.quote: Now all these arts are concerned with the tools of life, but not with life as a whole.
gives: They deal with the tools of life and not with life as a whole
support.follows: The other arts concern things used in living, and not life as a whole.
support.context: Letter 95: an objector says the pilot’s craft is learned from precepts, so the art of living can be too. “These arts” are the pilot’s and the other crafts.

support.quote: But in this art of living a voluntary mistake is the more shameful.
gives: in this one a mistake made on purpose is more shameful than one made by accident
support.follows: In the art of living, a deliberate mistake is worse than an accidental one.
support.context: Seneca’s example in Letter 95: a scholar is less ashamed of a grammar slip made on purpose than of one made by accident. In the art of living it is reversed.

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep reflecting on what may come, so that nothing comes upon me unforeseen and, whatever the evil is, I do not play the unschooled boy.
items.why: Marcus’s one exercise here is to practise what I have given up on (12.5), and his art of living stands ready for things that are “not foreseen” (7.33). Seneca’s exercise starts earlier: by thinking ahead he tries to leave nothing unforeseen. Article 3 already has this exercise from Letters 91, 76 and 78; here it stands beside Marcus’s “not foreseen”.

support.quote: We must see to it that nothing shall come upon us unforeseen.
gives: nothing comes upon me unforeseen
support.follows: We should arrange that nothing takes us by surprise.
support.context: Letter 107: Lucilius is upset that his slaves have run away. Seneca tells him to expect such things; what must not come “unforeseen” is any of life’s troubles.

support.quote: continual reflection will give you the power, no matter what the evil may be, not to play the unschooled boy
gives: I keep reflecting on what may come
whatever the evil is, I do not play the unschooled boy
support.follows: Constant reflection gives a person the power not to behave like an untaught boy, whatever evil comes.
support.context: Letter 107, on preparing the mind for what life brings. The “reflection” is thinking about troubles before they come; the “unschooled boy” is the unprepared.

items.label: breaks
items.t: I lay hold of today’s task, and then I depend less on tomorrow’s; while I am postponing, life speeds by. Philosophy, which I have been putting off until I have enough money, should come first: I begin with it.
items.why: 8.21 names the fault, preferring tomorrow to today, and gives no way back. Seneca gives one: take hold of today’s task, and begin with the thing I was putting off. The excuse “until I have enough” is from the sentence before the quoted words of Letter 17, where Lucilius says he has not yet enough.

support.quote: Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
gives: I lay hold of today’s task, and then I depend less on tomorrow’s
while I am postponing, life speeds by
support.follows: Whoever takes hold of today’s task depends less on tomorrow’s, and life runs on while we postpone.
support.context: The first letter, on saving one’s time: most of life slips away unused. “To-day’s task” is what this day’s hours are for; “postponing” is leaving it for later.

support.quote: this ideal, which you are putting off and placing second to other interests, should be secured first of all; you should begin with it
gives: which I have been putting off
should come first
I begin with it
support.follows: What is being put off behind other interests should be secured first: one should begin with it.
support.context: Letter 17: Lucilius will turn to philosophy once he has gained enough money. “This ideal” is that devotion to philosophy, which Seneca tells him to put first.

items.label: breaks
items.t: It does me no good to control a horse with the curb if my own passions bolt with me, or to beat many opponents at wrestling or boxing and then be beaten by anger.
items.why: 7.28 says what being better at throwing an opponent leaves unimproved. Seneca says the same of the wrestler and the rider, and names what defeats them: their own anger and passions.

support.quote: For what good does it do us to guide a horse and control his speed with the curb, and then find that our own passions, utterly uncurbed, bolt with us? Or to beat many opponents in wrestling or boxing, and then to find that we ourselves are beaten by anger?
gives: It does me no good to control a horse with the curb if my own passions bolt with me
to beat many opponents at wrestling or boxing and then be beaten by anger
support.follows: Mastering a horse or beating opponents is no use to someone whose passions run away with him and whom anger beats.
support.context: Letter 88, on which studies make a person good. Seneca has just said that neither athletic training nor the old Roman drill with horse and weapons teaches virtue.

items.label: breaks
items.role: While I am not yet able
items.t: While my training has not yet made me able, I do not demand of myself, a learner, what is demanded of a wise man. I press on and persevere: the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
items.why: Marcus shows one failure here, putting it off (8.21), and does not say how to go on while the training has not yet taken. Seneca admits that his own has not, and says how: a learner is judged as a learner, and presses on. He takes for granted that training is the way, so this is no answer to doubt. The opening clause comes from the end of Ep. 71.30, outside the quoted words, where Seneca says his principles are not yet so well trained that they come to his help in every crisis.

support.quote: it is a mistake on our part to make the same demands upon the wise man and upon the learner
gives: I do not demand of myself, a learner, what is demanded of a wise man
support.follows: A learner should not be held to what is asked of a wise man.
support.context: Letter 71: Seneca grants that many who profess wisdom, himself among them, are still frightened by slight threats; his own exhortations are “not yet followed”.

support.quote: Therefore let us press on and persevere. There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
gives: I press on and persevere
the greater part of progress is the desire to progress
support.follows: One should press on and persevere: most of the road is still ahead, but wanting to progress is the greater part of progressing.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 71: whoever is short of perfection slips back unless he keeps struggling ahead. The “road” is the way to wisdom, most of it still ahead.

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing outside me is needed: all that goes to make me a good man lies within myself (Ep. 80.3). But he also says that no one has the strength to rise above folly by himself; he needs a helping hand, and Seneca counts himself among those who need one (Ep. 52.2–3). Read in their letters the two do not conflict: 80.3 is about the equipment and expense an athlete needs, 52.2 about needing a teacher. This limits “does not wait for anything else” to things and does not extend it to people, and Marcus’s own 11.27 says that I am given the rules before I give them.

support.quote: No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it; he needs a helping hand, and some one to extricate him.
support.follows: Nobody is strong enough to get clear of folly alone; each needs someone to help him out.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. “It” is folly: the wavering between plans and wishes that Seneca has just described in himself and in Lucilius.

support.quote: We ourselves are not of that first class, either; we shall be well treated if we are admitted into the second.
support.follows: Seneca puts himself among those who need another’s help, not among those who find the way alone.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. In Epicurus’s classes the first reach the truth with no one’s help and the second need a guide. “We” are Seneca and Lucilius.

support.quote: All that goes to make you a good man lies within yourself.
support.follows: Everything needed to become a good man is within oneself.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca contrasts athletes, who need food, drink, oil and long training, with the mind, which feeds and exercises itself. “You” is Lucilius, or anyone.

items.t: Marcus’s art of living “does not fall”. Seneca’s fighter does: the only contestant who can enter with confidence has been downed in body but not in spirit, and rises as often as he falls (Ep. 13.2). In Ep. 80.3 even the mind may be laid low and trampled; what Seneca asks is that it not be conquered and that it struggle to its feet again. This limits “not to fall”: for Seneca falling is allowed, and what is not allowed is to stay down.

support.quote: who has been downed in body but not in spirit, one who, as often as he falls, rises again with greater defiance than ever
support.follows: The only contestant who can enter confidently is one who has been knocked down without losing heart and gets up every time he falls.
support.context: Letter 13: Seneca tells Lucilius that one’s powers are proved only by hard tests. The prizefighter is his figure for a person contending with Fortune.

support.quote: so that it might struggle to its feet again after it has been laid low, after it has been trampled under foot
support.follows: The mind can be toughened so that it gets up again after being knocked down and trampled.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca hears cheering from the stadium and asks, if a fighter’s body can be trained to take blows, how much more the mind? “It” is the mind.

amend.t: ; becoming good is an art, and nature does not give me virtue: I was born to attain it
; but I do not rise above my folly by my own strength alone: I need a helping hand
; yet as often as I fall I rise again

searches: nearest letter sections to the section by vectors (25)
art of living, art of life
postpon, put off, putting off, procrastinat
art to become good, unremitting practice, trained and taught
reason (with use of, make use, employ, exercis)
falls, fallen, thrown, laid low (with rise, get up, feet)
without books, without money, without equipment, even hunger, no bread
pupil, apprentice, schoolmaster, learner (with rule, master, teach, command)
despair, given up, hopeless (with practise, train, effort, persever): no match

rejected.why: “What do you need in order to become good? To wish it.” Names the wish where Marcus names reason. Left out so that the second claim carries one clause, the limit from Ep. 52.
How many train their bodies and how few their minds. A complaint about the crowd at the games; the next section, 80.3, is quoted.
One may reach philosophy “even without money for the journey”. Says what 17.6 says; one witness for “without bread” was enough.
“Wisdom itself is an art of living”, but in the mouth of an objector whom Seneca goes on to answer. His answer, 95.8 and 95.9, is quoted.
Wisdom “is the art of life”. A definition inside a technical argument about whether being wise is a good; nothing on how the art is learned. Seen in the search listing only.
Some reach virtue without long apprenticeship, by a fortunate temperament. A possible limit on the first claim, but Seneca treats them as exceptions and says the sluggish need constant work.
A pantomime need not inquire into the art of dancing. Dancing is only an example of an art that does not concern life as a whole; 95.8 says this directly. Seen in the search listing only.
Philosophy is not to be postponed until I have leisure. Same point as 17.5, which is quoted and answers the excuse of not having enough.
“Let us postpone nothing.” Said because death may come any day; 8.21 is about being good today, and 1.2 gives the remedy more plainly.
People who “do not live, but are preparing to live”. Describes the fault of 8.21 again and gives no way back.
Athletes take blows in training in order to be able to fight. About bearing pain in illness; Article 6 quotes the section before it for that.
Skilled wrestlers are kept up to the mark by practice. About one wise man helping another, not about what the skill is.
Lucilius has leaped up after Fortune had the upper hand. Applies the figure of 13.2 to him; 13.2 is quoted.
The man who has wrestled his way to wisdom deserves more credit. About kinds of temperament; “wrestled” is only a figure for effort. Seen in the search listing only.
What is short of perfection slips back unless it keeps struggling ahead. Leads to 71.36, which is quoted.
Sophisms do not make a man braver or more restrained. Close in form to 7.28, but about logical puzzles, not skill at winning; 88.19 has the wrestler himself.
“Make me more brave now, more just, more restrained!” Again against subtle studies; the “training” he cannot yet use is in logic.
Philosophy is a subject for daily practice, not for odd times. About giving it all one’s time; nearer to delay than to skill, and 1.2 and 17.5 cover delay.
Practise for poverty, and after long rehearsal it is even pleasant. About rehearsing poverty in particular; 107.4 gives the general exercise.
Do nothing without the approval of reason. About making one mind out of many readings; reason’s speech there is against riches and office.
“You are a reasoning animal”: my good is perfect reason. About what the good is; Article 5 covers what I was made for.

Ranked first by the vectors; read with 98.3 and 98.5. Possessions are of no use unless I equip myself against chance and say at each mishap “Heaven decreed it otherwise”. Not about training as a skill; 98.5’s thinking ahead is the exercise 107.4 already gives.
“Nothing ought to be unexpected by us.” The same exercise as 107.4, and already quoted in Article 3 with Ep. 76.34 and 78.29; read to confirm the overlap, not quoted again.

articles.title: What I turn to

claims.t: I gain by going back. By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony, the inner tuning that my rhythm belongs to; I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them.
claims.shared: Each passage tells me to go back and names what comes with it. 6.9 says “by continually going back”; 6.10 says “Go back here often”. With the going back 6.9 names “a firmer hold on the harmony”, and 6.10 names philosophy, “because of which the things there seem bearable”.
claims.changed: 6.9 goes back to the harmony and 6.10 to philosophy; the claim keeps them apart. The places gone back to are left to the claim on going back. “The inner tuning that my rhythm belongs to” is the editor’s gloss of “the harmony”: in 6.9 the harmony is the tuning of notes, set beside “the rhythm” of the sentence before and gone back to as I go back “into yourself”; the passage does not say that the harmony is the same as myself. “Because of philosophy” is 6.10’s “because of which”, said of philosophy and not given as the reason for going back; “the things at court” are 6.10’s “the things there”, which the sentence before names as the court. “I gain” is the editor’s word.

support.quote: For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.
gives: I gain by going back
By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony
support.follows: Going back to the harmony continually is what gives a firmer hold on it.

support.quote: Go back here often and rest in philosophy, because of which the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.
gives: I gain by going back
I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them
support.follows: Marcus is to go back often to philosophy and rest in it; philosophy is why the court seems bearable to him and he seems bearable there.

claims.t: There is one thing I want and take pleasure in: to act as a member of a community. I move and hold back as civic reason thinks right, and I rest in going from one social act to the next with god in mind.
claims.shared: Both passages say “one thing”, and in both the one thing is acting for a community: “social act” in 6.6, “civic reason” in 9.10. 6.6 makes it the thing to take pleasure in and rest in; 9.10 makes it the thing to want.
claims.changed: 9.10 says “one thing only”; 6.6 has no “only”, and the claim follows 6.6. “To act as a member of a community” is the editor’s summary of “social act” and “civic reason”, which are two different Greek words. 6.10 uses for resting in philosophy the same Greek verb that 6.6 uses for resting in social acts; no passage says how the two rests are related.

support.quote: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
gives: one thing
take pleasure in
to act as a member of a community
I rest in going from one social act to the next with god in mind
support.follows: The one thing to take pleasure in and rest in is going from one act for the common life to the next, with god in mind.

support.quote: want one thing only: to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right
gives: one thing
I want
to act as a member of a community
I move and hold back as civic reason thinks right
support.follows: The one thing to want is to move and to hold back as civic reason thinks right.

claims.t: I go back quickly and continually: into myself when circumstances throw me into confusion, stepping out of my rhythm no more than I am forced to; at a run to my own ruling part, the part of me that judges and decides; and to philosophy as to a mother, while I wait on the court as on a stepmother.
claims.shared: 6.9 and 6.10 both say “go back”: “go back quickly into yourself” and “continually going back to your mother”. 6.9 and 9.20 both ask for speed, “quickly” and “Run”, and both send me to what is my own: “yourself” and “your own ruling part”.
claims.changed: 9.20 says “Run to”, not “go back”; the claim lists the ruling part as one more place gone back to, which is the editor’s reading. Only 6.9 says “quickly” and only 6.10 says “continually”; the claim puts both words at its head. “Quickly” for 9.20 rests on the literal “Run”; the same Greek verb in 11.2 (“run to the parts”) may mean no more than turning straight to something. 6.10 does not say in so many words that the court is the stepmother and philosophy the mother; the claim follows the order of its words. 6.9 says “the rhythm”; the claim says “my rhythm”. “The part of me that judges and decides” is the editor’s gloss of “ruling part”, the Stoic name for the governing part of the soul.

support.quote: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to.
gives: I go back
