rejected.why: Nearest by vectors. A single norm for the whole of life, against living one way at home and another in public. About consistency, not about one thing wanted for the community.
“Hasten to find yourself first”: about being consistent in what one desires from day to day. Not a going back after being shaken.

Life is endurable once wisdom is begun. Near 6.10’s “bearable”, but it speaks of life as a whole, where 6.10 speaks of the things at court; backing the claim with it would widen what Marcus says. Removed after review.

Its first half, that philosophy studied intermittently goes back to its beginning, is not used: 6.10 says “continually” and “often”, so Marcus is not the intermittent student it speaks of. Only its sentence on putting affairs out of the way is quoted.

“Rejoice only in that which comes from your own store.” Looks like a limit on cheering myself with other people’s virtues, but it is aimed at goods that Fortune hands out; in Ep. 109.15 he rejoices in friends’ progress. No real disagreement.
The real good comes from a way of living “which treads but one path”. One path of life, not one thing wanted; the letter is about joy.
Loving the virtues of one’s peers gives pleasure. Close to 6.43, but said of wise men helping one another, and the pleasure is that of likeness; the match would need explaining.
Rejoice in friends’ advancement as in our own. About friendship and taking counsel; read to test Ep. 23.6, not quoted.
Seneca forces his mind to concentrate amid the noise of the street. He keeps the mind from straying; he does not speak of going back once shaken.
A mind that starts at sounds “has not yet withdrawn into itself”. A description of the unsteady mind in Letter 56, on noise; no instruction.
The sage will retreat into himself and live with himself, as Jupiter does when the world dissolves. A picture of the wise man’s self-sufficiency, not a habit amid duties.
A life “withdrawn into itself” is one that does not reach forward into the future. About anxiety over time to come.
Seneca never brings home the character he took out into a crowd. Read as the setting of Ep. 7.8, which is quoted.
One can live quietly even in the Forum if necessary, though he would flee it by choice. Bears on serving at court, but Ep. 62.1 already shows his other side in the item on the other business.
“Take refuge in philosophy” as a protecting emblem. Philosophy as cover in the eyes of other men; Ep. 103.4 says the refuge more simply.
Philosophy as an impregnable wall against Fortune. A fortress, not a place gone back to for rest.
Philosophy orders life and sits at the helm. A general praise of philosophy; nothing on going to it from other duties.
“Do not study philosophy merely during your spare time.” Same point as Ep. 53.9, which is quoted.
Philosophy, like Alexander, leaves other occupations only what she does not take. An image for the point of Ep. 53.9.
The wise man’s joy is not broken off whatever his business. Speaks of the perfected sage, not of someone returning.
We give wisdom only the time left over from our vices. About vices and not about duties.
A good man will fall back little by little from ambitious business. Advice to Lucilius to retire; the difference over business is already stated from Ep. 72 and Ep. 53.
Men love the rewards of their hardships and curse the hardships. Near 8.8, but it explains why men do not leave business; it does not forbid complaint.
Rulers give no greater privilege than peace and leisure. The ruler seen from outside; nothing on serving at court.
A philosopher “who appears at court” in a scoffer’s list of philosophers’ faults. A passing mention.
Keep a revered man in mind as witness and calm yourself by calling him to mind. The same device as Ep. 25.6, which is quoted; its purpose is restraint, not cheer.
Choose a Cato or a Laelius as protector or pattern. Same as Ep. 25.6.
“Do everything as if Epicurus were watching you.” Leads into Ep. 25.6, which is quoted.
Live with the Catos, with Laelius, with Socrates. The company of the great dead, said more directly in Ep. 62.2, which is quoted.
Live with Chrysippus and Posidonius; the only safe harbour is a firm stand against Fortune. Continues Ep. 104.21.
In pain, run over in memory what you have admired and the brave men who conquered pain. A practice of recollection, but for bearing pain.
People lament the louder for being heard. Near 9.10’s wish to be pitied, but it is about displays of grief in mourning.
Praying for death “courts pity”. About wishing for death.
Do not draw admiration by absurd austerity. About a philosopher’s dress and manner of living, not about toil.
It is as harmful to be scorned as to be admired. About keeping out of harm’s way.
“Your good qualities should face inwards.” Against seeking the praise of the many; Ep. 113.32 says the same of justice and is quoted.
“Work is the sustenance of noble minds.” Praises work as such, against praying for good fortune; says nothing on how to toil.
Strip things of what disturbs and see what each is at bottom. Near 11.2, but it removes a mask from what is feared; it does not divide what delights.
Tear the mask off the fortunate and you will scorn them. Looking down on what is admired, by unmasking and not by dividing into parts.
Of a splendid palace: “It is all show.” Contempt for display; no method of dividing.
“Bring my soul into harmony with itself.” The musical image of 6.9, set against what music teachers teach; nothing about going back.
A mind in which many arts and precepts blend into one harmony, like a chorus. About bringing many sources into one, not about returning.
Near by vectors. Equip yourself against the fickleness of chance and repeat it to yourself often. About desirable things and chance.
Near by vectors. Reason says: abandon riches, pleasures and the quest for office. A list of things to give up.
Near by vectors. Do not envy the great man in purple. About envy of rank, not about complaining of one’s own place.
“Live among men as if God beheld you.” Near 6.6’s “with god in mind”, but there God watches me; in 6.6 I remember god. Already used in Article 6.

articles.title: The morning, and the question before each action

claims.t: When I find it hard to get up, I remind myself that I am getting up to do a human being’s work: social actions, which are according to my nature. I share sleep with the animals that have no reason; this work is more my own, and more agreeable too.
claims.shared: Both passages meet the moment of getting up with one reminder: 8.11, that “to render social actions is according to the way you are made”; 5.1, “I am getting up to do a human being’s work”. Both name social actions and what is according to nature.
claims.changed: 8.11 sets sleep beside the animals, and 5.1 sets lying in bed beside the bees at their work; the claim keeps 8.11’s contrast, and claim 2 takes up 5.1’s bees. That this work is more agreeable is said by 8.11 alone.

support.quote: When you find it hard to wake from sleep, remind yourself that to render social actions is according to the way you are made and according to human nature, whereas sleeping is shared with the animals without reason as well.
gives: When I find it hard to get up
I remind myself
social actions
according to my nature
I share sleep with the animals that have no reason
support.follows: When waking is hard, I should recall that social action suits the way a human being is made, while sleep is shared with animals.

support.quote: And what is according to each one’s nature is more its own, more closely grown to it, and indeed more agreeable too.
gives: this work is more my own, and more agreeable too
support.follows: What fits a thing’s nature is more its own, and more agreeable to it as well.

support.quote: At dawn, when you are reluctant to get up, have this ready to hand: “I am getting up to do a human being’s work.
gives: When I find it hard to get up
I remind myself
I am getting up to do a human being’s work
support.follows: On a morning when I do not want to get up, I should keep ready the thought that I get up to do a human being’s work.

support.quote: You do not run to what is according to your nature?
gives: according to my nature
support.follows: I ought to hurry toward what is according to my nature, not hang back from it.

support.quote: But to you do social actions seem cheaper and worth less effort?
gives: social actions
support.follows: Social actions should not seem to me cheap or not worth the effort.

claims.t: The plants, the birds and the bees take part in the work of the universe, and so do all of us. Each does it in its own way: some knowingly, some without attending to it, even people asleep, even the one who finds fault with what happens. What is left to me is to understand among which of these workers I am placing myself, and to be willing to do what belongs to a human being.
claims.shared: Both passages see other beings at work on the universe and ask me to take my place among them: in 5.1 the plants and bees are “putting the universe together”, in 6.37 all of us, sleepers too, are “fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe”. Both say each does it in its own way.
claims.changed: 5.1 speaks of plants and animals and 6.37 of people; the claim puts them together. “These workers” are the people just named, as in 6.37, where the choice comes right after the one who finds fault: whether I work knowingly or as he does. What 6.37 says of the one who governs the whole, and its line in a play, are kept apart as said once.

support.quote: Do you not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees doing what is their own to do and, for their part, putting the universe together? And then you are not willing to do what belongs to a human being?
gives: The plants, the birds and the bees
take part in the work of the universe
Each does it in its own way
to be willing to do what belongs to a human being
support.follows: Plants and small creatures each do their own work and help put the universe together, so I should be willing to do a human being’s.

support.quote: We are all working together towards one finished result, some of us knowingly and with awareness, others without attending to it, just as Heraclitus, I think, says that even those who are asleep are workers and fellow workers in the things that happen in the universe.
gives: all of us
take part in the work of the universe
some knowingly, some without attending to it, even people asleep
support.follows: Everyone works toward one finished result, aware of it or not; even sleepers are workers in what happens in the universe.

support.quote: One works together in one way, another in another, and, into the bargain, so does even the one who finds fault and the one who tries to stand against the things that happen and do away with them, for the universe had need of such a person too.
gives: Each does it in its own way
even the one who finds fault with what happens
support.follows: Each works with the rest in a different way; even the one who finds fault with what happens does, since the universe needed him too.

support.quote: What remains, then, is for you to understand among which of them you are placing yourself.
gives: What is left to me is to understand among which of these workers I am placing myself
support.follows: Since everyone works for the whole somehow, what is left to me is to see which kind of worker I am making myself.

claims.t: At each thing I do, I stop and ask myself about it with my death in mind: what is this act to me, will I regret it, and is death terrible because it would take this away?
claims.shared: Both passages tell me to question myself at each action (8.2: “At each action ask yourself”; 10.29: “At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself”), and in both the question brings in death.
claims.changed: “With my death in mind” is the editor’s summary of two uses of death: 8.2 says “A little while and I am dead”; 10.29 asks whether death is terrible because it takes this away. Each passage’s own question is kept as it asks it. “What is this act to me” is the translators’ plainer reading of 8.2’s “How does this stand with me?”.

support.quote: At each action ask yourself: “How does this stand with me? Will I come to regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is cleared away.
gives: At each thing I do
ask myself about it
with my death in mind
what is this act to me, will I regret it
support.follows: At each action I should ask how it stands with me and whether I will regret it, remembering that I shall soon be dead.

support.quote: At each of the things you do, one by one, stop and ask yourself whether death is something terrible because of being deprived of this.
gives: At each thing I do
I stop
ask myself about it
with my death in mind
is death terrible because it would take this away
support.follows: At each thing I do, I should stop and ask whether death is terrible because it would take this thing away.

claims.t: When I have done good, I look for nothing more: I do not try to have it seen, and I want no return. I do not tire of doing good, but pass on to the next good act, as a vine bears its grapes again in season.
claims.shared: Three passages say that once the work is done nothing more is looked for: 7.43 “why do you look for a third thing”, 5.6 “looks for nothing more”, 8.2 “What more do I look for”. 7.43 and 5.6 both speak of one who has done good, and both turn away from having it seen: “to be seen to have done good”, “do not shout about it”.
claims.changed: 8.2 speaks of the work in hand, not of a good turn. 5.6’s “another thing” is read as the next good act, because the vine bears its grapes again. 7.43’s “do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit” becomes “I do not tire of doing good”, which drops its point that giving benefits the giver.

support.quote: When you have done good and another has had good done to them, why do you look for a third thing beside these, as fools do: to be seen to have done good as well, or to get a return?
gives: When I have done good
I look for nothing more
I do not try to have it seen
I want no return
support.follows: Once I have done good and someone has received it, it is foolish to want also to be seen doing it or to be repaid.

support.quote: No one tires of being benefited, and benefit is action according to nature. So do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit.
gives: I do not tire of doing good
support.follows: Giving benefit is itself a benefit to me, and no one tires of being benefited, so I should not tire of giving it.

support.quote: A third, in a way, does not even know what they have done, but is like a vine that has borne its grapes and looks for nothing more after it has once borne its own fruit.
gives: I look for nothing more
support.follows: The best kind of giver is like a vine that, having borne its grapes, looks for nothing more.

support.quote: A horse that has run, a dog that has tracked, a bee that has made honey, and a human being who has done good, do not shout about it, but pass on to another thing, as a vine passes on to bearing its grapes again in season.
gives: When I have done good
I do not try to have it seen
pass on to the next good act
as a vine bears its grapes again in season
support.follows: A human being who has done good, like a horse that has run, does not shout about it but goes on to the next thing.

support.quote: What more do I look for, if the work in hand is the work of a living being that has mind, is social, and is under the same law as god?
gives: I look for nothing more
support.follows: If what I am doing is the work of a social being with a mind, under the same law as god, I need look for nothing more.

claims.t: With whoever I meet and whatever anyone does, I ask myself about that person: what do they hold to be good and bad, and to what end are they doing this? When I know what they hold to be good and bad, nothing they do will seem strange to me, and I remember that they are compelled to do it. But I begin with myself.
claims.shared: Both passages tell me to put a question to myself about another person’s action, and both ask it of “this person”: 8.13 “What principles does this person hold”, 10.37 “To what end is this person doing this?”.
claims.changed: 8.13 asks it before meeting someone, 10.37 of anything anyone does; the claim takes both occasions. 8.13’s fig tree, doctor and helmsman are left out: they say again that nothing should seem strange.

support.quote: Whoever you meet, say to yourself at once, beforehand: “What principles does this person hold about what is good and what is bad?
gives: With whoever I meet
I ask myself about that person
what do they hold to be good and bad
support.follows: Before dealing with anyone, I should ask myself what that person believes to be good and bad.

support.quote: it will seem to me nothing surprising or strange if they do such-and-such things, and I will remember that they are compelled to do so.
gives: nothing they do will seem strange to me
I remember that they are compelled to do it
support.follows: Knowing what someone believes, I will find nothing strange in what they do, and will remember that they are compelled to do it.

support.quote: Train yourself, as far as you can, with everything that anyone does, to ask in your own mind: “To what end is this person doing this?” But begin with yourself, and examine yourself first.
gives: whatever anyone does
I ask myself about that person
to what end are they doing this
I begin with myself
support.follows: With anything anyone does, I should ask what it is for, and ask it of my own actions first.

single.label: Whether I am enough
single.t: Before a task I ask whether my mind is enough for it. If it is, I use it as a tool that the nature of the whole has given me. If it is not, I step back for someone who can do the work better, unless it is my duty for some other reason, or I do it as best I can and take on someone to help me.
single.quote: Is my mind enough for this or not? If it is enough, I use it for the work as a tool given by the nature of the whole. If it is not enough, either I step back from the work in favour of someone who can carry it out better, unless for some other reason it is my duty, or I do it as best I can, taking on to help me someone who, by making use of my ruling part as well, can do what is timely and useful for the community now.
single.why: Only this passage asks whether I am able for a task and what to do if I am not. Its aim, what is useful to the community, is already Article 1’s.
single.follows: If my mind is equal to a task I use it; if not, I give the task to someone better or do it with help.

single.label: A morning question
single.t: As soon as I wake, I ask myself whether it will make any difference to me if someone else blames what is just and right. It will not.
single.quote: Ask yourself as soon as you come out of sleep: will it make any difference to you if what is just and right is blamed by someone else? It will not.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of other people’s blame. It also asks its question on waking, as 5.1 and 8.11 do, but its question is about blame, not about the day’s work.
single.follows: If someone else blames what is just and right, that makes no difference to me.

single.label: Too much rest
single.t: Nature has set a measure for rest, as it has for eating and drinking. I fail when I go beyond that measure and stop short of what I can do in action. Then I do not love myself, or I would love my nature too, and what it wills.
single.quote: Nature, though, has given measures for this as well; it has given them for eating and drinking as well; and yet you go beyond the measures, beyond what is enough. But in your actions it is not so: there you stop short of what you can do. For you do not love yourself, since otherwise you would love your nature too, and what it wills.
single.why: Only this passage says what failing looks like here: too much rest and too little action. 8.11 knows that waking is hard but does not describe the failure.
single.follows: Going past nature’s measure in rest while falling short in action shows that I do not love my nature, and so do not love myself.

single.label: Waking again
single.t: I sober up and call myself back. Once I am awake again and understand that it was dreams that were troubling me, I look at what troubles me now as I looked at what troubled me in those dreams.
single.quote: Sober up and call yourself back. And when you have woken up again and understood that it was dreams that were troubling you, then, awake again, look at these things as you looked at those.
single.why: Only this passage gives a way back. Its waking is an image for coming to my senses, not the morning of 5.1 and 8.11, so it is not fused with them.
single.follows: Having seen that what troubled me were dreams, I should look at my waking troubles as I looked at the dreams.

single.label: Not a worthless part
single.t: Whatever I do, the one who governs the whole will make good use of me and take me in among those who help the work along. Even so, I must not become the part that Chrysippus likened to a cheap and ridiculous line in a play: poor in itself, though it still adds to the play as a whole.
single.quote: For the one who governs the whole will in any case use you well, and will take you in as some part of the fellow workers and of those who help the work along. But you, do not become the kind of part that the cheap and ridiculous line is in the play, the one Chrysippus mentions.
single.why: Only this passage says what kind of part I can fail to be. 5.1 asks me to work, but does not say I will be used whatever I do. What the cheap line is, poor in itself though it adds to the whole play, is from the translators’ note on Chrysippus (from memory), not from the passage.
single.follows: The one who governs the whole will use me well in any case, but I should not be the worthless line of the play.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 10.15 is 10.13, 8.11 is 8.12, 8.13 is 8.14–15, 7.5 is 7.5–7, 7.43 is 7.73–74, 6.37 is 6.42 and 6.29 is 6.31; 8.2, 5.1, 10.37, 5.6 and 10.29 have the same number.
Joins the questions of 8.2 and 10.29 by their form and by death, which both bring in. The words “with my death in mind” are the editor’s summary; each passage’s own question is kept as it stands.

Brings 8.2’s “What more do I look for” into the claim on doing good, though 8.2 speaks of the work in hand, not a good turn; and reads 7.43’s “do not tire of being benefited, in that you give benefit” as not tiring of doing good.

Keeps 10.15 said once and quotes it as printed, “is blamed”. The translators note from memory that the manuscripts may read “is done”; with that reading the question is whether it matters that someone else does what is right.
articles.limit: Claims 1 and 2 come near Article 5 (made for reason and fellowship) and Article 1 (each act aims at the common good); claim 3 near Articles 9 and 10 (each thing done as if leaving life now); claim 4 repeats Articles 9 and 11 (no show, no witness) and Article 19’s said-once 9.43d (looking for something back); and claim 5 is close to Article 19’s claims 1 and 6 (what they took to be good or bad, they can do nothing else, then I turn to myself). What this section adds is when and how: getting up in the morning; a question at each action; after a good act, passing on to the next as a vine bears again; and the question about others asked of everyone I meet, not only of someone who wrongs me. The middle of the statement joins questions that differ in content (regret, death, another’s aim) by their form alone.

statement.t: I get up for the work I was made for, I question each thing I do, and when I have done good I look for nothing more.

parts.words: I get up for the work I was made for
I question each thing I do
when I have done good I look for nothing more

statement.kind: Three moments of a day
statement.form: The statement follows a day: getting up, with claims 1 and 2 as its ground; questioning each action, mine and others’ (claims 3 and 5); and what I look for once the good is done (claim 4). The claims stand side by side; none is derived from another.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if I was not made for this work or if questioning my actions does no good.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, looking for nothing after doing good gains a second author. Under Why he adds the purpose of the whole life, against which each act is weighed; under Practice, death kept in mind at lying down and at waking, so that each morning is a gift, and a review of each day; under When it breaks, owning a fault as the sign that I am awake. He limits and challenges nothing.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a look back: besides questioning what I am about to do, I review each day.

items.quote: You need not look about for the reward of a just deed; a just deed in itself offers a still greater return.
gives: I look for nothing more
I want no return
items.follows: I need not look for a reward for a just deed, because the deed itself repays me more.
items.context: Letter 113, near its end: justice looks to another’s good and seeks nothing for itself, so one must be just without reward. “A just deed” is any act of justice toward others.

items.quote: Those who wish their virtue to be advertised are not striving for virtue but for renown.
gives: I do not try to have it seen
items.follows: Whoever wants his virtue made known is after fame, not virtue.
items.context: The close of Letter 113, on justice practised without reward: it makes no difference how many people know that one is upright. “Their virtue” is that justice.

items.label: why
items.role: The purpose of my whole life
items.t: Whenever I want to know what to seek or avoid, I consider how it stands to the purpose of my whole life, for whatever I do ought to be in harmony with it. No one can set the details in order without first setting that purpose before himself. If I do not know what harbour I am making for, no wind is the right wind.
items.why: Marcus asks of each action, mine or another’s, to what end it is done, and what it is to me in the face of death. Seneca puts a question before those: the purpose of the whole life, without which no single act can be set in order.

support.quote: As often as you wish to know what is to be avoided or what is to be sought, consider its relation to the Supreme Good, to the purpose of your whole life. For whatever we do ought to be in harmony with this; no man can set in order the details unless he has already set before himself the chief purpose of his life.
gives: I consider how it stands to the purpose of my whole life
whatever I do ought to be in harmony with it
No one can set the details in order without first setting that purpose before himself
support.follows: To judge what to seek or avoid, I measure it against the purpose of my whole life, which must be set first.
support.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good, opens with this rule for every choice. “The details” are the separate acts and choices of a life; “this” is the purpose of the whole life.

support.quote: When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
gives: If I do not know what harbour I am making for, no wind is the right wind
support.follows: Without a known aim, nothing that happens can help me toward it.
support.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good: our plans miscarry because they have no aim. The “harbour” is the chief purpose of one’s life; the winds are what chance brings.

items.label: practice
items.role: Death at both ends of the day
items.t: When I lie down to sleep, I tell myself that I may not wake again, and when I wake, that I may not go to sleep again. I go to sleep gladly and say that I have lived, and that the course Fortune set for me is finished. Then every morning I get up is a gift.
items.why: Marcus’s morning reminder in this section is about the work ahead, and death enters only at each action (8.2, 10.29). Seneca brings death to the two ends of the day, and from it he draws the morning as a gift.

support.quote: Say to me when I lie down to sleep: “You may not wake again!” And when I have waked: “You may not go to sleep again!”
gives: When I lie down to sleep, I tell myself that I may not wake again, and when I wake, that I may not go to sleep again
support.follows: At lying down and at waking I should be reminded that this sleep or this day may be my last.
support.context: Letter 49, on the shortness of life: Seneca asks philosophy for teaching against the fear of death. The words he wants said to him are reminders that any sleep or day may be his last.

support.quote: let us go to our sleep with joy and gladness; let us say: I have lived; the course which Fortune set for me Is finished.
gives: I go to sleep gladly and say that I have lived, and that the course Fortune set for me is finished
support.follows: Each night I should go to sleep glad, saying that I have lived and my course is finished.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: each day should be lived as if it completed one’s life. Seneca turns a rich man’s nightly mock funeral into a glad saying at bedtime.

support.quote: When a man has said: “I have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
gives: every morning I get up is a gift
support.follows: Once I have said “I have lived”, each further morning is something extra given to me.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age, ending the thought that each day should be lived as one’s last: whoever can say at night “I have lived” takes each new morning as a bonus.

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep watching myself and review each day. What makes us bad is that none of us looks back over his own life: our thoughts go only to what we are about to do.
items.why: Marcus’s questions in this section are asked before or at an action. Seneca adds the look back over the day, and says that thinking only of what comes next is what makes us bad.

support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day.
gives: I keep watching myself and review each day
support.follows: I should watch myself all the time and go back over each day.
support.context: Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees and makes a habit of it; “each day” is his own day, reported in order.

support.quote: For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life. Our thoughts are devoted only to what we are about to do.
gives: What makes us bad is that none of us looks back over his own life
our thoughts go only to what we are about to do
support.follows: Never looking back over one’s own life, and thinking only of what comes next, is what makes people bad.
support.context: Letter 83, giving the reason for reviewing each day: our plans for the future depend on the past, yet we think only ahead. “His own life” is one’s past conduct.

items.label: breaks
items.t: While I will not admit my faults, I am still in their grasp: only someone who is awake can tell his dream. Admitting a fault is a sign that my mind is sound, and I rouse myself so that I can correct my mistakes.
items.why: 6.29 tells me to wake up and see that it was dreams that troubled me. Seneca uses the same image for faults: being able to name them is the sign that I am awake.

support.quote: Why will no man confess his faults? Because he is still in their grasp; only he who is awake can recount his dream, and similarly a confession of sin is a proof of sound mind.
gives: While I will not admit my faults, I am still in their grasp
only someone who is awake can tell his dream
Admitting a fault is a sign that my mind is sound
support.follows: One who cannot confess his faults is still held by them; confessing them shows the mind is sound again.
support.context: Letter 53, on faults of the spirit: the worse a disease of the soul, the less it is felt, as deep sleep leaves no dreams. The “dream” stands for one’s own faults.

support.quote: Let us, therefore, rouse ourselves, that we may be able to correct our mistakes.
gives: I rouse myself so that I can correct my mistakes
support.follows: We should wake ourselves up so that we can correct our mistakes.
support.context: Letter 53, on faults of the spirit, after saying that only one awake can tell his dream. “Rouse” is waking from the sleep of one’s faults, which philosophy alone can do.

amend.t: ; and I review each day, not thinking only of what I am about to do

searches: review, examine myself, scrutinize, account of the day
return for, in return, repay, requite
to what end, what purpose, no wind
pardon, forgive, err through ignorance, not surprised, wonder at

rejected.why: Better men rise with the dawn. About the hour of rising, in a letter against those who turn night into day; claim 1 is about why I get up.
He who rests should act and he who acts should rest. Says what 5.1 already grants (“one must rest too”); no difference.
Reading the philosophers wakes one up to join those who worked for us. About writers of philosophy, not the universe’s work of claim 2.
Living for belly, sleep and lust. Already used in Article 5.
The wages of a good deed is to have done it. Fits claim 4, but the letter is about gratitude for benefits received; 113.31 says it of the deed itself.
The good man is eager to repay a benefit. About the receiver’s duty to return a favour, not the giver’s; no conflict with claim 4.
Act as if someone were watching. A watcher to restrain one, not a wish to be seen; does not conflict with claim 4.
Live as if in plain sight of all. Same point as 25.5: about hiding nothing, not about seeking credit.
Some reach the truth only with another’s help, and are not to be despised. About teachers; 7.5 is about help with a task, and is said once.
Find yourself first; be consistent. Near 10.37’s “begin with yourself”, but about a steady will, not about asking to what end.
Observe yourself for inconsistencies of life. About consistency, not the question before an action.
Examine yourself whether you have made progress. About progress in philosophy.
Observe others or yourself: goods are useless without defence against chance. Neither claim 5’s question nor its point.
Death hangs over us; think of everything that can happen as going to happen. About foreseeing misfortunes, not about questioning each act.
Every day should be ordered as if it closed the series. Leads into 12.9, which is quoted and says it as a practice.
“I must be just without reward.” Says the same as the sentence of 113.31 that is quoted.
Set a value on each thing, asking what it is. About my own opinions of things, not about what another person holds.
Do not heed what men will say of your death. About choosing one’s death.
One must often be just and disgraced at once. Near 10.15 on blame, but 10.15 is said once and takes no backing; adding it would repeat Article 22.

articles.title: Whose praise do I want?

claims.t: Before I want to please people or fear them as judges, I look right into their ruling parts and see what sort of people they are: what they are after and what they run from, and what they are like when they eat and sleep.
claims.shared: Three passages say the same thing to do: look into “their ruling parts” (9.32, 9.16, 4.31). 6.54 and 10.20 open with the same Greek words, “what sort of people those are” and “what they are like”, and 9.32 asks me to see their “little souls naked”. What they are after is in both 9.32 (“what sort of things they are in earnest about”) and 4.31 (“what sort of things they chase”).
claims.changed: The passages speak of people in general (“these people”, “they”); the claim speaks of those whose praise or judgment I care about, as 9.32, 9.16 and 6.54 do. “And at the wise as well” in 4.31 is left out, because its point is open: the wise may be a model or a target. The claim reads “they” who run from and chase things in 4.31 as everyone looked at, not the wise alone; the translators allow both. Of 10.20’s list, eating and sleeping are kept. The statement says “mind” where the claim keeps the passages’ “ruling parts”.

support.quote: What the ruling parts of these people are, what sort of things they are in earnest about, and for what sort of things they love and honour.
gives: I look right into their ruling parts
what they are after
support.follows: I should consider what rules in these people, what they take seriously, and what they give their love and honour for.

support.quote: Think of yourself as looking at their little souls naked.
gives: see what sort of people they are
support.follows: I should picture their small souls stripped bare, as they really are.

support.quote: Pass inside, right inside, into their ruling parts, and you will see what judges you are afraid of
gives: fear them as judges
I look right into their ruling parts
support.follows: If I go deep into these people’s ruling parts, I will see what kind of judges I am afraid of.

support.quote: Look closely into their ruling parts, and at the wise as well: what sort of things they run from, and what sort of things they chase.
gives: I look right into their ruling parts
what they are after
what they run from
support.follows: I should look closely into people’s ruling parts, and at the wise too, and see what they run from and what they chase.

support.quote: What sort of people those are whom they want to please, and for what sort of gains, and through what sort of activities.
gives: Before I want to please people
see what sort of people they are
support.follows: Anyone who wants to please people should consider what those people are like, what is gained, and what has to be done for it.

support.quote: What they are like when eating, sleeping, mating, emptying their bowels, and the rest.
gives: see what sort of people they are
what they are like when they eat and sleep
support.follows: I should picture these people as they are when they eat, sleep, mate and empty their bowels.

claims.t: The people whose praise I might want judge even themselves badly: they curse themselves, they are not pleased with themselves, and they do not know where they are or who they are. I do not want praise from such people.
claims.shared: 9.16 and 8.51 both turn from what these people think of me to what they think of themselves: 9.16 shows “what sort of judges they are of themselves as well”, and 8.51 names a person who “curses themselves” and “is not pleased with themselves”.
claims.changed: 9.16 says “what sort of judges”; that they judge themselves badly is the sense its context gives, and 8.51 says it outright. 8.51 asks questions (“Do you want to be praised by…?”); the claim gives the answer they expect.

support.quote: and what sort of judges they are of themselves as well.
gives: judge even themselves badly
support.follows: Looking into these people also shows what kind of judges they are of themselves.

support.quote: Do you want to be praised by a person who curses themselves three times an hour? Do you want to please a person who is not pleased with themselves?
gives: judge even themselves badly
they curse themselves, they are not pleased with themselves
I do not want praise from such people
support.follows: It makes no sense to want praise from someone who curses themselves, or to want to please someone who is not pleased with themselves.

support.quote: people who know neither where they are nor who they are
gives: they do not know where they are or who they are
support.follows: The people who clap know neither where they are nor who they are.

claims.t: I do not chase fame after death; I make a gift of the present time to myself. Those who would remember me will be people like the ones I find hard to bear now, and they too are mortal: each of them will very soon die, until the whole memory goes out; and whatever they say or think of me is nothing to me.
claims.shared: 8.42 and 4.16 both say that those who chase “fame after death” fail to reckon that the people who would remember them are mortal: “those people too are mortal” (8.42), “each of those who remember them will very soon die too” (4.16).
claims.changed: Both passages describe other people who chase fame after death; the claim says that I do not. 4.16 goes on to suppose that the memory never dies; that case is kept apart, under “If I doubt it”.

support.quote: Look: make a gift of this present time to yourself.
gives: I make a gift of the present time to myself
support.follows: I should give the time that is here now to myself.

support.quote: People who chase fame after death instead do not take into account that those people will be others of the same kind as these whom they find hard to bear; and those people too are mortal.
gives: I do not chase fame after death
Those who would remember me will be people like the ones I find hard to bear now
they too are mortal
support.follows: Those who would praise me later will be like the people I find hard to bear now, and they will die too.

support.quote: Whoever is worked up about fame after death does not picture that each of those who remember them will very soon die too; then in turn the one who takes over from that one, until the whole memory also goes out
gives: I do not chase fame after death
they too are mortal
each of them will very soon die
until the whole memory goes out
support.follows: Everyone who remembers me will soon die, and the one after them too, until all memory of me is gone.

support.quote: And what is it to you at all, if those people echo with sounds of such a kind, or hold a judgment of such a kind about you?
gives: whatever they say or think of me is nothing to me
support.follows: What later people say about me, or what they think of me, is nothing to me.

claims.t: When I want other people’s good opinion, I go against myself. I love myself more than anyone, yet I value their judgment of me above my own; I look down on people, yet I fawn on them; I will not speak well of those who live beside me, yet I want those who come after to speak well of me.
claims.shared: Each passage sets what people give others against what they want from them, and the two do not agree: 12.3 and 6.17 join the two halves with “yet”, and 11.13 with “Despising one another, they fawn on one another”. “I go against myself” is the editor’s name for the contradiction that each of the three shows in its own words.
claims.changed: The passages speak of “each person” (12.3) and of “they” (11.13, 6.17); the claim says “I”. 11.13’s second pair (wanting to be above others, taking the lower place), 12.3’s test of the god or teacher and its sentence on shame, and the last sentence of 6.17 are left out.

support.quote: each person loves themselves more than everyone else, yet sets less value on their own judgment about themselves than on that of others
gives: I go against myself
I love myself more than anyone, yet I value their judgment of me above my own
support.follows: People love themselves more than anyone, yet they value others’ judgment of them more than their own.

support.quote: Despising one another, they fawn on one another; and wanting to be above one another, they take the lower place beneath one another.
gives: I go against myself
I look down on people, yet I fawn on them
support.follows: People who despise one another fawn on one another, and in wanting to be above one another they put themselves beneath.

support.quote: The people who live at the same time as them and alongside them they are unwilling to speak well of, yet they set great store by being spoken well of themselves by those who come after, whom they have never seen and never will see.
gives: I go against myself
I will not speak well of those who live beside me, yet I want those who come after to speak well of me
support.follows: It is odd to refuse to speak well of those who live beside me and yet care much that people I will never see speak well of me.

claims.t: Praise does not make me better, and blame does not harm me. Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of it; my own good is my own action, not another person’s activity.
claims.shared: 4.16 and 9.32 both deny that praise and blame change what they fall on: in 4.16, “what is praised becomes neither worse nor better” and nothing is “ruined when it is blamed”; in 9.32, those who think they “do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises” are conceited.
claims.changed: 4.16 speaks of beautiful things, from law and truth to an emerald; the claim applies it to me. The Greek word for “beautiful” also means fine and noble. 6.46’s “lover of pleasure” is left out.

support.quote: At any rate, what is praised becomes neither worse nor better.
gives: Praise does not make me better
support.follows: Being praised makes a thing neither worse nor better.

support.quote: Which of these is beautiful because it is praised, or is ruined when it is blamed?
gives: Praise does not make me better
blame does not harm me
support.follows: Nothing is beautiful because it is praised, and nothing is ruined because it is blamed.

support.quote: When they suppose that they do harm by blaming or do good by singing praises, how much conceit.
gives: Praise does not make me better
blame does not harm me
support.follows: People who think their blame does harm, or their praise does good, think far too much of themselves.

support.quote: Everything that is beautiful in any way at all is beautiful of itself and ends in itself, and does not have praise as a part of itself.
gives: Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of it
support.follows: Whatever is beautiful is beautiful of itself, and praise is no part of its beauty.

support.quote: The lover of fame takes their own good to be another person’s activity; the lover of pleasure, their own feeling; the person who has sense, their own action.
gives: my own good is my own action, not another person’s activity
support.follows: Whoever loves fame puts their good in what someone else does; a sensible person puts it in their own action.

single.label: Slaves a little while ago
single.t: When people give themselves airs and scold from above, I remember that a little while ago they were slaves to many, and that in a little while they will be in the same case.
single.quote: Then what they are like when lording it and giving themselves airs, or getting angry and scolding from a position of superiority. Yet a little while ago they were slaves, to how many, and for what sort of things. And in a little while they will be in the same sort of case.
single.why: Only this passage says what the proud were a little while ago and will soon be again. Its first sentence feeds claim 1; this part stands alone.
single.follows: Those who give themselves airs and scold from above were slaves to many not long ago, and soon they will be in the same case.

single.label: Even if memory lasted
single.t: Even if those who remember me never died, and the memory never died, it would be nothing to me. To the living, praise is of use at most for getting some matter done.
single.quote: But suppose even that those who will remember are immortal, and the memory immortal: what then is that to you? And I do not speak of its being nothing to the dead; but to the living, what is praise, except perhaps for the sake of managing some matter?
single.why: Only this passage supposes the opposite of what claim 3 rests on, a memory that never dies, and says what holds then.
single.follows: Even an undying memory would be nothing to me; to the living, praise is at most useful for managing some matter.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 9.32 is 9.34, 8.42 is 8.44, 6.54 is 6.59, 4.16 is 4.19–20, 6.17 is 6.18, 8.51 is 8.52–53, 10.20 is 10.19, 12.3 is 12.4, 4.31 is 4.38, 9.16 is 9.18, 11.13 is 11.14 and 6.46 is 6.51; 10.10 is the same.

Reads 9.16’s “what sort of judges they are of themselves” as poor judges of themselves. The Greek says only “what sort”; the poor judgment is the sense of the context and is said outright in 8.51, which claim 2 joins to it.

Applies to me what the passages say of others: 4.16 of beautiful things (“what is praised becomes neither worse nor better”), and 12.3, 11.13 and 6.17 of “each person” and “they”. In claim 4, “I go against myself” is the editor’s name for the contradiction that each of the three passages shows in its own words; each is mapped to it for that reason.
Sets aside 10.10, the spider proud of its fly. It is about pride in a capture (the last hunter, of Sarmatians, is Marcus himself), not about anyone’s praise or judgment.
articles.limit: Article 22 already says that I fail when I want to be approved of, Article 10 that being remembered is of no account, Article 13 that praise from the many pulls me about, and Article 9 that I need no one as witness. Article 34 already says that those who remember me will soon follow me and that even remembrance lasting for ever would be empty; claim 3 and the item under “If I doubt it” say this again, here as reasons not to chase fame after death, with what 8.42 adds: those who would remember me will be like the people I find hard to bear now. What this article adds is the reason from the side of the people who give praise: I look into them and find poor judges, even of themselves; praise and blame do not change what they fall on; and those who would remember me will die too. 4.16 carries much of it: it feeds claims 3 and 5, the item under “If I doubt it” and two parts of the statement.

aside.10.10: About pride in a capture, from a spider’s fly to the Sarmatians Marcus himself fought. It shares with claim 1 the act of examining people’s principles, but turns it on pride in conquest, not on those whose praise or judgment I care about.

statement.t: Before I want anyone’s praise I look into their mind; praise makes me no better, and fame after death is nothing to me.

parts.words: Before I want anyone’s praise I look into their mind
praise makes me no better
fame after death is nothing to me

statement.kind: One question answered from three sides
statement.form: The section asks whose praise is worth wanting. Claims 1 and 2 answer from the people who give it: look into them, and they judge even themselves badly. Claim 5 answers from the thing praised: praise does not change it. Claim 3 answers from time: those who would remember me die too. Claim 4 shows what wanting praise does to me. The statement takes one part from the first three answers.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: seeing what sort of people they are (claim 1), not wanting praise from people I cannot praise (claim 2), and taking others’ word for what I am (claim 4). The article gains an audience of a few, one or none; a way to weigh judgments; and a way back: what I think of myself counts for more. He challenges two claims: he holds that those who come after will judge without prejudice, and that deserved praise from good people is a good.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement gains a clause: what I think of myself matters much more than what others think of me. Its last part stands only in the sense that what posterity says will not affect me; Seneca’s school holds that renown after death is a good, and so would deny that fame after death is worth nothing.

items.quote: when you wish to inquire into a man’s true worth, and to know what manner of man he is, look at him when he is naked
gives: see what sort of people they are
items.follows: To know what a person is worth and what kind of person they are, I should look at them stripped of everything they wear.
items.context: Letter 76: we value a man along with his trappings. To know his worth, Seneca says, strip away his estate, his titles, even his body, and consider his soul.

items.quote: Why do you take pleasure in being praised by men whom you yourself cannot praise?
gives: I do not want praise from such people
items.follows: It makes no sense to enjoy praise from people I could not praise myself.
items.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers: a lecturer leaves happy with the applause of the ignorant. The “men” are that audience, whom he could not praise himself.

items.quote: At present, you are taking the word of others for what you are.
gives: I value their judgment of me above my own
items.follows: Lucilius takes other people’s word for what he is, instead of looking into his own soul.
items.context: Letter 80: a king’s worth shows once his diadem is off. Seneca tells Lucilius to value himself by looking into his own soul, not by what others report.

items.label: action
items.role: An audience of few or none
items.t: I scorn the pleasure that the applause of the many gives. I am content if what I do reaches a few people, or one, or none at all.
items.why: Marcus asks whose praise is worth wanting and answers by looking at those who give it. He does not say how many people I need. Seneca says: a few, one or none.

support.quote: that you may scorn the pleasure which comes from the applause of the majority
gives: I scorn the pleasure that the applause of the many gives
support.follows: These sayings are meant to make me scorn the pleasure that the applause of the majority gives.
support.context: The close of Letter 7, on crowds, after three sayings about needing few listeners or none. Seneca tells Lucilius what the sayings are for.

support.quote: I am content with few, content with one, content with none at all.
gives: I am content if what I do reaches a few people, or one, or none at all
support.follows: A few people, one person or no one at all is enough for the one who said this.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: a man was asked why he worked so hard at an art that would reach very few people. This was his answer.

items.label: practice
items.t: I weigh people’s judgments and do not merely count them. How a person gives and receives praise shows me what kind of person they are.
items.why: Claim 1 looks into the ruling parts of those whose praise I might want. Seneca says what to look for there: how they give and take praise, and the weight of a judgment rather than the number of voices.

support.quote: it will make you weigh, and not merely count, men’s judgments
gives: I weigh people’s judgments and do not merely count them
support.follows: Philosophy teaches me to weigh what people judge, not only to count how many judge so.
support.context: Letter 29: what philosophy will do for Lucilius. “Men’s judgments” are what people think of him; Seneca would pity him if the whole city cheered him.

support.quote: you can tell the character of every man when you see how he gives and receives praise.
gives: How a person gives and receives praise shows me what kind of person they are
support.follows: How someone gives praise and how they take it shows what kind of person they are.
support.context: Letter 52: the applause of the theatre should differ from that of the school. Small signs show character, Seneca says, and praise shows it best.

items.label: breaks
items.role: The price, and the way back
items.t: To win the crowd’s approval I would have to use tricks and make myself like them. What I think of myself matters much more than what others think of me.
items.why: Claim 4 shows how wanting others’ good opinion sets me against myself, and gives no way back. Seneca names the price, becoming like the crowd, and the way back: my own view of myself counts for more.

support.quote: It takes trickery to win popular approval; and you must needs make yourself like unto them
gives: To win the crowd’s approval I would have to use tricks and make myself like them
support.follows: Winning the crowd’s approval takes tricks, and it means making oneself like the crowd.
support.context: Letter 29: Seneca quotes Epicurus, “I have never wished to cater to the crowd”. “Them” are the crowd, who approve only of those like themselves.

support.quote: However, what you think of yourself is much more to the point than what others think of you.
gives: What I think of myself matters much more than what others think of me
support.follows: What I think of myself matters much more than what others think of me.
support.context: Letter 29, on not catering to the crowd: having said that its favour is won only by becoming like it, Seneca sets one’s own view of oneself above its view.

items.t: Seneca disagrees about those who come after. Marcus says they will be people like those I find hard to bear now; Seneca says they will judge me without prejudice and without favour, and that I should have regard to them, and his school holds that renown after death is a good. He agrees with Marcus that what posterity says will not affect us. He is not consistent: in Ep. 113.32 he says it makes no difference how many people know that I am just.

support.quote: That man is born merely for a few, who thinks only of the people of his own generation. Many thousands of years and many thousands of peoples will come after you; it is to these that you should have regard.
support.follows: Whoever thinks only of their own generation lives for a few; I should have regard to the many generations that will come after me.
support.context: Letter 79: fame is the shadow of virtue and may come late, once envy is gone. “These” are the many peoples who will come after Lucilius.

support.quote: there will come men who will judge you without prejudice and without favour.
support.follows: Later generations will judge me without prejudice and without favour.
support.context: Letter 79, on fame that comes late: malice may silence everyone of one’s own day. The men “who will judge you” belong to later generations.

support.quote: We ourselves, indeed, shall not be affected by the talk of posterity
support.follows: What later generations say of us will not affect us.
support.context: Letter 79, on fame that comes late. Seneca grants that the dead will not feel what posterity says of them, and holds that it will still celebrate them.

support.quote: the renown which falls to one’s lot after death is a good
support.follows: Seneca’s school holds that renown after death is a good.
support.context: Letter 102 takes up an argument from an earlier letter, in which Seneca set out to prove his school’s belief that renown after death is a good.

support.quote: it makes no difference how many persons are acquainted with your uprightness
support.follows: How many people know that I am upright makes no difference.
support.context: The close of Letter 113, on justice that seeks no reward. “Your uprightness” is being just; how many people know of it, Seneca says, does not matter.

items.t: Seneca disagrees that my good is only my own action and never another person’s activity. Praise given to a good man by good men, when he deserves it, is a good, and it is his own good as well as theirs (Ep. 102.18–19). He agrees that the many are not the judges: glory rests on their judgments, renown on the judgments of good men (Ep. 102.17).

support.quote: It is my own good, in that I am praised, because I am naturally born to love all men
support.follows: Being praised by good people is my own good, because I am born to love all people.
support.context: Letter 102: renown is praise given to a good man by good men. Asked whose good it is, the one praised or the ones praising, Seneca answers: both.

support.quote: It is therefore a good belonging to both sides—this being praised when one deserves it
support.follows: Praise given to someone who deserves it is a good both for the one praised and for those who praise.
support.context: Letter 102: to praise the deserving is an act of justice, so it is a good of the one who praises and of the one praised. “It” is deserved praise.

support.quote: the latter depends upon the judgments of the many; but renown on the judgments of good men.
support.follows: Glory depends on what the many think; renown depends on what good people think.
support.context: Letter 102 separates renown from glory. “The latter” is glory, which depends on the many; renown depends on the judgments of good men.

amend.t: ; what I think of myself matters much more than what others think of me
; yet those who come after will judge me without prejudice and without favour, and I should have regard to them
; yet praise from good people, when I deserve it, is a good, and it is mine as well as theirs

after my, our, his, your death
what others think, opinion of you, others, men
pleased or displeased with himself, themselves, yourself

rejected.why: The great, envied from below, hold a different opinion of themselves. About the fears of the powerful, not about whose praise to want.
The fortunate come to fear what they strove for. About ambition and its fears.
Applause need not disturb your calm. A list of precepts against envying the great; the applause is for others, not for me.
A man who measures all souls by his own. About the equality of goods in triumph and defeat.
Tear off the actor’s mask of the great and you will scorn them. Ep. 76.32 says the same of seeing a person as they are, more plainly.
Strip a slave for sale before you judge him. The image behind 80.10; 76.32 is used for the point.
Those in purple are like actors; you measure the pedestal with the man. Sets up 76.32, which is used.
Strip the mask from men and from things. About fear of death and pain, not about judging people.
Men see more clearly in others’ affairs than in their own. About whether the wise can help the wise.
Foolish to praise in a man what comes from outside; a golden bit does not make a better horse. About external goods, not about what praise does.
Live as if before men’s eyes. About living openly, not about wanting praise.
Things are desired because they have been praised. About the value of things, not of praise.
We accept every flattery and see ourselves in the flatterer’s description. Near claim 4, but about believing praise, not about the contradiction Marcus names.
What to say to a flatterer. A practice against flattery; the article’s practice is to look into the one who praises.
Sour critics of others’ lives. About people who preach, in a letter on frugality.
Busybodies and self-tormentors suffer before they need to. About fear of loss.
Do not flatter yourself for despising useless luxury. About self-praise for small virtues.
Ranked near 8.42 by vectors; about welcoming death.
The talk of men has no concern with my purpose. Said of choosing one’s death; the context is suicide, not praise.
Crowds at the theatre, few at the lecture on the good man. About what people care to learn.
“Your deed will speedily be forgotten”: outside my task. Said of a man who goes to his death for honour; the match to claim 3 would need explaining.
Only the wise man plays one part. About inconstancy of character, not of wanting praise.
Watching those who did a noble deed once. About how we form the idea of virtue.
Utterance is not a good in itself. An objection Seneca answers in 102.14; quoting it would give the opposite of his view.
Renown is a judgment, not an utterance. A step in the logic; 102.17 to 102.19 give the conclusion.
Praise is a matter of the mind rather than of speech. A step in the logic of renown.
Seneca promises Lucilius fame among later generations. Says what 79.17 says, as a promise; 79.17 states the reason.
Fame is the shadow of virtue. Leads into 79.17, which is quoted.
Be your own spectator; seek your own applause. Said of bearing illness bravely without onlookers.
What is baser than philosophy courting applause? About lecturers; 52.11 and 52.12 are used.
That is not praise, it is merely applause. About the lecture hall; adds nothing to 52.11.
Only the first clause is used. “Your good qualities should face inwards” would need explaining.
Those who covet glory do not understand it. About Tubero’s plain furniture.
Glory is empty and fleeting. One item in a list of precepts, with no context of its own.
No past life lends us glory. About noble birth.
A soul pleased with itself for what displeases others. About the soul’s beauty, in a letter on style.
Satellius, a fawner on millionaires. An anecdote about borrowed learning.

articles.title: Wrongdoing harms the wrongdoer

claims.role: Where the harm of a wrong lies
claims.t: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it: it harms them and makes them bad, and they can be rid of it as soon as they wish. It does no harm to the person it is done to.
claims.shared: Three passages put the harm of a wrong in the one who does it: 8.53 says wickedness is “harmful only to the one” who has it, 9.4 that whoever does wrong does it “at their own cost” and does injustice “to themselves”, and 9.37 that if someone did wrong, “the evil is there”, with them.
claims.changed: 8.53 speaks of wickedness, 9.4 of doing wrong and acting unjustly, 9.37 of doing wrong; the claim calls all of them “a wrong”. Only 8.53 says that the wrong does no harm to the other person and that the wrongdoer can be rid of it.

support.quote: It is harmful only to the one who has also been given the power to be rid of it, as soon as they wish to.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it
it harms them
they can be rid of it as soon as they wish
support.follows: Wickedness harms only the one who has it, and that one can be rid of it as soon as they wish.

support.quote: Whoever does wrong does wrong at their own cost.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it
support.follows: The cost of a wrong falls on the one who does it.

support.quote: Whoever acts unjustly does injustice to themselves, making themselves bad.
gives: it harms them
makes them bad
support.follows: Whoever acts unjustly wrongs themselves, by making themselves bad.

support.quote: If the person did wrong, the evil is there.
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it
support.follows: If someone did wrong, the evil is there, with the one who did it.

support.quote: Wickedness in general does no harm to the universe, and wickedness in the particular case does no harm to the other person.
gives: It does no harm to the person it is done to
support.follows: Wickedness does no harm to the universe, and a particular wicked act does no harm to the person on the receiving end.

claims.t: Another person’s wrong is not an evil for me, and my being unfortunate does not depend on them. I leave their wrong with them.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the wrong of someone else, “my neighbour’s wickedness” in 8.53 and “another person’s wrongdoing” in 9.18, and both keep it away from me: 8.53 says it is not an evil for me, 9.18 that it must be left there.
claims.changed: 8.53 gives the reason, that god decided against it; 9.18 gives only the rule. “With them” reads the “there” of 9.18 as the place of the one who did the wrong, as the translators’ note does.

support.quote: For otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be an evil for me, which god decided against, so that my being unfortunate should not depend on someone else.
gives: Another person’s wrong
is not an evil for me
my being unfortunate does not depend on them
support.follows: My neighbour’s wickedness is not an evil for me: god decided that my being unfortunate should not depend on anyone else.

support.quote: Another person’s wrongdoing must be left there.
gives: Another person’s wrong
I leave their wrong with them
support.follows: Someone else’s wrongdoing is to be left where it is, with them.

single.label: Each mind rules itself
single.t: Another person’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine, any more than their breath or their flesh. We were made for one another, but each of us has a ruling mind with its own authority.
single.quote: To my faculty of choice, my neighbour’s faculty of choice is just as much a matter of indifference as their bit of breath and their bit of flesh. For however true it is that we have come to be for one another’s sake, still each of our ruling parts has its own authority.
single.why: Only 8.53 says why another person’s wrong cannot reach me: each ruling part has its own authority. No second passage of the section gives this ground.
single.follows: My neighbour’s power of choice is neither good nor bad for mine; though we exist for one another, each mind has its own authority.

single.label: Perhaps no wrong
single.t: When I think someone has done wrong, I also allow that perhaps they did not.
single.quote: But perhaps they did not do wrong.
single.why: Only 9.37 doubts that the wrong was done at all. It is a check before the claim applies, not a part of it.
single.follows: It may be that the person did not do wrong at all.

single.label: Nothing new
single.t: When I meet wickedness, and with everything else that happens, I keep this thought ready: this is what I have often seen.
single.quote: What is wickedness? This is what you have often seen. And with everything that happens, keep this at hand: this is what you have often seen.
single.why: Only 7.1 gives words to keep ready when wickedness is met. It speaks of how familiar wickedness is, not of whom it harms.
single.follows: Wickedness is what one has often seen, and the same thought is to be kept at hand for whatever happens.

single.label: Wrong done for pleasure
single.t: If I do wrong, a wrong done with pleasure is worse than one done in the pain of anger. In anger I am more like someone wronged first and forced by pain into anger; from desire I go to the wrong by an impulse of my own.
single.quote: the wrong done with pleasure is open to a greater charge than the wrong done with pain. And in general the one is more like a person who has first been treated unjustly and has been forced by pain into anger; the other is moved to do injustice by an impulse of their own, carried towards doing something from desire.
single.why: Only 2.7 compares wrongs, and it reports Theophrastus with Marcus’s approval. It is about how serious a wrong is, not whom it harms, and it shows what my own failing looks like.
single.follows: Theophrastus, whom Marcus approves, holds that a wrong done with pleasure deserves a greater charge than a wrong done in the pain of anger.

single.label: Wrong by not acting
single.t: I can act unjustly by not doing something, and not only by doing something.
single.quote: Often the one who does not do something acts unjustly, not only the one who does something.
single.why: Only 9.4 speaks of a wrong done by leaving something undone. It widens what counts as my wrong; no other passage of the section says it.
single.follows: Leaving something undone can be unjust, as well as doing something.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 8.53 is 8.55–56, 9.4 is 9.4–5, 2.7 is 2.10, 9.18 is 9.20, 9.37 is 9.38 and 8.9 is 8.10; 7.1 is the same.
Treats wickedness (8.53), doing wrong and acting unjustly (9.4), and wrongdoing (9.18, 9.37) as one thing, “a wrong”. The Greek uses three different words for them.
Reads “there” in 9.18 and 9.37 as “with the one who did the wrong”, as the translators’ notes do. The Greek says only “there”.
Keeps 2.7 as a said-once item under “When it breaks”. It reports Theophrastus’s ranking of wrongs with Marcus’s approval, and Marcus says that such a comparison is an everyday way of speaking.
articles.limit: Article 19’s claim 2 is this article’s claim 1, and Article 19 marks Ep. 81.22 as a challenge to it, as this article does for claim 1, because it lets the least part of a wrong reach the one wronged; Article 19’s claim 8 is the said-once 9.37b. What this article adds is leaving the wrong with the one who did it, which Article 21 says once (7.21b) and which here rests on 8.53 and 9.18, with the reason that another’s wrong is no evil for me. The articles disagree about the wrongdoer: Article 19’s claim 1 says that with their disposition they can do nothing else, while claim 1 here says they can be rid of the wrong as soon as they wish, as Article 15’s claim 4 says of my own wrong, and 2.7 calls a wrong done from desire an impulse of one’s own. Two fused claims rest on four passages, two of them one-line sayings; Article 1 (cutting myself off by wrongdoing) and Article 3 (nothing is unusual) come near.

aside.8.9: About regret: it argues that pleasure is neither useful nor good. It says nothing about wrongdoing or about whom a wrong harms.

statement.t: A wrong harms the one who does it, not the one it is done to, so I leave another’s wrong with them.

parts.words: A wrong harms the one who does it, not the one it is done to
I leave another’s wrong with them

inferences.why: No passage joins the two. 9.18 says to leave another’s wrong there without giving a reason; the step from where the harm lies to leaving the wrong with its doer is the editor’s.

statement.kind: A ground and the response it allows
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: the harm of a wrong lies with the one who does it. Claim 2 is what I do when the wrong is someone else’s: I count it no evil for me and leave it with them. The “so” that joins them in the statement is the editor’s. In the part “I leave another’s wrong with them”, 8.53 backs only “another’s wrong”; the leaving comes from 9.18.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if another person’s wrong could harm me after all.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, where the harm of a wrong lies gains a second witness and a challenge: he holds that the least and lightest part of a wrong reaches the one it is done to, and that bad people make one another worse. Practice gains forgetting wrongs on purpose and reading words and looks generously, and In action gains keeping watch against what people may do.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, except that its middle, that a wrong does no harm to the one it is done to, is challenged under Why: he holds that its least and lightest part reaches them. It also gains an ending: I forget another’s wrong on purpose.

items.quote: the first and worst penalty for sin is to have committed sin
gives: The evil of a wrong lies with the one who does it
items.follows: The first and worst penalty of wrongdoing is having done it.
items.context: Letter 97, on the wickedness of the age: Seneca agrees with Epicurus that wrongdoers never feel safe. “Sin” is wrongdoing, and its first penalty falls on the one who did it.

items.label: practice
items.t: I think little of the wrongs done to me and forget them, not by accident but on purpose. I do not misread a word or a look, and I make light of mishaps by reading them generously.
items.why: In this section Marcus says to leave another’s wrong where it is, and that perhaps no wrong was done; he gives no exercise for it. Seneca gives one: forget wrongs on purpose, and read words and looks generously.

support.quote: He despises the wrongs done him; he forgets them, not accidentally, but voluntarily.
gives: I think little of the wrongs done to me
forget them, not by accident but on purpose
support.follows: The wise man thinks little of the wrongs done to him and forgets them on purpose.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: the wise man takes lasting joy in what he has received. “He” is the wise man; “the wrongs done him” are injuries other people have done him.

support.quote: He will not misinterpret a word or a look; he makes light of all mishaps by interpreting them in a generous way.
gives: I do not misread a word or a look
I make light of mishaps by reading them generously
support.follows: The wise man does not misread a word or a look, and makes light of mishaps by reading them generously.
support.context: Letter 81, on weighing injuries against benefits. “He” is the wise man, who does not look for someone to blame and puts even people’s wrongs down to chance.

items.label: action
items.role: Guarding my life and goods against people
items.t: Other people are where my everyday danger comes from, so I watch for it, and I try to harm no one so that I am not harmed.
items.why: Seneca means danger to life and goods, which he sets beside fires and falling buildings, not an evil for the mind. Marcus says what another’s wrong is once it has been done; nothing in this section says to guard against it beforehand.

support.quote: it is from his fellow-man that a man’s everyday danger comes. Equip yourself against that; watch that with an attentive eye.
gives: Other people are where my everyday danger comes from
I watch for it
support.follows: A person’s everyday danger comes from other people, so one should arm oneself against it and watch it closely.
support.context: Letter 103, on the dangers of living among people. Seneca sets plots by people against accidents such as fires and falling buildings; “that” is the danger from people.

support.quote: Try, in your dealings with others, to harm not, in order that you be not harmed.
gives: I try to harm no one so that I am not harmed
support.follows: One should harm no one in dealings with others, so as not to be harmed.
support.context: Letter 103: from the danger people pose, Seneca draws a duty. “Harmed” means hurt by others in life and goods, the danger the letter opens with.

items.t: Seneca agrees that the worst of a wrong stays with the one who does it, but he does not say that none of it reaches the other person: “only the least and lightest portion” of it flows back on the one wronged (Ep. 81.22). He also says that bad people harm one another, each making the other worse (Ep. 109.4). Marcus says that a particular wickedness does no harm to the other person at all.

support.quote: When we do wrong, only the least and lightest portion of it flows back upon our neighbour; the worst and, if I may use the term, the densest portion of it stays at home and troubles the owner.
support.follows: Of a wrong we do, only the least part falls on our neighbour; the worst part stays with us and troubles us.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca says to avoid ingratitude for our own sake. “It” is the wrong we do; the “neighbour” is the one it is done to, here the benefactor.

support.quote: Evil men harm evil men; each debases the other by rousing his wrath, by approving his churlishness, and praising his pleasures
support.follows: Bad people harm one another: each makes the other worse by stirring his anger and praising his faults and pleasures.
support.context: Letter 109, on whether wise men can help one another. Seneca sets bad men, who harm and debase each other, against good men, who help each other.

amend.t: ; yet the least and lightest part of it does reach them, and bad people make one another worse
; and I forget it, not by accident but on purpose

searches: cannot be harmed, cannot receive or suffer injury
insult, abuse, slander near wise man, good man
wicked, wickedness near himself, itself, its own

rejected.why: “The worst punishment for crime lies in the crime itself”: the same point as 97.14, inside an argument that good cannot spring from evil.
Crime is punished the moment it is committed. Same point as 97.14; a third witness was not needed.
Bad deeds are lashed by conscience. The penalty is fear, not the wrong making one bad; a different harm from Marcus’s.
Never doing wrong brings peace of mind; wrongdoers tremble after the deed. About fear of punishment, not the harm the wrong itself does.
An evil conscience can find safety but never ease. Same point as 105.7.
