“More wretched to commit than to suffer injury.” A comparison: whether suffering injury harms at all would need explaining. Article 1’s letter.
Fortune can injure Lucilius; Seneca does not fear he will injure himself. About Lucilius’s character, not about wrongdoing.
The body is the only part of me that can suffer injury. Said of fortune and the body, not of wrongs done by other people.
“His neighbour’s wickedness … harms him”: a view of “certain men” that Seneca reports and then sets aside for Posidonius’s.
What does harm makes a man worse: a syllogism about pain and poverty that Seneca reports and then disputes.
What harms has no greater power than what receives harm. About no longer fearing death or the gods.
Contempt does injury but passes on. Advice on avoiding hatred; Letter 103 says the same more fully and is quoted.
Forget the injury and remember the kindness. About one man who has done both, weighing them against each other.
The ungrateful man clings to his injuries. About ingratitude; 81.24 gives the practice directly.
Much of evil lies in its novelty. About misfortunes thought over beforehand, not about wickedness.
“I see nothing new”: the words of men weary of life, not a thought kept ready as 7.1 asks.
Vices have countless forms. About the variety of vice, the opposite angle from 7.1.
The lustful suffer the evils they inflicted on others. About excess in pleasure; the step to Marcus’s claim would need explaining.
The gods cannot receive or inflict injury. About the gods, not people.
“A soul that cannot be harmed”: Seneca weighing how to translate a Greek term, not a claim about wrongs.
Wickedness goes on of itself. About the decline of the age.

articles.title: Short sayings

unfused.reason: The five passages of this section are separate short sayings, and no two of them say the same thing, so nothing here is fused. Four are kept side by side, each on its own; the fifth is half a sentence and is set aside.

single.label: Up or down
single.t: For a stone thrown upward, coming down is nothing bad, and going up is nothing good.
single.quote: For a stone that has been thrown upward, it is nothing bad to be carried down, and nothing good to be carried up.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of what is good or bad in what happens to a thing. It is an image, and Marcus does not say here what the stone stands for. It stands beside the statement, not as its ground.
single.follows: For a thrown stone, falling is not bad and rising is not good.

single.label: Hive and bee
single.t: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee in it either.
single.quote: What is not good for the hive is not good for the bee either.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of a community and its member. Article 3 says that what serves the whole is good for every part; this passage says that what is not good for the whole is not good for the part. It does not contradict Article 3, and it is not the same claim. It stands beside the statement, not as its ground.
single.follows: A bee cannot gain from what does not benefit its hive.

single.label: Upright on my own
single.t: I am to be upright on my own, not held upright by someone else.
single.quote: Upright, not held upright.
single.why: Only this passage of the section says it. The same rule ends modern 3.5 (Casaubon’s 3.6), which Article 22 quotes in its claim 2.
single.follows: Uprightness should be one’s own, not something that another keeps in place.

single.label: Fighting back
single.t: When I fight back against someone, the best way is not to become like them.
single.quote: The best way to fight back is to not become like them.
single.why: Only this passage of the section speaks of an opponent. The Greek does not say like whom; “them” stands for whoever is being fought.
single.follows: The best way to fight back against someone is to not become like them.

decisions: The editor recommended that this section get no article, since no two of its passages share a claim. It stands instead as four said-once items, so that the article numbers stay as planned; whether the section keeps an article is the owner’s decision.

The statement joins the two sayings about my own conduct (7.9 and 6.5) with a plain “and”. The stone (9.15) and the hive (6.49) are placed under Why as images that stand beside the statement, not as its ground, and each item says so.

Reads “not held upright” in 7.9 as not held upright by someone else, and writes “on my own”. The “not” itself is uncertain: according to the translators’ note it is an editor’s correction and the manuscripts read “or”, a report the note marks as from memory and unchecked.
Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek; passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. 9.15 is 9.17 in modern editions, 7.9 is 7.12, 6.49 is 6.54, 6.5 is 6.6, and 8.40 is the end of 8.41.
articles.limit: This section has no common topic, and the article states two separate rules without arguing for either. Both are said elsewhere: Article 22’s claim 2 says my mind must stand upright by itself, not set upright by anything else, and Article 19’s said-once 7.36a, never to feel toward inhuman people what they feel toward human beings, is near not becoming like those I fight; the stone of 9.15 is near Article 34’s claim 4, that having fallen no more harms a ball, and the hive of 6.49 neighbours Article 3’s claim 2 and Article 8’s claim 5, that if the city is not harmed, I am not harmed. Seneca’s advice in Ep. 7.8 not to hate the crowd is already in Article 1; here only the clause on not copying the bad is used.

aside.8.40: The quoted words are half a sentence: what becomes a “rounded sphere” (the mind) and the main clause (nothing touches it) are in the part of the passage left out, so the words cannot stand alone.

statement.t: I stand upright on my own, and my best way to fight back is not to become like those I fight.

parts.words: I stand upright on my own
my best way to fight back is not to become like those I fight

statement.kind: Separate sayings kept side by side
statement.form: No two passages of this section say the same thing. The statement puts two separate rules about my own conduct next to each other; it does not claim that one follows from the other or that they share a ground.

empty.practice: No passage in this section gives an exercise to repeat.
empty.breaks: No passage in this section says what failing at these rules looks like or how to come back.
empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what still holds if these rules are wrong.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: that a fall from a height has nothing evil in it, that a wise person’s good is shared with the people they live with, that the worst part of a wrong stays with the one who does it, that a person’s good is a free and upright mind subject to nothing, and that a slanderous companion rubs off on me and that I should not copy the bad because they are many. The article has no fused claims, so he backs none, and he limits nothing.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: my good is a free and upright mind that is subject to nothing.

items.label: why
items.t: A fall from a high place in life has nothing evil in it, if I consider the end: past death, nature lays no one lower.
items.why: 9.15 says that for a thrown stone, coming down is nothing bad, and does not say what the stone stands for. Seneca says it of a person who falls from prosperity, and gives his reason: death is the lowest point. This stands beside the stone, not as the statement’s ground.

support.quote: But this very fall has in it nothing evil, if you consider the end, after which nature lays no man lower.
gives: has nothing evil in it
if I consider the end
nature lays no one lower
support.follows: A fall from a height has nothing evil in it for one who considers the end, below which nature lays no one.
support.context: Letter 110: privileges have “built steps for themselves to the top of a precipice”. “This very fall” is the fall from that height; “the end” is death.

items.label: why
items.t: If I am wise, my good is a common good: it belongs to the people I live with, and to me as well.
items.why: 6.49 says that what is not good for the hive is not good for the bee. Seneca says something near it, but not the same: the wise man’s own good is shared with the people he lives with. 6.49 speaks of advantage, Seneca of the good. This stands beside the hive, not as the statement’s ground.

support.quote: But the wise man’s good is a common good—it belongs both to those in whose company he lives, and to himself also.
gives: my good is a common good
it belongs to the people I live with, and to me as well
support.follows: A wise man’s good is common: it belongs to the people he lives with and to himself.
support.context: Letter 85: a pilot’s art serves only his passengers, but the wise man’s good, his wisdom, serves the people around him and himself alike.

items.label: why
items.role: A wrong stays with the doer
items.t: When I do wrong, only the least part of it falls on the other person; the worst part stays with me and troubles me.
items.why: 6.5 says the best way to fight back is not to become like those I fight, and gives no reason. Seneca gives one that fits it, reading “become like them” as doing wrong in return, which is the editor’s step, not Marcus’s: a wrong harms the one who does it most. He says it of ingratitude, not of fighting back.

support.quote: When we do wrong, only the least and lightest portion of it flows back upon our neighbour; the worst and, if I may use the term, the densest portion of it stays at home and troubles the owner.
gives: When I do wrong, only the least part of it falls on the other person
the worst part stays with me and troubles me
support.follows: The worst part of a wrong stays with the one who does it, not with the one it is done to.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: Seneca urges Lucilius not to be ungrateful, for his own sake. “It” is any wrong we do, and ingratitude is his example.

items.label: why
items.t: A person’s good is a free and upright mind, which makes other things serve it and is subject to nothing.
items.why: 7.9 says to be upright, not held upright. Seneca, asked what a person’s good is, answers: a free and upright mind, subject to nothing. He does not define uprightness; he names it as one mark of that good.

support.quote: it is a free mind, an upright mind, subjecting other things to itself and itself to nothing
gives: a free and upright mind
makes other things serve it and is subject to nothing
support.follows: A person’s good is a free and upright mind that rules other things and is ruled by nothing.
support.context: Letter 124, on the true good: “it” is a person’s own good, which exists only when reason is perfected, and which few reach even in old age.

items.label: breaks
items.t: A slanderous companion rubs off on me, even when I am clean. I should not copy the bad simply because they are many.
items.why: 6.5 says not to become like those I fight, and does not say how that happens. Seneca shows one way it happens, through company; he says it of companions and the crowd, not of people one is fighting.

support.quote: the companion, if he be slanderous, rubs off some of his rust upon us, even though we be spotless and sincere
gives: A slanderous companion rubs off on me, even when I am clean
support.follows: A slanderous companion passes some of his rust on to us, however clean we are.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: Seneca warns Lucilius that company shapes character. “Us” is anyone, however clean, who keeps a slanderous companion.

support.quote: you should not copy the bad simply because they are many
gives: I should not copy the bad simply because they are many
support.follows: I should not copy bad people simply because there are many of them.
support.context: Letter 7, on crowds: “the bad” are the crowd met in public. Seneca has said one must either imitate it or loathe it, and here rejects imitating it.

amend.t: ; my good is a free and upright mind, which is subject to nothing

searches: become like, grow like, like them
common good, good of all, neighbour

rejected.why: A great soul “cannot stand upright unless it be propped by the divine”. The words clash with 7.9, but the prop is the god within the soul, not another person, so it is no real disagreement.
Bees and their king, used for the soul ruling the body’s functions. Not about a community and its member.
Bees gathering nectar, an image for reading many authors. Off the topic.
Bees sharing toil, as an example of animal instinct. Not about what is good for the member.
Propping one’s weakness with famous sayings. About learning by maxims, not about uprightness of character.
Toil is neither good nor bad. Close to 9.15, but about toil; Ep. 110.4 speaks of a fall, as the stone does.
Indifferent things take good or evil from virtue or vice. A general rule on indifferents, wider than the stone.
What annoys us does not necessarily injure us. About anger at slaves, not about fighting back.
We pay back injuries instead of benefits. About ingratitude, not about answering a wrong.
A soul upright and content with itself is the greatest good. Ep. 124.12 says the same more fully and is used.
Virtue stays equal whatever matter it deals with. About the equality of goods.
A life on the heights ends in a fall. A warning against a public career; does not say whether the fall is bad.
Our relations are like a stone arch. About what people owe one another; Article 1’s subject.
Live for your neighbour if you would live for yourself. Already in Article 1; Ep. 85.36 is nearer to the hive and the bee.
The soul in its own fortress, where every weapon falls short. Nearer to 8.40, which is set aside.
The wise man is equal to himself in all conditions. About steadiness under fortune, not about being upright without support.
Its second half (do not hate the many; withdraw into yourself; keep company that improves you) is already Article 1’s item S7.8a. Only the first clause, on not copying the bad, is used here.

articles.title: The sameness and meanness of things

claims.t: Everything in life is the same: it is now as it was in the time of those already buried. Watching it for a hundred years comes to the same as watching it for three.
claims.shared: 6.41 says that all things “are the same and from the same”; 9.12 that “everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried”. Both say that things do not change from one time to another.
claims.changed: 9.12 says “those we have buried”; the claim says “those already buried”. 6.41’s “and from the same” is left out. The “these things” of 9.36 are, in the part of its chapter left out here, the cause and the matter of things; the claim takes them as everything in life.

support.quote: For all things, up and down, are the same and from the same.
gives: Everything in life is the same
support.follows: All things, wherever one looks, are the same and come from the same.

support.quote: Everything now is as it was in the time of those we have buried.
gives: Everything in life is the same
it is now as it was in the time of those already buried
support.follows: Nothing is different now from how it was when the people we have buried were alive.

support.quote: To have observed these things for a hundred years or for three comes to the same.
gives: Watching it for a hundred years comes to the same as watching it for three
support.follows: Observing these things for a hundred years gives no more than observing them for three.

claims.t: Everything is foul in what it is made of. Underneath, each thing is water, dust, little bones and a goatish smell, and even marble is a callus of the earth, and gold and silver are sediment.
claims.shared: 9.12 calls all these things “filthy in their matter”; 9.34 speaks of “the rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing” and says that “all the rest is of this kind”. Both say that what everything is made of is foul.
claims.changed: 9.12 does not say what “all these things” are; the claim reads them as everything, as 9.34 does with “each thing” and “all the rest”. 9.12 also calls these things familiar and lasting a day; the claim keeps only their matter. 9.34’s first list (water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek) fits a body, and its second (marble, gold, silver) fits things; the translators note that “each thing” could also be read “each person”. Of the second list the claim drops clothing as little hairs and purple dye as blood.

support.quote: All these things are familiar in experience, lasting a day in time, and filthy in their matter.
gives: Everything is foul in what it is made of
support.follows: These things are well known, short-lived and dirty in what they are made of.

support.quote: The rottenness of the matter that underlies each thing: water, dust, little bones, a goatish reek.
gives: Everything is foul in what it is made of
Underneath, each thing is water, dust, little bones and a goatish smell
support.follows: The matter under each thing is rotten: water, dust, little bones and a goatish smell.

support.quote: Or again: marble is calluses of the earth, gold and silver are sediment, clothing is little hairs, and purple dye is blood, and all the rest is of this kind.
gives: marble is a callus of the earth, and gold and silver are sediment
support.follows: Even costly things are mean stuff: marble is hardened earth, gold and silver are sediment, and the rest is the same.

claims.t: The distaste I feel at the games, where the same things are always on show, or at the baths, with their oil, sweat and slimy water, I should feel about the whole of life: every part of it, and every object, is like that.
claims.shared: Both passages take something the reader already finds distasteful, the shows of the amphitheatre in 6.41 and bathing in 8.23, and carry it to all of life: “feel the same about the whole of life too” (6.41), “such is every part of life” (8.23).
claims.changed: 8.23 says how every part of life is; only 6.41 tells me to feel it. The claim says “the games” for the amphitheatre “and places of that kind”.

support.quote: Just as what goes on in the amphitheatre and places of that kind repels you, since the same things are always being seen, and the sameness makes the spectacle cloying, feel the same about the whole of life too.
gives: The distaste I feel
at the games, where the same things are always on show
I should feel about the whole of life
support.follows: The weariness I feel at a show where the same things keep coming round, I should feel toward the whole of life.

support.quote: As bathing appears to you (oil, sweat, dirt, slimy water, all of it disgusting), such is every part of life and every object.
gives: The distaste I feel
at the baths, with their oil, sweat and slimy water
the whole of life
every part of it, and every object, is like that
support.follows: Every part of life and every object is as disgusting as the oil, sweat and dirty water of the baths.

claims.t: If I do not know the things that happen in life, or am surprised at any of them, I am a stranger to the universe.
claims.shared: Both passages call a “stranger” the one who is unprepared for what happens: in 4.23 the one who “does not know the things that happen”, in 12.10 the one “surprised at anything at all that happens in life”.
claims.changed: Both passages speak of “the one who” and “the person who”; the claim says “I”. Only 4.23 says “to the universe”; 12.10 also calls that person ridiculous, which the claim leaves out. 4.23 opens with a list of bad characters with no verb, also left out.

support.quote: If the one who does not know the things that are in the universe is a stranger to the universe, no less a stranger too is the one who does not know the things that happen.
gives: If I do not know the things that happen
I am a stranger to the universe
support.follows: Not knowing what happens makes a person as much a stranger to the universe as not knowing what is in it.

support.quote: How ridiculous, and what a stranger, is the person who is surprised at anything at all that happens in life.
gives: the things that happen in life, or am surprised at any of them, I am a stranger
support.follows: Whoever is surprised by anything that happens in life is ridiculous and a stranger.

claims.t: The life in me is a little breath. It is no different in kind from water, dust and bones: it changes out of them and back into them, and it carries a corpse about.
claims.shared: Both passages use the same word, the “little breath” (9.34, 9.22), and both tie it to the matter that dies: in 9.34 it is “another thing of this kind”, in 9.22 the little breaths are “carrying corpses”.
claims.changed: Neither passage says whose little breath it is: 9.22 is a bare list, and 9.34 says “the little breath”. “The life in me” is the editor’s reading of both. The claim says “changes back into them” for 9.34’s “changing out of these things and into these”. “The life in me” is the breath, not the mind: Article 12, claim 4, keeps the mind apart from the breath. Article 31, claim 2, gives the same image of carrying a corpse to the soul.

support.quote: And the little breath too is another thing of this kind, changing out of these things and into these.
gives: a little breath
It is no different in kind from water, dust and bones: it changes out of them and back into them
support.follows: Even the little breath of life is made of the same mean stuff, and changes out of it and into it.

support.quote: Children’s tantrums and toys, and “little breaths carrying corpses”, so that the scene of the Calling Up of the Dead strikes home more vividly.
gives: a little breath
it carries a corpse about
support.follows: Children’s tantrums and toys, and little breaths carrying corpses, make the scene of the dead called up strike home more vividly.

single.label: Out of season
single.t: If I ask for my child when the child is no longer given to me, I am as mad as someone who asks for a fig in winter.
single.quote: To ask for a fig in winter is the act of someone mad. Such is the person who asks for their child when it is no longer given.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of wanting what is no longer given. It calls that madness, as 12.10 calls surprise ridiculous, but one is about wanting and the other about being caught unprepared, so they are not fused.
single.follows: Asking for a child who is no longer given is as mad as asking for a fig in winter.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 9.12 is 9.14, 9.34 is 9.36, 6.41 is 6.46, 8.23 is 8.24, 4.23 is 4.28–29 (the sentence quoted opens 4.29), 9.22 is 9.24, 12.10 is 12.13, 9.36 is 9.37 and 11.29 is 11.33.

Reads 9.36 as being about sameness. Its “these things” point back to the cause and the matter of things, in the part of its chapter left out here, which also asks what in them is new; the claim takes a hundred years and three as equal for that reason.
Reads the “little breaths carrying corpses” of 9.22 as the life in a person, as 9.34 uses “little breath”. 9.22 is a list with no verb and does not say what it is describing.

Follows the project English of 6.41, “feel the same about the whole of life too”, for claim 3’s “I should feel”. The Greek has a bare infinitive with no verb to govern it, and it can also be read as a statement: this is what happens to you with the whole of life too.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that nothing that happens is unusual, and Article 34, claim 8, that the same things happen in every age, only with other people; what this article adds is the ground, that things are always the same and foul in their matter, and that being surprised shows a stranger. It pulls against Article 5, claim 3, where what looks rotten looks different, even pleasing, to someone who knows nature well: both are Marcus’s, and in the editor’s reading that one looks at matter with nature’s eye so as to accept it, while this one strips things down to their matter so as to stop prizing them. The article states a way of seeing and does not argue for it, gives no action beyond a feeling and a warning, and sets aside three of the twelve passages.

aside.11.28: Two lines of verse with no comment, a heart that laughed and people who will find fault with virtue; they belong with other people’s blame, not with the sameness of things.
aside.11.20: A bare mention of the fable of the mountain mouse and the house mouse, with no verb and no comment; any lesson drawn from it would be the editor’s.
aside.6.51: An exclamation at how many of those born with me have already died; it belongs with the sections on death and time and says nothing of sameness or of matter.

statement.t: Everything in life is the same as it always was and foul in what it is made of, and I am no stranger to it.

parts.words: Everything in life is the same as it always was
foul in what it is made of
I am no stranger to it

statement.kind: Two grounds, an exercise and a warning
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the grounds: things are always the same, and foul in their matter; claim 5 carries the second to the life in me. Claim 3 turns both into a feeling about the whole of life, and claim 4 says that being surprised at what happens shows a stranger.

empty.action: No passage in this section says what I should do because things are the same and foul; it asks me only to see them so, and to feel about them as I feel at the games and the baths.
empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what holds if things are not always the same or not foul; the article states this way of seeing and does not argue for it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, being surprised at what happens gains a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: what to do, which is to think ahead; what surprise costs; a way back after a loss; and words to say when wealth dazzles me. He limits the distaste for life as a whole, which must not turn into hating life, and he challenges the little breath: for him the soul is heavenly, not of one kind with dust and bones.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a task: I see to it that nothing comes upon me unforeseen.

items.quote: We should not manifest surprise at any sort of condition into which we are born, and which should be lamented by no one, simply because it is equally ordained for all.
gives: or am surprised at any of them
items.follows: We should not be surprised at any condition we are born into, since it is laid down for everyone alike.
items.context: Letter 107: Lucilius’s slaves have run away, and Seneca answers that every trouble has happened to many. The “condition into which we are born” is the human lot of loss and death.

items.label: action
items.t: I see to it that nothing comes upon me unforeseen: reflecting again and again on what may come keeps me, whatever the trouble, from acting like an unschooled boy.
items.why: In this section Marcus says that whoever is surprised at what happens is a stranger to the universe, but not what to do about it. Seneca says what to do: reflect on what may come, continually. Article 3 has a like item from Ep. 91.4.

support.quote: We must see to it that nothing shall come upon us unforeseen.
gives: I see to it that nothing comes upon me unforeseen
support.follows: We should make sure that nothing comes upon us unforeseen.
support.context: Letter 107, on bearing what life brings: the prepared meet danger bravely, the unprepared panic at trifles. “Us” is anyone facing the troubles of life.

support.quote: continual reflection will give you the power, no matter what the evil may be, not to play the unschooled boy.
gives: reflecting again and again on what may come keeps me, whatever the trouble, from acting like an unschooled boy
support.follows: Constant reflection lets us meet any trouble without acting like an unschooled boy.
support.context: Letter 107, on bearing what life brings: troubles weigh more when unfamiliar. “The evil” is whatever may come; “the unschooled boy” is the one it catches unprepared, who panics.

items.label: breaks
items.t: What surprises me weighs on me more: strangeness adds to the weight of a misfortune, and I feel more pain from what also takes me by surprise.
items.why: Marcus says that being surprised shows I am a stranger to the universe; he does not say what surprise costs. Seneca says it adds to the pain.

support.quote: Strangeness adds to the weight of calamities, and every mortal feels the greater pain as a result of that which also brings surprise.
gives: strangeness adds to the weight of a misfortune
I feel more pain from what also takes me by surprise
support.follows: A misfortune hurts more when it is strange and comes as a surprise.
support.context: Letter 91: the city of Lyons has burned down, and the news has shaken Seneca’s friend Liberalis. The “calamities” are disasters like this fire.

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I lose something, I keep in memory what I had and the enjoyment it gave me. Having it can be taken from me; having had it, never.
items.why: 11.29 shows what failing looks like, asking for a child who is no longer given, and gives no way back. Seneca gives one for every loss: to keep in memory what I had. It also tempers the distaste of claim 3: what I have enjoyed I keep in memory with thanks, as Article 32 says of its claim 3.

support.quote: Simply this—to keep in memory the things we have lost, and not to suffer the enjoyment which we have derived from them to pass away along with them.
gives: I keep in memory what I had and the enjoyment it gave me
support.follows: Against our losses, our resource is to remember what we lost and to keep the enjoyment it gave us.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune’s fickleness: Seneca has just quoted a consolation to a woman who lost her son. “The things we have lost” are whatever Fortune takes.

support.quote: To have may be taken from us, to have had, never.
gives: Having it can be taken from me; having had it, never
support.follows: What we have can be taken away; that we have had it cannot.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune’s fickleness, in Seneca’s answer to every loss. “To have” is to possess a thing now; “to have had” is its past enjoyment.

items.label: practice
items.t: When a show of wealth dazzles me, I ask why I should wonder or gape at it: it is all show, displayed and not possessed, and it passes away while it pleases. Beneath the gilding there is ugly wood.
items.why: Marcus sees costly things for what they are made of (9.34). Seneca adds words to say to myself when such a show dazzles me, and says that its splendour is only a surface.

support.quote: Accordingly, I say to myself, whenever a show of that sort dazzles my eyes, whenever I see a splendid palace with a well-groomed corps of attendants and beautiful bearers carrying a litter: Why wonder? Why gape in astonishment? It is all show; such things are displayed, not possessed; while they please they pass away.
gives: When a show of wealth dazzles me
I ask why I should wonder or gape at it
it is all show, displayed and not possessed, and it passes away while it pleases
support.follows: A display of wealth is nothing to marvel at: it is shown, not owned, and it passes while it pleases.
support.context: Letter 110, on true and false riches: Seneca has watched a parade of wealth go by. “A show of that sort” is such a display: palaces, attendants and litters.

support.quote: For we know that beneath all this gilding there lurks some ugly wood.
gives: Beneath the gilding there is ugly wood
support.follows: Under gilded ceilings there is only ugly wood.
support.context: Letter 115, on superficial blessings: we admire marble veneers and gilded ceilings as children admire toys. “All this gilding” is the gold laid over ceilings.

items.t: Seneca knows the feeling of 6.41 from the inside. He says that we slip into being cloyed with doing and seeing the same things, that philosophy itself pushes us there, and he speaks the complaint, how long must I endure the same things, in the first person. Then he warns: I must neither love nor hate life overmuch. He says that what makes people hate their lives is idle leisure, and that to one who surveys the universe the truth never palls. He is not consistent: in Ep. 77.6 a Stoic he praises tells a sick friend weighing death that even mere surfeit may make one wish to die.

support.quote: Others also are moved by a satiety of doing and seeing the same things, and not so much by a hatred of life as because they are cloyed with it.
support.follows: Some come to want death not from hating life but from being cloyed with doing and seeing the same things.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca warns against a reckless craving for death. “Others” are those who feel it from weariness of life; he counts himself among them.

support.quote: not to love or to hate life overmuch
support.follows: We need to be warned not to love life too much, and not to hate it too much.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: having armed Lucilius against the fear of death, Seneca warns him against loving or hating life to excess.

support.quote: To one who roams through the universe, the truth can never pall; it will be the untruths that will cloy.
support.follows: To one who surveys the universe the truth never grows stale; only untruths cloy.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: once we know good and evil, life will not weary us. “The truth” is what one learns by surveying the universe.

support.quote: only idle leisure is wont to make men hate their lives
support.follows: It is only idle leisure that makes people hate their lives.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: a life that surveys great and divine things never tires of itself. “Their lives” are the lives of the idle.

items.t: Seneca does not hold that the soul is of one kind with the body. For him it is heavenly, mixed for a time with what is earthly and only detained in the body as in a heavy prison; it bears the body as a burden to oversee, not to love. In 9.34 the little breath changes out of water, dust and bones and back into them. The disagreement is narrower than it looks: Marcus’s word is “little breath”, the stuff of life, while Seneca speaks of the soul that thinks and goes to the gods. Seneca is not consistent here either: in Ep. 65.16 the soul longs to return to the elements of which it was once a part.

support.quote: When the day comes to separate the heavenly from its earthly blend, I shall leave the body here where I found it
support.follows: At death what is heavenly in me will be separated from its earthly mixture, and I will leave the body behind.
support.context: Letter 102, on our immortality: Seneca gives the soul’s own words. “I” is the soul; “the heavenly” is the soul too, and “its earthly blend” the body.

support.quote: I am not apart from them now, but am merely detained in a heavy and earthly prison.
support.follows: Even now the soul is not apart from the gods; it is only held in the body as in a heavy prison.
support.context: Letter 102, on our immortality, in the soul’s own words. “Them” are the gods it will go to at death; “a heavy and earthly prison” is the body.

support.quote: it regards the body also, since it is a burden which must be borne, not as a thing to love, but as a thing to oversee
support.follows: The soul at its height treats the body as a burden to bear and to oversee, not as something to love.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life: the soul that has risen to the gods looks down on the body. “It” is that soul, and “the body” is its own.

amend.t: ; I see to it that nothing comes upon me unforeseen
; but I must not hate life overmuch, and if I roam through the universe, the truth will never cloy
; but my soul is heavenly, only detained in the body, an earthly burden that I bear and do not love

rejected.why: “None of these things is unusual or unexpected.” Article 3 already uses it for “none of it is unusual”; its bathing establishment is about things thrown at you, not about disgust.
Send the mind ahead to meet every problem. Article 3 uses it; 107.4 says the same here, with the unschooled boy, nearer to the stranger of 4.23.
“What can happen that is beyond belief? Or what that is new?” Said to a father on his son’s death, about how common death is; Article 3 covers that, and 98.11 gives the way back.
People are surprised at losing anything, though they must lose everything. Says what 107.6 says; the next section, 98.11, is used.
The daily round of food, sleep and lust is always the same. Said to persuade a sick man that living is no great matter; named in q1 as Seneca’s inconsistency, not quoted.
None of your pleasures is new to you; a hundred or a thousand measures make no difference. A rebuke to a glutton clinging to life; about pleasures, not about all things.
Nothing is fouler than gold and silver dragged out of the mud. Near 9.34, but “these things of earth” needs its context to be seen as gold and silver; a backing that needs explaining is dropped.
We are like children who prize every toy. Near 9.22’s toys, but 9.22 is used here for the little breaths, and the comparison is not a claim of this article.
You should not be surprised that new places bring no benefit. About restless travel, not about what happens.
All past time lies in the same place. About how short past time seems, not about things being the same.
The universe keeps changing and never stays the same. About change, the opposite emphasis, and nearer to the sections on change.
The midday shows in the arena. Seneca’s distaste for the games is at their cruelty, not at their sameness.
The body weighs on the soul, which longs to return to the elements. Named in q2 as Seneca’s inconsistency; 102.22 says the soul is heavenly more plainly.
The clogging burden of a body. Says the body is a burden; 92.33 says it with the soul’s view of the body, and is used.
The soul leaves the body as a child leaves the afterbirth. About the body after death; nearer to the articles on death.
The body is a covering, like the afterbirth that perishes at birth. About death as a birth; nearer to the articles on death.
Grown men fear like boys in the dark. About fear, not about the meanness of things.
Satiety is the limit of eating, whether one eats more or less. An argument about equal goods.

articles.title: How my soul uses itself

claims.t: My soul sees itself, and it sees the whole: it goes round the whole universe and knows the reason that runs through all of it.
claims.shared: 11.1 and 11.11 both say that the soul sees itself (11.1: “it sees itself”; 11.11: it sees “the truth within itself”; the Greek verb is ὁρᾷ in both). 11.1, 11.11 and 5.26 all say that it takes in the whole: “the whole universe”, “the truth of all things”, “the reason that runs through the whole of substance”.
claims.changed: 11.11 says the soul sees this when it is true to its own form; the claim drops the condition. 5.26 speaks of the soul that has skill and understanding; the claim says “my soul”.

support.quote: it sees itself, it analyses itself
gives: My soul sees itself
support.follows: The reasoning soul sees itself and analyses itself.

support.quote: shines with a light by which it sees the truth, the truth of all things and the truth within itself
gives: My soul sees itself
it sees the whole
support.follows: When the soul keeps its own form, it sees by its own light the truth of all things and the truth within itself.

support.quote: it goes round the whole universe and the void around it and its shape
gives: it sees the whole
it goes round the whole universe
support.follows: The reasoning soul takes in the whole universe, the void around it and its shape.

support.quote: The one that knows beginning and end, and the reason that runs through the whole of substance
gives: it sees the whole
knows the reason that runs through all of it
support.follows: The soul that has skill and understanding knows beginning and end, and the reason that runs through all substance.

claims.role: What is mine and what is not
claims.t: I am a soul and a body, and the soul carries the body like a corpse. Whatever is not my mind’s own activity is indifferent to it, dead things and smoke; all of its own activity is in its power, and everything lies in that.
claims.shared: 6.30 and 4.34 both say what I am made of, a body and a soul (“a little body and a soul”; “a little soul carrying a corpse”). 6.30 and 12.26 both set the mind’s own activity against everything else and dismiss the rest: it is “indifferent” in 6.30 and “dead things and smoke” in 12.26.
claims.changed: 6.30 calls the body little and 4.34 the soul; the claim drops both words. 6.30 says “mind” and 12.26 “the ruling part”; the claim says “my mind” for both. 12.26 counts even what lies within choice among “the rest”; the claim keeps to 6.30’s line between the mind’s own activity and everything else. 4.34 makes me the soul and the body what it carries; the claim joins this to 6.30’s “made of a little body and a soul”.

support.quote: I am made of a little body and a soul.
gives: I am a soul and a body
support.follows: I am made of a small body and a soul.

support.quote: You are a little soul carrying a corpse, as Epictetus used to say.
gives: I am a soul and a body
the soul carries the body like a corpse
support.follows: As Epictetus used to say, I am a small soul carrying a dead body.

support.quote: To the mind, whatever is not its own activity is indifferent; and whatever is its own activity, all of that is in its power.
gives: Whatever is not my mind’s own activity is indifferent to it
all of its own activity is in its power
support.follows: Only the mind’s own activity makes a difference to it, and all of that activity is in its power.

support.quote: As for the rest, it is either within choice or outside it: dead things and smoke.
gives: Whatever is not my mind’s own activity is indifferent to it
dead things and smoke
support.follows: Everything other than how the ruling part uses itself, whether within choice or outside it, is dead things and smoke.

support.quote: For everything lies in that.
gives: everything lies in that
support.follows: Everything lies in how the ruling part uses itself.

claims.t: At every turn I ask myself how my ruling part is using itself now, and for what, and whether I have the soul of a child, a tyrant, a farm animal or a wild beast.
claims.shared: 5.11 and 12.26 ask the same question: how the soul, the ruling part, is being used (“am I using my own soul for now?”; “How is the ruling part using itself?”; the Greek verb is χρῆσθαι in both). 5.11 and 9.39 both name the beasts it can sink to: “a farm animal’s”, “a wild beast’s”; “turned into a wild beast”, “grazing”.
claims.changed: 5.11 says “my own soul” and names the ruling part a sentence later; the claim says “ruling part”, as 12.26 does. 9.39 is a question whose construction is open; the claim takes only its list of what the ruling part can become. 5.11’s youth and silly woman are dropped. 12.26 asks how the ruling part is using itself; 5.11 asks for what; the claim keeps both.

support.quote: “Just what, then, am I using my own soul for now?” Ask yourself this at every turn
gives: At every turn I ask myself
how my ruling part is using itself now
and for what
support.follows: At every turn I should ask myself what I am using my soul for now.

support.quote: How is the ruling part using itself?
gives: how my ruling part is using itself now
support.follows: The question to ask is how the ruling part is using itself.

support.quote: And whose soul, then, do I have now? Not a small child’s, surely? Not a youth’s? Not a silly woman’s? Not a tyrant’s? Not a farm animal’s? Not a wild beast’s?
gives: whether I have the soul of a child, a tyrant
a farm animal or a wild beast
support.follows: I should ask whose soul I have now, and hope it is not a child’s, a tyrant’s, a farm animal’s or a wild beast’s.

support.quote: Do you say to the ruling part: “You are dead, you are ruined, you have turned into a wild beast, you are playing a part, you are running with the herd, you are grazing”?
gives: a farm animal or a wild beast
support.follows: Marcus asks whether he tells his ruling part that it is dead, ruined, a wild beast, an actor, one of a herd, a grazing animal.

claims.t: My soul does violence to itself and becomes worse than itself when it is beaten by pleasure or pain, or when it pretends, saying or doing what it does not mean. Nothing I could find is worth that. I value nothing above my soul, and I do not make my good fortune depend on what goes on in other people’s souls.
claims.shared: 2.14 and 2.3 both say that the soul does violence to itself (the Greek verb is ὑβρίζειν in both). 11.1 and 2.3 both say that the soul should rank nothing above itself: 11.1 that it values nothing above itself, 2.3 by reproaching a soul that does not respect itself and puts its good fortune in other people’s souls.
claims.changed: 2.3 is a reproach; the claim states its opposite as what I do. 8.44’s four states (brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright) and 2.14’s other ways of self-harm are left in their passages. The first sentence reads 2.14’s violence and 8.44’s worsening as one thing, so 2.14’s conditions govern both; 8.44 names its own states and does not speak of pretending.

support.quote: The human soul does violence to itself most of all
gives: My soul does violence to itself
support.follows: The human soul can do violence to itself, and in some ways more than in others.

support.quote: Do violence, do violence to yourself, soul
gives: My soul does violence to itself
support.follows: In bitter irony, Marcus tells his soul to do violence to itself.

support.quote: my soul should be in a bad way and be worse than itself: brought low, craving, shrinking in, taking fright
gives: becomes worse than itself
support.follows: Something can put my soul in a bad way and make it worse than itself: brought low, craving, shrinking in, afraid.

support.quote: Third, it does violence to itself when it is beaten by pleasure or by pain.
gives: when it is beaten by pleasure or pain
support.follows: The soul does violence to itself when pleasure or pain beats it.

support.quote: Fourth, when it plays a part and does or says something in a feigned and untrue way.
gives: or when it pretends, saying or doing what it does not mean
support.follows: The soul does violence to itself when it pretends, doing or saying something feigned and untrue.

support.quote: And what will you find that is worth that?
gives: Nothing I could find is worth that
support.follows: Nothing I could find would be worth making my soul worse than itself.

support.quote: valuing nothing above itself
gives: I value nothing above my soul
support.follows: It belongs to the reasoning soul to value nothing above itself.

support.quote: you do not respect yourself but place your good fortune in the souls of others
gives: I value nothing above my soul
I do not make my good fortune depend on what goes on in other people’s souls
support.follows: Marcus reproaches his soul for not respecting itself and for placing its good fortune in other people’s souls.

claims.t: When my life ends, my soul may go out or be scattered, or it may hold together. Whichever it is, my soul has reached its own goal at whatever point my life stops: the task set before it is complete, and it can be ready to leave the body this moment.
claims.shared: 11.1 and 11.3 both speak of the moment life ends and say the soul is complete or ready then (“wherever the limit of life comes upon it”; “if it must this moment be released from the body”). 11.3 and 4.17 both leave open what becomes of the soul, and both say it may “hold together” (συμμεῖναι in both).
claims.changed: “Whichever it is” is the editor’s join of the two sentences. 11.1’s “end” (τέλος) is the soul’s goal, not its ceasing to be, so the claim says “goal”. 4.17 adds that souls which hold together do so only for a while and are then taken back into the whole; the claim keeps only that they may hold together. 11.3 says the soul is ready; the claim says it can be.

support.quote: it reaches its own end wherever the limit of life comes upon it
gives: When my life ends
my soul has reached its own goal at whatever point my life stops
support.follows: Wherever the reasoning soul’s life is cut off, it has already reached its own goal.

support.quote: wherever it is overtaken, it makes what was set before it full and in need of nothing more, for itself
gives: the task set before it is complete
support.follows: Wherever death overtakes the reasoning soul, it has made what was set before it full, needing nothing more.

support.quote: What a soul it is that is ready, if it must this moment be released from the body
gives: When my life ends
it can be ready to leave the body this moment
support.follows: Marcus admires a soul that is ready to be released from the body this very moment.

support.quote: either be extinguished or be scattered or hold together
gives: my soul may go out or be scattered
or it may hold together
support.follows: Released from the body, a soul may be put out, be scattered, or hold together.

support.quote: the souls that pass over into the air, after holding together for a while, change and are poured out and are set alight
gives: or it may hold together
support.follows: If souls go on existing, they hold together in the air for a while, and then change and are taken back into the whole.

claims.t: My mind does not move as bodies do, as an arrow flies or as the elements go up, down and round. Even when I am cautious or turning a question over, it still goes straight toward the target set before it. I let no action fly at random: even the smallest is done with reference to my end.
claims.shared: 8.57 and 6.16 both set the mind’s or virtue’s movement apart from the movement of bodies: the arrow, and the elements going up, down and round (φέρεσθαι and φοραί, one root in the Greek). 2.14 and 8.57 both give the mind’s action a target: it is done “with reference to the end” and travels “toward what is set before it”.
claims.changed: “Bodies” is the editor’s word for the arrow and the elements together. 8.57 puts the difference from the arrow in the manner (cautious, turning about), and says the mind none the less travels straight; the claim keeps it there. 6.16 speaks of the movement of virtue and 8.57 of the mind; the claim reads both as my mind’s movement. 2.14 counts aimless action among the ways the soul does violence to itself; the claim keeps only the aim.

support.quote: Fifth, when it lets some action or impulse of its own fly at no target, but does anything whatever at random and without attention, when even the smallest things ought to be done with reference to the end.
gives: toward the target set before it
I let no action fly at random
even the smallest is done with reference to my end
support.follows: The soul harms itself when it acts at random; even the smallest things should be done with reference to the end.

support.quote: Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it turns about in considering something, travels straight none the less, and toward what is set before it.
gives: Even when I am cautious or turning a question over, it still goes straight
toward the target set before it
support.follows: Even when it is cautious or turning a question about, the mind still travels straight toward what is set before it.

support.quote: An arrow travels in one way, the mind in another.
gives: My mind does not move as bodies do
as an arrow flies
support.follows: The mind does not travel in the way an arrow travels.

support.quote: Up, down, round in a circle: such are the motions of the elements. The movement of virtue, though, is in none of these
gives: My mind does not move as bodies do
as the elements go up, down and round
support.follows: Virtue does not move as the elements move, up, down or round in a circle.

single.label: Things say nothing
single.t: Things stand outside the doors, on their own; they know nothing about themselves and pronounce nothing. It is my ruling part that pronounces on them.
single.quote: Things stand outside the doors, themselves by themselves, knowing nothing about themselves and pronouncing nothing. What, then, pronounces on them? The ruling part.
single.why: Only 9.13 says that the ruling part pronounces on things. It is near the line drawn between the mind’s own activity and everything else, but no other passage here says who judges things.
single.follows: Things say nothing about themselves; whatever is said about them is said by the ruling part.

single.label: Its own virtues
single.t: Love of those near me, truthfulness and a sense of shame also belong to my soul.
single.quote: Also the rational soul’s own are love of those near it, and truthfulness, and a sense of shame
single.why: Only 11.1 names these as the soul’s own. 2.3’s “respect yourself” (αἰδεῖσθαι) is the verb of 11.1’s αἰδώς, “a sense of shame”, but 2.3 speaks of respect for oneself, not of a virtue the soul owns. The words after them, valuing nothing above itself, are fused with 2.3 in the claim on how my soul harms itself.
single.follows: Love of those near it, truthfulness and a sense of shame belong to the reasoning soul.

single.label: Following reason
single.t: When I follow reason in everything, I am at once unhurried and quick to move, cheerful and composed.
single.quote: Someone who follows reason in everything is something at once unhurried and quick to move, at once cheerful and composed.
single.why: Only 10.14 describes the person whom reason leads. It says what such a person is like, not where the mind is going, so it is not fused with the claim on going straight toward the end.
single.follows: Whoever follows reason in everything is unhurried yet quick to move, cheerful yet composed.

single.label: Ready for reasons
single.t: My readiness to leave the body should come from my own judgment, not out of mere defiance: in a reasoned and dignified way that could convince someone else too, without theatrics.
single.quote: this readiness should come from a judgment of one’s own, not by way of bare opposition, as with the Christians, but in a reasoned and dignified way, and in a way that could convince someone else too, without theatrics
single.why: Only 11.3 says where the readiness should come from. The claim on the end of life says the soul can be ready; this says how the readiness is reached.
single.follows: Readiness to die should rest on one’s own reasoned judgment, not on bare defiance or on show.

single.label: Time is short
single.t: I have one life, and it is almost finished. If I spend it doing violence to my soul, no chance will be left to honour it.
single.quote: you will have no chance left to honour yourself. For each person has one life, and yours is almost finished
single.why: Only 2.3 says that time is running out for the soul to honour itself. It is the urgency behind the way back from self-harm.
single.follows: Each person has one life; Marcus’s is almost over, and soon he will have no chance left to honour himself.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek; passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 2.14 is 2.16, 2.3 is 2.6, 11.11 is 11.12, 4.17 is 4.21, 4.34 is 4.41, 5.26 is 5.32, 9.39 is 9.39b, 6.30 is 6.32, 8.44 is 8.45b, 12.26 is 12.33, 6.16 is 6.17, 8.57 is 8.60, 10.14 is 10.12b, 9.13 is 9.15 and 3.16 is 3.15–16a; 11.1, 5.11 and 11.3 are the same.

Reads soul, mind and ruling part as one thing: 5.11 moves from the soul I use to “this part, the one they call the ruling part”, and asks about both together; 6.30 moves from “soul” to “mind”, and 12.26 says “the ruling part”. 12.26’s “that” (everything lies in that) is read as how the ruling part uses itself, not as the ruling part itself, as the translators’ note allows.
Uses 9.39 only for its list of what the ruling part can become, since its construction is open, and reads 6.16’s “movement of virtue” as the right movement of the mind.

Keeps six fused claims, more than usual, because the section has eighteen passages and each group has a component that two passages both say. In the claim on self-harm, 2.3’s reproach is turned into what I do.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one: Article 4 that what rules in me moves itself, Article 2 that reason should lead, Article 1 and Article 21’s claim 5 that every act has an aim, Article 12 that I ask what I am using my mind for (claim 3 here), that I go straight toward a target (claim 6) and that my mind pronounces on things (9.13), Article 13 that nothing is better than the spirit within me (claim 4), and Articles 10 and 34 the cases of what death does (claim 5). What this section adds is the use the soul makes of itself: everything lies in it, and it can do violence to itself, which I read as giving in to pleasure or pain, so Article 8’s “nothing from outside touches my mind” is not denied; and claim 5 says without condition what Article 17’s claim 2 says only of a disciplined mind, while Article 35 and 2.3 here warn that the time can run out. 11.1 feeds three claims and a said-once item, so the article leans on one long passage, and the claim under If I doubt it answers a doubt about the soul’s survival, not about the statement itself.

aside.3.16: Its first sentence is about the many senses of ordinary words and a sight that is not of the eyes. Its second divides a person into three, body, soul and mind, each with its own share (sensations, impulses, principles), and it is the one passage here that keeps soul and mind apart; the article reads them as one and divides only into soul and body.

statement.t: Everything lies in how my soul uses itself: it can see itself and the whole, or do violence to itself.

parts.words: Everything lies in how my soul uses itself
it can see itself and the whole
or do violence to itself

statement.kind: One power and its two uses
statement.form: The first part is what everything depends on: the use the soul makes of itself (the claims on what is mine and on the question I keep asking). The second and third are its two uses, seeing itself and the whole, and doing violence to itself. The claims on going straight toward the end and on being ready when life ends show the good use in action and at death.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the claims on what my soul sees, on going straight toward its end and on being ready when life ends gain a second author. Practice gains a daily review, When it breaks gains the soul that turns from king to tyrant, which also extends the statement, and If I doubt it gains a reason to fear neither end nor change. He limits the claim on what is mine: the body is to be cherished with care, though not lived for.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement goes on to say what a soul that loses control becomes: it turns from a king into a tyrant, a prey to its emotions.

items.quote: Tell me rather how closely in accord with nature it is to let one’s mind reach out into the boundless universe!
gives: it goes round the whole universe
items.follows: It is in accord with nature for the mind to reach out into the boundless universe.
items.context: Letter 102, on hints of immortality: Seneca turns from petty argument to the soul’s greatness. “One’s mind” is the human soul, whose homeland he calls the whole firmament.

items.quote: For whatever we do ought to be in harmony with this; no man can set in order the details unless he has already set before himself the chief purpose of his life.
gives: even the smallest is done with reference to my end
items.follows: Everything we do should fit the chief purpose of our life, and no one can order the details without first setting that purpose before himself.
items.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good: Seneca tells Lucilius to weigh every choice against the purpose of his whole life. “This” is that Supreme Good, the purpose of life.

items.quote: The archer must know what he is seeking to hit; then he must aim and control the weapon by his skill. Our plans miscarry because they have no aim.
gives: I let no action fly at random
items.follows: An archer must know his target before he aims; our plans fail because they have no aim.
items.context: Letter 71, on the Supreme Good. The archer stands for anyone who acts; the “aim” our plans lack is the chief purpose of life, which Seneca goes on to name as the honourable.

items.quote: Death either annihilates us or strips us bare. If we are then released, there remains the better part, after the burden has been withdrawn; if we are annihilated, nothing remains
gives: my soul may go out or be scattered
or it may hold together
items.follows: Death either destroys us or strips us bare; if we are released, the better part remains, and if we are destroyed, nothing does.
items.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca sets aside fears of the underworld. “Us” are human beings at death; the “burden” withdrawn is the body, and the better part left is the soul.

items.quote: as if death were about to call me away in the very act of writing. I am ready to depart
gives: it can be ready to leave the body this moment
items.follows: Seneca writes as if death might call him away mid-sentence, and says he is ready to go.
items.context: Letter 61, on meeting death cheerfully, written in old age: Seneca writes as if death might take him while he is still writing. “To depart” is to die.

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep watching myself, and I review each day. What makes us wicked is that no one looks back over his own life.
items.why: Marcus asks at every turn how his soul is being used now. Seneca adds a second look, back over the day, and says why it matters: we go wrong because we never look back.

support.quote: I shall keep watching myself continually, and—a most useful habit—shall review each day. For this is what makes us wicked: that no one of us looks back over his own life.
gives: I keep watching myself
I review each day
What makes us wicked is that no one looks back over his own life
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself and review each day, because people go wrong by never looking back over their own lives.
support.context: Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, and says he watches himself and reviews every day; “his own life” is each person’s past conduct.

items.label: breaks
items.t: My soul is a king while it respects what is honourable and gives the body no base commands. When it is uncontrolled and passionate, it turns that kingship into tyranny and becomes the prey of its emotions.
items.why: 5.11 asks whether I have a tyrant’s soul, the soul of a person who is a tyrant. Seneca uses “tyrant” for the soul’s own rule over the body gone bad, and so explains what a soul that has lost control turns into: a ruler ruled by its emotions.

support.quote: our soul is at one time a king, at another a tyrant. The king, in that he respects things honourable, watches over the welfare of the body which is entrusted to his charge, and gives that body no base, no ignoble commands.
gives: My soul is a king while it respects what is honourable and gives the body no base commands
support.follows: The soul is sometimes a king and sometimes a tyrant; as king it respects what is honourable and gives the body no base commands.
support.context: Letter 114, on style as a mirror of character. Seneca has just called the soul the king of the body; here he says it can also be its tyrant.

support.quote: But an uncontrolled, passionate, and effeminate soul changes kingship into that most dread and detestable quality—tyranny; then it becomes a prey to the uncontrolled emotions
gives: When it is uncontrolled and passionate, it turns that kingship into tyranny and becomes the prey of its emotions
support.follows: A soul without control turns its rule into tyranny and is then preyed on by its uncontrolled emotions.
support.context: Letter 114, on style as a mirror of character. “Kingship” is the soul’s rule over the body; Seneca has just said that a soul which yields to pleasure loses it.

items.label: doubt
items.t: Death is either an end or a change. I do not fear ceasing to exist: it is the same as not having begun. Nor do I shrink from changing into another state.
items.why: 11.3 and 4.17 leave open what becomes of the soul, and 11.3 says it can be ready. Seneca gives a reason not to fear either outcome.

support.quote: And what is death? It is either the end, or a process of change.
gives: Death is either an end or a change
support.follows: Death is either an end or a change.
support.context: Letter 65, on the first cause: Seneca asks what death is in general and answers that it is ending or change; the next sentences apply this to himself.

support.quote: I have no fear of ceasing to exist; it is the same as not having begun. Nor do I shrink from changing into another state, because I shall, under no conditions, be as cramped as I am now.
gives: I do not fear ceasing to exist: it is the same as not having begun
Nor do I shrink from changing into another state
support.follows: Seneca does not fear ceasing to exist, which is like not having begun, nor changing into another state, where he will be less cramped.
support.context: The close of Letter 65, on the first cause. Seneca answers his own question about death; “cramped” refers to the soul shut in the body.

items.t: Seneca does not call the body a corpse. He grants that we have an inborn affection for it and are entrusted with its guardianship, and says we should cherish it with the greatest care, while never living for it and being ready to give it up when reason demands. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. He is not consistent: elsewhere he calls the body a burden to be borne, not loved (Ep. 92.33).

support.quote: I confess that we all have an inborn affection for our body; I confess that we are entrusted with its guardianship.
support.follows: We all love our bodies by nature, and we are entrusted with their guardianship.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. Seneca grants that we love our bodies, then says we must not be their slaves; “its guardianship” is our charge of the body.

support.quote: We should conduct ourselves not as if we ought to live for the body, but as if we could not live without it.
support.follows: We should treat the body as something we cannot live without, not as what we live for.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. Seneca sets out how far the body is to be served: enough to keep it, never as the end of life.

support.quote: We should cherish the body with the greatest care; but we should also be prepared, when reason, self-respect, and duty demand the sacrifice, to deliver it even to the flames.
support.follows: We should take the greatest care of the body, and be ready to give it up when reason, self-respect and duty require.
support.context: Letter 14, on withdrawing from the world. The sentence closes his account of the body: cherish it, but be ready to sacrifice it.

support.quote: it regards the body also, since it is a burden which must be borne, not as a thing to love, but as a thing to oversee
support.follows: The soul treats the body as a burden it must carry, to be overseen and not loved.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. “It” is the soul that has risen to the height Seneca has just described, set over all things; from there it looks down on the body.

amend.t: ; yet I am entrusted with the body’s guardianship, and I cherish it with the greatest care, though I do not live for it
; when it loses control, it turns from a king into a tyrant and becomes a prey to its emotions

searches: use of the soul, mind or reason
either the end or change, extinguish, scattered
rôle, play a part, one man
cherish the body, care of the body
harms or injures himself or itself
ready to die or depart, prepared for death

rejected.why: The soul’s rational and irrational parts, in an argument about the primary good. Not about how the soul uses itself.
The body as a weight on a soul that longs to be freed. Near 4.34, but it does not say the soul carries a corpse; Letter 14 is used for the body.
A soul resplendent only with its own good. About praising what is a man’s own; matching it to “indifferent” would need explaining.
The upright soul as a god dwelling in a body. About what to seek, not about the soul’s use of itself.
Virtue fastened to useless flesh. Harsher than Letter 14 and about the happy life; Ep. 92.33 is used to show his other side.
The soul that gazes upon truth, as a definition of the first good in an argument about equal goods.
A sluggish soul shows in the gait. About style as a sign of character.
The soul as the body’s king. Ep. 114.24, which says how it becomes a tyrant, is quoted instead.
Doing nothing without reason’s approval. About reading and composition.
The departed soul cares nothing for its remains. About burial, not about readiness.
The soul claims all time and will go to the gods. A hope of survival that Marcus leaves open.
The good is a flawless mind that counts nothing outside itself its own. Close to the claim on what is mine, but it names the good, and the match needs explaining.
Examine yourself to see whether you have progressed in philosophy or in life. About progress, not about the soul’s use now.
Play accuser, judge and intercessor of yourself. A search for faults; Ep. 83.2 is the daily review.
We are lit and put out like a lamp. Ep. 65.24 says both outcomes more plainly.
Seneca rejects the view that a crushed soul is scattered. A side argument about one kind of death.
Sotion on souls passing into beasts. About abstaining from meat.
Questions about the soul’s nature, listed as studies that do not make us better.
The wise man trembles and feels pain, as sensations of the body. 2.14 speaks of being beaten by pain, not of feeling it, so there is no difference to record.
Put yourself under the control of reason. About wisdom as freedom; it would back only a said-once item.
One virtue makes the soul straight and unswerving. A list of virtues; backing “I go straight” with it would need explaining.
The soul is always in motion, like a flame. About ambition and rest.
The clogging burden of the body. Ep. 24.18, on what death does to it, is quoted instead.
Live every day as if it were a complete life. An effort to make each day complete, not 11.1’s claim that the soul has its end wherever life stops.
Ask yourself whether you would die for your country. A test of whether one believes that only the honourable is good.

articles.title: All things pass

claims.t: All things are changing, and I am changing with them, all the time and quickly. The whole is like a river in flood: each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen.
claims.shared: 9.17 and 9.27 both say that all things change (“All things are in change”; earth “will change, and those things too will change without end”), and 9.17 and 6.14 both put the person among them. 4.35 and 9.27 both picture the whole as a rushing stream (“a violent current”; “a torrent”), and 4.35 and 6.14 both say that a thing is gone as soon as it is seen.
claims.changed: 9.17 speaks of the universe, 4.35 of eternity as a river, 9.27 of the substance of the whole as a torrent; the claim calls all three “the whole”. 2.9 speaks of things vanishing, not changing; the claim takes from it only the speed.

support.quote: All things are in change.
gives: All things are changing
support.follows: Everything is changing.

support.quote: You yourself too are in continual alteration and, in a certain respect, in perishing, and so is the whole universe.
gives: I am changing with them
all the time
support.follows: I too am always being altered, and in a way perishing, and so is the whole universe.

support.quote: Then earth itself will change, and those things too will change without end, and those again without end.
gives: All things are changing
support.follows: Even the earth will change, and what it changes into will change again, without end.

support.quote: Flows and alterations renew the universe continually
gives: All things are changing
all the time
support.follows: The universe is renewed all the time by flows and alterations.

support.quote: Each person’s life itself, too, is something of the kind: like the vapour that rises from blood and the breath drawn in from the air.
gives: I am changing with them
support.follows: A person’s life is a passing thing too, like vapour rising from blood or a breath drawn in.

support.quote: How quickly all things vanish, the bodies themselves into the universe, the memories of them into eternity.
gives: and quickly
support.follows: All things vanish quickly: bodies into the universe, and the memory of them into eternity.

support.quote: Eternity is a kind of river of things that come to be, and a violent current. For as soon as each thing has been seen it has been carried past, and another is being carried past, and yet another will be carried along.
gives: and quickly
The whole is like a river in flood
each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen
support.follows: Time is like a fast river: each thing is swept past as soon as it is seen, and others follow it.

support.quote: The substance of the whole is a torrent: it carries everything along.
gives: The whole is like a river in flood
support.follows: The stuff of which everything is made is like a torrent that sweeps all things along.

support.quote: It is as if someone began to love one of the little sparrows flying past, and it has already gone out of sight.
gives: each thing is carried past as soon as it has been seen
support.follows: Loving one of these passing things is like loving a sparrow that is out of sight the moment one notices it.

claims.role: Nature’s work, always of one kind
claims.t: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole, and it loves this work: it changes what exists and makes new things like the old. Nothing comes that is new in kind; what will be is of the same kind as what has been.
claims.shared: 4.29 and 9.33 both say that the nature of the whole loves change (“loves nothing so much as to change”; “in this the nature of the whole delights”) and that it makes new things like the old (“new things like them”; “others like them”). 6.34, 7.27 and 9.33 all say that what comes is “of the same kind” as what was.
claims.changed: 8.5 says that change is nature’s work and 4.29 that nature loves it; the claim puts the two in one sentence. “New in kind” is the editor’s wording for 8.5’s “nothing new” read beside 6.34’s “of the same kind”.

support.quote: The nature of the whole has this as its work: to move what is here over to there, to change it, to lift it from here and carry it there.
gives: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole
support.follows: The work of the nature of the whole is to move things from one place to another and to change them.

support.quote: the nature of the whole loves nothing so much as to change the things that exist and make new things like them
gives: Changing things is the work of the nature of the whole
it loves this work
it changes what exists
makes new things like the old
support.follows: Nothing pleases the nature of the whole more than changing what exists and making new things like it.

support.quote: And in this the nature of the whole delights, the nature in accordance with which all things come about well, and from eternity have come about in the same kind of way, and without end there will be others like them.
gives: it loves this work
makes new things like the old
what will be is of the same kind as what has been
support.follows: The nature of the whole delights in change, and things of the same kind as before will keep coming about without end.

support.quote: All things are transformations, not so that one need fear something new. All things are familiar
gives: Nothing comes that is new in kind
support.follows: All things are changes of what was, so nothing new and strange comes that one need fear.

support.quote: Whoever has seen what is now has seen everything: all that has come to be from the everlasting past and all that will be without end. For all things are of the same stock and of the same kind.
gives: Nothing comes that is new in kind
what will be is of the same kind as what has been
support.follows: Whoever has seen the present has seen all past and future, since all things are of the same kind.

support.quote: It is possible to foresee what will be as well. For it will certainly be of the same kind, and it cannot step out of the rhythm of what is happening now.
gives: what will be is of the same kind as what has been
support.follows: The future can be foreseen, because it will be of the same kind as what happens now.

claims.t: When I reflect on how fast things change and on how small a part of eternity and of substance is mine, I picture nothing that passes as great. I do not prize what runs past me, and I look down on everything mortal.
claims.shared: 9.27 and 12.25 both say that reflecting leads to holding things cheap (“a person who reflects on … will look down on everything mortal”; “Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great”). 6.14 and 2.9 say the same of what passes: no one would prize it, and it is “cheap and contemptible”.
claims.changed: 12.25 says “nothing” and names one exception, kept as a said-once item; the claim says “nothing that passes”. 9.27 says what a person who reflects will do; the claim says it of me.

support.quote: For a person who reflects on wave after wave of changes and alterations, and on their speed, will look down on everything mortal.
gives: When I reflect
how fast things change
I look down on everything mortal
support.follows: Whoever thinks about how fast changes follow one another will look down on everything mortal.

support.quote: How small a part of boundless, gaping eternity has been portioned out to each one: for it vanishes very quickly into the everlasting. And how small a part of the whole of substance, and how small a part of the whole of soul.
gives: how small a part of eternity and of substance is mine
support.follows: Each of us has been given a tiny share of endless time, of all substance and of all soul.

support.quote: Reflecting on all this, picture nothing as great
gives: When I reflect
I picture nothing that passes as great
support.follows: Whoever reflects on how small their share is should picture nothing as great.

support.quote: In this river, then, which of these things running past would anyone prize, a thing it is not possible to stand on?
gives: I do not prize what runs past me
support.follows: Nothing running past in this river is worth prizing, since no one can stand on it.

support.quote: What all the things perceived by the senses are like, and above all those that lure with pleasure or frighten with pain or are loudly celebrated through vanity: how cheap and contemptible and filthy and quick to perish and dead.
gives: I picture nothing that passes as great
support.follows: The things of the senses, above all what tempts, frightens or is famous, are cheap, quick to perish and dead.
