claims.t: I constantly keep in mind the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists, and against all that exists each thing is a fig seed, and against all of time a turn of a drill. I fix my attention on each thing and think of it as changing, and already dissolving.
claims.shared: 10.19 and 9.31 both tell me to hold the whole of time and of what exists in mind (“the whole of eternity and the whole of substance”; “encompassed the whole universe in thought … surveying everlasting eternity”) and to think of each thing as it changes (“think of it as already dissolving and in change”; “thinking of the swift change of each particular thing”). 4.29 says to observe change “continually”, as 10.19 says “constantly”.
claims.changed: 10.19 and 4.29 are instructions to “you”, and 9.31 is a fragment without a main verb; the claim states them as what I do.

support.quote: An impression, constantly, of the whole of eternity and the whole of substance, and that all particular things are, set against substance, a fig seed, and set against time, a turn of a drill.
gives: I constantly keep in mind
the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists
against all that exists each thing is a fig seed, and against all of time a turn of a drill
support.follows: I should keep all of time and all substance always in view, and see each thing against them as a fig seed or a moment.

support.quote: Fixing attention on each object, think of it as already dissolving and in change
gives: I fix my attention on each thing
think of it as changing
already dissolving
support.follows: Whatever I look at, I should think of as already changing and coming apart.

support.quote: By having encompassed the whole universe in thought, and by surveying everlasting eternity, and by thinking of the swift change of each particular thing
gives: the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists
think of it as changing
support.follows: One holds the whole universe and all of time in thought, and thinks of how fast each thing changes.

support.quote: Observe continually that all things come about by change
gives: I constantly keep in mind
think of it as changing
support.follows: I should keep observing that everything comes about through change.

claims.t: When I say that everything goes badly, I forget that a loss is nothing but a change, and that change is nothing bad for what is changed. The elements I am made of change too, and do not grumble.
claims.shared: 9.33 and 10.7 both say that losing or perishing is only change (“Loss is nothing other than change”; “let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered””). 4.35 and 10.7 both deny that change is bad for what is changed.
claims.changed: 9.33 asks “you” why you say that all goes badly; the claim makes it my failure. 8.16 adds that my own elements change without complaint.

support.quote: Why then do you say that all things have come about badly and all things will always go badly
gives: When I say that everything goes badly
support.follows: It is wrong to say that everything has gone badly and always will.

support.quote: Loss is nothing other than change.
gives: a loss is nothing but a change
support.follows: Losing something is only its changing.

support.quote: The parts of the whole, all that are by nature contained by the universe, must perish; but let “perish” be said in the sense of “be altered”.
gives: a loss is nothing but a change
support.follows: The parts of the universe must perish, and here perishing means being altered.

support.quote: Now if this is by nature both bad and necessary for them, the whole would not be well managed
gives: change is nothing bad for what is changed
support.follows: If being altered were bad for the parts, the whole would be badly managed, which is not believable.

support.quote: There is nothing bad for things that are in the course of change, just as there is nothing good for things that come to exist out of change.
gives: change is nothing bad for what is changed
support.follows: Being changed is not bad for a thing, just as coming out of a change is not good for it.

support.quote: which are the elements of the universe and of you. And these too change, and do not grumble.
gives: The elements I am made of change too, and do not grumble
support.follows: My elements, which are also the universe’s, change and do not complain of it.

claims.t: Even if no nature orders things, a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of: it goes back where it came from, or its elements are scattered. Either way it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it.
claims.shared: 10.7 and 7.27 both give two accounts of dissolution, and both name “a scattering of the elements” among them (7.27: “some such scattering of elements”). 10.7 and 8.16 both say that a thing is dissolved into what it was made of (“into the things out of which each is put together”; “dissolved into what is its own”).
claims.changed: In 7.27 the second account is the atomists’; in 10.7 the person imagined leaves out nature as the one who orders things. The claim takes both as what still holds without nature. 10.7 speaks of parts of the whole; “a thing’s death” follows 8.16’s “what has died”.

support.quote: And if someone were to leave nature out of it and explain these things by the way they naturally are, even so it would be ridiculous to say that the parts of the whole are naturally such as to change, and at the same time to be surprised or annoyed as though at something happening against nature, especially when the dissolution is into the things out of which each is put together.
gives: Even if no nature orders things
a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it
support.follows: Even without nature as the one who orders things, it is absurd to expect change and then be annoyed when a thing comes apart into its parts.

support.quote: For it is either a scattering of the elements out of which it was compounded, or a turning of the solid into the earthy and of the breath-like into the airy, so that these too are taken back up into the reason of the whole
gives: it goes back where it came from
its elements are scattered
support.follows: Dissolving either scatters a thing’s elements or turns them into earth and air, which the whole takes back.

support.quote: What grew from earth goes back to earth, and what sprouted from a seed of the upper air, back to the vault of heaven.
gives: it goes back where it came from
support.follows: What came from the earth returns to the earth, and what came from the sky returns to the sky.

support.quote: Or else this is a dissolution of the interlockings among the atoms, and some such scattering of elements that cannot be affected.
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
its elements are scattered
support.follows: Or else death is a coming apart of the atoms’ links and a scattering of elements that nothing can act upon.

support.quote: What has died does not fall outside the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into what is its own
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
support.follows: What dies stays in the universe, changes there, and is dissolved into its own parts.

single.label: Without lament
single.t: What the gods send me I bear, in toil and without lament.
single.quote: But the sailing wind that blows from the gods must be borne, in toils without lament.
single.why: A line of verse Marcus copied, and the only place in the section that speaks of bearing what the gods send. 8.16 says the elements change without grumbling, but it speaks of the elements, not of what I bear.
single.follows: What the gods send must be borne, with toil and without lament.

single.label: Everything a seed
single.t: Everything that exists is in a way the seed of what will come from it, and not only what is sown in the earth or in a womb.
single.quote: For everything that exists is, in a way, the seed of what will come from it. But you picture as seeds only those that are cast into earth or womb, and that is very much a layman’s view.
single.why: Only this passage calls everything a seed. It goes with the claim that nature makes new things like the old, but no second passage says it.
single.follows: Whatever exists is a seed of what will follow it, not only seeds sown in earth or womb.

single.label: Old and young alike
single.t: Everything I see will soon perish, and so will those who watched it perish; whoever dies very old will be brought level with whoever died before their time.
single.quote: Everything you see will very quickly perish, and those who have looked on as it perished will very quickly perish themselves, and whoever dies in extreme old age will be brought level with the one who died before their time.
single.why: Only this passage draws from the speed of change that a long life and a short one end level. The speed itself is in claim 1.
single.follows: Since everything and everyone perishes quickly, dying very old comes to the same as dying young.

single.label: What is great
single.t: The one thing I count as great is to act as my own nature leads and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.quote: except this: to act as your own nature leads, and to undergo things as the common nature brings them.
single.why: Only this passage names what is still great when nothing that passes is. It is kept beside the claim it limits.
single.follows: The only thing to picture as great is acting as one’s own nature leads and undergoing what the common nature brings.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.27 is 7.49–51, 6.14 is 6.15, 4.29 is 4.35–36, 10.19 is 10.17–18, 9.31 is 9.32b–33, 9.27 is 9.28b–29a, 9.17 is 9.19, 2.9 is 2.12a, 12.25 is 12.32, 6.34 is 6.37–38, 4.35 is 4.42–43, 8.5 is 8.6, 9.33 is 9.35 and 8.16 is 8.18; 10.7 is the same.
Reads “perish” in 10.7, “perishing” in 9.17 and “loss” in 9.33 as one thing, because 10.7 and 9.33 each say that it is change.

Sets “nothing that passes is great” beside “nothing bad” in the statement. 4.35 pairs a denial of bad with a denial of good in one sentence, but the statement’s “great” comes from 12.25, 9.27, 6.14 and 2.9, not from 4.35.

Leaves out what belongs to other articles: that what I give back at death I took in only “yesterday and the day before” (10.7, 6.14), the subject of Article 33; that all things are linked and dear to one another (6.34), Article 4’s subject; and the changes of ruling powers that open 7.27.
articles.limit: Article 3 already says that I accept what happens without complaint, which claim 5 comes near, and that none of it is unusual, which claim 2’s “nothing comes that is new in kind” comes near, though claim 2 speaks of one kind across all time, not of the ordinariness of what happens to me; Article 5 says that nature makes new things of what it takes back. Claims 5 and 6 come near Article 36 (no change of my life, its ending included, is bad) and Article 10 (death is a dissolving of my elements), the said-once 9.31 is Article 35’s point that a long life and a short one come to the same, and claims 2 and 6 come near Articles 30 and 33 on sameness and on matter reshaped. What this article adds is change itself, in all things and not only in my death: it is everywhere, fast and of one kind, it is nothing bad, and nothing that passes is great.

statement.t: All things change, and I with them; the change is the work of nature and nothing bad, and nothing that passes is great.

parts.words: All things change, and I with them
the change is the work of nature
nothing bad
nothing that passes is great

statement.kind: A fact, its source and two judgments
statement.form: Claim 1 states the fact: all things change, quickly, and I with them. Claim 2 gives its source, the nature of the whole, which loves change and keeps to one kind. The statement then sets two judgments side by side: change is nothing bad (claim 5) and nothing that passes is great (claim 3). Claim 4 is the exercise that keeps the fact in view, and claim 6 says what holds without nature.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five claims gain a second author: that all things change and I with them, that I look down on what passes, the practice of seeing all of time, that a loss is only a change, and that a thing is resolved into its elements. The ground gains one good that does not perish; what breaks gains the fear of a death already under way and the weariness that sameness can breed. He backs the third claim’s contempt for what passes in Letter 58 and limits it in Letter 98: what I lose I keep in memory, with thanks.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, and he adds what Marcus’s section does not name: a good that does not pass, the real good of wisdom and virtue.

items.quote: Even I myself, as I comment on this change, am changed myself.
gives: I am changing with them
items.follows: Seneca himself changes even while he speaks about change.
items.context: Letter 58, on Plato’s classes of being: what we see and touch is in flux, our bodies above all. “This change” is that flux.

items.quote: the universe, too, immortal and enduring as it is, changes and never remains the same
gives: All things are changing
items.follows: Even the universe, which lasts for ever, changes and never stays the same.
items.context: Letter 58, after saying that a man flows away like a river: the universe too keeps everything it had, but always in a new arrangement.

items.quote: Let us despise everything that is so little an object of value that it makes us doubt whether it exists at all.
gives: I look down on everything mortal
items.follows: We should look down on things of so little worth that we can doubt they exist at all.
items.context: Letter 58 draws a use from Plato: what the senses show is in flux and not truly real. “Everything so little an object of value” is those passing things.

items.quote: Place before your mind’s eye the vast spread of time’s abyss, and consider the universe; and then contrast our so-called human life with infinity
gives: the whole of eternity and the whole of what exists
items.follows: I should picture all of time and the whole universe, and set a human life against that infinity.
items.context: Letter 99 consoles a father whose young son has died. Set against all of time and the universe, Seneca says, a long life is little more than a child’s.

items.quote: everything which seems to perish merely changes
gives: a loss is nothing but a change
items.follows: What seems to perish only changes.
items.context: Letter 36 answers a craving for longer life: nothing that vanishes from sight is annihilated. “Everything which seems to perish” includes our own death.

items.quote: Whatever is will cease to be, and yet it will not perish, but will be resolved into its elements.
gives: a thing’s death is only its dissolution into what it was made of
items.follows: Everything that exists will cease to be, yet it does not perish but is resolved into its elements.
items.context: Letter 71: everything, the stars and the earth included, is born, grows and is destroyed. “Whatever is” means each of those things.

items.quote: they are surprised at losing anything, although some day they are bound to lose everything
gives: it is ridiculous to be surprised or annoyed at it
items.follows: It makes no sense to be surprised at losing one thing when one is bound to lose everything.
items.context: Letter 98, on the fickleness of Fortune: people forget where each day pushes them. “Losing anything” means their goods, and in the end their life.

items.label: why
items.role: One good that does not pass
items.t: All the good things that mortals chase are mortal too. The real good, which is wisdom and virtue, does not perish: it is the only lasting thing a mortal can have.
items.why: Marcus says here that nothing that passes is great, and 12.25 names one great thing, acting as my nature leads. He does not say that anything does not pass. Seneca names it: the real good, wisdom and virtue, does not perish.

support.quote: “All the Good of mortals is mortal.”
support.follows: Every good that mortals have is itself mortal.
support.context: Letter 98 quotes Metrodorus, consoling his sister for the death of her son. The “Good of mortals” is the goods people rush after in crowds.
gives: All the good things that mortals chase are mortal too

support.quote: For the real Good does not perish; it is certain and lasting and it consists of wisdom and virtue; it is the only immortal thing that falls to mortal lot.
support.follows: The real good, wisdom and virtue, does not perish; it is the only immortal thing a mortal can have.
support.context: Letter 98, Seneca’s comment on Metrodorus’s saying that all the good of mortals is mortal: the real good is the one exception.
gives: The real good, which is wisdom and virtue, does not perish
it is the only lasting thing a mortal can have

items.label: breaks
items.role: A death that happens every day
items.t: When I fear that death will come to me once, I forget that it comes every day: every moment is the death of what I was, and the last hour only completes it.
items.why: Marcus says that I am in continual alteration and in a certain respect perishing (9.17), but he draws nothing from it about the fear of death. Seneca does: what I fear as one future event is already happening.

support.quote: every instant means the death of our previous condition. Will you not stop fearing lest that may happen once which really happens every day?
support.follows: Each moment ends what we were before, so it is foolish to fear that death will happen once.
support.context: Letter 58: after Heraclitus’s river, Seneca says that we mortals are carried past as fast. “That” which happens every day is death.
gives: When I fear that death will come to me once
it comes every day
every moment is the death of what I was

support.quote: the final hour when we cease to exist does not of itself bring death; it merely of itself completes the death-process.
support.follows: The last hour of life does not bring death by itself; it only completes a dying that was already under way.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: we die every day, as a water-clock empties drop by drop. “The final hour” is the moment we cease to exist.
gives: the last hour only completes it

items.label: breaks
items.t: Seeing that I do nothing new and see nothing new can make me sick of living. The wish to die that grows from that weariness is a weakness, and I avoid it.
items.why: Marcus draws comfort from sameness: nothing new comes that I need fear (8.5), and forty years show as much as ten thousand (7.27). Seneca shows the same thought turning into weariness of life, a failure Marcus does not name here.

support.quote: Others also are moved by a satiety of doing and seeing the same things, and not so much by a hatred of life as because they are cloyed with it.
support.follows: Some people want to die not because they hate life but because they are sick of doing and seeing the same things.
support.context: Letter 24, on the urge to die: besides those who despise life and those who find it irksome, some are moved by weariness. “It” is life, of which they are cloyed.
gives: can make me sick of living

support.quote: I do nothing new; I see nothing new; sooner or later one sickens of this, also.
support.follows: Whoever thinks that he does and sees nothing new will sooner or later grow sick of it.
support.context: Letter 24: the words Seneca gives to a man cloyed with life, who sees nature go round and return. “This” is that endless round.
gives: Seeing that I do nothing new and see nothing new

support.quote: above all, he should avoid the weakness which has taken possession of so many,—the lust for death.
support.follows: The brave and wise man should above all avoid the lust for death.
support.context: Letter 24: the brave and wise man should not rush out of life. “The weakness” is the lust for death, which takes the noble and the craven alike.
gives: The wish to die that grows from that weariness is a weakness, and I avoid it

items.t: In Letter 58 Seneca, like Marcus, tells me to despise what passes (Ep. 58.28); in Letter 98 he tells me to keep what I have lost in memory and to be thankful for having had it. Fortune can take the thing from me, but not the fact that I had it. This limits claim 3 and does not contradict it: Marcus’s word in 9.27, “look down on”, can also mean simply to think little of.

support.quote: to keep in memory the things we have lost, and not to suffer the enjoyment which we have derived from them to pass away along with them
support.follows: We should keep in memory what we have lost, and not let the enjoyment we had of it pass away with it.
support.context: Letter 98 asks what resource we have in the face of losses. “Them” are the things we have lost: goods, and the people we loved.

support.quote: To have may be taken from us, to have had, never.
support.follows: What we have can be taken from us; that we had it cannot.
support.context: Letter 98, on losses brought by Fortune: having a thing can be taken away, having had it cannot.

support.quote: A man is thankless in the highest degree if, after losing something, he feels no obligation for having received it.
support.follows: It is deeply ungrateful to lose something and feel no gratitude for having had it.
support.context: Letter 98, on losses brought by Fortune: whoever loses a thing still owes thanks for having received it.

amend.t: ; but the real good, wisdom and virtue, does not perish
; but what I have lost I keep in memory, and I am thankful for having had it

rejected.why: Nothing that vanishes is annihilated, and we shall be restored to the light of day. Goes beyond Marcus to a personal return; 36.11 is used for the change itself.
Life and death go by turns; what was broken up is put together again. Says what claim 2 and Article 33 say; 71.13 is used and is plainer.
Cato: why be angry if I die a little before the general destruction? About one’s own death and timing, nearer the shortness of life.
The soul either goes to a better life or returns to the universe. Its first case is an afterlife Marcus does not consider in this section.
Nothing is free from change, not even the universe. Said to bear a change of government; 58.24 says the same more directly.
Heraclitus’s river and we mortals carried past as fast. Close to claim 1, but its second half is used for the fear of death and one witness was enough.
We crave sense-things as if they lasted. Platonic, about turning to the ideas; 58.28 states the contempt plainly and is used.
Nature rules by changing seasons; eternity consists of opposites. About adapting to Nature’s law, used in Article 6’s search.
Periods of time separate us, but death levels us. Matches 9.31’s levelling, which is a said-once item and takes no backing.
We die every day. The commonplace that 24.20 explains; 24.20 is quoted.
Who understands that he is dying daily? About the value of time, not change.
The balanced mind laughs at the succession of ages and the changes of Chance. About freedom from worry over the future.
All past time slips into the same abyss. About how short past time seems, the subject of the shortness of life.
A single day scatters what years built. About sudden disaster to cities, not the steady change of all things.
We must not cry out at calamities; such are the laws of the world we entered. About Fortune and disaster; Article 3 covers not complaining.
Every trial has been overcome by someone. About endurance, not change.
Mortal things decay and are replenished; things divine are one. Used to argue the equality of goods.
Most people are swept along like objects afloat in a river. About people without purpose, not the flow of things.
Men clutch at life as those carried down a stream clutch at briars. About clinging to life, not change.
Death has its fixed rule, equal for all; who can complain? About death’s fairness, nearer the dead and forgotten.
We know by what successive changes Nature summons back the year. Part of a consolation for an early death.

articles.title: The same matter, reshaped

claims.t: Out of the same material, the nature of the whole makes one thing after another, and each very quickly changes into something else: what was part of one becomes part of another, and so on without end.
claims.shared: Both 7.17 and 5.13 follow the same material from one thing into the next: in 7.17 the material of a little horse is used “for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else”; in 5.13 a part of me “will change into another part of the universe, and so on”. 7.17 and 6.4 both say that this is quick: “for the briefest time”, “very quickly change”.
claims.changed: 7.17 gives the image of wax and names the shapes; the claim keeps the names and drops the wax. 5.13 says it of the parts of me; the claim says it of everything, as 7.17 and 6.4 do.

support.quote: The nature of the whole, out of the whole of substance as if out of wax, at one moment shaped a little horse; then it melted that down and used its material for a little tree, then for a little human, then for something else.
gives: Out of the same material, the nature of the whole makes one thing after another
into something else
what was part of one becomes part of another
support.follows: Nature makes one thing after another out of the same substance, melting each down and using its material for the next.

support.quote: Each of these existed for the briefest time.
gives: each very quickly changes
support.follows: Each thing made in this way exists only for a very short time.

support.quote: All existing things will very quickly change
gives: each very quickly changes
support.follows: Everything that exists will very soon change.

support.quote: So every part of me will be assigned, through change, to some part of the universe, and that in turn will change into another part of the universe, and so on to infinity.
gives: into something else
what was part of one becomes part of another
and so on without end
support.follows: Each part of me will pass by change into some part of the universe, and that part into another, without end.

claims.t: I am made of matter and of a cause, which is what in me acts and shapes the matter. Neither will perish into nothing, just as neither came out of nothing: the matter vanishes into the substance of the whole, and the cause is taken back up into the reason of the whole, the reason that orders all things.
claims.shared: 5.13 names two things I am made of, “what is causal and what is material”; 7.7 names the same pair for all things, “everything material” and “every cause”. 7.7 and 4.12 both say that what goes is “taken back up into” a reason: “the reason of the whole” and “its seminal reason”.
claims.changed: “What in me acts and shapes the matter” is the editor’s explanation of the cause; 5.13 says only “what is causal”. 4.12 says “you” will be taken back up into “its seminal reason”, the reason of what gave birth to me; the claim says it of the cause and of the whole, as 7.7 does. “The reason that orders all things” is the editor’s gloss of 7.7’s “the reason of the whole”. No passage here says in so many words that this reason orders anything; 6.4’s left-out second saying speaks of “the reason that governs”, without saying what it governs.

support.quote: I am made up of what is causal and what is material, and neither of these will perish into what is not, just as neither came to be out of what is not.
gives: I am made of matter and of a cause
Neither will perish into nothing
just as neither came out of nothing
support.follows: Neither the causal nor the material in me will perish into nothing, just as neither came from nothing.

support.quote: Everything material very quickly vanishes into the substance of the whole
gives: the matter vanishes into the substance of the whole
support.follows: Everything material soon disappears into the substance of the whole.

support.quote: every cause is very quickly taken back up into the reason of the whole
gives: the cause is taken back up into the reason of the whole
support.follows: Every cause is soon taken back up into the reason of the whole.

support.quote: or rather, you will be taken back up into its seminal reason, through change.
gives: is taken back up into the reason
support.follows: More exactly, I will be taken back up, through change, into the seminal reason of what gave birth to me.

claims.role: Death is the change birth was
claims.t: My death is the same kind of change as my birth. I came to be through change, as my parents did, and I go back into what I came from: the same things from which my father and mother drew what made me, and from which I have been fed every day.
claims.shared: 4.5 and 5.13 both set birth and death side by side as one kind of thing: “Death is the same kind of thing as birth”; “It was through a change of this kind that I too came to be”. 4.5, 4.12 and 5.4 all say that I go “into” what I came from: “a dissolving into the same”, “vanish into what gave birth to you”, “breathing my last into that from which I draw breath”. 5.13 and 4.12 both say that I “came to be” or “came to exist”, and 4.12 that I did so “as a part within something”.
claims.changed: 4.5 speaks of death in general; the claim says “my death”. 5.4 does not name what it falls on; the claim calls it “the same things”, without naming the earth.

support.quote: Death is the same kind of thing as birth, a mystery of nature: a combining out of the same elements, a dissolving into the same.
gives: My death is the same kind of change as my birth
I go back into what I came from
support.follows: Death is the same kind of thing as birth: a combining out of the same elements and a dissolving into them.

support.quote: It was through a change of this kind that I too came to be, and my parents
gives: My death is the same kind of change as my birth
I came to be through change, as my parents did
support.follows: I came to be, as my parents did, through the same kind of change that will pass my parts on.

support.quote: You came to exist as a part within something.
gives: I came to be
support.follows: I came to exist as a part of something larger than me.

support.quote: You will vanish into what gave birth to you
gives: I go back into what I came from
support.follows: I will vanish into what gave birth to me.

support.quote: breathing my last into that from which I draw breath every day, and falling on that from which my father gathered the bit of seed, my mother the bit of blood and my nurse the bit of milk; from which every day, for so many years, I have been fed and watered
gives: I go back into what I came from
the same things from which my father and mother drew what made me
from which I have been fed every day
support.follows: When I die I breathe out into what I breathe every day and fall onto what my parents drew me from and what has fed me.

claims.t: There is nothing terrible in my coming apart, just as there is nothing good in my being put together. My ending belongs to the way I am made: nature aimed at it no less than at my beginning, and it does not go against the reason on which I am built.
claims.shared: 8.18 and 4.5 both say that the end belongs to the way a thing is made: nature “has aimed at the ending of each thing”, and death is not “contrary to the reason on which it is built”. 7.17 and 8.18 both set the end beside the beginning and weigh them alike: “taken apart” and “put together”, “ending” and “beginning”.
claims.changed: 7.17 says it of “a little box”, after a horse, a tree and a human made of wax; the claim says it of me. “Belongs to the way I am made” is the editor’s phrase for what 8.18 and 4.5 both say: 8.18 that nature aimed at the ending, 4.5 that death does not go against the reason on which a living being is built.

support.quote: But there is nothing terrible for a little box in being taken apart, just as there is nothing good in its being put together.
gives: There is nothing terrible in my coming apart, just as there is nothing good in my being put together
support.follows: Being taken apart is nothing terrible for a thing, just as being put together is nothing good for it.

support.quote: Nature has aimed at the ending of each thing not a bit less than at its beginning and its course.
gives: My ending belongs to the way I am made
nature aimed at it no less than at my beginning
support.follows: Nature aims at the end of each thing just as much as at its beginning and its course.

support.quote: it is not contrary to what follows in sequence for a living being with mind, nor contrary to the reason on which it is built.
gives: My ending belongs to the way I am made
it does not go against the reason on which I am built
support.follows: Death goes neither against what comes next for a being with a mind nor against the reason on which that being is built.

single.label: Until I rest
single.t: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest.
single.quote: I make my way through the things that accord with nature until I fall and rest
single.why: Only this passage says what I do in the meantime: I go on through what accords with nature. No second passage says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: I go on through what accords with nature until I fall and rest.

single.label: One whole or not
single.t: Whether the stuff of the world is one continuous whole or not, what exists changes either way: if it is one, things go up in vapour; if it is not, they are scattered.
single.quote: either they will go up in vapour, if substance is indeed a unity, or they will be scattered
single.why: Only this passage gives two pictures of what the world is made of and says what happens to things under each. 5.13 also allows for another picture, but a different one, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: If the stuff of the world is one continuous whole, things will go up in vapour; if not, they will be scattered.

single.label: Even in finite cycles
single.t: Even if the universe is governed in cycles that come to an end, nothing stops me from saying that the change which made me and will pass me on is endless both ways: back through my parents and forward through my parts.
single.quote: and, for one who goes back, into another infinity. For nothing prevents one from saying so, even if the universe is governed in finite cycles.
single.why: Only this passage asks whether the endless change still holds if the universe runs in cycles with an end. “So” covers both infinities 5.13 has just named, forward through my parts and back through my parents. 6.4 allows for a different picture, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: Going back through one’s ancestors leads into another infinity, and one may say so even if the universe runs in finite cycles.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 7.17 is 7.23, 6.4 is 6.4–5, 7.7 is 7.10, 4.12 is 4.14–15 and 8.18 is 8.20; 5.13, 4.5 and 5.4 are the same.

Reads the pair “what is causal and what is material” in 5.13 and the pair “every cause” and “everything material” in 7.7 as the same two things in me, and explains the cause as what in me acts and shapes the matter. In the statement, “the whole” that I came out of is the editor’s word for 4.5’s “the same elements”, 5.13’s parts of the universe and 4.12’s “something” of which I am a part.

Reads “a change of this kind” in 5.13 as the change just described, by which my parts pass into other parts of the universe. So 5.13 is taken to say that I came to be by the same kind of change as the one that ends me, and it backs “My death is the same kind of change as my birth” beside 4.5.

Applies 7.17’s last sentence, said of “a little box”, to me, since the human made of wax is one of the shapes in the same passage. Leaves out, as being about other things: the second saying of 6.4 (modern 6.5: the reason that governs knows on what material it acts) and of 4.12 (modern 4.15: lumps of incense falling earlier or later); 7.7’s “the memory of everything is very quickly buried in eternity”, which is about memory, not matter; 4.5’s “not a thing anyone would be ashamed of”, whose shame the passage does not explain (claim 4 quotes the reason that follows it); and 5.4’s “which bears me as I tread on it”, about how the earth serves me while I live.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this. Article 32 (“All things pass”) says that change is nothing bad for what is changed (its claim 5) and that a thing’s death is its dissolution into what it was made of (its claim 6). Article 10’s claim 4 says that death is a dissolving of my elements, according to nature, and so not bad. Article 36 says that my death is one more of the changes I live through (its claim 2) and that nature, not I, fixes the time and limit of my death, which is not bad (its claim 3). Claims 3 and 4 here come near all of these, and Ep. 30.11, 82.15 and 82.16 are used in Article 10 or 36 as well. Article 6 says once that everything is from nature and goes into nature (4.19), and Article 5 (its claim 3) that nature throws nothing away but takes it back into herself and makes new things out of it, which comes near claims 1 and 2 here; Ep. 36.10 is used there as well. What this article adds is that nothing of me perishes into nothing, that what I am made of is shaped into something else, that my death is the same change as my birth, and that my ending was intended as my beginning was. No passage gives an exercise or describes failing.

statement.t: What I am made of came out of the whole, goes back into it and is shaped again, and my ending belongs to the way I am made.

parts.words: What I am made of came out of the whole
goes back into it
is shaped again
my ending belongs to the way I am made

statement.kind: One cycle traced, and what it means for the end
statement.form: Claims 1 to 3 follow the same material through one cycle: it is made into one thing after another, none of it goes into nothing, and I go back into what I came from. Claim 4 says what this means for my ending: it was intended as my beginning was.

empty.practice: No passage in this section gives an exercise to repeat; they describe what happens to what I am made of.
empty.breaks: No passage in this section describes what failing looks like here or how to come back from it.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claims 1, 2 and 3 each gain a second author, and the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: an exercise for facing death, what failing looks like and the way back, and what holds if death is simply the end. He limits claim 4: death is no evil, but it keeps a look of evil.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and takes in the other case: if death is the end and not a change, ceasing to exist is the same as never having begun.

items.quote: she but resolves that which she has compounded, and compounds again that which she has resolved.
gives: Out of the same material, the nature of the whole makes one thing after another
items.follows: Nature takes apart what she has put together, and puts together again what she has taken apart.
items.context: Letter 30, on facing death calmly: death’s rule is the same for everyone. “She” is Nature, and what she takes apart and puts together again are living things.

items.quote: Whatever is will cease to be, and yet it will not perish, but will be resolved into its elements.
gives: will perish into nothing
items.follows: Everything that exists will come to an end, yet it will not perish: it will be resolved into its elements.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: everything, earth and stars included, is born, grows and is destroyed. “Whatever is” is every thing in the world.

items.quote: re-absorbed into the world of things, from which they have come forth
gives: I go back into what I came from
items.follows: Things that vanish from sight are taken back into the world they came from.
items.context: Letter 36, to someone who craves a longer life: things that vanish from sight go back into the world. Seneca adds that they come forth again, a return Marcus does not speak of here.

items.label: doubt
items.role: If death is simply the end
items.t: Death is either an end or a change. If it is an end, I do not fear ceasing to exist: it is the same as never having begun, and a lamp is no worse off when it is put out than before it was lit.
items.why: Marcus’s passages here hold that nothing of me goes into nothing; none asks what is left if death is simply the end. Seneca takes that case and answers it: ceasing to exist is the same as not having begun.

support.quote: And what is death? It is either the end, or a process of change.
gives: Death is either an end or a change
support.follows: Death is one of two things: an end, or a change.
support.context: The close of Letter 65, on the first cause: God is to the universe as the soul is to the body. Seneca then asks what death is.

support.quote: I have no fear of ceasing to exist; it is the same as not having begun.
gives: I do not fear ceasing to exist
it is the same as never having begun
support.follows: Seneca does not fear ceasing to exist, because that is the same as never having begun.
support.context: The close of Letter 65: having said that death is either an end or a change, Seneca takes the first case. “It” is ceasing to exist.

support.quote: would you not say that one was the greatest of fools who believed that a lamp was worse off when it was extinguished than before it was lighted?
gives: a lamp is no worse off when it is put out than before it was lit
support.follows: A lamp is no worse off once it is put out than it was before it was lit.
support.context: Letter 54, written after an asthma attack: death is non-existence, as before birth. The lamp stands for us, lit at birth and put out at death.

items.label: practice
items.t: Death is not a thing I can easily ignore. I harden my mind by long practice, so that it learns to bear the sight and the approach of death.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section gives an exercise. Seneca gives one, long practice in facing death, and gives it because death is hard to ignore.

support.quote: although death is something indifferent, it is nevertheless not a thing which we can easily ignore. The soul must be hardened by long practice, so that it may learn to endure the sight and the approach of death.
gives: Death is not a thing I can easily ignore
I harden my mind by long practice
so that it learns to bear the sight and the approach of death
support.follows: Death is hard to ignore, so the mind must be hardened by long practice until it can bear death’s sight and approach.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death: Seneca has just said that we naturally shrink from dying. This hardening is his answer to that fear.

items.label: breaks
items.role: Going out as I came in
items.t: Failing is to be worse when I die than when I was born, and the fault is mine, not nature’s. Nature brought me into the world without desires or fears; the way back is to go out as I came in.
items.why: Marcus says that I go back into what I came from, and describes no failing. Seneca names one: dying worse than I was born, with desires and fears that nature did not give me.

support.quote: we are worse when we die than when we were born; but it is our fault, and not that of Nature.
gives: to be worse when I die than when I was born
the fault is mine, not nature’s
support.follows: People are worse when they die than when they were born, and the fault is theirs, not nature’s.
support.context: Letter 22: Seneca corrects Epicurus, who said that everyone leaves life as one just born. “We” are people in general, who die more afraid than they were born.

support.quote: I brought you into the world without desires or fears, free from superstition, treachery and the other curses. Go forth as you were when you entered!
gives: Nature brought me into the world without desires or fears
to go out as I came in
support.follows: Nature brought each of us in without desires or fears and tells us to leave as we came.
support.context: Letter 22: Nature’s imagined rebuke to people who die full of fears. “I” is Nature, “you” is all of us, and “as you were when you entered” means as at birth.

items.t: Seneca agrees that death is no evil, but he says it is not as indifferent as how one’s hair is cut. There is implanted in us a love of ourselves and an abhorrence of dissolution, so death keeps a look of evil (Ep. 82.15). This limits the claim that there is nothing terrible in coming apart; it does not contradict it.

support.quote: death is not so indifferent as the question whether your hair should be worn evenly or unevenly.
support.follows: Death matters more to us than how our hair is cut, though both are called indifferent.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death: Seneca says the things called indifferent differ among themselves, and gives death as his example.

support.quote: Death belongs among those things which are not indeed evils, but still have in them a semblance of evil; for there are implanted in us love of self, a desire for existence and self-preservation, and also an abhorrence of dissolution
support.follows: Death is no evil, but it looks like one, because love of self and a shrinking from dissolution are planted in us.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death: why death, though no evil, still looks like one. The “abhorrence of dissolution” is our own coming apart.

amend.t: ; and if death is simply an end, ceasing to exist is the same as never having begun
; yet death keeps a look of evil for me, since an abhorrence of dissolution is implanted in me

searches: before I was born, before our birth
whence we came, from which they have come
born (with destined to die, must die)

rejected.why: Whatever has been put together is broken up and put together again. Says what Ep. 30.11 says, which is quoted, and puts it as a hope the mind lacks.
Everything that seems to perish merely changes; you are destined to return. The return of the same person is not in Marcus’s section.
Its second sentence, that we shall be restored to the light, is left out for the same reason; only the first sentence is quoted.
The universe keeps all it had in a new arrangement. Said of the universe as a whole; claim 1 is already backed by Ep. 30.11.
Cause and matter as the two sources of everything, in a letter on how many causes there are. Says nothing of what becomes of either when a thing ends.
All things are made of matter and God. About which of the two is higher, not about change.
The day of death is the birthday of your eternity. A birth of the soul into eternity, not the same change as birth; the match with claim 3 needs explaining.
The body is cast off as the afterbirth is. About the soul leaving the body, which Marcus does not discuss here.
Sotion’s doctrine of souls passing from body to body. A Pythagorean view Seneca reports, not his own claim.
Death is non-existence, which I knew before I was born. Ep. 54.5, quoted, says it with the lamp.
Death either annihilates us or strips us bare. Says what Ep. 65.24 says, in a letter on the terrors of the underworld.
Even if I am annihilated, my courage is no less. The wise man’s hope of the gods; Ep. 65.24 states the case more plainly.
Rehearse this thought every day. “This thought” is that a long life is no blessing, not the facing of death.
To depart calmly needs long practice. Said of an old friend’s illness; Ep. 82.16 gives the practice in general.
Practise how to welcome death or invite it. Includes choosing death, which this section does not touch.
Whoever can die as free from care as at birth has caught the message of wisdom. Repeats Ep. 22.15, which is quoted.
Whoever is born is destined to die. About mourning another’s death.
Be reconciled to fate, by which all things are dissolved. About the burning of a city and fortune’s reach.
To glide off to one’s haven when nature slips the cable. About wearing away in old age.

articles.title: The dead and the forgotten

claims.t: Everyone dies: those who treated the sick, who foretold other people’s deaths, or who killed many in war died themselves, and whole courts and, in a way, whole cities have died.
claims.shared: 4.39 and 3.3 name the same three kinds, each dying after doing to others what then came to them: doctors and Hippocrates after treating the sick, astrologers and the Chaldaeans after foretelling deaths, champions and the conquerors after killing many. 4.39 and 8.29 add whole cities and a whole court; 6.42 says it of people of every kind.
claims.changed: The names are dropped. “Everyone dies” widens 6.42’s “people of every kind, of every kind of occupation and from every sort of nation”. 4.39 hedges the cities (“so to speak”); the claim keeps the hedge as “in a way”.

support.quote: Keep in mind continually that people of every kind, of every kind of occupation and from every sort of nation, are dead
gives: Everyone dies
support.follows: I should keep in mind that people of every kind, every occupation and every nation are dead.

support.quote: Keep in mind continually how many doctors have died, after many times knitting their brows over the sick
gives: those who treated the sick
died themselves
support.follows: I should keep in mind how many doctors have died after frowning over the sick many times.

support.quote: Hippocrates, after curing many illnesses, fell ill himself and died.
gives: those who treated the sick
died themselves
support.follows: Hippocrates cured many illnesses and still fell ill and died.

support.quote: how many astrologers, after foretelling other people’s deaths as if that were something great
gives: who foretold other people’s deaths
support.follows: Astrologers who made much of foretelling other people’s deaths are among the many who have died.

support.quote: The Chaldaeans foretold the deaths of many, and then what was fated caught up with them too.
gives: who foretold other people’s deaths
died themselves
support.follows: The Chaldaeans foretold many deaths, and then their own fated end caught up with them.

support.quote: how many champions, after killing many
gives: who killed many in war
support.follows: Champions who killed many are among the many who have died.

support.quote: after so many times wiping out whole cities completely and cutting down in battle many tens of thousands of horsemen and foot soldiers, one day went out of life themselves as well
gives: who killed many in war
died themselves
support.follows: Conquerors who destroyed cities and cut down tens of thousands in battle one day left life themselves.

support.quote: how many whole cities have, so to speak, died
gives: in a way, whole cities have died
support.follows: Even whole cities have, so to speak, died.

support.quote: The death of a whole court.
gives: whole courts
support.follows: A whole court, such as that of Augustus with all its people, has died.

claims.t: I shall soon be dead, and those who bury me or remember me will soon follow: one person buries another and dies in turn, and a little later not even our names are left.
claims.shared: 4.39 and 8.24 tell the same story, someone who buries another and then dies in turn: “One buried this person and was then laid out”; “Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla.” 8.19 and 10.34 say the same of those who keep a memory: “short-lived is … the one who remembers”, and those who will receive “the fame that comes after death” are little leaves too. 4.6 and 10.34 both say I shall soon be dead.
claims.changed: 4.6 says “you and this man” of someone who annoys me; the claim keeps only that both die and are forgotten. 10.34 speaks of the one who carried me out to burial; the claim says “those who bury me”, and leaves the mourner who comes after.

support.quote: within a very short time both you and this man will be dead, and a little later not even your names will be left
gives: I shall soon be dead
a little later not even our names are left
support.follows: Very soon both I and the man who annoys me will be dead, and a little later even our names will be gone.

support.quote: A little while and you will close your eyes
gives: I shall soon be dead
support.follows: In a little while I shall close my eyes in death.

support.quote: already someone else will be mourning the one who carried you out
gives: those who bury me
will soon follow
support.follows: Soon after I die, the one who carried me out to burial will be mourned by someone else.

support.quote: Short-lived is the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered.
gives: remember me
will soon follow
support.follows: Whoever praises or remembers is as short-lived as whoever is praised or remembered.

support.quote: little leaves in the same way are those who will receive in succession the fame that comes after death
gives: remember me
will soon follow
support.follows: Those who will in turn keep a person’s fame after death fall like leaves as well.

support.quote: One buried this person and was then laid out, another buried that one, and all of it in a short time.
gives: those who bury me
one person buries another and dies in turn
support.follows: One person buries another and is soon laid out himself, and all of it happens in a short time.

support.quote: Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla.
gives: one person buries another and dies in turn
support.follows: Lucilla buried Verus, and then it was Lucilla’s turn.

claims.t: Even those who shone soon turn into tales and then fade even from the tales, and the rest are forgotten the moment they die. Even remembrance that lasted for ever would be empty.
claims.shared: All three say “tale”: 4.28 “turn into tales”, 8.24 “changed into tales”, 12.20 “a tale, or not even a tale”. 4.28 and 8.24 also say that the tale fades in its turn (“complete forgetting buries them”; “faded even out of the tales”) and that some are forgotten at once (“unseen, unheard of”; “not remembered even for a short while”).
claims.changed: 4.28 says “all things” fade and then says it means the famous; 12.20 speaks of those at the height of fame or fortune. The claim calls both “those who shone”, 4.28’s word. The last sentence, that everlasting remembrance is empty, is said by 4.28 alone.

support.quote: For all things quickly fade and turn into tales, and quickly too complete forgetting buries them. And I say this of those who shone in some wonderful way; for the rest, the moment they have breathed their last, are “unseen, unheard of”.
gives: Even those who shone
soon turn into tales
fade even from the tales
the rest are forgotten the moment they die
support.follows: Even those who shone quickly become tales and are then wholly forgotten; everyone else is unheard of from the moment they die.

support.quote: And what is everlasting remembrance at all? All of it empty.
gives: Even remembrance that lasted for ever would be empty
support.follows: Even a remembrance that lasted for ever would be wholly empty.

support.quote: some not remembered even for a short while, some changed into tales, and some by now faded even out of the tales
gives: turn into tales
fade even from the tales
the rest are forgotten the moment they die
support.follows: Of the dead, some were not remembered even briefly, some became tales, and some have faded even out of the tales.

support.quote: Smoke and ash and a tale, or not even a tale.
gives: turn into tales
fade even from the tales
support.follows: Those who were at the height of fame or fortune are now smoke, ash and a tale, or not even a tale.

claims.t: Having ended is no harm to what has ended. Nothing is terrible for the dead in being long dead, whether they were famous or never named at all, any more than it harms a ball to have fallen or a bubble to have burst.
claims.shared: Both passages ask what harm there is in having ended, and expect the answer “none”: 6.42 “What, then, is terrible in this for them?” of the long dead; 8.19 “what harm … to have fallen? … what harm to have burst?” of a thrown ball and a bubble.
claims.changed: Both passages put it as a question; the claim states the answer they expect. 8.19 also asks what good it is to the ball to rise and to the bubble to hold together, and adds a lamp; the claim keeps only the harm of ending.

support.quote: What, then, is terrible in this for them? And what for those who are not even named at all?
gives: Having ended is no harm to what has ended
Nothing is terrible for the dead in being long dead
whether they were famous or never named at all
support.follows: Being long dead is nothing terrible for the famous dead, nor for those never named.

support.quote: So what good is it to the little ball to be carried upward, or what harm to be carried downward, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to the bubble to hold together, or what harm to have burst?
gives: Having ended is no harm to what has ended
it harms a ball to have fallen or a bubble to have burst
support.follows: A thrown ball is not harmed by falling, nor a bubble by bursting.

claims.t: What deserves my serious effort is one thing: to be just and truthful, kind even to liars and the unjust, and without affectation.
claims.shared: 4.28 and 6.42 both name “one thing”: “This one thing” is what one should put serious effort into; “One thing here is worth a great deal”. All three name justice (“thought that is just”, “truth and justice”, “to show oneself just”), and 4.28 and 6.42 both name truth (“never to lie”, “with truth”).
claims.changed: Each passage adds something the claim leaves out: 4.28 social actions and welcoming what happens, 12.20 self-control and following the gods.

support.quote: What then is there that one should put serious effort into? This one thing: thought that is just, actions that are social, speech such as never to lie
gives: What deserves my serious effort is one thing
to be just and truthful
support.follows: What deserves serious effort is just thought, social action and speech that never lies.

support.quote: One thing here is worth a great deal: to live life through with truth and justice, kindly towards the liars and the unjust.
gives: What deserves my serious effort is one thing
to be just and truthful
kind even to liars and the unjust
support.follows: The one thing of great worth is to live with truth and justice, and to be kind to liars and the unjust.

support.quote: how much more philosophical it is, in the material one has been given, to show oneself just, self-controlled, following the gods, without affectation
gives: to be just
without affectation
support.follows: It is wiser to be just, self-controlled and without affectation in the life one has been given.

claims.role: Leaving when the time is done
claims.t: When my time is done I leave life with good grace, as a passenger gets off at the harbour and as a ripe olive falls, grateful to the tree that grew it.
claims.shared: Both passages picture a life that has run its course and then is left: the olive falls “when it has grown ripe” (4.39); the voyage has reached harbour, “get off” (3.3). Only 4.39 says how: “with good grace”.
claims.changed: 3.3 speaks to me in the second person; the claim is in the first. The two images are kept side by side.

support.quote: So pass through this instant of time in accord with nature and come to rest with good grace, as an olive might fall when it has grown ripe, speaking well of the earth that bore it and grateful to the tree that grew it.
gives: When my time is done I leave life
with good grace
as a ripe olive falls, grateful to the tree that grew it
support.follows: I should live this brief time according to nature and end it with good grace, as a ripe olive falls, grateful to its tree.

support.quote: You went on board, you sailed, you came to harbour: get off.
gives: When my time is done I leave life
as a passenger gets off at the harbour
support.follows: When the voyage of my life has reached harbour, I should get off.

claims.t: Again and again I go over the dead one after another, the famous and those I know of, and I ask where they are now.
claims.shared: 12.20 and 4.39 both tell me to go over people again (“Go back continually over”; “Go over as well all those you know, one after another”). 12.20 and 10.31 both then ask where they are (“where is all that now?”; “where, then, are those people?”).
claims.changed: 12.20 names the indignant and those at the height of fame or fortune; the claim says “the famous”. 4.39 says “all those you know”, which may include people known by report; the claim says “those I know of”.

support.quote: Go back continually over those who were exceedingly indignant at something, those who were at their height in the greatest fame or disasters or enmities or fortunes of whatever kind.
gives: Again and again
go over
the famous
support.follows: I should keep going back over people who were once furious, famous or in great fortune or disaster.

support.quote: Go over as well all those you know, one after another.
gives: go over
the dead one after another
those I know of
support.follows: I should go over, one after another, the dead I know of.

support.quote: Then stop and consider: where is all that now?
gives: I ask where they are now
support.follows: Having recalled them, I should stop and ask where all that is now.

support.quote: where, then, are those people? Nowhere, or wherever it may be.
gives: I ask where they are now
support.follows: The people of earlier times are nowhere now, or wherever it may be.

claims.t: When I look at people now, I picture those of earlier times who were like them. The same things happen in every age, only with other people.
claims.shared: 4.27 and 10.27 both say that every age shows the same things: the times of Vespasian and of Trajan (“all the same things”), the courts of Hadrian, Antoninus and others (“only with other people”). 10.27 and 10.31 both tell me to picture the earlier ones: “set before your eyes”, “picture”.

support.quote: when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars; and with each person the one who corresponds
gives: When I look at people now
I picture those of earlier times
who were like them
support.follows: For each person I see, myself included, I should picture someone of the past who corresponds.

support.quote: set before your eyes whole plays and scenes of the same kind, all that you have come to know from your own experience or from older history
gives: I picture those of earlier times
support.follows: I should picture whole scenes of the same kind, from my own experience and from history.

support.quote: Think continually how all things of the kind that happen now happened before as well, and think of them as going to happen.
gives: The same things happen in every age
support.follows: What happens now happened before, and it will happen again.

support.quote: For all of those were of this kind, only with other people.
gives: who were like them
only with other people
support.follows: Those past courts were just like the present, only with other people.

support.quote: Think, for the sake of an example, of the times of Vespasian, and you will see all the same things
gives: The same things happen in every age
support.follows: In the times of Vespasian I would see all the same things that happen now.

claims.changed: The names of the courts and of the people paired in 10.31 are dropped, and 10.31’s “when you look at yourself, picture one of the Caesars” is folded into “people now”. 10.27’s “think of them as going to happen” is left out; the claim looks back only.

claims.t: When I go wrong, I strain after things and chase them as if they would last for ever, though those who strained with all their strength soon fell, and what people strain after is cheap. The way back is to do what fits my own constitution and be content with it: it is enough to get across this short stretch of life in good order.
claims.shared: “Strain” is the word of three passages: 4.27 “strained with all their strength”, 12.20 “everything that people strain after”, 10.31 “Why then do you strain?”. 10.34 says the same of chasing things “as if they were going to last for ever”.
claims.changed: “When I go wrong” is the editor’s frame for the label. 4.27 speaks of others who neglected what fits their constitution; the claim turns that into the way back for me.

support.quote: Why then do you strain? Why is it not enough for you to get across this short stretch in good order?
gives: strain after things
it is enough to get across this short stretch of life in good order
support.follows: There is no need for me to strain; getting across this short stretch in good order should be enough.

support.quote: you run from all things and chase all things as if they were going to last for ever
gives: chase them as if they would last for ever
support.follows: I avoid and chase everything as if it would last for ever, though life is short for all.

support.quote: see how many people strained with all their strength and a little later fell and were broken up into the elements
gives: strain after things
those who strained with all their strength soon fell
support.follows: Many people strained with all their strength and soon fell and were broken up into the elements.

support.quote: how cheap everything is that people strain after
gives: strain after things
what people strain after is cheap
support.follows: Everything people strain after is cheap.

support.quote: people who neglected to do what fits their own constitution, to hold on tight to that and to be content with that
gives: The way back is to do what fits my own constitution and be content with it
support.follows: Those I knew went wrong by neglecting what fitted their constitution instead of holding to it and being content with it.

claims.role: Whatever death turns out to be
claims.t: Death may be an end for me, or a move somewhere else. If it is another life, there are gods there too; if it is a state without sensation, I stop being a slave to the body.
claims.shared: Both passages give death in alternatives without choosing between them: an end (8.24 “your little breath be put out”; 3.3 “a state without sensation”) or a move elsewhere (8.24 “move away and be posted somewhere else”; 3.3 “to another life”).
claims.changed: 3.3 calls the body “a vessel” that is “earth and gore”; the claim says “the body”. 8.24 has a third case, the compound scattered, which the claim folds into “an end”.

support.quote: either your little compound will have to be scattered, or your little breath be put out, or else move away and be posted somewhere else
gives: Death may be an end for me
or a move somewhere else
support.follows: At death my little compound will be scattered, or my little breath put out, or the breath will move and be posted elsewhere.

support.quote: If to another life, nothing is empty of gods there either. And if in a state without sensation, you will stop putting up with pains and pleasures and being a slave to a vessel that is so much worse than the thing that serves it
gives: Death may be an end for me
or a move somewhere else
If it is another life, there are gods there too
if it is a state without sensation, I stop being a slave to the body
support.follows: If death leads to another life, there are gods there too; if to no sensation, I am freed from pains, pleasures and the body.

single.label: A small corner
single.t: Whatever praise or memory I have is held in a corner of one region, where people do not all agree, nor does anyone agree even with themselves; and the whole earth is a point.
single.quote: And besides, in a corner of this region, and not even here do all agree, nor does any one person even agree with themselves; and the whole earth is a point.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of where fame is held, not of how long it lasts. Other passages say fame is short; none says it is small. The Greek clause has no subject or verb; “praise or memory” is supplied by the editor from the sentence before.
single.follows: Praise and memory live in a small corner, among people who disagree, on an earth that is itself a point.

single.label: Attention in proportion
single.t: I give each action the attention it is worth and no more. If I do not spend myself on lesser things more than is fitting, I shall not give up in frustration.
single.quote: And here it is necessary to remember that the attention given to each action also has its own worth and proportion. For in this way you will not give up in frustration, if you do not occupy yourself with the lesser things more than is fitting.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of measuring attention to each action. It is kept as a warning against one way of failing.
single.follows: Attention to an action has its proper measure; not overspending it on lesser things keeps me from giving up in frustration.

single.label: A practice
single.t: When I kiss my child, I may say inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” Those are not words of ill omen. Nothing that points to a work of nature is, or the reaping of grain would be ill-omened too.
single.quote: A person kissing their small child, Epictetus used to say, should add inwardly: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” “Those are words of ill omen.” “Nothing is of ill omen,” he said, “that points to some work of nature. Otherwise the ears of grain being reaped is of ill omen too.”
single.why: Only this passage gives words to say to someone I love. It is Epictetus’s saying, which Marcus records.
single.follows: Epictetus taught that thinking of a loved child’s death is not ill-omened, since death is nature’s work, like the harvest.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 4.39 is 4.48, 6.42 is 6.47, 4.28 is 4.33–34, 10.31 is 10.31a, 4.27 is 4.32, 12.20 is 12.27, 8.24 is 8.25, 8.19 is 8.20b–21, 8.29 is 8.31, 11.30 is 11.34–35; 4.37 is 4.46, 7.15 is 7.18, 8.35 is 8.37; 3.3, 4.6, 10.27 and 10.34 are the same. In 8.24 “Lucilla buried Verus, then Lucilla” the Greek has no verb and “buried” is the translators’ supply; 4.39 has “buried” for the first act and “laid out” for the second, so claim 2 says only that the burier dies in turn.

Quotes the claim and leaves the lists of names in 4.39, 3.3, 6.42, 4.28, 8.24, 10.31, 12.20 and 8.29. Also left out, as repeating a claim or belonging to another section: 4.39’s philosophers and tyrants and “yesterday a little slime, tomorrow a mummy or ash”, 10.31’s “smoke and nothing”, 11.30’s grape and raisin (change), 8.29’s “the last of his own family”, and 4.28’s Clotho (accepting what fate spins, Article 3’s subject).
Reads 4.39 and 3.3 as one list in two forms: the same three kinds (healers, foretellers of death, killers in war) die after doing to others what then comes to them.
Puts 3.3 and 8.24 under “If I doubt it”: neither says that death is nothing, only what holds whichever form it takes. Ten passages feed two or more claims; 4.39 and 12.20 feed four each.
articles.limit: Other articles already say parts of this one: Article 10 that I shall soon be nowhere and forgotten and live justly meanwhile (its said-once 7.31b and its claim 4 come near claims 8 and 10 here); Article 27’s claim 3 that those who would remember me die too (claim 2); Article 29’s 9.15a that coming down is nothing bad for a thrown stone (claim 4); Article 30’s claim 1 that life now is as in the time of those already buried (claim 8); Article 17 and Article 36’s claim 4 that I go graciously (claim 6); and Article 36’s 8.55a, death as no sensation or a different kind (claim 10). What this article adds is the others: the dead before me, the skilled and the great among them, those who bury and remember them, and the exercise of going over them. Ten claims rest on thirteen of the section’s seventeen passages, and 4.39 and 12.20 feed four claims each, so the article leans on two long passages.

aside.4.37: Heraclitus on the death of each element into the next belongs with the chapter on change; the rest of the passage is about people who live as if asleep and do what was handed down.
aside.7.15: About change being necessary to the nature of the whole; it says nothing of the dead or of being forgotten, and belongs with the chapter on change.
aside.8.35: That those who sat by the coffins of Verus and Hadrian died too is said more plainly by 4.39 and 8.24. Its questions whether the dead would be aware of such mourners, or pleased, are set aside: they mock the mourning and say nothing of fame, and 6.42 and 8.19 already ask what harm ending does.

statement.t: I keep in mind that all before me, the greatest too, are dead and soon forgotten, and I put my effort into living justly.

parts.words: I keep in mind
all before me, the greatest too, are dead
soon forgotten
I put my effort into living justly

statement.kind: A remembrance and the effort that answers it
statement.form: Claims 1 to 4 are what I keep in mind: everyone dies, those who outlive me follow, fame becomes a tale, and having ended harms no one. Claim 5 is the effort Marcus himself draws from that (“What then …?” in 4.28, “here” in 6.42), and claim 6 is how to leave. Claims 7 and 8 say how the remembering is done, claim 9 is the failure it corrects, and claim 10 says what holds whatever death turns out to be.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that everyone dies, that those who outlive me follow, that death is a harbour, and what death may be. The action side gains an answer to the objection that my own deed will be forgotten or little thanked, the practice side gains thinking of my own death beside the deaths of those I love, and the claim about fame is challenged: he holds that whatever fame virtue earns does not pass away.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains an answer to the objection about my own deed: if I am told my deed will soon be forgotten, that lies outside my task. He challenges only how completely the famous are forgotten, not that I and those before me die.

items.quote: The whole race of man, both that which is and that which is to be, is condemned to die.
gives: Everyone dies
items.follows: Every human being, now living or still to come, will die.
items.context: Letter 71: the wise man, reviewing his life as Cato would, says that all people and all great cities will perish. “The whole race of man” is everyone, now and to come.

items.quote: we follow closely those whom we have lost
gives: will soon follow
items.follows: Those who mourn the dead follow them after only a short interval.
items.context: Letter 99 consoles a father on his son’s death. “We” are the bereaved, and “those whom we have lost” are the dead they mourn.

items.quote: it is the harbour, where we must some day put in, which we may never refuse to enter
gives: as a passenger gets off at the harbour
items.follows: Death is a harbour that every voyage reaches and that no one may refuse to enter.
items.context: Letter 70 likens life to a voyage. “It” is the voyage’s end, death, which fools take for a dangerous reef; whoever reaches it early has no more cause to complain than a quick sailor.

items.quote: the soul at death is either sent forth into a better life, destined to dwell with deity amid greater radiance and calm, or else, at least, without suffering any harm to itself, it will be mingled with nature again, and will return to the universe
gives: or a move somewhere else
If it is another life, there are gods there too
items.follows: At death the soul either goes on to a better life with the divine or returns unharmed into nature.
items.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: great souls should accept whatever fate brings, because at death the soul either goes to a better life with the divine or returns unharmed into nature.

items.label: action
items.t: When I am told that my deed will soon be forgotten, or bring me few thanks, I answer that this lies outside my task. My thoughts are on the deed itself, and I know that it is honourable.
items.why: Marcus answers forgetting in general: everlasting remembrance is empty (4.28), and justice is the one thing worth effort. Seneca adds an objection put to the doer about his own deed, that it will be forgotten or thanked little, and answers it with the deed’s own honour.

support.quote: “Your deed will speedily be forgotten,” or “Your fellow-citizens will offer you scant thanks.” He will answer: “All these matters lie outside my task. My thoughts are on the deed itself. I know that this is honourable.
gives: my deed will soon be forgotten, or bring me few thanks
this lies outside my task
My thoughts are on the deed itself, and I know that it is honourable
support.follows: Told that his deed will be forgotten or thanked little, the good man says this is not his concern: the deed is honourable.
support.context: Letter 76: a brave man about to give his life for an honourable deed, with no joy to expect from it. The objections are put to him, and “the deed” is that act.

items.label: practice
items.t: I think as often of my own death as of the deaths of those I love, and I remember that death keeps no order of age: whatever can happen at any time can happen today.
items.why: Marcus’s practice here is to go over the dead, and 11.30 gives words to say over a child: “Tomorrow, perhaps, you will die.” Seneca adds my own death beside the deaths of those I love, thought of continually, and says outright that death keeps no order of age.

support.quote: let us continually think as much about our own mortality as about that of all those we love
gives: I think as often of my own death as of the deaths of those I love
support.follows: I should think as continually of my own death as of the deaths of those I love.
support.context: Letter 63, on grief for friends: Seneca wept too much for Serenus, a younger friend he never thought would die first. “Those we love” are friends like him.

support.quote: Now is the time for you to reflect, not only that all things are mortal, but also that their mortality is subject to no fixed law. Whatever can happen at any time can happen to-day.
gives: death keeps no order of age
whatever can happen at any time can happen today
support.follows: Everything dies, and in no fixed order, so whatever can happen at any time can happen today.
support.context: Letter 63, on the death of Seneca’s younger friend Serenus: “no fixed law” means that the young need not die after the old, as Seneca had assumed.

items.t: Seneca disagrees about the fame of virtue. He holds that whatever fame virtue earns cannot pass away, and that a few great men hold out against oblivion for a long time (Ep. 79.17, 21.5). He grants that the dead do not feel what is said of them, and in 21.5 that even the great go at last into the same silence. He is not consistent: in 21.5 the silence comes at last; in 79.17 the fame does not pass.

support.quote: If there is any reward that virtue receives at the hands of fame, not even this can pass away.
support.follows: Whatever fame virtue earns cannot pass away.
support.context: Letter 79: virtue may be hidden or suppressed in its own day, but later generations will judge it fairly. The “reward” is the fame virtue receives from them.
