support.quote: We ourselves, indeed, shall not be affected by the talk of posterity; nevertheless, posterity will cherish and celebrate us even though we are not conscious thereof.
support.follows: The dead will not feel what later people say of them, yet later people will honour them.
support.context: Letter 79, closing the argument that virtue is never lost to view. “We” are those whose worth was not known in their lifetime.

support.quote: some few great men will raise their heads above it, and, though destined at the last to depart into the same realms of silence, will battle against oblivion and maintain their ground for long
support.follows: A few great men stand above the flood of time for long, though at the last they too go into silence.
support.context: Letter 21, on the renown Seneca’s letters will bring Lucilius. “It” is “the deep flood of time” that will roll over us all.

amend.t: ; if I am told my deed will soon be forgotten, that lies outside my task
; yet whatever fame virtue earns does not pass away, though the dead do not feel it

searches: where are they, where is he
nothing new, same round, same things
slayer, follows him, gone before, on ahead
as if it would last, live for ever, eternal

rejected.why: “The slayer soon follows the slain”: about gladiators killed early or late in the games. Ep. 99.6 says the same of mourners and is quoted.
“Posted on ahead”: the same consolation as Ep. 99.6, which is quoted and says it more plainly.
“We shall soon come to the goal which this friend has reached”: backs the second claim, but Ep. 99.6 says it without a condition.
“Slipped at once from the memory of men”: about favourites who lose their position, not about the dead.
Grandees sunk in oblivion while Epicurus’s friend is remembered: the same argument as Ep. 21.5, which is quoted.
“He still lives! … passed over into posterity”: praise of one man who died young; Ep. 79.17 states the view itself.
Fame is the shadow of virtue and may come late: Ep. 79.17, the conclusion of the same argument, is quoted.
Epicurus’s renown shone after his death: an example for Ep. 79.17, which is quoted.
“Equal in death”: about rank and funeral monuments, not about the skilled dying; Ep. 71.15 says that all die.
Great cities will be blotted out by time: in a letter on the burning of Lyons, about cities still standing.
Alexander learns how small the earth is: about his false greatness; it would only meet 8.19, a said-once item, which takes no backing.
Losing those we love is like trees losing leaves: a consolation that they can be replaced, not that those left behind fall too.
The same harbour image as Ep. 70.3, but it leads into when one may choose to die.
“Let us die in harbour”: about retiring from public life, not about death.
How many are arranging funerals right now: says only that death is common, which Article 3 already has.
About proving that philosophy’s words are deeds; not about the dead or being forgotten.
Nothing that vanishes is annihilated: about change and return, the subject of the chapter on change.
Heraclitus’s river: about change, the subject of the chapter on change.
“Important to die honourably”: advice to a man deciding whether to end his life.
Death went before us and follows us: about not existing before birth.
Madness not to reflect that one is mortal: said against luxurious kitchens.
Every day counts toward death: about the shortness of life, the subject of Article 35.
Every life is short beside eternity: about the shortness of life, the subject of Article 35.
Remember how noble it is to round out one’s life before death: about hurrying to finish, not about the dead.

articles.title: The length of a life and the use of its time

claims.t: How long I live does not matter. The longest life comes to the same thing as the shortest, and dying many years from now rather than tomorrow is no great gain.
claims.shared: Three passages set a long life beside a short one and find no difference that counts. 2.12 says it “makes no difference” how long one sees the same things, 4.42 asks “what difference is there” between a child of three days and a Nestor, and 4.38 calls many years from now against tomorrow “nothing great”.
claims.changed: 2.12 and 4.42 speak of anyone’s life, 4.38 of the day I die; the claim says “I” throughout. It keeps the conclusion and drops the grounds: in 2.12 that one loses only the present moment (it returns in claim 5), in 4.42 the endless time on either side. 2.12b’s own ground, that all things are of one kind and come round again, is dropped.

support.quote: it makes no difference whether a person will see the same things for a hundred years, or for two hundred, or for time without limit
gives: How long I live does not matter
support.follows: All things come round the same, and seeing them for a hundred years, two hundred, or without end makes no difference.

support.quote: So the longest comes to the same thing as the shortest.
gives: The longest life comes to the same thing as the shortest
support.follows: The longest life and the shortest come to the same thing.

support.quote: In this, then, what difference is there between a child three days old and a Nestor of three generations?
gives: How long I live does not matter
The longest life comes to the same thing as the shortest
support.follows: Set against endless time, a child three days old and a man who lived three generations do not differ.

support.quote: so too think it nothing great that it should be many years from now rather than tomorrow
gives: How long I live does not matter
dying many years from now rather than tomorrow is no great gain
support.follows: That my death should come many years from now rather than tomorrow is to be counted nothing great.

claims.role: The time is limited and running out
claims.t: A limit of time is marked out for me, just as my body has been given a fixed weight, and I am content with my time as I am with the size of body I was given. My life is being used up day by day, and death is coming.
claims.shared: 2.1 and 6.44 both say that time has been “marked out” or “marked off” for me, as a limit or as an amount. 3.1 and 4.14 both say that death is on its way: one “comes nearer to death at every moment” (3.1), and “what must come hangs over you” (4.14).
claims.changed: 2.1 draws from the limit that I must use the time; 6.44 that I should be content with it, as with the size of body, so many pounds, that I was given. The claim keeps the contentment here and leaves the use to claim 3. 4.14 does not name death: “what must come” is read as death, as the translators’ note reads it.

support.quote: a limit of time has been marked out for you
gives: A limit of time is marked out for me
support.follows: A limit has been set to my time, and I must come to see that it has.

support.quote: For just as you are content with the amount of matter that has been marked off for you, so too with time.
gives: A limit of time is marked out for me
my body has been given a fixed weight
I am content with my time as I am with the size of body I was given
support.follows: As I am content with the amount of body marked off for me, I am to be content with the time marked off for me.

support.quote: You are not upset, are you, that you weigh so many pounds and not three hundred?
gives: my body has been given a fixed weight
support.follows: I am not upset that I weigh so many pounds and not three hundred.

support.quote: life is being used up day by day and a smaller part of it is left
gives: My life is being used up day by day
support.follows: Each day uses up some of my life and leaves less of it.

support.quote: one comes nearer to death at every moment
gives: death is coming
support.follows: Every moment brings a person nearer to death.

support.quote: What must come hangs over you.
gives: death is coming
support.follows: What must happen to me already hangs over me.

claims.t: I hurry to become good and to come to my own rescue while it is still possible; once my time is gone, it will not be possible again.
claims.shared: “While it is possible” stands in both 4.14 and 3.15, and 2.1 says the other side of it: once the time is gone “it will not be possible again”. “Hurry” stands in both 3.1 and 3.15, each time after a “so”.
claims.changed: What I hurry to do is said differently: 4.14 says become good, 3.15 come to my own rescue, 2.1 clear away the clouds. The claim keeps the first two side by side and leaves out the image of the clouds.

support.quote: So one must hurry
gives: I hurry
support.follows: Because death comes nearer and the mind may give out first, one must hurry.

support.quote: So hurry to the end
gives: I hurry
support.follows: Since he will not read what he saved for old age, Marcus must hurry on to the end.

support.quote: While you live, while it is possible, become good.
gives: become good
while it is still possible
support.follows: While I am alive and still able to, I am to become good.

support.quote: come to your own rescue, if you care at all about yourself, while it is possible
gives: to come to my own rescue
while it is still possible
support.follows: If I care about myself at all, I am to come to my own aid while I still can.

support.quote: If you do not use it to clear away the clouds, it will be gone, you will be gone, and it will not be possible again.
gives: once my time is gone, it will not be possible again
support.follows: If I do not use my time to clear away the clouds, it and I will be gone, with no second chance.

claims.t: I fail by putting things off: I am given time again and again and make no use of it, and I store up reading for old age that I will never read. To find my way back, I stop wandering and let go of empty hopes.
claims.shared: 2.1 and 3.15 both find the failure in deferring: 2.1 in “putting these things off”, 3.15 in what “you were putting away for yourself for old age”.
claims.changed: The Greek verbs differ: 2.1 has “put off”, 3.15 “store away”. The claim reads 3.15’s storing up reading for old age as a way of putting things off. The way back is said only by 3.15.

support.quote: Remember how long you have been putting these things off, and how many times you have been given a set time by the gods and make no use of it.
gives: putting things off
I am given time again and again and make no use of it
support.follows: Marcus has long put these things off, and has again and again been given time and not used it.

support.quote: For you are not going to read either your little notebooks or the deeds of the ancient Romans and Greeks and the extracts from the writings, which you were putting away for yourself for old age.
gives: putting things off
I store up reading for old age that I will never read
support.follows: Marcus will not read the notes, histories and extracts he was saving for his old age.

support.quote: Stop wandering.
gives: I stop wandering
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to stop wandering.

support.quote: letting go of empty hopes
gives: let go of empty hopes
support.follows: Marcus is to let go of empty hopes.

claims.t: A longer life may not be the gain it seems. Even if I lived longer, at death I would lose only the present moment, since no one can lose the past or the future; and my mind might not stay able to understand things, for my grasp of things can give out first, while my breathing and eating go on.
claims.shared: 2.12 and 3.1 both suppose a longer life (“Even if you are going to live three thousand years”; “if a person were to live longer”), and both give a reason why it may not bring what it seems: in 2.12 the longest-lived loses no more than the one who dies soonest; 3.1 says it is unclear whether the mind will last.
claims.changed: “A longer life may not be the gain it seems” is the editor’s summary of two different reasons, and the claim keeps both. “At death” is the editor’s gloss on 2.12’s “lose”. 2.12 supposes thousands of years; the claim says only “longer”, as 3.1 does. The “since” and the “for” are Marcus’s own “For” in 2.12 and 3.1.

support.quote: Even if you are going to live three thousand years, or even three times ten thousand
gives: Even if I lived longer
support.follows: Marcus supposes a life of three thousand years, or even thirty thousand.

support.quote: the one who lives longest and the one who will die soonest lose an equal amount
gives: A longer life may not be the gain it seems
support.follows: Whoever lives longest loses no more than whoever dies soonest.

support.quote: For the present is the only thing a person is going to be deprived of
gives: at death I would lose only the present moment
support.follows: The only thing anyone is going to be deprived of is the present.

support.quote: For no one could lose either the past or the future
gives: no one can lose the past or the future
support.follows: No one can lose the past or the future, since no one has them.

support.quote: if a person were to live longer, this at least is unclear, whether their mind will later on be equal, unchanged, to the understanding of things
gives: A longer life may not be the gain it seems
Even if I lived longer
my mind might not stay able to understand things
support.follows: If I live longer, it is not certain that my mind will still be fit to understand things.

support.quote: the grasp of things and the power to follow them give out first
gives: my grasp of things can give out first
support.follows: The grasp of things and the power to follow them give out before the rest of a person does.

support.quote: there will be no lack of breathing, of taking nourishment
gives: while my breathing and eating go on
support.follows: A person who begins to lose their wits still goes on breathing and taking food.

single.label: A practice
single.t: To help myself think little of death, I call to mind those who clung on to life a long time, and I ask what more they have than those who died young.
single.quote: A layman’s help toward contempt of death, but an effective one all the same, is to call back to mind those who clung on and lingered in life. What more do they have, then, than those who died before their time?
single.why: Only 4.42 gives this exercise: recalling the long-lived dead. Its last sentence, on the child and Nestor, feeds claim 1; this part is the practice.
single.follows: Recalling people who held on to life a long time is a plain but effective help toward thinking little of death.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek instead of Casaubon. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s. In modern editions 2.12 is 2.14, 4.42 is 4.50, 2.1 is 2.4, 4.14 is 4.17, 3.15 is 3.14, 4.38 is 4.47 and 6.44 is 6.49; 3.1 is the same.

Holds two things in one statement that a reader may hear as opposed: the length of a life does not matter, and I must hurry. The passages hold both: no length is worth more than another, but the time I have is limited and being used up.

Reads 3.15’s reading stored up for old age as putting things off, beside 2.1’s “putting these things off”. The Greek verbs differ (2.1 “put off”, 3.15 “store away”); the shared word “putting” is the English’s.
Reads “what must come” (4.14) as death, as the translators’ note does, and places the longer life supposed by 2.12 and 3.1 under “If I doubt it”: what holds if my time turns out not to be short.
articles.limit: Article 10 already says that all I live is the present and that how long I live does not matter, Article 17 that my time is short, Article 32 (said once, 9.31b) that whoever dies very old is brought level with whoever died before their time, Article 24 (said once, 8.21a, beside the same Ep. 1.2) that I must not put off becoming good, and Article 9 (said once, 6.27e) that it is shameful if my soul gives out before my body. What this article adds is the two held together: no length is worth more than another, yet the time is limited and being used up, so its use cannot wait; and that a longer life may not be the gain it seems. It stands in some tension with Article 31’s claim 5, that my soul has reached its goal at whatever point my life stops, since here I can still run out of time to become good; and 3.1 feeds three claims, so the article leans on it.

statement.t: How long I live does not matter; my time has a limit, and I hurry to become good while it is still possible.

parts.words: How long I live does not matter
my time has a limit
I hurry to become good while it is still possible

statement.kind: Two grounds that seem to pull apart, and the use that answers them
statement.form: Claim 1 says the length of a life counts for nothing; claim 2 that the time is limited and running out. They do not conflict: no length is worth more than another, but whatever length I have is being used up. Claim 3 is what I do about it, claim 4 how I fail at it, and claim 5 what holds if I live long after all.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author: young and old alike are short-lived beside eternity, a limit is fixed and life is taken a little each day, I hasten, and while I postpone, life speeds by. In action, Practice and If I doubt it each gain something Marcus does not say here, and claim 5 is limited: age need not harm the mind, though Seneca also says that wisdom is hard to learn when old.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains an end point: once I have made my life complete, I wait in peace for the rest of my time.

items.quote: all of us, whether young or old, live, in comparison with eternity, on the same level as regards our shortness of life
gives: The longest life comes to the same thing as the shortest
items.follows: Measured against eternity, the young and the old alike have the same short life.
items.context: Letter 99 copies Seneca’s letter to Marullus, whose small son had died: what to say to anyone who mourns someone who died young. “All of us” is everyone.

items.quote: There is indeed a limit fixed for us, just where the remorseless law of Fate has fixed it
gives: A limit of time is marked out for me
items.follows: Each of us has a limit to life, fixed where Fate has fixed it.
items.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning ahead, written after Cornelius Senecio died suddenly in the midst of his plans. “A limit” is the end of each person’s life.

items.quote: For every day a little of our life is taken from us
gives: My life is being used up day by day
items.follows: Each day takes a little of our life from us.
items.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca takes up a commonplace Lucilius once argued, that we die every day. “Our life” is each person’s span, lessened day by day.

items.quote: Proceed, then, Lucilius, and hasten, lest you yourself be compelled to learn in your old age, as is the case with me.
gives: I hurry
items.follows: Lucilius should hasten with his study now, so as not to be learning it in old age, as Seneca is.
items.context: Letter 76, on learning wisdom in old age: Seneca, old, attends lectures on how to be a good man, and urges Lucilius to hasten to that study now.

items.quote: While we are postponing, life speeds by.
gives: putting things off
items.follows: While we put things off, life runs past us.
items.context: Letter 1, on saving time: Seneca urges Lucilius to hold every hour and lay hold of today’s task. “Postponing” is leaving that task to tomorrow.

items.label: action
items.t: I hurry to make my life complete before death comes, and then I wait in peace for the rest of my time: a happy life is not made happier by being longer.
items.why: Marcus says that the length of a life does not matter and that I must hurry, and leaves the two side by side. Seneca joins them: I hurry to make my life complete, and then I wait in peace for the time that remains.

support.quote: Hasten ahead, then, dearest Lucilius
gives: I hurry
support.follows: Lucilius is to hurry on.
support.context: Letter 32, on progress: life is short and others hold Lucilius back, so Seneca urges him to hasten, as if an enemy were at his back.

support.quote: remembering continually what a noble thing it is to round out your life before death comes, and then await in peace the remaining portion of your time
gives: make my life complete before death comes
I wait in peace for the rest of my time
support.follows: It is a noble thing to complete one’s life before death comes and then wait in peace for the time that remains.
support.context: Letter 32, on progress: Seneca urges Lucilius to hasten as if an enemy were at his back. To “round out your life” is to make it complete, reaching the happy life before death.

support.quote: for such a life is not made happier for being longer
gives: a happy life is not made happier by being longer
support.follows: A life that is already happy does not become happier by lasting longer.
support.context: Letter 32, on progress, end of Seneca’s plea to hasten: “such a life” is the happy life, held by one who has rounded out his life before death.

items.label: practice
items.t: I begin to live at once and count each day as a separate life. If I put the finishing touches to my life every day, I am never short of time.
items.why: Marcus’s practice in this section looks at other people, the long-lived dead. Seneca gives one for each of my own days: complete my life daily, so that time is never lacking.

support.quote: begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life
gives: I begin to live at once and count each day as a separate life
support.follows: One should start living now and treat each day as a whole life of its own.
support.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning ahead, after a friend’s sudden death: Seneca’s conclusion, set against those who live for hope alone.

support.quote: One who daily puts the finishing touches to his life is never in want of time.
gives: If I put the finishing touches to my life every day, I am never short of time
support.follows: Whoever completes his life each day never runs short of time.
support.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning ahead: the flaw Seneca names is a life always left unfinished, with part of it put off. “His life” is one’s own.

items.label: doubt
items.role: Not knowing where the limit is
items.t: I do not know how near my limit is, so I set my mind as if I had come to the very end, and I put nothing off.
items.why: Claim 5 asks what holds if my life turns out longer. Seneca answers from the other side: I cannot know how long it will be, and that alone is reason to act as if I were at the end.

support.quote: but none of us knows how near he is to this limit. Therefore, let us so order our minds as if we had come to the very end. Let us postpone nothing.
gives: I do not know how near my limit is
I set my mind as if I had come to the very end
I put nothing off
support.follows: No one knows how near the end is, so one should think as if at the end and put nothing off.
support.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning ahead, after Senecio died suddenly with his plans unfinished. “This limit” is the end of life that Fate has fixed.

items.t: Seneca, himself old, finds age in his body but not in his mind (Ep. 26.2), and holds old age, its passions spent, to be the best time to reach wisdom (Ep. 68.14). Yet he also says that wisdom is hard to learn thoroughly when old (Ep. 76.5). So age need not bring the failure that claim 5 fears, though it may.

support.quote: I feel that age has done no damage to my mind, though I feel its effects on my constitution
support.follows: Seneca’s age has worn his body but has not harmed his mind.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: Seneca, now among the worn-out, takes stock of himself. “Age” is his own old age, felt in the body, not, he says, in the mind.

support.quote: You need not think, however, that any time of life is more fitted to the attainment of a sound mind than that which has gained the victory over itself by many trials
support.follows: No time of life suits gaining a sound mind better than one that has mastered itself through many trials.
support.context: Letter 68, on wisdom and retirement: Lucilius asks what use is wisdom learned only at the end. “That” time of life is old age, past the passions of youth.

amend.t: ; once I have made my life complete, I wait in peace for the rest of my time
; yet age can leave my mind unharmed while my body feels it

rejected.why: “It matters not how long the action is spun out, but how good the acting is.” In a letter on taking one’s own life, where it argues one may stop when one chooses.
If old age shatters the mind he will leave life. Near 3.1, but it is about ending one’s own life; not written into a personal rule.
Few reach extreme old age without impairment. Backs claim 5, but it is an argument for ending one’s life before the debt falls due.
The wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can. On taking one’s own life.
What difference does it make how soon you depart. Already used in Article 6.
His age incomplete, his life complete. Close to w1; 32.3 joins completion to hurrying, which is this article’s point.
The old man is very little superior to the child. “Very little” is not “the same”; 99.31 says it outright.
A balanced mind knows that a day differs not a whit from eternity. About freedom from worry over the future; would need explaining to back claim 1.
One day is equal to all days through resemblance. Nearer 2.12’s sameness of all things, which the article leaves out.
An honourable life cut to a single day is equally honourable. Same point as 32.3, which is quoted.
The time we spend in living is but a point. On the brevity of life, not on length not mattering; near Article 10’s instant.
Time cannot suffice even for necessary things. Against superfluous study; 3.15 is about reading saved for old age, not superfluous reading.
When time is so scant, madness to learn superfluous things. Against dialectic; same reason as 49.5.
Most of life passes in doing ill, doing nothing, or what is beside the point. A further way of failing; left out to keep the items few.
They postpone everything; such persons do not live but prepare to live. Same as 1.2, in a letter against hair-splitters.
The fool is always getting ready to live. Close to claim 4, but 1.2 says “postponing” in so many words.
Old men preparing for new careers. About beginning late, not about saving things for old age.
Life is short and we make it shorter by fresh beginnings. About inconstancy; 32.3 from the same letter is quoted.
Weeping that one will not be alive a thousand years from now. An argument about not existing before and after, not about length.
Each day counts to the credit of death. Says what 24.20 says; one witness suffices.
We are worn away and every day reduces our powers. About the manner of dying in old age, which 26.4 calls easy.
Exercise of the mind need not be hampered by old age. A remark in a letter on bodily exercise; 26.2 and 68.14 say it of the mind itself.
Philosophy is not to be postponed until leisure. About leisure, not old age; 1.2 is used for postponing.
Late starters ply the spur; our time of life is best for these pursuits. 68.14 states the point about the mind; 76.5 is used for hastening.
Death interrupts life and does not steal it. On things returning; Article 33’s ground, not this one.
An untimely death after a full life. Same point as 32.3; also rejected in Article 6.

articles.title: Meeting death well

claims.t: Dying is one of nature’s works, and it is also good for nature.
claims.shared: Three passages say that death is one of nature’s things: 9.3 “one of the things nature wills”, 10.36 “one of the things that accord with nature”, 2.10 “a work of nature”. 9.3 and 10.36 even share the words “this too is one of the things”.
claims.changed: The claim uses 2.10’s word, “work”, for all three. Only 2.10 adds that death is also good for nature.

support.quote: since this too is one of the things nature wills
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works
support.follows: Death too is one of the things that nature wills.

support.quote: for this too is one of the things that accord with nature
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works
support.follows: Being untied from my own people at death, without being pulled back, is one of the things that accord with nature.

support.quote: This, though, is not only a work of nature but also something good for nature.
gives: Dying is one of nature’s works
it is also good for nature
support.follows: Dying is a work of nature, and it is also good for nature.

claims.t: I have already lived through many small deaths: activities that stopped, and ages of my life that gave way to the next. None of them was bad, and neither is the ending of my whole life.
claims.shared: 9.19 and 12.17 both say that the ending of an activity is “nothing bad” and that, “in the same way”, neither is the ending of a whole life. 9.3 and 9.19 both name the ages of life (being young and growing old; childhood, youth, old age) as changes of the same kind as dying; 9.19 calls each of them “a death”.
claims.changed: 12.17 adds “at the right time” to both endings; the claim leaves the time to claim 3. 9.19 says the changes are “nothing terrible”, 12.17 that they suffer “nothing bad”; the claim says “bad”. 9.3 also names teeth, beard, grey hair and childbirth, and 9.19 the stages of a life under grandfather, mother and father; the claim keeps the ages. “Small deaths” is the editor’s word for 9.19’s “every change of these too is a death”.

support.quote: For as it is with being young and growing old, with growing and reaching one’s prime, with getting teeth and a beard and grey hair, with begetting and carrying a child and giving birth, and with all the other natural activities that the seasons of life bring, so it is with being dissolved.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next
support.follows: Dying is a change like growing old, getting grey hair or giving birth: one of the natural activities the seasons of life bring.

support.quote: The ending of an activity, the stopping and, as it were, the death of an impulse, of a judgment: nothing bad.
gives: activities that stopped
None of them was bad
support.follows: When an activity, an impulse or a judgment ends, nothing bad has happened.

support.quote: Now pass on to the ages of life: childhood, for example, adolescence, youth, old age. For every change of these too is a death. Surely that is nothing terrible?
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next
I have already lived through many small deaths
None of them was bad
support.follows: Each passage from one age of life to the next is a kind of death, and none of them is terrible.

support.quote: In the same way, then, neither is the ending and stopping and change of your whole life.
gives: neither is the ending of my whole life
support.follows: The ending of my whole life is no more terrible than the smaller endings before it.

support.quote: Any single activity, whichever it is, that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad in that it has stopped
gives: activities that stopped
None of them was bad
support.follows: An activity that stops at the right time suffers nothing bad by having stopped.

support.quote: In the same way, then, the sum made up of all the actions, which is a life, if it stops at the right time, suffers nothing bad just in this respect, that it has stopped
gives: neither is the ending of my whole life
support.follows: A life, the sum of a person’s actions, suffers nothing bad by stopping, if it stops at the right time.

claims.t: It is nature, not a tyrant or an unjust judge, that sends me away, and nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit. My death is not a bad thing, and when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole, it is a good one.
claims.shared: 12.17 and 12.27 both say that the end of a life is fixed by another and not by me: “The right time and the limit are given by nature”; “what is complete is fixed by the one who … ; you are responsible for neither”.
claims.changed: 12.27 names nature as the one who sends me away, then says what is complete is fixed by “the one” responsible for the putting together and the dissolving, a masculine word in the Greek (god, or the magistrate of the image); the claim calls it nature, as 12.17 does. 12.27 does not say whose putting together and dissolving is meant; the claim reads them as mine, from “you are responsible for neither”, and keeps only that the limit is not my doing. 12.17 says death is not bad “if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial”; the claim drops that condition, and “not I” stands in for its first half.

support.quote: sent away from the city not by a tyrant, nor by an unjust judge, but by nature, which brought you in
gives: It is nature, not a tyrant or an unjust judge, that sends me away
support.follows: It is nature, which brought me into life, that sends me out of it, not a tyrant or an unjust judge.

support.quote: For what is complete is fixed by the one who was responsible then for the putting together and is responsible now for the dissolving; you are responsible for neither.
gives: nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit
support.follows: What is complete is fixed by the one responsible for the putting together and the dissolving, and neither is my doing.

support.quote: The right time and the limit are given by nature
gives: nature, not I, fixes the right time and the limit
support.follows: It is nature that gives the right time and the limit of a life.

support.quote: So for each person the stopping of life is not a bad thing, since it is not a shameful thing either, if indeed it is both outside one’s choice and not unsocial; and it is a good thing, if indeed it comes at the right time for the whole, benefits the whole and is carried along with the whole.
gives: My death is not a bad thing
when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole, it is a good one
support.follows: If it is not chosen and not against the community, the end of a life is not shameful and so not bad; it is good when it comes at the right time for the whole.

claims.t: When my death comes I go graciously, not as one torn away, and with goodwill toward the people I leave.
claims.shared: 12.27 and 10.36 both tell the one who is dying to “go away” and to be “gracious” (the same Greek word in both). 9.3 and 10.36 both ask for goodwill toward the people left behind: “care for them and bear with them gently”, “friendly, well-disposed and gracious”.
claims.changed: In 12.27 one goes graciously because the one who dismisses is gracious; in 10.36 one stays gracious toward the people who want one gone. The claim keeps the manner and drops both reasons. 9.3’s waiting for death and being well pleased with it are left to Article 10, which says them.

support.quote: So go away graciously, for the one who dismisses you is gracious too.
gives: I go graciously
support.follows: I should leave graciously, since the one who dismisses me is gracious too.

support.quote: Still, do not for that reason go away less kindly toward them, but keeping to your own habit: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.
gives: I go graciously
with goodwill toward the people I leave
support.follows: Even toward people who are glad to see me go, I should leave as I always was with them: friendly, well-disposed and gracious.

support.quote: not as one being torn away; rather, just as in a person who dies an easy death the little soul slips easily out of the body, such too must the withdrawal from these people be.
gives: not as one torn away
support.follows: I should leave the people of my life not as one torn away, but as easily as the soul slips from the body in an easy death.

support.quote: rather one must even care for them and bear with them gently
gives: with goodwill toward the people I leave
support.follows: One must care for the people one is leaving and bear with them gently.

claims.t: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving. They do not share my principles, and even those I struggled for want me to go; there is nothing here to hold on to.
claims.shared: 9.3 and 10.36 both give the same help for dying: look at the people you are leaving and you will go more easily (9.3 “put you at ease”, 10.36 “go out more easily”). Both end on what would “hold” one in life: 9.3 only the company of people with the same principles, 10.36 nothing, since even one’s partners want one gone.
claims.changed: 9.3 calls this a layman’s rule and adds that one must not take offence at these people; 10.36 says that even a good and wise person has someone glad to see him go. The claim keeps the looking and what it shows, and leaves the goodwill to claim 4. 9.3e says “the things you are about to leave”; the people are read from the words the edition restores in brackets for a gap (“[at what kind of] characters”) and from the “them” that follows, and the translators’ note leaves open whether “the things” include people.

support.quote: what will most put you at ease about death is to stop and look at the things you are about to leave
gives: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving
support.follows: What most eases a person about death is to stop and look at what they are about to leave.

support.quote: So you will think of this as you die, and you will go out more easily, reasoning: “I am leaving a life of this kind, in which my very partners, for whom I struggled so much, prayed, took thought, those very people want me to go
gives: To go more easily, I look at the people I am leaving
even those I struggled for want me to go
support.follows: Dying, I will go more easily if I remember that even the partners I struggled and prayed for want me to go.

support.quote: remember that the release will not be from people who hold the same principles as you
gives: They do not share my principles
support.follows: The people death releases me from are not people who share my principles.

support.quote: For this alone, if anything at all, would pull one back and hold one in life: if one were allowed to live together with those who have made the same principles their own.
gives: there is nothing here to hold on to
support.follows: The one thing that could hold a person in life is living with people who share their principles.

support.quote: Why, then, would anyone hold on to a longer stay here?
gives: there is nothing here to hold on to
support.follows: There is no reason to hold on to a longer stay in such a life.

single.label: A rest
single.t: Death is a rest: from the impacts on my senses, from being pulled by impulse like a puppet on strings, from working through thoughts step by step, and from serving the body.
single.quote: Death is a rest from the impacts on the senses, from the tugging of impulse on the puppet strings, from the step-by-step course of thought, and from service to the flesh.
single.why: Only this passage says what death gives: rest from what has worked on me all my life. No other passage of the section says it, so it is not fused.
single.follows: Death ends the blows on the senses, the pull of impulse, the step-by-step working of thought and the service of the body.

single.label: When I am afraid
single.t: If I am afraid of death, I am like a child afraid of a work of nature. The way back is to look at dying by itself and take apart what I have imagined into it, until I judge it to be nothing but a work of nature.
single.quote: if a person looks at it by itself alone and, by dividing up the notion, dissolves the things imagined into it, they will no longer judge it to be anything other than a work of nature; and if anyone is afraid of a work of nature, they are a child.
single.why: Only this passage says how to take the fear apart: look at dying by itself and remove what is imagined into it. 8.55 also speaks of fear, but argues by cases.
single.follows: Looked at by itself, with what was imagined into it taken away, dying is only a work of nature, and fearing it is childish.

single.label: Either way
single.t: If I fear death, I fear either having no sensation or having a different kind. With none, I will sense nothing bad; with a different kind, I will be a different living thing and will not have stopped living.
single.quote: Whoever fears death fears either the absence of sensation or sensation of another kind. But if you no longer have sensation, you will have no sensation of anything bad either; and if you acquire a rather different kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living thing, and you will not stop living.
single.why: Only this passage argues by both cases. It holds whatever death turns out to be, even if it is not the natural change the other passages describe, which is why it stands under doubt.
single.follows: Whatever death is, it brings either nothing to feel, so nothing bad, or a new kind of feeling and a life that goes on.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 12.27 is 12.34–36, 2.10 is 2.12b, 12.17 is 12.23, 9.19 is 9.21, 8.55 is 8.58 and 6.26 is 6.28, while 9.3 and 10.36 are the same.

Leaves out most of 12.27. Its middle paragraph (12.35: to someone for whom only what comes at the right time is good, and to whom a longer or shorter look at the universe makes no difference, not even death is a thing to fear), “five years or three” and the three acts turn on how long a life is, the subject of the section on the shortness of life (Article 35); claim 3 takes the right time from 12.17. Its first remark, that even those who judge pleasure good have despised death, is left out because its “despise death” pulls against 9.3’s “Do not despise death”, a tension the translators kept visible.

Reads “the one who was responsible then for the putting together” in 12.27 as nature, since the same passage has just named nature as the one who brought you in. The Greek word is masculine, so it may be god or the magistrate of the play image.

Leaves out the end of 9.3, “Come sooner, death, in case I too should perhaps forget myself”. It is a cry of weariness at living among people of other principles, not a way of meeting death, and the article does not turn it into a rule.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one: Article 10 (claim 4) that I wait for death cheerfully as a dissolving according to nature, so 9.3’s waiting is left to it; Article 17 that dying is one of the acts of my life, near claim 1; Article 33 that my death is a change of the same kind as my birth and that nature aimed at my ending (claims 3 and 4), and Article 32 that change is nothing bad for what is changed (claims 5 and 6), both near claim 2; Article 34 that I leave life with good grace (claim 6) and that death is an end or a move (claim 10, which 8.55 here says again); Article 6 that what comes is timely. What this section adds is the small deaths of my own ages and activities, the right time for the whole as the ground for calling death good, and above all how I leave the people of my life: graciously, not torn away, with goodwill, helped by seeing that nothing among them holds me. Claim 5 rests on a bleak view of those people that only two passages hold, and the article argues that death is not bad rather than proving it.

statement.t: My death is nature’s work, like the passing of my ages before it, so I go graciously and leave the people of my life kindly.

parts.words: My death is nature’s work
like the passing of my ages before it
I go graciously
leave the people of my life kindly

inferences.why: 12.27 says “So go away graciously” and 10.36 grounds going without force in nature; drawing graciousness from nature and the ages of life together is the editor’s step.

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Claims 1 to 3 are the ground: death is nature’s work, like the small deaths of my ages and activities, and its time is set by nature, not by me. Claims 4 and 5 are the conduct that follows, how I leave the people of my life and what makes leaving easier; the editor’s “so” joins the ground to that conduct only, not to any clause another author adds. The said-once items add what death gives, how fear is undone, and what holds if death is not what the ground says.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the ages of a life gain a second author. Practice gains a daily rehearsal, When it breaks gains the longing for death, and If I doubt it gains what remains of me either way. He limits claim 3, since death keeps a look of evil, and claim 5, since those I hold dear can be a reason to stay.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement takes one more clause, which stands apart from Marcus’s ground: I neither rush out of life nor long for death. The ground stands, and two claims beneath it are limited.

items.quote: We lose our childhood, then our boyhood, and then our youth.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next
items.follows: Childhood, boyhood and youth are each lost in turn.
items.context: Letter 24, on despising death: we die a little every day. The ages that are lost one after another are stages of that daily dying.

items.quote: He says that it is as foolish to fear death as to fear old age; for death follows old age precisely as old age follows youth.
gives: ages of my life that gave way to the next
items.follows: Death follows old age just as old age follows youth, so fearing it is as foolish as fearing old age.
items.context: Letter 30: Seneca reports his old friend Bassus, who is near death and talks of it freely. “He” is Bassus; the saying is about death in general.

items.label: practice
items.t: Leaving calmly when the inevitable hour comes takes long practice. I practise every day so that I can leave life content, instead of clutching at life as people swept down a stream clutch at briars and rocks.
items.why: Marcus’s practice here is to look at the people I am leaving, at the hour itself. Seneca adds that the calm has to be learned long before, by rehearsing it every day.

support.quote: This is a great accomplishment, Lucilius, and one which needs long practice to learn,—to depart calmly when the inevitable hour arrives.
gives: Leaving calmly when the inevitable hour comes takes long practice
support.follows: To leave life calmly when the hour comes is a great thing, and it takes long practice to learn.
support.context: Letter 30: Seneca admires his old friend Bassus, who faces his own death with a calm face. “The inevitable hour” is the hour of death.

support.quote: Rehearse this thought every day, that you may be able to depart from life contentedly; for many men clutch and cling to life, even as those who are carried down a rushing stream clutch and cling to briars and sharp rocks.
gives: I practise every day so that I can leave life content
instead of clutching at life as people swept down a stream clutch at briars and rocks
support.follows: Going over the right thought every day lets one leave life content instead of clinging to it.
support.context: Letter 4, on the terrors of death. “This thought” is the one just before it: no one lives in peace who thinks too much about making life longer.

items.label: breaks
items.t: Failing can also mean wanting death. I do not rush out of life or let a longing for death take hold of me; if I run toward death because I am tired of life, it is the way I live that has driven me to it.
items.why: Marcus names fear as the failure. Seneca names the opposite one, a longing for death. In 9.3 Marcus touches it in “Come sooner, death”, a sentence this article leaves out, and perhaps in “nor violent”, which the translators note may mean pushing toward death.

support.quote: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life; he should make a becoming exit. And above all, he should avoid the weakness which has taken possession of so many,—the lust for death.
gives: I do not rush out of life or let a longing for death take hold of me
support.follows: A wise person does not hurry out of life, leaves it fittingly, and guards against the longing for death.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death. Seneca warns that despising death can turn into wanting it: leaving life in haste, even when reason seems to advise an end.

support.quote: to run towards death because you are tired of life, when it is your manner of life that has made you run towards death
gives: if I run toward death because I am tired of life, it is the way I live that has driven me to it
support.follows: Whoever runs toward death out of tiredness with life has been driven there by the way he lives.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: Seneca quotes Epicurus, who blames those who crave death as much as those who shrink from it, and calls this running absurd.

items.label: doubt
items.t: Death either ends me or strips me bare. If it releases me, the better part of me remains, free of its burden; if it ends me, nothing remains, neither good nor bad, and that is no different from never having begun.
items.why: 8.55 argues from sensation: none, or a different kind. Seneca’s two cases are about what remains of me, the better part or nothing, and he likens nothing to the time before I was born.

support.quote: Death either annihilates us or strips us bare. If we are then released, there remains the better part, after the burden has been withdrawn; if we are annihilated, nothing remains; good and bad are alike removed.
gives: Death either ends me or strips me bare
If it releases me, the better part of me remains, free of its burden
if it ends me, nothing remains, neither good nor bad
support.follows: If death releases us, our better part remains without its burden; if it destroys us, nothing remains, good or bad.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death, after dismissing the terrors of the underworld as fit only for children. “The burden” is the body.

support.quote: For what does it matter whether you do not begin at all, or whether you leave off, inasmuch as the result of both these states is non-existence?
gives: that is no different from never having begun
support.follows: Never beginning and leaving off end in the same non-existence, so it does not matter which.
support.context: Letter 54, written after an attack of asthma: we are lit and put out like a lamp. “Both these states” are the time before birth and the time after death.

items.t: Seneca counts death indifferent: not an evil, but not a good either. It still keeps a look of evil, because we love ourselves, want to go on existing and recoil from dissolution, so we cannot easily ignore it and the soul must be hardened by long practice to endure its approach. This limits claim 3 rather than contradicting it: Marcus calls death good only when it comes at the right time for the whole and benefits the whole (12.17), and Seneca speaks of death in itself.

support.quote: Death belongs among those things which are not indeed evils, but still have in them a semblance of evil
support.follows: Death is not an evil, but it still looks like one.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death. Seneca explains why death, though indifferent, is feared: love of self and a recoil from dissolution are born in us.

support.quote: although death is something indifferent, it is nevertheless not a thing which we can easily ignore. The soul must be hardened by long practice, so that it may learn to endure the sight and the approach of death.
support.follows: Death is neither good nor bad, yet we cannot easily ignore it, and the soul must be trained long to endure its approach.
support.context: Letter 82, on the natural fear of death: Seneca’s conclusion from the recoil from dissolution that is born in us, and what it asks of us in practice.

items.t: Seneca does not let the people I leave be only a reason to go. Those I hold dear can be a reason to stay: a good man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he pleases, and holds on to life even at great cost when they need him. This limits claim 5; 9.3 too allows that living with people of one’s own principles would hold one in life.

support.quote: sometimes, even in spite of weighty reasons, the breath of life must be called back and kept at our very lips even at the price of great suffering, for the sake of those whom we hold dear
support.follows: Sometimes, for the people we love, we must hold on to life even when it costs us much suffering.
support.context: Letter 104: Seneca, old and ill, has weighed letting himself die, and keeps himself alive for his wife Paulina. “Those whom we hold dear” are such as she.

support.quote: because the good man should not live as long as it pleases him, but as long as he ought.
support.follows: A good man lives as long as he ought to, not as long as he likes.
support.context: Letter 104, on Seneca keeping himself alive for his wife Paulina: the reason he gives for holding on to life for those one loves.

amend.t: ; still, it keeps a look of evil, and I cannot easily ignore it
; and I neither rush out of life nor long for death
; but for the sake of those I hold dear, I live as long as I ought, not as long as I please

searches: die every day, daily death, dying daily
work of nature, law of nature
linger, as long as he ought (with death)

rejected.why: “Not suddenly torn from life, but withdrawn bit by bit” is the bodily decline of old age, not the manner of going that 10.36 asks for.
Gliding into harbour when nature slips the cable: a gradual death in old age. Matching it to nature’s taking apart would need explaining.
Thrust out, but going as if willingly. About willingness, which Article 6 already has from Letter 61; “willingly” is not “graciously”.
Practise how to welcome death “or even to invite it”: recommends inviting death, while the passages used (24.25, 104.3) warn against hurrying it.
Death frees many from torture, want and weariness. Close to 6.26, a said-once item, which takes no backing.
Death interrupts life but does not steal it; what vanishes comes back. About return, which no passage of the section says.
On being remembered after death. Off the topic.
We stop shuddering at death once we know the limits of good and evil. Near 2.10, a said-once item; said in a letter on bearing illness.
Its “death ought to be despised more” means fearing it less; it does not disagree with 9.3’s “Do not despise death”, which means not to be disdainful. Only its first two sentences are used.
“The last but not the only death.” Says what Ep. 24.20 says for claim 2; a third witness was not needed.

Neither love nor hate life overmuch, even when reason advises an end. Ep. 24.25 continues it and is used for the warning against longing for death; 24.24 adds only the balance, which that item does not need.
Live in the body as if about to leave it. A practice, but in a letter that defends choosing one’s death; Letters 30 and 4 give the practice without that.
To think on death is to think on freedom; love of life is the one chain. About freedom from slavery, with a way out by choice.
We die daily and should value each day. About the use of time, the subject of the section on the shortness of life.
Nature divides a short life into infancy, childhood, youth and age. About how short life is, not about death as a change.
No one is the same in old age as in youth. About the flux of bodies in an argument on being, not about death.
Death is non-existence, known before birth. Ep. 54.5 says the same and is quoted.
It is not important to live, but to die honourably: advice that helps Marcellinus toward suicide, while 24.25 and 104.3 warn against hurrying death.
Desire whatever circumstances demand. Already quoted in Article 6.
One is braver at the moment of death than when approaching it. An observation about courage, not a way of meeting death.
Nature takes apart what she put together. Article 33 uses it for its claim 1; this article leaves that ground to Article 33.
Dying well means dying gladly. It backed being well pleased with death, which this article now leaves to Article 10.

articles.title: What I learned, and from whom

claims.t: I keep free of anger. I do not give so much as a sign of it, and I am not irritable even when I explain something; I am at once free of passion and most affectionate.
claims.shared: Three passages name freedom from anger as a thing Marcus took from someone: 1.1 “freedom from anger” (from Verus), 1.6 “never giving so much as a sign of anger” (from Sextus), 1.12 “never … angry” (from Maximus). 1.5 adds one occasion for it: explaining.
claims.changed: 1.12 lists anger among several things Maximus never was; only anger is kept. Each passage names what Marcus took from one person; the claim says “I”.

support.quote: From my grandfather Verus: good character and freedom from anger.
gives: I keep free of anger
support.follows: Marcus took good character and freedom from anger from his grandfather Verus.

support.quote: never giving so much as a sign of anger or of any other passion, but being at once most free of passion and most affectionate
gives: I keep free of anger
I do not give so much as a sign of it
I am at once free of passion and most affectionate
support.follows: From Sextus Marcus took this: never to show even a sign of anger or other passion, and to be both free of passion and most affectionate.

support.quote: never hurrying or hanging back or at a loss or downcast or putting on a grin, or again angry or suspicious
gives: I keep free of anger
support.follows: Maximus, as Marcus saw him, was never in a hurry or hanging back, never downcast, and never angry or suspicious.

support.quote: and not being irritable when explaining
gives: I am not irritable even when I explain something
support.follows: From Apollonius Marcus took this: not to be irritable when explaining things to others.

claims.t: Illness does not change me: I stay the same in sharp pain, in grief and in illness, and in illness I keep good spirits, as in any other hardship. When an attack has passed, I go straight back to my usual work at full strength.
claims.shared: 1.5 and 1.12 both name illness as something that does not change the man: Apollonius was “always the same … in long illnesses”, and Maximus kept “good spirits in illness as in other hard circumstances”. 1.13 says what comes after it: his father came back from headache “at full strength”.
claims.changed: “Grief” stands for 1.5’s “the loss of a child”; “an attack” stands for 1.13’s attacks of headache.

support.quote: being always the same, in sharp pains, at the loss of a child, in long illnesses
gives: Illness does not change me
I stay the same in sharp pain, in grief and in illness
support.follows: From Apollonius Marcus took this: to be always the same, whether in sharp pain, at the loss of a child or in long illness.

support.quote: From Maximus: self-mastery and being carried off course in nothing; and good spirits in illness as in other hard circumstances
gives: Illness does not change me
in illness
in illness I keep good spirits, as in any other hardship
support.follows: From Maximus Marcus took self-mastery, and good spirits in illness as in any other hardship.

support.quote: after his attacks of headache, coming straight back fresh and at full strength to his usual work
gives: When an attack has passed, I go straight back to my usual work at full strength
support.follows: Marcus’s father, after attacks of headache, went straight back to his usual work, fresh and at full strength.

claims.t: I am slow to believe slander, glib talk or tales of spells. I am not content with a rough grasp of a matter, or with the impressions that first come to hand.
claims.shared: 1.2, 1.4 and 1.3 each refuse a quick belief: “slow to accept slander”, “nor quickly assenting to glib talkers”, “disbelieving what is said by those who deal in marvels”. 1.4 and 1.13 share the word “content”: not “content with a rough grasp”, not “content with the impressions that lay to hand”.
claims.changed: “Tales of spells” stands for 1.3’s marvel-mongers and sorcerers. 1.13 puts its words as a thing no one could say of his father; the claim says them of me.

support.quote: and being slow to accept slander
gives: I am slow to believe
slander
support.follows: From the man who brought him up, Marcus learned to be slow to accept slander.

support.quote: and reading with care, and not being content with a rough grasp of the whole, nor quickly assenting to glib talkers
gives: I am slow to believe
glib talk
I am not content with a rough grasp of a matter
support.follows: From Rusticus Marcus took this: to read with care, not to rest content with a rough grasp, and not to agree quickly with glib talkers.

support.quote: and disbelieving what is said by those who deal in marvels and by sorcerers about spells and about the driving out of spirits and things of that kind
gives: I am slow to believe
tales of spells
support.follows: From Diognetus Marcus took this: not to believe what marvel-mongers and sorcerers say about spells and driving out spirits.

support.quote: and careful inquiry in council, and persistence, and not “he gave up the search too soon, content with the impressions that lay to hand”
gives: I am not content
the impressions that first come to hand
support.follows: Marcus’s father inquired with care in council and kept at it; no one could say he stopped too soon, content with first impressions.

claims.t: I do good, and I share what I have readily and without holding back.
claims.shared: 1.11 and 1.12 both say “doing good”; 1.1 and 1.11 both name sharing readily (“readiness to share”, “sharing readily”).
claims.changed: 1.11’s “unsparingly” may go with the sharing alone or with the doing good as well; the claim takes it with the sharing.

support.quote: From my mother: reverence for the gods, and readiness to share
gives: I share what I have readily
support.follows: From his mother Marcus took reverence for the gods and a readiness to share.

support.quote: and doing good and sharing readily, unsparingly
gives: I do good
I share what I have readily
without holding back
support.follows: From his brother Severus Marcus took this: doing good, and sharing readily and unsparingly.

support.quote: and doing good
gives: I do good
support.follows: Among the things Marcus took from Maximus is doing good.

claims.t: I train myself to live plainly, far from the way the rich live, and to need little: when comforts are there I use them without fuss, and when they are not, I do not need them.
claims.shared: 1.2 says “needing little”, and 1.13 says of comforts “when they were not he did not need them”. 1.1’s “plainness in the way of living” and 1.3’s pallet bed and animal skin are the same plain life, the one as a habit and the other as training.
claims.changed: “Comforts” stands for 1.13’s “the things that add to the ease of life”. “Train” is read from 1.3’s “the Greek training” (ἀγωγή, which can also mean the Greek way of life), and 1.3 says that Marcus wanted the pallet bed, not that he slept on it. 1.2’s hard work and 1.3’s pallet bed and animal skin are dropped; the claim keeps the plain life they belong to.

support.quote: and also plainness in the way of living, far from the way the rich live
gives: to live plainly, far from the way the rich live
support.follows: From his mother Marcus took a plain way of living, far from the way the rich live.

support.quote: From the man who brought me up: becoming neither a Green nor a Blue, nor a Small-Shield or a Big-Shield man; and bearing hard work, and needing little
gives: to need little
I do not need them
support.follows: From the man who brought him up, Marcus learned to bear hard work and to need little.

support.quote: and wanting a pallet bed and an animal skin, and everything of that kind that belongs to the Greek training
gives: I train myself to live plainly
support.follows: From Diognetus Marcus took the wish for a pallet bed, an animal skin and the rest of the Greek philosophers’ hard training.

support.quote: using the things that add to the ease of life, of which fortune gave him plenty, without conceit and at the same time without apology, so that when they were there he took them without affectation, and when they were not he did not need them
gives: to need little
when comforts are there I use them without fuss, and when they are not, I do not need them
support.follows: Marcus’s father used the comforts fortune gave him without conceit or apology, and did not need them when they were not there.

claims.t: When someone turns against me, in anger or by finding fault, even without reason, I am ready to make it up: I try to bring them back to their usual self, I am easy to reconcile with as soon as they are willing, and I forgive.
claims.shared: 1.4 and 1.10 both speak of someone who is angry or finds fault, and both end with a return: “willing to come back”, “bring them back”. 1.12 adds forgiving.
claims.changed: “I am ready to make it up” is the editor’s summary of 1.4’s “easy to reconcile” and 1.10’s “bring them back”. 1.4’s “have done wrong” is folded into “turns against me”. Neither passage says at whom the anger or the fault-finding was aimed: 1.4 speaks of “those who have been angry”, 1.10 of “a friend who finds some fault”. The claim takes both as aimed at me, and “turns against me” is stronger than 1.10’s “finds some fault”.

support.quote: and, towards those who have been angry and have done wrong, being easy to win back and easy to reconcile, as soon as they themselves are willing to come back
gives: When someone turns against me
in anger
I am ready to make it up
I am easy to reconcile with as soon as they are willing
support.follows: From Rusticus Marcus took this: to be easily won back and reconciled with those who were angry and did wrong, once they want to return.

support.quote: not making light of a friend who finds some fault, even if they happen to be finding fault without reason, but trying actually to bring them back to their usual self
gives: When someone turns against me
by finding fault, even without reason
I am ready to make it up
I try to bring them back to their usual self
support.follows: From Catulus Marcus took this: not to brush off a friend’s complaint, even an unfounded one, but to try to bring the friend back to their usual self.

support.quote: and forgiving
gives: I forgive
support.follows: Among the things Marcus took from Maximus is forgiving.

single.label: Reason alone
single.t: I look to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while.
single.quote: and looking to nothing other than reason, not even for a little while
single.why: Only 1.5 says what to look to. 1.6’s “the idea of living according to nature” is near it but is a different idea, so the two are not fused.
single.follows: From Apollonius Marcus took this: to look to nothing but reason, not even for a short time.

single.label: The mark of a sound soul
single.t: To hold out when I must go without, and to stay sober when I can enjoy, is the mark of a soul that is sound and unbeaten.
single.quote: What is recorded of Socrates would fit him: that he was able both to go without and to enjoy those things which most people are weak at going without and give way in enjoying. To be strong, and to hold out and stay sober in each of the two, is the mark of a man who has a soul that is sound and unbeaten
single.why: Only 1.13 gives a reason for any of these lessons, and it is Marcus’s own judgment on a saying about Socrates that he applies to his father. Claim 5 says what to do; this says what doing it shows.
single.follows: Being able both to go without and to enjoy, holding out in the one and staying sober in the other, is the mark of a sound and unbeaten soul.

single.label: Needing correction
single.t: I keep in mind that my character needs correcting and treatment.
single.quote: From Rusticus: getting the impression that my character needed correcting and treatment
single.why: Only 1.4 says that the writer’s own character was at fault. It shows what failing looks like and that it can be treated.
single.follows: From Rusticus Marcus got the impression that his character needed correcting and treatment.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers stay Casaubon’s; in modern editions 1.1 is 1.1–4, 1.2 is 1.5, 1.3 is 1.6, 1.4 is 1.7, 1.5 is 1.8, 1.6 is 1.9, 1.10 is 1.13, 1.11 is 1.14, 1.12 is 1.15 and 1.13 is 1.16.

Turns “From X: Y” into “I Y” only where Marcus names a quality or a habit as taken from that person. Bare descriptions of his father’s days, such as the formal dress from Lorium or the cloak at Tusculum, are not made into rules.

Leaves out four further parallels to keep the article to six claims: being tight and slack in turn (1.5 and 1.13 use the same image of a string), saying plainly what I think (1.11, 1.12, 1.13), making no show of learning or virtue (1.4, 1.6, 1.13), and valuing my teachers (1.1, 1.10).

Reads the anger in 1.4 and the fault-finding in 1.10 as aimed at Marcus himself; neither passage says at whom. Claim 3 quotes 1.13’s “he gave up the search too soon, content with the impressions that lay to hand”, whose text the translators call doubtful; the claim’s second sentence also rests on 1.4.
articles.limit: Book 1 gives thanks and does not argue, so the article is mostly a list of qualities with little ground: only 1.13 gives a reason, and only for needing little. Four parallels and many lessons said once by a single teacher are left out. Other articles argue what this one lists: Article 2 that I do not judge in a hurry and Article 21 that I keep a sure grasp of each impression (claim 3), Article 19 that anger is weakness and that I bear with those who wrong me (claims 1 and 6), Article 8 that pain is the body’s to see to (claim 2), and Article 18 that I take without conceit and let go readily (claim 5); this article adds that each was learned from a particular person, and the occasions: slander and glib talk, a friend’s complaint, grief and long illness, comforts present or absent.

statement.t: I live as the people who brought me up and taught me showed me: even-tempered, careful in what I believe, and needing little.

parts.words: the people who brought me up and taught me showed me
even-tempered
careful in what I believe
needing little

statement.kind: Lessons from many people aligned into one
statement.form: Book 1 is a list of what Marcus took from each person in his life. Where two or more of them gave him the same thing in different words, the lessons are aligned into one claim; the statement names three of those claims and the people they came from.

empty.doubt: No passage in this section asks what would hold if these lessons were wrong; Book 1 gives thanks and does not argue.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, freedom from anger, steadiness in illness, slowness to believe and easy reconciliation each gain a second author. The article gains a reason for learning from people, what happens when a teacher’s habit is broken, and what holds if a teacher was wrong. He limits the training in hardness: a few days at a time, as a test, not a penance or a show.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a reason: what I ought to do is learned from one who does it.

items.quote: anger should be avoided, not merely that we may escape excess, but that we may have a healthy mind
gives: I keep free of anger
items.follows: Anger is to be avoided, not only to escape excess but to keep the mind healthy.
items.context: The close of Letter 18, on a saying of Epicurus that ungoverned anger begets madness. “Anger” is the passion itself, which Seneca says can flare from any small cause.

items.quote: It is your body that is hampered by ill-health, and not your soul as well.
gives: Illness does not change me
items.follows: Illness hampers the body, not the soul.
items.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill and complains that his illness keeps him from all his duties. “Your soul” is Lucilius’s mind, which the illness does not reach.

items.quote: we agree too quickly with what people say
gives: I am slow to believe
items.follows: We are too quick to agree with what people tell us.
items.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. “What people say” is rumour of trouble to come, which, Seneca says, we accept without testing or examining it.

items.quote: men should know that you are the sort of person who can be offended without danger; and your reconciliation should be easy and sure
gives: I am easy to reconcile with
items.follows: People should know that I can be offended without danger, and that I am easily and surely reconciled.
items.context: Letter 105, on living safely among others. Seneca says how not to be feared: an easy disposition, so that whoever offends you need not fear you and can make it up.

items.label: why
items.t: I learn what to do from people who do it. A teacher whose life I have seen is a witness to what he teaches, and the way by rules is long, while the way by examples is short and helpful.
items.why: Marcus names what he took from each person and never says why a life teaches better than a lesson. Seneca says why, and like Marcus he names his own teachers.

support.quote: What ought to be done must be learned from one who does it.
gives: I learn what to do from people who do it
support.follows: What one ought to do is learned from someone who does it.
support.context: Letter 98 ends on an old friend bearing a painful ulcer with courage. Seneca calls watching him studying philosophy by practice; “one who does it” is such a man.

support.quote: I, at any rate, listen in a different spirit to the utterances of our friend Demetrius, after I have seen him reclining without even a cloak to cover him, and, more than this, without rugs to lie upon. He is not only a teacher of the truth, but a witness to the truth.
gives: A teacher whose life I have seen is a witness to what he teaches
support.follows: Having seen Demetrius lie down without cloak or rugs, Seneca hears his words differently: he teaches the truth and also bears witness to it.
support.context: Letter 20, on practising what you preach. Demetrius is a Cynic philosopher Seneca knew; his bare bed shows that he lives the poverty he teaches.

support.quote: the way is long if one follows precepts, but short and helpful, if one follows patterns
gives: the way by rules is long, while the way by examples is short and helpful
support.follows: Following rules is a long way; following examples is short and helpful.
support.context: Letter 6, on sharing knowledge. Seneca sends Lucilius books but says living together will teach him more; the “patterns” are living people whose conduct one watches.

items.label: breaks
items.t: Some of the habits my teachers gave me stay with me and some I break; where I have stopped abstaining from something, I keep to a limit close to abstaining.
items.why: Marcus does not say what happens when a lesson is not kept. Seneca, speaking of the habits he took from his teacher Attalus, says that some stayed and some were broken, and how he kept near the broken ones.

support.quote: And that is why some of these habits have stayed with me, Lucilius.
gives: Some of the habits my teachers gave me stay with me
support.follows: Some of the habits Seneca took up as a young pupil have stayed with him.
support.context: Letter 108, on the approaches to philosophy. “These habits” are the limits on food and drink Seneca took up after hearing his teacher Attalus praise poverty and moderation.

support.quote: Other resolutions have been broken, but after all in such a way that, in cases where I ceased to practice abstinence, I have observed a limit which is indeed next door to abstinence
gives: some I break
where I have stopped abstaining from something, I keep to a limit close to abstaining
support.follows: Where Seneca broke a resolution and stopped abstaining, he still kept a limit close to abstaining.
support.context: Letter 108 again: Seneca lists the resolutions from Attalus’s teaching that he kept for life (no perfume, no wine) and says what became of the ones he broke.

items.label: doubt
items.t: When I cannot be sure that a teacher’s reason is true, I leave the question open and can still keep the plain habit he taught: if the reason is true, the habit is purity; if not, it is thrift.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if a teacher was wrong. Seneca’s teacher Sotion answers for one plain habit: keep it either way. Seneca adds that he later gave the habit up, at his father’s request (Ep. 108.22).

support.quote: while holding to your own view, keep the whole question in abeyance in your mind
gives: When I cannot be sure that a teacher’s reason is true, I leave the question open
support.follows: Keep your own view, but leave the question open in your mind.
support.context: Letter 108: Sotion, Seneca’s teacher, speaking of Pythagoras’s belief that souls pass into animals. “The whole question” is whether that belief is true.

support.quote: If the theory is true, it is a mark of purity to refrain from eating flesh; if it be false, it is economy.
gives: can still keep the plain habit he taught
if the reason is true, the habit is purity; if not, it is thrift
support.follows: If the reason for not eating meat is true, abstaining is purity; if it is false, abstaining is still thrift.
support.context: Sotion’s conclusion, as Seneca remembers it from his youth. “The theory” is that souls pass into animals, the reason Pythagoras gave for eating no meat.

items.t: Seneca limits the training in hardness. He agrees with Marcus about display, as 1.4 rejects “making a show … of the man of discipline”, and his mean is 1.13’s: comforts used without conceit and without apology. The limit lands on 1.3’s wish for a pallet bed and an animal skin. Philosophy, Seneca says, asks for plain living but not for penance, and a couch on the bare earth and other forms of self-display are to be avoided (Ep. 5.2, 5.5); a real pallet he prescribes for three or four days at a time, sometimes more, as a test (Ep. 18.7). He also praises lasting hardness in Demetrius (Ep. 20.9), so what he limits is penance and display, not hardness itself.

support.quote: Philosophy calls for plain living, but not for penance; and we may perfectly well be plain and neat at the same time.
support.follows: Philosophy asks for plain living, not for self-punishment; one can be plain and neat at once.
support.context: Letter 5, on the philosopher’s mean. Seneca warns Lucilius against making a show of philosophy by an odd way of life; “plain living” is simple but ordinary.

support.quote: Repellent attire, unkempt hair, slovenly beard, open scorn of silver dishes, a couch on the bare earth, and any other perverted forms of self-display, are to be avoided.
support.follows: Rough dress, unkempt hair, a bed on the bare ground and other shows of hardship are to be avoided.
support.context: Letter 5 again: these are the habits of those who want to be noticed rather than to improve. Seneca says inwardly we should differ, outwardly conform.

support.quote: Let the pallet be a real one, and the coarse cloak; let the bread be hard and grimy. Endure all this for three or four days at a time, sometimes for more, so that it may be a test of yourself instead of a mere hobby.
support.follows: For a few days at a time, Seneca would have Lucilius sleep on a real pallet and eat hard bread, as a test of himself.
support.context: Letter 18, on festivals and fasting. Seneca prescribes set days of poverty as training, so that Lucilius learns he can bear want; “all this” is the pallet, cloak and bread.

amend.t: ; what I ought to do is learned from one who does it
